this game is basically a depression simulator, but in the absolute best way possible. I’m giving it a massive thumbs up because it’s a straight-up masterpiece, no cap.

Unlike your average FPS where you’re some super soldier running around no-scoping enemies, this game gives you the ultimate reality check. You play as regular, helpless civilians just trying to survive in a besieged city. And let me tell you, it hits different. You’re not trying to get a crazy kill-death ratio, you’re literally just trying to find a moldy piece of bread and some meds so your squad doesn't get cooked and die.

The vibes are insanely bleak. You'll spend your days building water filters, upgrading your shelter, and feeding your crew. Then, at night, you go out to scavenge. The tension is off the charts, bro. Every time you send someone out, you're lowkey sweating, hoping they don't get caught lacking by armed thugs.

And the moral choices? Bruh. They will destroy you. There was a time I had to steal food from a helpless elderly couple just to keep my own people alive. I sat staring at my monitor feeling like an absolute villain. The guilt is real, and the game actually punishes you for it—your characters will literally get depressed and give up if you do too much shady stuff. You really have to balance your survival instincts with your humanity.

Mechanically, it’s a massive W. The resource management is super tight. You will fail, you will lose your favorite survivors, and you will feel completely hopeless at times. But when you finally survive until the ceasefire, the feeling of relief is insane. Visually, the charcoal-sketch art style is gorgeous and fits the grim mood perfectly.

This game is a GOAT of the survival genre. It’s emotionally devastating, highly addictive, and will make you want to touch grass and appreciate your real life immediately after closing it. 10/10, absolutely phenomenal experience. Prepare to question your own morals, though.
The game keeps pausing when alt-tab even if you play in window mode. I tried everything and couldn't find a solution. Avoid it if you enjoy or need multitasking while playing.

In general, this is a good game. Its strengths lie in the atmosphere, music, and art style. The missions are quite solid, and it’s nice that you can optimize them to some extent.

My negative opinion is based on a number of small issues. The most important one is the lack of a proper tutorial and the odd way the game teaches you its systems. You end up spending too much time just figuring out what everything does and how it works. You basically have to lose a few times just to understand the interface and mechanics, which are quite obscure. It’s one of those games that you need to play with a wiki open in the background.

The game is nearly impossible if you don’t understand the mechanics, but becomes too easy once you do. In the end, the obscurity of the systems is the main obstacle.

It’s also too repetitive. While I recognize there is some randomness, it’s not enough to keep the ‘day phase’ engaging.

After about 10 hours, I drifted off to other titles. I have fond memories of it, and I’ll leave it at that.

It says 6 hours of play. It's a lie, I played probably closer to 50-60 hours on xbox. If for no other reason that the theme and tone of this game, I cannot recommend it enough. Too often in the gaming world we glorify and live out our fantasies as noble, yet violent heroes in a war against evil. I can't think of a single game that takes a peek at the unfortunate civilians stuck within a warzone. Enter "This War of Mine". Dark, morose, challenging, with moral questions abound of "Do I get involved and try to be a hero" or "Do I descend into desperation and steal from the innocent for my own preservation". It even touches on participation, where you choose whether to barter what meager goods you have with the military forces in your area. It's not a building or living sim, but more of a psuedo-simplistic colony/survivor sim where you build up your home defense during the day, and send out a single raider in the night to gather supplies. Sleep, protection, food, sickness, and depression/desperation are all factors that you need to manage for your tiny house amidst the war that rages around your little city. The personalities are simplistic but give a believable environmental tone, and if you really embrace the ambiance, gives a stark peek of war from the view of those who don't wage it, but live within it. Controls are easier with a controller vs. keyboard and mouse, but I'm entirely biased.

The game can feel punishing if you try to explore because the gameplay is so awkward, there is no confidence when entering combat unless you have a gun, which is still a decent chance for you to mess up. The characters are meaningfully different from each other and I like how they communicate. The overall message of the story and just trying to survive everyday is very impactful and nudges the ever present, deeply rooted question of war and conflict.

In this day and age, this game is a must. A welcome and gentler reminder, for those of us fortunate enough not to experience war first hand, about what war really entails for most of those who get embroiled in it. 

You get to witness people starving to death, girls being rounded up by shady military personnel for unspeakable ends, kids running from snipers to ensure their grandma can receive the medicine she needs to survive, even though she might die the next morning. Bleak, sure... but you also witness kindness and charity, and despite the struggle, you can feel hope.

This is not a game to play mindlessly. You must let yourself get involved in the story - you must forget this is a game at all. It is a window into a reality most of us won't have (hopefully) to experience in real life. 

I've completed only single run successfully in this game, but every run I've lost reminded me of what real people, in real life, are experiencing around the world right now. And it touches your soul. It makes you feel for them... it makes you a better human. Even as the one I succeeded in came to its conclusion, I felt happiness and sadness, because as I came back to reality, I thought how this is the story of so many people around the world - how so many have suffered the same way, struggled the same way, and in the end, felt the same way when thinking about their neighbors, friends, and work colleagues who sadly didn`t make it through.

Couldn't recommend this game enough. It deserves all the awards it has gotten and some more.

A video maker from my homeland once made a “review” on this game, which can be summurised as follows: “HA HA HA, WAR CRIMES FONI, HUMAN SUFFERING FONI, YOU WOULD BECOME A BANDIT ANYWAY”. 
And guess what? He’s right. It’s all fun and games watching fictional characters suffer losses, gain industrial-scaled PTSDs and believing that you’re above any of it.

UNTIL YOU BECOME SUCH CHARACTER.

When ordinary people around you get murdered, one by one, by UAVs, short-range missiles or, if they’re especially unlucky, by stray bullet from crack-headed marksman who believes it’s funny…
When both sides of a conflict become indistinguishable from each other to the point of transforming words “war crime” into a meme…
When the sounds of sirens (and sometimes explosions) become your midnight alarm clock…
When there’s no certainty that you, or people you knew, will live to meet sunrise, and deaths are treated as yet another fact of life…
Suddenly This War Of Mine stops being so funny. At least, for me.

Pray to God, Allah, Buddha, Monolith, Karl Marx, – whatever freaking deity you believe in, - that you will never have to cover from air strikes with artillery barrages or clear the rubble where normal peaceful people used to live. When your government commits a horrific action – it’s YOU who’s going to pay the price for it. It’s ALWAYS you.

BTW, do you know what’s the most unrealistic part of This War of Mine? It’s not game mechanics, personal stories or anything like it.
It’s a light shining in darkness. If you stick to your guns, retain your humanity, don’t murder innocents and help your community – all of your characters will receive a happy ending when the truce finally comes into power.
In reality, however, there’s no good ending, no matter what you do. The war still ravages the land, people still enlist for fun and profit in the name of ideas they can’t even explain, and innocent civilians die, just as they had centuries before today.

♥♥♥♥ THE WAR!

By end-game I survived fine. I didn't even build half the stuff that was available, because supplies were scarce. It didn't really matter. I did manage to do a largely-ethical run however - no killing, and barely any stealing (and only stealing from real bad folk). I didn't feel the game was 100% polished - there was a couple of times when things unexplicably triggered, such as a 'fight' scenario during a scavenge run when no-one was hostile or fighting me.

But the integrity of the game mechanics stuck with me. It really puts you in the headspace of someone who's surviving on limited resources, which, given the world's current state of affairs, is probably useful knowledge. Time to build my underground bunker I suppose.

I will say that by the last 5 nights I was pretty bored with the game. Perhaps it was just that it got fairly easy, or that it was easy to cheat the save system (if you force-quit the game during a scavenge run, the save reverts back to the previous day) when a character died. Maybe if I'd played with a little more integrity, it would've gotten harder. But you get kind of hooked into the characters and don't want them to die, and it gets tedious to lose progress. Also, the game mechanics around stealth/hostile people and fighting aren't really explained to you, so you're more or less just thrown into it and so you die.

Fighting during scavenge runs is a chumps game anyway, I think. There's certainly plenty to be gained, but the chance of dying is too high. I just got caught out a couple of times.

4 thumbs up out of five.

I didn’t pick up This War of Mine because I was looking for a good time. It was cheap, it had a reputation, and I had a feeling it might be something… different. Something heavier. Still, I wasn’t prepared for how uncomfortable it would make me. Not loud, not shocking. Just this slow, constant pressure that builds the longer you play. And again, the strange part is… I respect the hell out of it.

This game doesn’t put you in the role of a hero. There’s no glory here, no big moments where you feel powerful. You’re not fighting a war. You’re stuck in one. Just trying to get through the next day. You manage a group of civilians hiding in a broken shelter. During the day, you patch things up, cook, rest, try to keep people from falling apart. At night, you go out scavenging in a city that’s just as desperate as you are. And that’s where it starts to hit. Because the game doesn’t just ask: can you survive? It asks: what are you willing to do to survive?

You find yourself in situations where nothing feels right. You need food. You find someone weaker than you who has some. You need medicine. Someone else needs it too. And the game doesn’t step in and say what’s “good” or “bad.” It just lets you decide… and then shows you what that decision does to your people. Not in some dramatic, over-the-top way. Just small things. They get sad. They get quiet. They sit there, smoking, not saying anything. And somehow that’s worse.

There’s no real sense of control here either. You can make good decisions, plan carefully, do everything right… and things can still go to hell. Someone gets sick. Someone gets hurt. Supplies don’t last. Winter comes. You’re not building something stable. You’re holding things together with whatever you can find. Barely.

What surprised me most is how personal it started to feel. These aren’t just “units” or “characters.” You start paying attention to them. You notice who’s tired, who’s breaking, who’s still holding it together. And when something goes wrong, it doesn’t feel like you failed a system. It feels like you let someone down. That’s a weird thing to get from a game.

It’s not fun. Not in the usual sense. Sometimes it’s frustrating. Sometimes it feels unfair. Sometimes you just sit there staring at the screen, wondering if you really want to make the next decision. And yet… it’s incredibly well made. There’s no excess here. No pointless mechanics, no distractions. Everything serves the same purpose: to put you in that situation and let you deal with it. No safety net. No power fantasy. No clean ending where everything feels resolved. Just people trying to get through something awful.

I understand why this game gets so much praise. And I also understand why some people bounce off it immediately. This isn’t something you play to relax. It’s something you experience… if you’re willing to sit with it.

For me, it’s a bit like The Long Dark, but sharper in a different way. That game asks if you can survive nature. This one asks what kind of person you are when survival starts to cost something. And that question stays with you longer than you’d expect.

I don’t “enjoy” this game in the traditional sense. But I respect it. A lot. And I’ll probably go back to it… even if part of me really doesn’t want to.

I am trying to defend our base from bandits. Posting one guard every night and blocking every other entrance just to protect our stuff. My daughter is fast asleep and I went out scavenging.
I did the best I could for us to survive… even if it meant making bad decisions.
I chose a place marked “Caution.” There could be bandits. Soldiers. Trouble.
So I brought my knife.
I searched the place for anything, moving carefully and avoiding the people inside.
I avoid conflict as much as possible.
Then I heard two people talking.
They sounded… normal. Friendly.
So I stopped hiding. I continued my search out in the open.
The loots I'm getting doesn't have a "Private" written on, so I assumed it's safe to loot.
Then one of them spotted me.
“I’ve got you now,” he said, or something along those lines.
I stopped rummaging and pulled out my knife.
I climbed up to the roof.
He followed.
After he climbed, he pointed his gun at me, so I attacked him.
I stabbed him 3 times, he pushed me, I got hurt a little.
Then I attacked him again.
He went down.
As he neared his death, he pleaded, “Please don’t do this.”
I... couldn’t stop.
I looted his body and ran for the exit.
I got home, everyone was safe.
We were not raided. I feel relieved.
But then the other survivors seemed so... down.
Why are they... looking at me like that?

Only then did it hit me.
Everyone back there was just like us… struggling to survive, clinging to what little they have.
Turns out I was not a survivor... I... was the bandit.

[h1]This War of Mine[/h1]

[b]This War of Mine[/b] isn’t your typical shooter or strategy game — it’s a grim, emotional survival sim that drops you into a war-torn city and says, “Survive. Somehow.” You don’t play as soldiers; you’re civilians trying to scrape by, scavenge food, avoid snipers, and make gut-wrenching moral choices while winter and war conspire against you. Think The Sims meets apocalyptic misery, with a soundtrack of fear, hunger, and distant gunfire.

[b]Why it hits hard:[/b]
• Emotional survival: Decisions aren’t just tactical — stealing, trading, or saving people comes with heavy consequences.
• Atmosphere: Dark, muted visuals and ambient sounds make you feel the weight of war.
• Complex choices: Every decision matters — morality is never black and white, and sometimes survival means being cruel.
• Randomized stories: Each playthrough brings different survivors, events, and dilemmas.

[b]The tough spots:[/b]
• Depressing as heck: This game will crush your soul, especially if you get attached to your survivors.
• Slow pacing: Scavenging can feel tedious and repetitive at times.
• Steep learning curve: Early decisions can be unforgiving — there’s no hand-holding.
• Limited action: Don’t expect combat thrills; it’s about tension, stealth, and survival, not gunfights.

[u]Overall:[/u]
This War of Mine is a sobering, brutal experience that makes you rethink the word “survival.” It’s less about winning and more about enduring — the desperation, tough choices, and fleeting victories will stick with you.

This War of Mine was one of the first games I got on Steam almost 10 years ago, and the concept hit me instantly. We are used to seeing combat and FPS, but I had never seen a game that seeks to portray how it feels for the rest of the people, those who live around the conflict and are stuck there with no way out.
As someone who has never been even close to a war zone, I have no idea if this is realistic or not. All I know is that it made me care about the characters, feel their struggles, worry about their well-being and hope for the end.
In this game, the same moral decisions carried weight they didn't in other scenarios. The game deeply humanizes its characters, and you see the "villains" stand in a grey moral area: people who do bad things, not because they are mean or evil, but because they are selfish, they are desperate, they want to survive. You get to know the characters, their stories, understand their morals and the impact every decision has on each one.
The art in this game also does an amazing job of conveying the tragic scenario. The music is somber, the drawings have rough edges, and it works perfectly for the depressing atmosphere. But there are also gleams of hope: you can hear soft music on the radio, kids laughing when they are happy.
I never had issues with bugs in the game that bothered the playing experience. The UI is simple, resources are scarce, and the winter is relentless. You do what you can, but it shows how easy it is for someone in a bad situation to end up in one even worse: an untreated cold or a small wound can become deadly. The days can be monotonous, the nights are tense, the work gets repetitive, but I like it. It pays off when your characters are safe and fed.
This is what matters most. It's a game that really goes for feelings, so you have to feel how everything is deliberate and reflect on what it means. That is the experience This War of Mine brings. And this is why I keep coming back to it. When you start to become numb to the grim reality of the world, this game can remind you how it feels to be human.

10/10 – War Is Hell, and So Is My Emotional State 

This War of Mine is not a “fun” war game.

It is a powerful, exhausting, emotionally heavy experience about surviving in a besieged city as civilians.

You’re not a hero. You’re not a soldier. You’re just trying to keep people fed, warm, and alive.

Every choice hurts:
Do you steal from strangers?
Do you help others at your own risk?
Do you let someone starve so everyone else can live?

The game constantly forces you to confront the human cost of survival. Characters develop depression, guilt, and trauma based on your decisions. And you feel responsible for all of it.

It’s beautifully designed. It’s brutally honest. It stays with you long after you stop playing.

Is it fun? Not in the traditional sense.
Is it important? Absolutely.
Is it unforgettable? Yes.

Highly recommended. Please play it. Carefully.

This is not just a game; it's a profound emotional experience. Unlike most war games that focus on soldiers and glory, This War of Mine puts you in the shoes of the forgotten ones—the civilians.

While attempting to reflect the horrors of war, two distinct and opposing tendencies manifest themselves over the course of this game: that is, the moral against the immoral. As a general rule, survival games such as this one most often degenerate into min/max, "spreadsheet"-style gameplay. And so to succeed in this game you must choose a resource to target, go to the right location at night, choose the right tools, make sure to feed your characters before they get "very hungry", click in the right places to fight adversaries, and so on. Unfortunately, the attempt to suture morality onto this mechanical gameplay, and the subsequent attempt to tether the min/maxing to consequences in this moral superstructure, utterly fails. Morality finds itself concretely expressed in the form of the mood of your characters, as well as their dialogue. As resources begin to dwindle, you are confronted with a choice: spiral into death, or steal and kill (technically you can trade, too, but this again turns the game into pure optimisation and the entire idea of morality becomes superfluous). 

At this point the contradiction between the moral and the immoral enters into its sharpest and most acute struggle. The actual form this struggle is expressed in is also extremely disappointing. The game treats morality in the most absolute terms: if you steal (absolutely no exceptions) this is immoral. If you kill an elderly man and his wife this is immoral. On the other hand, if you kill some men beating a woman at a brewery, this is moral. What makes this even more ironic is that the woman was being beat for theft! The game is unable to handle the fact that the moral only exists in its identity with the immoral. It is absolutely possible for any one of the above events to be both moral and immoral (I should take a moment to make it clear that I am speaking within the bounds of bourgeois morality, which is what the game reflects). This is indicative of a broader failure of the game, i.e. the inability to overcome the insoluble contradictions of liberalism as the game instead attempts to reconcile and gloss over contradiction. 

Whether a work of art, a game in this case, is progressive in character is determined, in part, by whether or not it fights against the social relations of the day. Furthermore, and Benjamin talks about this in his essay The Author as Producer, a work of art must break out of the confines of the form which contains it. This War of Mine fails to do any of this. This is epitomised by the fact that the bourgeois idea of private property is accepted wholesale. In order to break out of its confines, it would be necessary for this game to question the very premises of bourgeois legality and private property as an idea. Instead we are conditioned by the game rules (i.e. morality) to respected the holy and consecrated bourgeois right, risking our characters falling into depression if they fail to do so. To challenge these social relations, it would be necessary for the game to include politics, something it tries so hard to shirk (which is such an absurd thing to do, as war is inextricably tied up with politics, and vice versa). This is the kernel of the reason for this game's inability to develop a progressive character. 

Finally, the game also simply fails to actually depict the horror of war. This is ultimately a failure of the game mechanics themself (of course this is not to suggest that min/max-type games are inherently reactionary or progressive (that would be a manifestation of ultra-leftism) but the point is that a game's mechanics and the social relations of the period form a unity, and they must be understood precisely in this unity, not independently of one another). The computer-controlled characters are utterly inept and your own characters are essentially vessels for the distorted morality of the game. Survival in a time of war is reduced to little more than resource managment.

This War of Mine is a game with something to say that would very much like you to know that it's said it, and doesn't really care how it says it.

This game would like to bludgeon you over the head with the idea that war is awful and being in a war is awful (a fact apparently considered profound to the world of 2014). It does this by placing you in the shoes of a group of survivors working out of a safehouse and having to operate with limited resources in harsh conditions and surroundings.

Resources are few, and you will have to struggle to scrape by if you don't want to enter the path of moral ambiguity or bankruptcy. Basic materials will only get you so far, and it won't be long until you have no choice but to steal or kill to get something you want - and your characters will care about the sacrifices they have to make.

That's the premise, at least. In practice, you'll be able to obtain at least semi-considerable resources until the game ceases providing you with safe (or relatively safe) POIs in which to scavenge in, despite the fact you're in an entire bombed out city, where finding basic materials would likely not be that much of a problem.

When those eventually dry, you'll be left with two choices: Steal from the vulnerable, or put yourself at risk in dangerous areas that can potentially make your life much worse, and face the eventuality of being forced to take a life. 

Let's go through those options:
Most players, I think, will choose danger over theft from the innocent first, especially remote danger like an active sniper somewhere in the distance, so let's start there. 

Danger mostly comes in the form of hostile NPCs, though in at least one case it takes the form of the aforementioned sniper which only becomes a material hostile later in the game. They can (generally) be stealthed around, though the game's movement and interaction is extremely clunky, so it's risky - that being said, this game's NPCs are dumb as bricks and will walk into any trap or walk directly past any number of obvious corners  in their mission to scare the player into thinking there's a threat.

Once you understand the game's combat mechanics, you can generally completely clear any given area with a knife, especially if you just jack your first victim's weapons - but that's *mechanical*. As we mentioned previously, raiding dangerous locations risks having to take a life, and this game boasts a morale system for your survivors that punishes the sacrifices you have to make to survive. 

... killing a human is not chiefly among those moral considerations.

While your characters will care immensely if a true innocent is killed, only the most hyper-empathetic of characters will *ever* care about murdering or stealing from thugs or combatants. Their thoughts on the matter will be passing at worst, and if there is *any* reaction to the actions they're taking, it's likely to be very slight and easily fixed with a bit of radio. Even those that do only care outside of many scripted events that can happen on location - a schoolteacher who can't fathom theft from her enemies can get into a heated gunfight with two snipers in a construction site and, assuming she survives, be totally unbothered by the whole experience, morally and mentally.

Sounds like we've got quite the pragmatic group, no? If you aren't actively committing war crimes and shooting civilians dead, they must not be super touchy-feely. Perhaps, then, it'll be manageable to do some light theft, as long as direct conflict with the owners is avoided - let's, say, steal a few items from an already well-off and well-stocked family.

Even the most pragmatic of your characters will care immensely. Roman and Katia, the two Morally Grey survivors, will both have a decent chance of reacting negatively to theft, no matter how minor it is, no matter who it was stolen from, and no matter why it as stolen. An old man can be dying in your shelter of a horrible illness and one of your survivors will become depressed over your choice to take some medicine from the closet of a family with plenty left to spare, apparently totally unable to rationalize even to the point of "My friend is literally slowing dying in front of me" potentially justifying the action. Breaking into a warehouse when you are fully stocked, picking a fight with its armed occupants, slaughtering them all without remorse, and taking everything inside of it is more justifiable than petty theft to save a life in the eyes of your survivors.

If you return to take something else, or if you had actually come to truly rob a container blind, your characters will be hit with a completely fresh and equally potent - if not *stronger* - wave of guilt for everything they had taken before, combined with everything they had already taken, as it was apparently not considered you would return to a location you stole from.

Outside of bandits and stealing from the innocent, your remaining option for resource gathering is traders, which will sell largely arbitrary selections of goods that may or may not assist you in whatever you're doing around the shelter. They'll occasionally make their way to you themselves, but there are for more traders located in various neutral POIs - ranging from selling food to medicine to just raw junk and scrap. Generally built out of civilian areas, the traders are one of the few systems in the game I'd call truly interesting to engage with - just because each individual trader will value different things, and the value of those different things varies depending on the weather conditions and current events of the city. An easy example is one of the few non-civilian traders; that being the military base's trader, who overvalues vodka and moonshine.

Speaking of the military base - to really drive home how nonsense this game's morality can be, your survivors don't care at all if you respond to the soldiers who are open to trade by murdering them all and looting the base entirely clean. They are treated as no better - potentially even worse - than bandits, despite each individual soldier you kill almost certainly wanting to be here about as much as you do. You can loot their entire stock and off their corpses after clearing the base quite easily, and be set for most of the rest of the game, with only cursory trading and looting done to make sure you don't run out of the ever elusive Scrap Wood and Scrap Electronics.

As I opened with: This War of Mine desperately wants you to know what it's said, but didn't take any care to say it in a way that could be considered valuable or profound. Almost all of its narrative fails in execution and hits massive walls of dissonance in gameplay. To think it has done something impressive requires you to buy into its own presentation and hype.

Let me start by saying: [b] This War of Mine [/b] is my [u] FAVORITE [/u] game of all time.

Where as most games about war revolve around the action, the killing, the war itself, This War of Mine delves deeply into the [i] human cost [/i] of war itself. Your characters will starve, they will get depressed, and they will [spoiler] commit acts out of desperation and even commit suicide. [/spoiler]

You will be riddled with tough choices, and even tougher situations. As with most every day people living through a war, the goal is not to [i] harm others [/i] but rather to [i] ensure that you and your community [b] Survive. [/b][/i] You will need to build your base to prevent looters. You will need to actively defend yourself when patrolling for supplies. You can help others in your community to prolong their survival, or wait out their demise and loot what remains. 

Making ethically bad decisions can affect your gameplay drastically. Whether this is good or bad, is up to you, and the playthrough you have. Each one is different, difficult, and a fun journey. Often, some, or none of your characters will survive to the end. Often times, your neighbors will ask for help. Often times, your characters will cry, or wish they had a book, or reminisce. This is the nature of [b] war. [/b]

This War of Mine is a game that depicts the much more harsh realities of surviving a war: Desperate, trapped in a city besieged by an army willing to commit whatever atrocities they wish, you're trapped inside; not as a soldier, but as a helpless civilian. Reminiscent of another title, Orphan Age, this dives into the nitty-gritty of surviving a war-torn city, like avoiding leaving during the day unless you wish to get your wig split playing "Spot the Sniper", or facing moral dillemmas: Would you steal from the sick and dying if it meant you may survive another day? Maybe you can, but your character might not be able to live with that guilt. There are many ways to lose the game, by simply dying as another casualty of war, committing suicide, dying by trying to escape in desperation, abandoning your shelter, even if you do survive, your characters would more than likely be racked with survivor's guilt, PTSD, and are forever scarred by the war. Not to mention buying this game and subsequent DLCs sends money to the Charity War Child, which is an organisation that helps support children in war-torn areas. This game is a reality check against the romanticization of war, and worth the purchase and playing experience.

You already know or imagine what this game is about by reading the reviews other people made. So instead of reviewing this game I'm gonna use this space to give you some advice from a story I've read about the Bosnian war.

[b]If you are a hoarder or a panic-buyer, don't tell anybody.[/b]

Because if you are live in a country going through a major crisis that includes a shortage of goods and food, if your neighbors and their loved ones are starving to death, and they learn you had anything to do with it, they'll pick their pitchforks and torches and go against you without listening to reason.

In the Bosnian war, there was a family who knew that things were getting worse, and this family had enough food to last a long time. But the trick was to make sure the neighbors didn't find out, because otherwise they'd get raided. There were other people who stockpile stuff, but others quickly found out who had the food because that house was heavily fortified with lots of barricades. They asked "Hey, they must be guarding something valuable there", so everybody raided there.

That family had a father who was smart, he said "We have enough food to last a long time, but we have to be safe and sensible about this", so they made sure to not stand out. His family did nothing more than their neighbors did like setting a guy with a gun in the front door to counter attack potential looters and that was it. They didn't barricade the whole house to indicate that they have enough food to last seasons. And they also made sure that while they were eating enough to survive they made sure to only eat enough to survive.... because if everyone is low on food all your neighbors are incredibly thin to unhealthy levels, and you are 300 pounds that's enough giveaway about your food supplies.

That family survived the war effectively in the end. Nobody in their family starved to death, everyone was well taken care of. They were a little bit thinner, but they were okay.

After about four hours with The Final Cut, I’m starting to see why this game is so highly praised. It’s not your typical RPG, there’s almost no combat so far, but the writing and atmosphere are phenomenal. Every conversation feels meaningful, and the dialogue choices genuinely shape how my character thinks and behaves.

You think you understand it, you think you will make it in first try, but no, it will take you several times, with frustration, but each time you are ready, with more knowledge to get it done this time. For me, it was about three 10+ hour sessions - three days to do it. The vibe is there, from visuals, to sounds and music, to story and action. This game's mechanics and style for me is something like a mix of early Fallout's to Fallout Shelter, plus something what Frostpunk could have taken influence off of - there's definitely a trend of this type of 2D, 2.5D survivor type games. This is a pretty solid little survival crafter with a realistic take on what it must be like to be a civilian during times of war. It often forces you to make very tough decisions, many of which are ethical in nature. It makes you wonder how far you could go to survive in such conditions. Will you be ruthless or kind towards other survivors? Will you neglect people in your group in favor of others? Little things like that add a lot to the game.

The gameplay comes in two parts: managing your shelter and going outside to loot. The shelter management is a lot of fun and involves just the right amount of work so that most of your days aren't wasted rolling your thumbs since you'll be busy crafting or enhancing things. The way you use the ressources available to you is crucial for your group's survival, especially in the first days when the wrong choices can have severe consequences. On one hand, you'd like to build a hatchet, but then again maybe you'd better wait and build a trap so you could get meat in a couple of days... Little choices like that come to you on a daily basis.

The second part of the game is the looting at night. I'm not a big fan of this part, because it involves a few core things I don't like. First of all, all characters are slow - most precisely when they're not running - due to the fact that you only have the choice between running and stealth walk. Running is out of the question if you have any indication that there may be hostile characters. The stealth walk is really slow and only adds frustration to the game most of the time, since time is breathing down your neck and you need to leave before the countdown ends.

Then, there's the horrendous fighting mechanics that will definitely end up with you dying in your first few playthroughs. It's by far the worst aspect of the game. It's extremely clumsy and frustrating. The characters in this game are almost all inept at fighting except for maybe two of them, and there is no way to train or augment your skills. I understand they want to make it realistic - not all survivors can fight - but it removes a huge chunk of the game if you don't and it makes things way harder for you to survive because your characters are very limited in what they can do. They don't have anything to counterbalance their lack of combat skills. They can't craft unique things. They can't salvage for specific things. They don't have special abilities, except maybe the ability to play guitar ( which is useless 99% of the time ). They can't make peace with hostile characters, even those they encounter the first time. They only have one skill, like "good cook", and that's it. In my opinion the game suffers a lot from this simplicity and you quickly end up disliking a lot of characters who are completely useless and, on top of that, don't have any personality except for their written backstories that you get a few days in-between ( and you end up not reading them because nobody likes to read a bunch of paragraphs with no voice overs while playing their video games ).

The crafting, while quite efficient, lacks depth. Electricity ( generators, gas, lighting, electric heating, etc. ), for example, should've been in the game. Power issues could've added a lot to it. There's only a few things you can craft that aren't super necessary, namely alcohol or cigarettes, and eventually you'll just end up making those because they are easy to make and you can trade a lot, a lot of stuff in exchange for them, making you well-off and quite overpowered about halfway through your survival journey. Food only comes in three items, one that's a whole meal and the other two, combined, making a full meal. In my opinion, a very fun feature of most survival crafters is to be able to collect food of all sorts and just gazing upon your stored food and other items. Unfortunately, you can't do that in that game, and all items you collect aren't physically viewable, they're just simplistic, white, drawn icons on an inventory screen.

I feel like the developers who made this game built it to give themselves a moral high ground over other games that involve wars, but by doing so they got themselves in a bind that kept them from going further and exploring different avenues with more "evil" characters like the thugs you encounter. I think it would've added an interesting dynamic to the game if we could've been the thugs, soldiers or rebel militia and see the consequences of our actions later on.

The war you need to survive through clearly has an eastern, central europe vibe which makes sense since the development team is from Poland. I kinda wish we could've explored different settings though, such as wars in the middle east or asia, like trying to survive through a dictatorship or something like that. I feel like the many stories this game has kinda all fall in the same basket and don't really stand out from one another because of this.

11 bit studios took pride in their game's anti-war narrative to the point that they made public statements on the war in Ukraine, but are dead silent when it comes to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. This is clearly still a big issue in the TWOM community, as indicated by the many, many posts about this. This is what happens when you try to get a moral high ground with any kind of media. It backfires because once you take a public stance, people will expect you to do it all the time and will interpret your silence for approval of whatever's going on.

Other than that, the game does a lot of things right! The fact that survivors are different from one another is great, it's just that there should've been more content there. Collecting and then using ressources is a lot of fun. The music and sound effects are really good and make the game really atmospheric, as the tag indicates. The game is very dark in terms of colors, but it fits the setting. Going through the war and making it alive, especially when you manage to keep the same survivors from the beginning, feels very rewarding. It's quite the journey. The replay value is so-so but it's a very good experience for the first time, despite the few frustrating points I've given the game. 7/10.

This War of Mine is one of the most brutal and depressing games I’ve ever played — and that’s exactly what makes it so powerful. It doesn’t put you in the role of a soldier or a hero, but of ordinary people caught in the middle of war, just trying to make it through each day. Every decision has weight, and most of them feel awful. Do you steal from someone weaker than you, knowing it might mean their death? Or do you go hungry and risk losing your own people?

I loved the challenge of organizing, scavenging, and trying to survive, but I never once had a truly successful run. No matter how careful I was, things always broke down in the end — someone got sick, we were raided, or I got killed. It’s relentless, and every game over was brutal but captivated me.

What makes it so compelling is how human it feels. The fatigue, the hunger, the fear, the small moments of relief — it captures the psychological desolation of war in a way I’ve never seen before in a game. It’s hard, it’s bleak, and sometimes it feels hopeless… but that’s what makes it unforgettable.

Brutal, yes — but brilliant.

I keep coming back to this game over and over. The mechanics can be a little clunky at times, but it’s still one of the best games ever made. This War of Mine really puts you in the shoes of a war-torn civilian, and while it’s “just a game,” it does an incredible job of making you feel the constant tension and dread of living under those conditions. It’s hard to even imagine what real people experiencing this go through, but this game makes you pause and think about it.

This War of Mine isn’t out here handing you some shiny trophy for “winning.” Nah, it’s more like, “how shredded is your conscience when you finally make it out?” And honestly? That messes with me in the way that makes you rethink your life choices, not in a “hey, let’s fire it up at the next birthday party” sort of way. I swear, this game leaves you marked up, but for whatever reason, I still open it back up every now and then, just to see if the ache’s still there.

Here’s the thing: most games put you on some ridiculous hero pedestal, right? But this one, nope you’re just some regular nobody. You’re exhausted, half starved, trying to sleep on a pile of bricks while the ceiling leaks sadness. Your “missions” turn into raiding some grandma’s cupboards or watching your buddy fade away ‘cause nobody’s coming. Grim doesn’t even cover it. But you can’t deny it there’s this raw honesty to it. Most games wouldn’t go near this with a 10 foot pole.

Honestly, This War of Mine just grabs you, shakes you up, and doesn’t give one damn about your “fun.” If you’re looking to kick back and farm XP, just walk away. This thing rips you apart and then leaves you alone with your thoughts, making you wonder how you’d actually hold up if everything went sideways. Fun? Nope. Fair? Not a chance. But that’s the twisted charm, man it sticks with you, like some bad dream you can’t quite shake no matter how many times you close your laptop.

Best of luck to ya! Hope you survive the war!

This War of Mine captures the quiet, relentless brutality of civilian life in a war zone better than any shooter ever could. You don’t play a soldier or a hero. You guide ordinary people as they scavenge for food, medicine, and warmth while shells fall outside. Every decision is heavy: do you steal from a sick neighbor so your group can last one more day? Do you risk the night for scraps that might not exist? The game never judges, but it never lets you forget the cost.

Its influence reaches far beyond gaming. In 2020, Poland made history by adding This War of Mine to its high school recommended reading list–the first video game anywhere to be recognized as essential literature. The government even offers it free for students and teachers, complete with lesson plans.

And when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, developer 11 Bit Studios turned empathy into action, donating a week of profits to the Ukrainian Red Cross with over $850,000 raised in days.

What makes this all resonate is how the game itself refuses spectacle. The charcoal visuals, the mournful score, and the slow grind of survival pull you into a place where every small victory feels borrowed and every loss hits like real grief. Raw, haunting, and unforgettable. This War of Mine depicts the horrors of war and makes you feel them. Proof that games can be both art and witness.

I'm gonna be honest, I've played a lot of looting survival games and this was perhaps the weakest of them all. The gameplay loop is rather limited and uninteresting, with you simply sending one character out each night, over and over again. You can never manage to carry enough resources to meet your needs, at least in my attempted experience, and for whatever reason you can only send out one guy to loot ♥♥♥♥. Why? At least let me make use of my survivors when it comes to the most important aspect of the game. There is also minuscule replayability, everything feels the exact same over and over again.

Perhaps the most exciting possibility in the game is the combat, which I got to experience once and it was kinda thrilling. I was cornered during a looting run and had to fight off two defenders with just my crowbar. I then get back home and everyone is depressed as if I had gone and killed innocents. He defended himself, but they are all horribly depressed? Man up and quit your crying, you did what you had to do. There is also no combat when enemies show up at night. All you can do is hope that your guys can do their job and fend them off. Missed opportunity, and all it ends up feeling like is your hard-looted stuff gets whisked away and you can't do ♥♥♥♥ to stop it. 

Also in terms of resource management, the game seems to try to make things harsh. It makes sense when considering the setting is an actual war zone. However, with the limited amount of looting capacity and no ability to improve it, you're sort of stuck trying to balance base improvements vs sustenance, but you always fall short. There is also a severe lack of bandages while there is an overabundance of medicine, which cannot be used to treat the wounds you are always sustaining with night raids. 

TLDR: The concept is fertile with possibilities, but all you get is a bunch of not-men sitting around feeling sorry for themselves. They can't defend themselves, and if they kill someone that meant them harm then they get unreasonably depressed. They are melodramatic and hardly fun to play as considering the setting. The depression should be felt by the player for the decisions they are forced to make, not forced upon them by the characters.

Runs at a modest [b]20–30 FPS[/b] on my potato, but thanks to the game's gritty, sketchbook art style, it’s [i]still very enjoyable.[/i]
[b]No crashes.[/b]
[b]Audio? Chef’s kiss.[/b] The sound design is [i]so crisp[/i] you’ll hear the sadness in every creaking floorboard and gunshot.

[b]Storyline:[/b]
Every playthrough is different. Random survivors, random tragedies, random emotional damage. So yeah—can’t really sum up the story. Just know:
[i]You will suffer. And love it.[/i]

[b]Gameplay:[/b]
It’s a full-on [b]Mouse1 clicker simulator™️[/b].
There’s not even a control settings menu because you literally just click everything. It kinda feels like a mobile game, and while I think that’s by design, I really wish there was some keyboard integration to smooth things out.

Here’s what I’d love 11 bit studios to consider for quality of life:

[list]
[*][b]TAB to open, ESC to close inventory[/b]. Drag and click to open is tiring.
[*][b]Number keys to select characters.[/b] Clicking portraits or the people every time? [i]Tiring.[/i] Let me keep my cursor on the 'eat' button and press 1–4 to switch people.
[*][b]Weapon hotkeys (1–4) during scavenging.[/b] Why must I open my backpack, click a gun, then click “equip,” then exit... every time? Just let me press [b]1 for shotgun[/b], [b]2 for rifle[/b], [b]3 for scoped rifle[/b], [b]4 for pistol[/b], paired with best melee. Smooth, simple, satisfying.
[*][b]SPACEBAR to shoot/attack locked targets.[/b] Right now, if you misclick while trying to shoot a moving enemy, you just... walk into their line of fire like an idiot. Mouse1 to select, SPACEBAR to execute—[i]easy fix, better gameplay.[/i]
[*][b]ASD to adjust time.[/b] Personally, I’m not a fan of speeding things up, but slowing down time? YES PLEASE. Let me [b]SHIFT[/b] into slow-mo for sneaky takedowns or intense looting sequences.
[*][b]Raids are kind of meh.[/b] You don’t actually defend your shelter—it just says “you were raided” and whether you survived based on RNG and gear. Would love [i]actual combat segments[/i].
[/list]


[b]Final thoughts:[/b]
Do I recommend this game? [b]Yes—especially for the story.[/b]

PT/BR

Joguei This War of Mine por cerca de 2 horas na Steam, mas antes disso já tinha passado mais de 12 horas jogando por outros meios alternativos 💻.
Comprei o jogo na loja oficial só pra apoiar os devs, porque acho a proposta válida e bem feita, mesmo com várias críticas que carrego 🎁.
Recomendo com ressalvas — e, sendo honesto, com fortes inclinações a não fazer isso de novo 💸.

A proposta do jogo é, de fato, diferente do que estamos acostumados nos jogos de guerra ⚔️.
Aqui, não somos soldados com armas e objetivos heroicos — somos civis comuns tentando sobreviver em meio ao caos, fome, frio e medo ❄️.
E isso, por si só, já torna o jogo interessante 🎮.
A atmosfera pesada, a trilha sonora melancólica e o visual sombrio fazem com que você realmente sinta o peso daquela situação 🌫️.
A ideia é muito boa 💡.
Mas, com o tempo, comecei a me sentir mais frustrado do que envolvido 😓.

Um dos pontos que mais me incomodou foi o ritmo 🐌.
O jogo é extremamente lento em algumas partes ⏳.
Quando você vai explorar uma casa abandonada ou uma escola, por exemplo, mesmo que não tenha inimigos nem ameaças por perto, você precisa voltar lá 2, 3, 4, até 5 vezes só pra pegar todos os recursos 🛠️.
Isso torna a experiência cansativa, repetitiva, meio sem propósito 🔁.
Em vez de me sentir tenso ou imerso, eu só ficava pensando: "Lá vamos nós de novo..." 🥱.
E o mais frustrante é que isso poderia ser facilmente resolvido com algumas opções simples, como um sistema de “fast loot” 🏃‍♂️ — onde pegar tudo de uma área já vasculhada fosse automático — ou a possibilidade de levar mais de um sobrevivente por expedição, pra otimizar o tempo e tornar tudo menos maçante 🤝.
Esses ajustes deixariam a gameplay mais fluida, sem comprometer o peso dramático da experiência 🚪.
Do jeito que está, acaba quebrando muito o clima de urgência que o jogo quer passar 🚨.

E já que estamos falando de exploração… pelo amor de Deus, como é que esses personagens conseguem montar rádios, aquecedores, destiladores, painéis de metal, até instrumentos musicais… mas NENHUM DELES SABE FAZER UMA MOCHILA?! 🎒❌🧠
Sério, não existe sequer a opção de montar uma sacola com pano velho ou amarrar dois panos com um fio de cobre — que aliás, você tem aos montes 💼🧶.
Eles conseguem criar circuitos eletrônicos funcionais no meio do apocalipse 🧲📻, mas transportar 8 unidades de madeira exige múltiplas viagens a pé, na neve, com a mãozinha 🍂👋.
É tão ilógico que chega a ser cômico 🤡.
Você olha pro abrigo cheio de engenhocas e pensa: “Alguém aqui já ouviu falar em carregar coisas?” 🚚💡
Se a ideia era trazer realismo e profundidade, isso tira completamente o sentido — parece que o jogo escolheu ser difícil não pela narrativa, mas pela teimosia absurda 🤯🔧.

Outro ponto que me soou exagerado foi a questão moral dos personagens 🤔.
Tudo é muito profundo, filosófico, dramático demais 🎭.
É como se cada decisão (mesmo as mais óbvias pra sobrevivência) virasse um dilema existencial 🧠.
Entendo que o jogo quer passar o lado psicológico da guerra, mas às vezes parece forçado, como se os personagens estivessem "pensando demais" em situações onde o instinto de sobrevivência deveria ser mais forte 🧍‍♂️.
Fica uma sensação de artificialidade emocional — como se os civis fossem filósofos deprimidos em vez de pessoas desesperadas por viver mais um dia 🛌.

E por fim, a mensagem anti-guerra, que é importante, sim — mas o jogo martela tanto isso o tempo todo, que chega uma hora em que parece mais uma propaganda do que uma experiência interativa 📢.
Ao invés de me fazer refletir naturalmente, me senti empurrado pra pensar de um jeito só, como se o jogo estivesse gritando na minha cara: “GUERRA É RUIM, VOCÊ ESTÁ SE SENTINDO MAL, NÉ?” 😣.
A imersão se perde aí também 🌀.

No geral, eu acho This War of Mine um jogo único, com uma ideia nobre e importante, mas que exagera em alguns aspectos e acaba se sabotando ⚖️.
É mais uma experiência emocional do que um jogo divertido — e às vezes nem emocional é, só arrastado 🪨.
Vale a pena jogar pelo menos uma vez, mas prepare-se: o peso que ele tenta passar não vem só da história… vem da paciência também 🧘.








English:

I’ve played This War of Mine for about 2 hours on Steam, but before that, I had already spent over 12 hours playing it through alternative means 💻.
I bought it officially just to support the devs, because I think the concept is solid and well-executed — even though I’ve got a bunch of criticisms to go with it 🎁.
I recommend it with caution — but honestly, I’m heavily leaning toward not doing that again 💸.

The concept is definitely different from what we’re used to in war games ⚔️.
Here, you’re not a soldier with guns and heroic goals — you’re just regular civilians trying to survive in the middle of chaos, hunger, cold, and fear ❄️.
And that alone already makes the game interesting 🎮.
The heavy atmosphere, the melancholic soundtrack, and the grim visuals really make you feel the weight of the situation 🌫️.
The idea is really good 💡.
But over time, I found myself feeling more frustrated than immersed 😓.

One of the things that bothered me the most was the pacing 🐌.
The game is extremely slow in certain parts ⏳.
When you go out to scavenge an abandoned house or a school, for example — even if there are no enemies or threats nearby — you have to go back 2, 3, 4, even 5 times just to grab all the resources 🛠️.
This turns the experience into something tedious, repetitive, and kind of pointless 🔁.
Instead of feeling tense or immersed, I kept thinking, “Here we go again...” 🥱.
And what’s worse is that this could easily be fixed with a few simple options — like a “fast loot” system 🏃‍♂️, where grabbing everything in an already-searched area is automatic — or the ability to bring more than one survivor per scavenging run to make things smoother 🤝.
These small changes would make the gameplay way more fluid without killing the game’s dramatic tone 🚪.
The way it stands, it just kills the sense of urgency the game tries so hard to create 🚨.

And since we’re talking about scavenging… for the love of logic — how can these people build radios, heaters, metal workshops, even musical instruments… but not a single one of them can make a backpack?! 🎒❌🧠

Another thing that felt overdone was the moral depth of the characters 🤔.
Everything is so deep, philosophical, and overly dramatic 🎭.

Ahoy, Swoonds here.
Have you ever wanted to simulate the thrill of war from the thrilling perspective of a depressed civilian eating cat food in a bombed-out kitchen?
Did you play The Sims and think, “What this needs is more PTSD and war crimes”?
Then boy, do I have the antidepressant replacement for you:
This War of Mine – the only survival game where the final boss is seasonal depression.

🎭 THE PREMISE
You don’t play as the hero.
You don’t play as the villain.
You play as some guy named Boris, who’s 48, hungry, smokes 12 cigarettes a day, and once cried because he stepped on a rat trap.

This isn’t Call of Duty.
There are no killstreaks.
There’s no "winning."
Only not dying.
And sometimes dying less horribly than others.

Set in a nameless Eastern European war zone that’s definitely not Sarajevo but might as well be, This War of Mine puts you in control of a group of regular civilians trying to survive the horrors of war.
Which mostly means: building beds, crying in them, and getting stabbed by an old man over a can of soup.

⛺ THE GAMEPLAY
Daytime:
Stay indoors. Snipers will turn your skull into wall art.
Build stoves, furniture, rat traps. Board up the windows.
Spend five hours debating if you should burn your last book for warmth, or read it and remember hope.

Nighttime:
Choose someone to go scavenge.
Then proceed to sneak through ruined hospitals, snuff out grandmothers, and rob corpses for expired meds.
Will you loot an orphanage?
Will you steal insulin from a dying man?
Will you come home, traumatized, to find your friend hung himself in the bathroom?

That’s called emergent gameplay, baby.

💉 THE SURVIVAL
Food? Rare.
Medicine? Priceless.
Ammo? Practically made of unicorn tears.

Everyone has vices.
Pavle’s depressed.
Katya’s depressed.
Bruno is hungry and depressed.

Keep your people warm, fed, and sane.
Or don’t.
And watch your camp unravel into a Lovecraftian breakdown of existential dread and cold soup.

Sometimes, the most strategic choice is who you let starve next.

🔫 COMBAT
Combat in This War of Mine is less “Rambo” and more “Oh God, that man had a family.”
It’s clunky.
It’s brutal.
It’s usually avoidable.
But when it happens, it’s savage, fast, and always morally bankrupt.

You will shoot a man in the spine, loot his shoes, and cry about it later over a half-eaten potato.

Sometimes, you’ll get shot just because you made a noise while scavenging.
Sometimes, you’ll stab a soldier in the dark because they were guarding medicine.
Sometimes, the biggest enemy is your conscience.

💔 THE CHOICES
You want to help that old couple, but you also need food.
You want to treat that sick child at the door, but you only have one pill left.
You want to be the good guy,
but the good guy is dead.

Every choice has weight.
Every action changes how your survivors feel.
Push them too far and they’ll spiral into guilt, rage, or suicide.

This isn’t about “winning.”
It’s about enduring.
And endurance costs everything.

🧱 THE AESTHETIC
The visuals are grim charcoal sketches come to life.

The music is melancholic Eastern Bloc electronica, occasionally interrupted by screams.

The UI is depressing in a sexy, minimalist way.

The whole game oozes bleak Eastern European realism.
It feels less like playing a game and more like being waterboarded with emotions.

🛠️ THE DLC
Want to experience more trauma?
Play the Stories DLC, where you follow individual tales of loss, regret, and grey morality.
One story features a dad sheltering his daughter.
Another has you protecting the sick.
Another lets you question if mercy is worse than vengeance.

It’s like The Road, but interactive.
And more painful.
But still fun, somehow?

🧠 THE REALIZATION
This War of Mine isn’t really about war.
It’s about the people caught beneath it.
The forgotten. The helpless. The ones who didn’t choose this.
And what happens when survival costs your soul.

But also…
sometimes you make moonshine and trade it for 30 cans of tuna.
So it’s not all bad.

🏆 FINAL SCORE
This War of Mine is not a fun game.
But it’s an important one.
It’s harsh, it’s heavy, it’s hopeless,
and it’ll haunt you long after you stop playing.

9 out of 10 broken radios
Would recommend to anyone who thinks games can’t make you feel bad.
Because they can.
And they will.
And you’ll say, “One more run.”
And you’ll cry again.

If you are into survival base management games then this is something that is right up your alley. 

I played and came back to this game quite a few times because I found it very engaging. You start out with 2-4 civilian characters with unique qualities, and have to manage a base in a war torn country until you either buy your escape from the city you are trapped in or last until a ceasefire is declared. The weather can get freezing cold, supplies can be difficult to come across, and gangs can raid your base at night, and you have to defend your base, acquire resources, and manage things as best you can. 

I found out fairly quickly that mass producing cigarettes is probably the best way to get through a playthrough since there is a trading aspect to the game where you can trade goods for other goods. Cigarettes are the easiest thing to make, you can make lots of them, and then you can trade them for things you need to get through really difficult parts of your playthrough. Each game can last from 30 to 80 days where during the day you manage your base and look after your characters, and then there is a night phase where you can choose one character to go scavenge a certain location that may have food, building materials, weapon materials, scrap parts, medicine, etc... Certain characters may be able to carry more stuff than other characters, some may be able to sneak around quietly, some have combat experience and can kill hostile enemies with greater ease. 

The one major downside to this game is THERE IS NO SAVE GAME OPTION. If something goes wrong in your playthrough like a character dying or a particularly bad raid on your base at night, you're not going to be able to just quickly reload an earlier autosave and try again. That burned me a few times in different playthroughs of this game, especially when I was trying to get all of the steam achievements in order to 100% complete the game. 

Overall though this is fun game to pick up if youre into survival base-building management games, on sale or not.

"Refusing to fight for what one believes is right is not an act of cowardice. It is the realization that war is futile."

This War of Mine – A Game That Left a Scar, Not Just an Impression

I’ve played countless war games, but none have ever made me stop, sit in silence, and just feel the weight of survival like This War of Mine. This isn’t about soldiers, medals, or glory. This is about civilians—trapped in the crossfire, starving, freezing, breaking, enduring.

You don’t win This War of Mine. You outlast it. Maybe.

What makes this game so hauntingly powerful is its brutal honesty. Every choice feels heavy: Do I rob an elderly couple to feed my group? Do I risk venturing out under sniper fire for medicine? Can I bear to leave a wounded stranger begging at my door while I protect the last of our supplies?

This game doesn’t offer “fun” in the traditional sense—it offers perspective. The kind that lingers with you after you close the game. The kind that makes you look at news headlines differently. It's art, in the most raw and human way possible.

Every character has a name, a past, a breaking point. And by the time the war ends—if it ends—you’re not celebrating victory. You’re just wondering what kind of person you became to survive.

If you’ve never played a game that truly challenges your morality, your empathy, and your humanity, this is the one. This War of Mine doesn’t want to entertain you. It wants to make you understand.

Most war games put you on the front lines with a rifle in your hands and adrenaline in your veins. This War of Mine does the opposite — it drops you behind the lines, in the rubble of a city under siege, where survival isn't about glory, but about desperation, morality, and hard choices.

This is war through the eyes of the civilians.

Inspired by the Siege of Sarajevo, This War of Mine tasks you with managing a group of ordinary people trying to survive in a war-torn city. These are not soldiers — they're teachers, chefs, musicians, and mechanics. They're cold, hungry, injured, and scared. And it’s your job to help them make it through another day.

The gameplay mixes resource management, crafting, stealth, and emotional storytelling. By day, you fortify your shelter, cook food, care for the wounded, and try to stave off depression. By night, you send someone out to scavenge for supplies — often facing brutal moral dilemmas in the process.

Do you steal from an elderly couple to feed your starving group? Do you risk injury to save a stranger calling for help? Do you ignore a knock at the door because you're low on meds? Every decision has a cost, and survival often means sacrificing your humanity.

The game’s art style is hand-drawn, bleak, and hauntingly beautiful. The grayscale palette is punctuated by muted colors, adding to the sense of despair. The ambient soundtrack is minimal and melancholic — never overpowering, always appropriate.

And yet, the most powerful element is silence. The game gives you space to feel. To stare at your characters as they sit in sorrow. To reflect after a gut-wrenching choice. It doesn’t yell at you. It lets the weight of war speak for itself.

While the mechanics are relatively simple — crafting, managing hunger, sleep, and morale — the emotional complexity runs deep. Each playthrough is procedurally generated, offering different characters, stories, and events. No two runs feel the same, especially with the growing burden of your decisions over time.

The game isn’t without its rough edges. The AI during scavenging can be a bit rigid, and the pacing in late-game scenarios can feel slow once your base is fortified. But those are minor blemishes on an otherwise unforgettable experience.

This War of Mine isn’t just a game — it’s a statement. It has been used in classrooms, praised by humanitarian organizations, and even added to the Polish educational curriculum. It forces players to think not just tactically, but ethically. It reminds us that war is not just fought with bullets, but with hunger, trauma, and loss.

The developers further supported this message with the “Stories” DLCs and the Final Cut, which refined visuals and added new content while maintaining the game’s somber tone.

This War of Mine is a raw, emotional, and humanizing portrayal of war that lingers long after the screen goes dark. It’s not “fun” in the traditional sense — and that’s exactly the point. It’s a powerful piece of interactive storytelling that deserves a place among the most important games of its generation.

If you’re looking for a game that challenges not just your skills but your conscience, This War of Mine will leave a lasting impression — and maybe a heavy heart.

Bleak, haunting, and human, [i] This War of Mine [/i] flips the script on war games by showing you not the soldiers, but the civilians. Trapped in a besieged city, starving and broken, you’re only trying to survive day by day, minute by minute. It’s a masterclass in emotional storytelling, where every decision feels like a quiet tragedy waiting to happen.

You control a small group of civilians trying to survive in a war-torn city inspired by the Siege of Sarajevo. During the day, you manage your shelter—crafting, upgrading, tending to wounds and depression. At night, you venture into the city to scavenge for food, medicine, and supplies, sometimes at great moral cost. It puts you in impossible situations and forces you to live with what you’ve done. It's not about victory or heroism, but survival and guilt. If you're looking for a game that sticks with you long after the screen goes dark, this is it.

🕯️[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] One of the most emotionally affecting games ever made. I felt grim after surviving another day.

[*] Moral choices are nuanced and brutal. There are no “good” or “bad” endings, just compromises and consequences.

[*] Unique war narrative. It shows the civilian cost of war, rarely explored in games, and doesn’t flinch from the horror.

[*] Distinct survivors with personalities. Each character has their own skills, flaws, and even journal entries that evolve based on your actions. Some have more useful skills than other.

[*] Visually stunning in a stark, graphic-novel way. The pencil-sketched 2.5D art style matches the tone perfectly—gritty and grey, but beautiful.

[*] Great replayability. Different characters, random events, changing locations, and shifting weather conditions make every run feel unique.

[*] Powerful end-game. If you make it to the ceasefire, you get an epilogue describing how each character feels about your choices. Some of my people didn't love how I pushed them, but I was only trying to help them survive!

[*] Surprisingly good mod support with an in-game launcher. 

[*] Goes on sale and is super cheap! Seriously, it's only a dollar right now. 
[/list]

[b] ⚠️ Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Bleakness isn’t for everyone. This is a grim, heavy game that doesn’t offer much in the way of hope or joy. It can be emotionally exhausting.

[*] Micromanagement fatigue. The shelter loop can feel repetitive over long sessions, especially in late-game when resources dwindle.

[*] Combat is clunky and punishing. You can defend yourself, but the mechanics are stiff and often not in your favor.

[*] Random events can be unfair. Sometimes people die or get sick with little warning or no way to prevent it. That’s war, sure, but it can feel frustrating.

[*] Depression mechanics can spiral. Once a character becomes emotionally broken, it’s hard to bring them back. One death can tank everyone’s mood.
[/list]

This War of Mine initially makes a strong impression - survivors fending for their lives, foraging supplies, food, and even staving off attackers not in a zombie scenario or post-apocalyptic hellscape, but in a realistic civil war in the fictional country of Pogoren. I don't believe such a scenario had been tackled before, at least not as famously, as in this game, so I was immediately interested. At first, the game had me entirely hooked, I was playing multiple multi-hour sessions at a time, and despite some initial troubles, I got into the swing of things pretty quickly. Managing my characters was fun and challenging at first. However, as time went on, I ended up realizing how shallow the game truly was both mechanically and thematically. Although the game attempts to show the true horrors of the civilian perspective of war, you don't see a whole lot and the moral choices you have to make end up losing their emotional effect pretty quickly. As it turns out, the mechanically advantageous choices are all the immoral ones, and on repeat attempts, there's practically no reason to go for anything else other than some self-imposed limitation. The game is, unfortunately, lacking in variety: the trader always has the same supplies, multiple runs will have the same areas to scavenge with no differences (there is some variance, but largely it's the same areas), you'll always have a cold front or a crime wave, et cetera. Once you've played maybe, six attempts, you've seen it all, and the game doesn't offer much more. The stealth, combat, and scavenging mechanics are all fairly basic and offer little depth. Even when it comes to the anti-war themes the game tries to push, it can't help but feel unbelievably surface-level and spoonfed to the player. The worldbuilding memos the player finds are too impersonal, and the character interactions are so threadbare that it becomes difficult to care.

At least the presentation isn't bad, the game is clearly low-budget but it has at times fairly striking art direction. The grim, almost monochrome, paper sketch style fits the tone very well and at the very least makes the game look as grim as it wishes it was. Asset quality is fairly low, but when compared to how pulled back the camera is, this is hard to notice even at high resolutions. Environments are surprisingly detailed and seem to tell better stories than the actual writing does. My only real complaint is the lack of anti-aliasing, which can make the game look overly cheap at points. The soundtrack is well-produced and can be suitably atmospheric, but I can't help but feel it's too overbearing and "epic" sounding for the kind of intimate stories this game wants to tell.

A Grim Premise That Becomes Repetitive and Emotionally Numb

This War of Mine sets out to deliver a powerful message — war seen not through the eyes of soldiers, but of civilians simply trying to survive. And for the first few hours, it succeeds. The art style is bleak and effective, the atmosphere oppressive, and your choices feel weighty. But once the novelty wears off, the cracks begin to show.

The gameplay loop quickly becomes repetitive. Scavenge by night, manage resources by day, repeat. There’s little mechanical variety, and most decisions boil down to the same few options, just dressed differently. After a while, the emotional impact dulls because the events feel more like scripted systems than organic experiences.

Character development is shallow. The survivors have backstories, but they rarely evolve during gameplay. Their reactions to trauma or loss start to feel robotic rather than human. Depression mechanics, while meant to add realism, often just become frustrating — especially when characters spiral with little player agency to stop it.

Controls and interface aren’t great either. Managing your shelter feels more like dragging icons across a screen than making meaningful decisions, and movement during scavenging can feel awkward and imprecise.

What should have been a heartbreaking, introspective journey turns into a grind that struggles to stay engaging. I respect what This War of Mine tries to do, but I didn’t find myself emotionally moved — just worn down.

[h1]The Game That Doesn't Offer Hope – And That’s Exactly the Point[/h1]

[h3]Surviving the Unsurvivable[/h3]
[hr]
[b]This War of Mine[/b] isn't about being a hero. It's not about saving the world, conquering evil, or even winning. It's about surviving, barely, while your soul crumbles piece by piece.

You don’t play as a soldier. You play as [b]Pavle[/b], [b]Katia[/b], [b]Bruno[/b]—everyday civilians trapped in a city destroyed by war. People who didn’t ask to be part of the conflict, yet now fight every day not for victory, but for the next can of food, a warm bed, or simply one more day.

[h3]A War Story With No Glory[/h3]
[hr]
There’s no grand narrative here. The story is simple: war is hell, and it’s even worse when you’re not holding a gun. The game drops you into a grey, frozen, bombed-out hellhole and says: “Figure it out.” And you do. But the cost is always personal.

You will make horrifying choices.
Will you steal medicine from the hospital?
Will you rob an elderly couple to keep your group alive?
Will you send someone into sniper fire just to find two pieces of wood and a half-rotten tomato?

There’s no good answer. Only survival.

[h3]Gameplay That Hurts (in the Right Way)[/h3]
[hr]
Imagine The Sims, if instead of designing a dream house, you’re barricading windows with trash and wondering if rat meat is still technically food. The gameplay is simple on the surface – click to scavenge, click to craft, click to sleep – but underneath it’s a war of attrition against hunger, cold, wounds, and your own morals.

You micromanage emotions, not just needs. One day [b]Bruno[/b] is making a stove. The next, he’s sitting in the corner, broken, because you forced him to loot a shelter full of crying kids.
[u]And yes, you made that call.[/u]

[h3]Atmosphere That Bleeds Through the Screen[/h3]
[hr]
Bleak doesn’t begin to cover it. The entire world is drained of color, covered in ash and snow. The music is minimal, haunting—like grief whispering through a ruined city. There’s no joy, no relief. Just cold, hunger, and silence.
And somehow, it’s perfect.

You’re not meant to enjoy This War of Mine.
You’re meant to endure it.
To feel it.
To remember it.

[h3]Morality as a Game Mechanic[/h3]
[hr]
The hardest part of this game isn’t surviving – it’s living with what you did to survive. There’s no morality system. No red vs. blue points. Just people. Hurt, tired, starving people. And the decisions you make on their behalf.

Some nights, I sat frozen, hovering over a choice I didn't want to make. And then I made it. And I hated myself for it.
[u]That’s what makes this game unforgettable.[/u]

[h3]Still Alive – And Still Growing[/h3]
[hr]
It’s hard to believe, but [b]This War of Mine[/b] first came out in 2014. And yet, ten years later, in 2024, it received a brand new DLC with a completely original standalone story. That kind of post-launch support is rare—especially for a game that was never about hype, but about message.

And for me?
[u]This is one of my favorite games of all time.[/u]
I keep coming back to it—not for fun, but for the feeling. That raw, reflective, haunting experience that no other game quite replicates. It leaves a mark. Every time.

[h3]Performance & Steam Deck[/h3]
[hr]
On PC, the game runs flawlessly. Even older machines will handle it well, since the art style is stylized and performance-light. No crashes, no bugs, just smooth, haunting gameplay.

On the [b]Steam Deck[/b]? Surprisingly great. The interface scales well to the smaller screen, controls are intuitive with a few tweaks, and the experience translates beautifully. Curling up with this game in handheld mode feels intimate – and somehow, even more painful.

[b]Steam Deck Experience: 9.0/10[/b]

[h3]Skills? Or Just Survival Instincts?[/h3]
[hr]
Each character brings different strengths. [b]Pavle[/b] can run fast. [b]Bruno[/b] cooks better meals. [b]Katia[/b] trades more effectively. These aren’t skills in the traditional "RPG" sense – they’re survival traits. You’ll learn to value every edge. And when someone dies, it's not just a lost pawn – it's a part of your survival strategy gone forever.

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]
[hr]
This War of Mine is not a game you play to relax. It's not fun in the usual sense. But it's one of the most powerful gaming experiences I've ever had. It's emotionally brutal, relentlessly honest, and utterly unforgettable.

There are games that entertain.
There are games that challenge.
Then there are games like this – that matter.

[b]Final Score: 10/10[/b]
