This War of Mine.This is a story about war, but instead of fighting, you have to
survive. In war, the ones who suffer the most are often innocent people who have nothing to do with the conflict. They are civilians trapped in a dangerous situation,struggling to find food, water, and safety. This War of Mine is inspired by the Bosnian
War (1992-1996) and tells the story of people trying to stay alive in a war-torn city.
Every choice you make matters, and every action has consequences.The game hasa simple 3D view, allowing you to watch your characters move and do things in realtime. Unlike most war games that focus on shooting and fighting, this game focuses on survival. Your characters need basic things like food, water, shelter, and clothes to
live. But because of the war, these things are very hard to find. Every day, you must search for supplies in different places to keep your group alive.
However, the problem is that most places with food and resources are alreadyoccupied by others who are also trying to survive. This leads to difficult choices. For example, one day, you might find a house with plenty of food, but inside, there is an old couple. They are deaf and cannot protect themselves. You must decide whether
to take their food to keep your group alive and Let old age take the old couple away or leave it and risk your people starving.These choices affect not only the game but also the emotions of your characters. If someone steals from the weak, they may feel guilty and become depressed. If things get worse, they might lose hope and even take their own life. On the other hand, if you choose not to take food, your group might suffer from hunger or illness. Another important part of the game is dealing with neighbors. Some neighbors may come to help, while others may ask for your
help. Sometimes, you will face very hard decisions. For example, one morning, two children come to your shelter begging for medicine to save their sick mother. But at the same time, one of your own group members is also very sick and needs the same medicine. If you give the medicine away, your friend might not survive. If you
keep it, the children’s mother might die. There is no easy answer every choice has a consequence.Besides finding supplies and making tough decisions, you also have to protect your shelter. Some nights, thieves might try to break in and steal your food,medicine, or other important items. If you do nothing, you could wake up and find
that everything is gone. But if you fight back, your characters could get hurt or even die.
This War of Mine is a game that shows what war is like for civilians. It is not about winning or losing .it is about surviving. You have to make difficult choices and live with the result

That being said, it's a well designed game with lots of interesting moments and difficult choices, and it's unlike anything else on the market to this day.

Certainly a powerful story game on the commentary of war the difficult choices made during it. Very few choices you make in this game feel like they mean much, and making it to the end with everyone alive is a challenge, especially on longer war duration settings. There are a multitude of heartbreaking scenes and stories you'll stumble across, and the dialogue the characters have in response to your actions truly adds to the effect.

My friends tell me this game is legendary and that they don't understand how I haven't heard of it before; and frankly, [b]I'm[/b] surprised I haven't heard of it before, either. This just happens sometimes, I suppose.

This is a survival strategy game where the protagonists are just a group of ordinary civilians huddling together in a shelled building, trying to navigate life in a besieged city. Food, medicine and fuel are hard to come by and the shelter gets raided regularly by other survivors. You are regularly faced with difficult choices, like deciding whether or not to share limited medical supplies with a neighbour, since your own people might need it soon. Or risking your life to help an injured person pinned down by a sniper. The picture is bleak, often desperate, but there is an undercurrent of determination, even hope. And given the conflicts currently raging around the world with countless civilians caught in the crossfire, I think this game is very relevant to give just a glimpse of what hardships war brings.

If most war games let us “experience war,” This War of Mine makes us “live through war.” The helpless nights, the struggle to survive—these are just fragments in a game, but for many in the real world, they are daily reality. As global tensions continue to shift, countless people are still displaced by conflict. We may feel a fleeting sense of sorrow while playing, but for them, there is no chance to start over.
I hope games like this not only allow us to appreciate their artistic brilliance but also serve as a wake-up call: war is never just a game, and there are no true winners.

This War of Mine – A Hauntingly Beautiful Experience
This War of Mine is not your typical war game. Instead of putting you in the boots of a soldier, it throws you into the harsh reality of civilian survival in a war-torn city. Every moment of the game is a test of morality, resourcefulness, and emotional endurance. And I absolutely loved every minute of it.

Atmosphere & Music – A Perfectly Crafted Experience
One of the strongest aspects of This War of Mine is its ability to immerse you completely. The hand-drawn, grim art style sets the perfect tone for the bleak world you’re forced to navigate. But what really elevates the experience is the music. The soundtrack is hauntingly beautiful—subtle yet powerful, enhancing every decision you make. Whether you’re scavenging abandoned homes or just sitting in the shelter, the music ensures that the weight of your actions never fades.

Gameplay – A Complete and Engaging System
The gameplay is incredibly well-designed, striking a perfect balance between resource management, exploration, and character interaction. Every decision feels meaningful—do you steal from helpless survivors to keep your own group alive, or do you risk going hungry to keep your morality intact? These choices never feel black and white, making every playthrough feel unique and personal.

The day-night cycle is a fantastic mechanic that keeps the tension high. During the day, you manage your shelter, care for your survivors, and make tough choices about crafting and rationing supplies. At night, you venture out into the city, scavenging for materials while facing the constant danger of enemy patrols, hostile survivors, or even moral dilemmas that leave a lasting impact.

Characters – Unique and Memorable
Every survivor has a story, and they all feel incredibly human. From a father trying to protect his daughter to a journalist struggling to keep his integrity, each character brings a different perspective to the war. Their personalities and skills influence gameplay, and watching their mental and physical states deteriorate due to starvation, illness, or guilt makes for an incredibly emotional journey.

The interactions between characters add depth to the game. Seeing them comfort each other after a tough decision or struggle with guilt after doing something desperate makes them feel real. It’s these moments that make you attached to them, which makes losing a survivor feel devastating.

Final Thoughts – A Masterpiece of Storytelling and Gameplay
This War of Mine is a rare gem in gaming. It’s not just about survival—it’s about the human cost of war. The music, the gameplay, and the characters all come together to create an unforgettable experience. It’s engaging, emotional, and thought-provoking in a way that few games manage to be.

I would love to see more stories, more characters, and more expansions to explore different perspectives of war. This is a game that sticks with you long after you’ve put it down. If you haven’t played it yet, do yourself a favor and experience this masterpiece.

This game is an experience that everyone with a pulse and a shred of human emotion should have. It is brutal, ruthless, tragic, and beautiful. Getting through a scenario with all of your survivors feels like a real accomplishment. You feel genuine relief when you realize that the war is over.

The stories add another layer to this game, showing different experiences of people in wartimes: a father trying to save his daughter, a group of people trying to preserve their culture in the face of oppression, a man who is determined to report the truth to his listeners regardless of the cost, and now a woman trying to recover her scattered memories along with the stories she's collected as a journalist.

If that's not enough, 11 Bit Studios has raised money for War Child, and donated all proceeds from sales to sending aide to Ukraine back when the war first started.

This game is a lesson in humanity in the most desolate times. It is a work of art. If you haven't already, please experience it for yourself.

This game is not kind, but in the best way. While it is not brutal in it's imagery -- you won't watch someone die horribly of illness or injury up close and personal -- but it is *honest.* War is not a happy thing for anyone involved, but especially for civilians who are caught in the crossfire. This game brings those realities to us in such a way that, at least for me, stayed with me long after I set it down. Much like the game devs said some years ago in a message I remember them posting: we can step away from this game. There are many, many of those who are not nearly as lucky. There are many out there who this "game" is their reality, and this is a beautifully made and developed means of putting just a fraction of that into perspective for it's players. 

I applaud the development team for continuously keeping this game something special and always staying true to their message in the causes they champion and the charities they donate to. I truly believe this is a game everyone should give a chance, even if only for a day. From the music to the art to the characters and stories (and even in the classic mode) I think it can give something to everyone.

I've likely rambled quite a bit, and apologies if I sounded pretentious at any point, as that was very far from my intention.

This truly is a wonderful game, and I hope that many will give it a chance, and if not, consider donating to any of the charities they've mentioned here before -- or any that helps the victims of war.

Overall amazing game - it possesses a unique concept unlike any other war-based game I've played before. You play as "normal folk" trying to survive through a war that can last weeks, each character has their own set of skills, strengths and "weaknesses" which makes every playthrough a unique experience. 

I like how there is an element of strategy involved in how you structure your base, manage your inventory and controlling characters when they go out scavenging for materials at night. Though there is a little bit of a learning curve when you begin, after a couple of playthroughs you will manage to survive the war without any casualties.

The gameplay itself is not very complicated, but the complexity lies within the order of decisions you take.
Overall it's a highly recommendable game for anyone that looks for a somewhat unique experience. 
It's a game that shows what war means for regular people and the suffering that comes with it.

The game is challenging, and sometimes you will fail, but that's kind of the point; feeling hopeless as a civilian in war, and not an elite fighter. 
It can be played as point and click, but I personally prefer playing with a controller.
Either way it's good, and while there are tips and guides out there, I recommend not reading them at least the first few times you play; just more immersive that way I think, learning the consequences of mistakes and experiencing the really sad aspects of the game.  Definitely recommend this one.

 There are times when you make it through half your gameplay and you have everything to be self-sustainable and you just spike the ball and run out the clock just to see if your pacifist run yielded a good aftermath.

If they wanted it to "feel" real, at any point in the game after you end the day an artillery strike wrecks your house, killing or wounding your party, and destroy half your stuff. As you go towards different locations you should see the aftermath of battles, with dead and injured soldiers and dead, disfigured civilians. Shock me with children begging their mothers or fathers to get up. Let me see how a kind character I'm playing gets hit or executed while a bunch of soldiers barge in the house as the others only look in terror and pray it is not them next. The objective of the game should not be just to get your happy ending because you were extra careful not to do anything to alter that, but to be a gruelling testament of the unfairness of war. Even if it would be frustrating, let my character die beyond my control from drone strikes, artillery shells or just being in the wrong place at the wrong time. For three or four days now, I have played nothing but "This War of Mine". I am a veteran of Iraq and I remember all too well the hardships it brought upon the civilians, especially in the beginning of the war. I remember being heartbroken at the sight of children crying and begging for food on the side of the road.

This "game" puts you square in the middle of the experiences of those civilians. It is a brutal, kill or be killed world - where an act of unimaginable violence may let you live another day, but it can also break your heart and soul. Some days, you are offered a chance at compassion - and if you take that chance, risking your own safety and resources for others, you may find you feel a bit better about yourself.

Then there are the times where you are stuck between a rock and a hard place. You are unarmed, scavenging for anything to save your friends, and you peep through a keyhole and see a soldier brutally beating - and possible worse - a woman. He has an AK-47, you have a lockpick and a rumbling stomach. So you sit there and watch - afraid that any noise may turn his violent attention upon you. When it is all done, you hide until he leaves and then, shamefully, pick over the bloodied body of the woman for anything she may have scavenged before the soldier got to her.

This is "This War of Mine" - a dark, beautiful, haunting, exhilerating, and horrible tale.

What's that tagline, "The first casualty of war is innocence"? It applies here - in a way you would have never imagined coming from a computer game.

This War of Mine is a gripping war survival game, you play as civilians trying to survive another day in their war-torn city. You must manage your resources which include food, water, wood etc, to ensure the survival of your characters. In addition to resource management, you also need to keep an eye on the needs of your characters such as their hunger, energy and happiness levels. 

You can keep onto of these by making sure proper beds are made, you have enough food and collecting/making luxury items such as cigarettes and books to keep them happy. How you get these items is either through trading, or getting lucky on your nightly scavenges, but more on that later.

Gameplay is easy to grasp, using your mouse to click on locations to get your selected character to move and do various things, cook, sleep, hide, build etc. Double clicking makes them sprint, however there is a noise penalty for when you do sprint in the forementioned scavenges! Not all the places you visit will be empty, or friendly… A few of them might have some rather nasty pieces of work living there and if they hear noises, be sure they’ll come to investigate and some of them will not hesitate in killing you upon spotting you! 

At night, if you choose to send someone on a hunt, starts this high intensity timed (you must be back before sunrise!) stealth mission. There are a few mechanics that can help you sneak your way around a night level. You can peak through doors and have a small line of sight into the next room, enemy noises are indicated by red ‘sonar waves’ that alert you to someone or something being around, and if you are spotted you can hide in a few nooks and crannies. You can fight your way out; I personally find the melee combat a little clunky, but the shooting is robust enough, it does feel a bit like an afterthought in terms of how these encounters were meant to go. Killing someone will have a bad effect on your characters mood, remember these are just civilians and not murderers. 

And that is in essence the game, survive, for as long as you can. Build your base up to increase your chances of survival and see how long you can last and honestly, I love it!

The art style is so lovely, this hand drawn sketchy look about the environments and people. There is also very little colour used, which helps emphasis the bleakness of the land and time this game is set in. The music is moody and dramatic and really helps the mood of this game. 

The DLCs are also worth it, with each of them having a unique story around set characters, some of them really got to me whilst I played. 

I’d highly recommend purchasing this game, even when it isn’t on sale, because not only does it help support people but it is also really worth your time and money.

There's something quite unique about this game and I can definitely appreciate that it's more about the experience and the story than the gameplay. You are meant to suffer and you are meant to make difficult choices where you don't win. Civilians in war seldom prosper and so it's realistic that they are left to suffer and struggle.

Having said all that, the game has some restricting factors that really make it unpleasant beyond the thematic elements:

* The RNG (random number generator) is a big component of the game. I tried this game the first time in 2018 and struggled to learn its mechanics. I never could get my protagonists to the end of the war, as is the goal of the game. I came back this year to try again, this time using a guide, and learned that RNG plays a huge part in success or failure. Sometimes you roll a safe place, sometimes a deadly place.
* Making a mistake is unforgivable and the roguelike component means all your hard work is lost. If you're sinking hours into a game and invested in your protagonists and get a bad RNG roll to a deadly location, you're often facing a game over screen
* The economy system is weird. There's wood everywhere but you can only carry four logs at a time. There's lots to pick up but you can never take what you need. You're always desperate for something. Every time you feel you're making progress, something goes wrong. I get that this is part of the story of the hopelessness of war, but it's frustrating as a core mechanic.

It feels to me like there's a thumbs up game here with a few tweaks to make it more suitable for a general audience, potentially even a handholding version for people who are learning how to play. As it sits, going in blind is a very difficult proposition and I feel like you have to really like roguelikes, survival games of managing minuscule resources, and be comfortable with brutal RNG in order to really give this game the endorsement that 94% of the people have given it so far. Given the flaws I see in it, I wouldn't recommend it to people who are not searching for those specific traits in a game.

This War of Mine : By Triple F

"This War of Mine" is a survival strategy game developed by 11 bit studios that takes an unflinching look at the civilian experience of war. Released in 2014, the game is set in the fictional city of Pogoren, which has been ravaged by conflict. Instead of focusing on soldiers or combat, "This War of Mine" tells the story of ordinary people struggling to survive amidst the devastation. By shifting perspective to the civilian experience, it offers a sobering, emotional, and thought-provoking gameplay experience that sets it apart from most war-themed games.

In "This War of Mine," players manage a group of civilians who must gather resources, build shelter, and make difficult moral choices to survive. Each day brings new challenges, as players balance the need for food, medicine, and warmth against the ever-present threat of violence. The game’s day-night cycle shapes the flow of gameplay; during the day, characters stay indoors to avoid snipers, and players can craft items, repair the shelter, and manage resources. At night, players send one survivor to scavenge for supplies in the dangerous city, a tense and risky process that adds an element of suspense and urgency. This balance between day and night activities creates a constant feeling of tension, as players must plan carefully to keep their group alive.

Resource management is central to "This War of Mine" and creates some of the game’s most challenging decisions. Food, medicine, and building materials are all scarce, and players are frequently forced to choose who receives limited resources and who goes without. As the days pass and supplies dwindle, these decisions become increasingly difficult, especially as characters suffer from hunger, illness, or depression. This resource scarcity is realistic and forces players to confront the harsh realities of survival in wartime. Each choice feels impactful, as mismanaging resources can lead to sickness, conflict, or even death within the group.

The moral complexity of "This War of Mine" is one of its most defining features. The game presents players with ethically challenging scenarios, such as choosing whether to steal food from vulnerable civilians or leave empty-handed. These moments highlight the desperation that comes with survival and make the game emotionally challenging in ways that few others are. Characters react to these decisions, experiencing guilt or relief depending on the choices players make. Watching a character sink into depression after an ethically questionable act reinforces the gravity of these decisions and adds an unsettling sense of realism, as players are constantly reminded that every action has consequences.

The visual design of "This War of Mine" emphasizes the bleakness of its setting, employing a hand-drawn, monochromatic art style that reflects the desolation of a city torn apart by war. Shadows and muted colors convey the oppressive atmosphere, while the detailed environments immerse players in the dire reality of the characters’ lives. Each location has a distinct look, from ruined apartment buildings to abandoned schools, all bearing signs of past lives disrupted by conflict. The visuals, paired with the ambient sound design, create a hauntingly immersive experience, enhancing the game’s themes of survival and loss.

Sound design in "This War of Mine" plays a critical role in setting the tone, with a minimalistic, somber soundtrack that underscores the game's melancholy themes. Environmental sounds, such as distant gunfire, footsteps, or the hum of radio static, serve as constant reminders of the surrounding danger. Characters respond audibly to their physical and emotional states, groaning in pain or muttering anxiously, which further humanizes them and deepens the emotional impact. The quiet yet tense audio design keeps players on edge, adding another layer to the game’s immersive and often distressing atmosphere.

On a final note, "This War of Mine" is a powerful, unorthodox take on the survival genre that challenges players not only to make tactical decisions but to confront the moral and emotional toll of war on civilians. Its emphasis on resource management, difficult moral choices, and haunting atmosphere create a deeply engaging experience that is as thought-provoking as it is challenging. By focusing on the civilian experience, the game offers a rarely seen perspective on war, making it a memorable and impactful experience for those willing to grapple with its tough themes. For players looking for a game that goes beyond traditional mechanics and explores the human cost of conflict, "This War of Mine" stands out as a poignant and unforgettable title.

I love this game.

The concept and world building is strong on the surface, but the game does not back it up. The gameplay loop is one of resource management and keeping track of what supplies are needed and what structures to build, which work well enough. And the pattern of what offenses/defenses occupy each of the different areas change with good variation. 

But the characters lack any real depth or memorability. Lines are often repeated several times within minutes amongst all or a majority of the inhabitants, and beyond some perks like extra bag space to scavenge for items, or less resources used for cooking, or bargaining bonuses while trading, there is no characteristic which make each person unique. The game even knows this by condensing their bio into one word descriptions so you can remember: Pregnant, good cook, old etc.

And there aren't that many characters so it feels lazy and ultimately there is no emotional connection when someone dies or gets killed. And at a surface level I can't see of any benefit to having a campaign playing without one of the characters that has 15 slots of inventory space in their backpack for scavenging.

It takes about one or two campaigns to understand what the best way to level up is and the more you play and learn how to game the system, the less connected the narrative becomes and I found myself just counting down the minutes to when I can go collect resources. 

I wish it was possible to have the characters contribute something beyond being a husk to carry stuff to the house. And that the visitors also had some variation beyond being the same trader or someone asking for help off-screen.

The controls are not something I ever grew to love - a basic system of clicking to select and pointing to areas for characters to navigate to. Often times I had accidentally selected the wrong character to go somewhere and it took too many clicks to try and get a simple action to be done. All issues that I think one would typically get used to after playing several times.

But I did not see a reason to stick through the grind. The characters always get sad, the day structure and rhythm is the same between playings, and the way to win is also roughly by approaching the structure upgrades in the same way.

It's not a bad game, but don't go into it expecting something that changes the way you think about war games. I wanted to give it more time for it to grow on me because maybe it would, but after playing for 20 in-game days a second time I had my scavenger killed because of what I felt was some type of misclick/navigation issue that meant my character was carrying a weapon off-screen and got killed.

It's brutal, human and pretty difficult. Even more difficult than Frostpunk, another game from 11 Bit Studios which inspired me to buy this one.

However, a lot of the difficulty disappears once you observe one simple mechanic:
[spoiler] When you only eat on the second day that you're 'very hungry', you can manage to eat only once in 3 days (5th day, 8th day, 11th day etc.) without negative side effects [/spoiler]

This War of Mine: A Brutal Journey into Survival
"I’m 6 hours in, and that’s a straight 6 hours."

That’s how I started my journey into This War of Mine. A game that promised a stark contrast to the usual fare of forgiving, shallow survival titles. Little did I know, I was about to embark on a harrowing tale of survival, where every decision, every action, would echo through the bleak landscape of war-torn city.

"At the beginning of my hours, I was hopeful and treated others I met with the same kindness I normally would."

The early days were filled with optimism. I shared my supplies, took in those in need, and built a semblance of a home. But as the days turned into weeks, the harsh realities of war crept in. But seriously this game is personally one of the most shocking experience I had with a video game. This game perfected the craft of conveying the feeling of despair one would have when they find themselves stuck in a battlefield not as a combatant but helpless regular civilians. 
The core system of this game revolves around the idea of "the price of survival". You will be constantly fighting in your mind about different choices in game that may turn out to be the difference of Life and death of you group. These choice ranges from easier ones such as what limited resource do you choose to bring home every night, to things that interrogates your morality such as do you steal medicine from a hospital for you dying friend. Aside from this core system about choices, this game is also brutal with most of the mechanics reinforcing how fragile the civilians you control were. Many of them are not physically fit, unable to fight or move around quietly, and often emotionally devastated. This is the games way of reminding you as a player that these people are just like us, ordinary people who find themselves stuck in that inescapable hell. They are not coldblooded soldiers that would not think twice before executing an order, but mere people who will feel guilty and demotivated under a brutal situation like this.
On my first play through of this game I was extremely frustrated by this mechanic about the emotional state of the characters since they cry about almost every thing and beat themselves up for problems that has nothing to do with them. This is extremely frustrating for me as a player as this state of depression comes with a string of debuff that punishes me as a player for doing the right thing for the survival of the crew. At some point I even thought that why wouldn't the devs must create these characters instead of making avatars of the player which would create even better immersion and make the gameplay much smoother. However, I eventually realized that this mechanic is essential for the game to convey how truly hopeless one would feel when they find themselves in a situation like this. For the characters we control, the situation we saw in game is their reality and despite how ridiculous the situation seems, it still wouldn't turn people into a cold-blooded machine that would do anything for survival. Deep down these characters know what they do (the commands you give them) is for the purpose of ultimate survival, but this does nothing to soothe the emotional trauma they are going through. They do not have the luxury of calmness we as a player enjoy sitting in front of a computer as to us, this is merely a situation that wouldn't even matter as soon as we switch of the game. This is also why this game would not work if the characters we control are made as an avatar of the player. the weight of every decision will be lost as the consequence feels a lot less. A great example to my point is the act of killing in this game. If we control a character to kill for whatever reasons, the character we control will have to live the rest of his life with this murder whether it is justified or not whilst we as player could do it without feeling the emotional weight. 
I would also like to mention the aesthetics of this game is spot on in making you as the player feel depressed and helpless. The monotone color scheme takes away the flashiness about war that many other modern media tells us. This monotone color scheme is also contrasted with light sources in game which often emits bright red color that give the player the feeling of danger and unease. When a human being is exposed to excessive sensation towards any of his or her five senses, these sense will go numb as a mechanism to protect the persons mind and keep their sanity. The things that the player sees on screen is exactly how the characters see the world before them as their sense to colors become dull as "safe" and "danger" is the only information visual information that the characters need. The environment is also presented as a sort of dulled painting or photo where there is sense of uncertainty, which stems from the characters self-protecting mechanism towards the brutal memory of war. Now instead of describing war as a bright and exciting playground, war is presented as a fuzzy mess that is nothing but hell. As a character from the game, there is nothing you would like to remember from this experience  regardless of how much do you want to forget it. 
The devs nailed all of these elements and created an absolutely phenomenal atmosphere, which made this game and unforgettable experience for me.

This game hits all the right spots for me.
1. Very replayable. While the outcome will roughly be the same the details will end the story with a spectrum of variety due to many variables. Makes you want to play it over and over to see how well you can manage with different survivors and conditions.
2. Intelligent story telling. It is very stingy with the amount of things it will allow you to dictate at the start. It strongly encourages you to take a random mess and overcome a harsh situation. Or not. Has a bit of Rim World, but with way more heart breaking penalties for misfortune or bad decisions. There are no do overs.
This can be frustrating to some players, but I'm the type that eats this style up.
3. Beauty. It's a very nice looking game. Very well animated. They even took the time to make someone playing a song on the guitar move their hands on the fret board and strum to the actual song. Many little authentic details everywhere help you forget these are just pixels and not people.
4. Challenging. The devs had the guts to rip yours out. They took big chances infuriating their market by enforcing permanent outcomes while at the same time encouraging you to invest in a story that can easily reach an unacceptable destination. I love games with the audacity to piss me off.
5. A very reasonably adult themed game. I was pleasantly suprised by the lack of bias social commentary. All forces are desperate and possibly dangerous. Including you. The people in your shelter depend on you to make the tough choices, while at the same time may be just as threatened emotionally by those actions which can be catastrophic. Much thought went into this dynamic.

Despite coming out in 2014, This War of Mine is not only one of my favorite survival games, but also one of my favorite games of all time. The setting places you in the middle of a war-torn Eastern European fictional city of Pogoren, but rather than controlling either of the combatants, you control a group of 1-4 civilians of which there are many to choose from, with varying specialties/vices, who are just trying to survive the day-to-day as their homes are destroyed around them. 

The replay value is always one of the first thing I mention when talking about this game. There are various scenarios that can happen during the day as you upgrade your shelter, from the trader coming by to offer supplies, to shady individuals with interesting propositions, to other survivors who need shelter, upon which letting them in adds them to your base, and much more. The amount of different levels to scavenge at during the night time part of the gameplay is even more impressive. They can be randomly selected or handpicked before you start a new game, and the different scenarios that could be happening at those scavenging locations give the game endless hours of replayability.
This War of Mine also brings ethics into question and forces you to make very difficult moral decisions sometimes, and some of them weigh heavier on different characters. There are genuinely some characters who are okay with doing anything to survive, including murder, while other characters may become sad and question their individual morals for even stealing from other survivors. This also attributes to the replay value of trying different survival tactics, since if you try to murder several people for supplies with emotionally weaker characters night after night, it can break them, leading them to acting dangerously unhinged and unpredictable.
Regardless of the lack of voice acting, you can still feel the general despair from the amazingly sorrowful soundtrack and the survivors' conversations/behaviors within your base, and you feel for the survivors in your shelter. This is especially true in the game's stories DLC, where you are given three narratives to follow as you play, which are very engaging despite all three stories having different end goals, besides surviving, of course.

TL;DR I wholeheartedly believe This War of Mine holds up to this day and is worth full price. That being said, as often as it goes on sale, it is without a doubt that I think it's a STEAL!

I first saw This War of Mine as a recommendation on Steam. I never heard about the game before and I didn't particularly like the screenshots, but I decided to buy it anyway since it was on huge discount.
This War of Mine is a strategy game about surviving the war in a fictional town of Pogoren, somewhere in Eastern Europe. You control a group of several people bunched together in one of the apartment block ruins scattered around the city. The military is waging war with the resistance and the whole city is completely cut off. Food and resources are hard to come by and most of the people you knew are gone, either fled the city or killed. People that meant something in the world before the war are reduced to begging and thieving.
The game basically has two distinctive parts: day and night. During the day, you'll work on crafting items and building your base. At night, you'll be scavenging around the city for equipment and materials. I have to say this dynamic works well, but there are a lot less things to do during the day. Sometimes, a neighbor will knock on your door around noon, asking for help or looking to trade items. On other days, your characters will mostly just sit around during the day, doing nothing. The daylight part of the game basically only includes crafting items, some of which you'll have to wait for couple of hours until they're finished. In practice, you'll start preparing your items in the morning and wait until afternoon when they're ready. There is an option for skipping the rest of the day, but unfortunately you cannot speed up time. So if you want to be efficient at crafting, you'll just have to wait until each day ends in its natural course. Needless to say, this is very annoying. At night, you'll be barging into peoples homes trying to scavenge something you can eat or use for crafting. Sometimes you'll run into unfriendly characters that you'll have to run or hide from. Of course, once you get access to weapons, you can also show them who's the boss. Combat is  clunky and you never know how it will turn out, so for the most part it's better to stick with hiding and stealing.
The game features over 10 campaigns with different characters, as well as a couple of story-driven scenarios. The objective in both is the same - to survive for 45 days, after which you are saved by the peacekeeping squads. I've played through several campaigns, and it pains me to say that all of them were completely the same. I got the same apartment, same things happened every time and I got the same ending. This appears to be a common thing with 11bit games, as I faced the same situation in one of their other games, Frostpunk (which is interestingly also a survival strategy game). There is a very limited number of items you can craft and you'll almost surely craft all of them in your first playthrough. So my point is - only buy the base game if possible. 11bit is one of those bastard studios that sells DLCs with no actual additional content, aiming only to squeeze you out of your money for nothing in return. That being said, the first playthrough was great for me and I had a lot of fun. It lasted about 10 hours, which is remarkably about the same amount of time this game is good for.

This War of Mine is an interesting game, but doesn't really offer much. If you like survival strategy games, I advise you to buy only the base game, and only on sale. Everything beyond that just isn't worth it.

This War of Mine is a simple point-and-click resource management game that in my opinion tries too hard at conveying a message instead of being an actually enjoyable game and unfortunately fails at both those tasks.

You play as a group of civilians struggling to survive in a war-torn city. Your goal is to scavenge for resources and upgrade your safehouse to keep everyone alive in these awful times. The gameplay loop gets boring pretty quick as all you really do is click icons and count resources. Click on the food icon, click on the upgrade icon, realise you need some extra scrap, travel to the next house over, click on the loot icon and so on. Other than the occasional NPC interaction this is all the game really has to offer. Even the combat is reduced to clicking on a fight icon. Because of this the gameplay feels more like a mobile game that had been ported to PC. Another issue is that this game is painfully slow, especially in the beginning when you don’t have the proper tools to do stuff. Often I found myself doing nothing and waiting for a progress bar to finish loading, again something I’d expect from a mobile game. 

As for the obvious message of “war is hell”, which This War of Mine puts incredible emphasis on, I found it rather incompetently delivered. While some elements like the derelict environment and radio transmissions got the point across decently, those were greatly undermined by the dull writing present everywhere else in the game. Constant text boxes popping up over my characters’ heads bluntly reminding me how upset they are, NPCs with cliche stories of sick family members and a general lack of subtlety. The worst part is the sadness/morality system which will make your entire crew, no matter how well fed and entertained, spiral into suicidal wrecks upon committing the slightest of microaggressions against another person. Despite living in an active warzone the tipping point for these grown men is stealing some junk from an armed mob or refusing to enter a sniper’s sightline to save someone. And it’s not just a minor negative stat, your survivors will refuse to do anything or straight up kill themselves if you abstain from being a hero for a few days.

Overall, while I can appreciate the devs trying to experiment with an original perspective, the implementation ultimately results in tedious and unfulfilling gameplay and subpar storytelling, for which I give this game a score of 3/10.

You will find things you can't really assign value to initially, since you don't know how much of it you will need, when it will become usable, and for some items, what its used for at all, until you upgrade certain tools.
Your first time in combat will also likely be weird and risky since its hard to be sure you are doing it right so its better to just try that out early so you don't risk wasting a run. 
The pacing of the game is also pretty slow since there is no fast forward button, which makes the trial and error of the early game experience costly in terms of IRL time.

That being said, once you figure out the crafting tree, and the basic mechanics, the game is pretty easy for a seasoned survival game player like myself, since the difficulty of the game is mostly in decision making.
I'd recommend this game to people who are new to the perma-death style survival genre.

The game basically has a cycle of craft + eat during day, occasionally trading, and sending someone to scavenge at night. The inventory capacity and stack sizes of the items are such that you will be spending the first few hours making repetitive trips to the same place night after night just slowing chipping away at the loot that is left there. Nothing different ever happens on these subsequent trips, you just go, fill your tiny pockets, and leave, and you do it all over again until the game decides you can't go there anymore "because war" and you need to go somewhere else, that somewhere else eventually being somewhere with hostile guys with guns who will try to kill you. So that's it, that's the game. The game makes no effort to judge you for your kind or cruel actions. If you make one of your guys knife an elderly couple to death he just says he's sad but nothing changes. I got to day 13 which took every bit of 2.5 hours and by the time I finally got gunned down by some rapist with an AK I was glad I had an excuse to stop playing. Losing a character when you only start with 3 is crippling because ideally you want to be able to rotate between guard/sleep/scavenge. The game is supposedly "about" the horrors of war as a civilian but really it is painfully ambivalent to your actions as a player. The only consequence that matters is failing the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ combat and getting a character killed. That is the only way you'll lose because everything else about the game is braindead simple.

Maybe the game is more enjoyable as a roleplay thing where you try to be a good person (and inevitably die lol) but I don't see the point. None of the moral decisions have emotional weight, nor meaningful consequences. Kill a sick dad and his son? +2 sad points +100000 loot. The game is positively sterile. I don't understand the hype, and I *really* don't understand the people with 100s of hours of playtime. 2.5h in and I was bored to tears. This game doesn't evoke any emotion because it has no characters. They are sims that may proclaim they ought to smoke more and kill less but they really don't seem to mind.

"This War of Mine," developed by 11 bit studios, is a harrowing survival game that puts you in control of a group of civilians trying to survive in a war-torn city. Unlike traditional war games, it focuses on the struggles and moral dilemmas faced by non-combatants.

The game features a unique day-night cycle where you manage your shelter, scavenge for supplies, and make difficult decisions that impact your group's survival. Its somber art style and haunting soundtrack add to the immersive and emotional experience.

Pros:

-Deeply emotional and impactful storytelling.
-Unique perspective on war and survival.
-Challenging resource management and moral choices.
-Atmospheric art style and soundtrack.

Cons:

-Can be emotionally draining.
-Some repetitive elements.

Overall, "This War of Mine" is a powerful and thought-provoking survival game that offers a unique and sobering perspective on the human cost of war. 9/10

With 8 hours of gameplay, here are my personal pros and cons for This War of Mine so far:

Pros:
- Soundtrack. The music has a somber tone. A combination of bittersweet and hopeless. Fitting.
- Art-style. The locations truly feel war-scarred, rough, and bleak. The menu overlay matches, too.
- Sense of progression. Felt special to get a knife for the first time, let alone a gun, later.
- Specialization. Each character had a thing they were good at, rewarding playing to their strengths.
- Radio. Fantastic world-building mechanism which went a long way to provide a story.
- Traders. Game has simple internal economy and traders hint how under/overpriced their stuff is.

Cons:
- Character movement. Clunky. Stairs are annoying to traverse. Turning around 180° is an ordeal.
- The combat. It's bad. Sometimes you assassinate as planned, other times you just instantly die.
- Saving. Needs to auto-save at home AND scavenge locations too, else death means replaying everything.

Overall, I think the game is good. If I knew what I knew now, I'd spend $10-15 to buy it again.

Whenever I come back to the game its always frustrating, though. The combat is so close to being good, but frequent bugs, inconsistent mechanics, and weird interactions mostly ruin it. This is almost acceptable for new players because the game really doesn't want you to play it as a Rambo simulator, but its immensely annoying for veteran players who are looking for some variety of gameplay.

Then there's the bugs. Saves fail, items disappear, characters get stuck, interactions don't work as intended, and on and on and on. Again, its not likely that a new player sees too many of these in their first run, but over time these things become painfully obnoxious. Speaking of saves, I've always wished that along with saving at the end of the night it also saved at the end of the daytime period. That would certainly mitigate a lot of the most annoying stuff.

(I was gifted this game by a friend so if you're reading this, thank you!) This War of Mine is a survival game. The controls themselves and basically everything is super simple to learn and use but surviving is still very very hard. Bandits and soldiers who aren't very friendly, wounds that can get worse, sickness especially when winter comes, lack of food and materials... Having to go out and scavenge each night maybe steal, maybe kill someone who wasn't even a threat to you just for a bit more food then your guys get depressed and the never ending downward spiral begins.

+The game looks, sounds nice and plays well. Nothing is too hard to understand and a mouse is all you need to play.
+Several different characters some run faster and some have more inventory slots so you can loot more stuff, tons of different locations to visit and try to loot from, they all have their own backstories and sometimes give their opinions on whatever is going on.
+Even though the gameplay loop is simple and everything in the game is super easy to understand and use its still very hard to survive. Just how much stuff you need and how little you have it always causes problems. Seeing a trader come to your door is like christmas! This combination of easy to play, hard to win is enjoyable. It does get a bit silly at times with just how much stuff you need just to build one single thing but if it was any other way that might make the game much easier which wouldn't be as fun.
+I originally thought there was no end and it was an endless game about survive for as long as you can and thats not true, the war eventually does end. There are different "stages" too like winter where it'll get much colder, your guys will be all sick but you can melt snow and make as much water as you want then if you have meat you can cook tons of food.

-Having to survive as civilians in a war zone is different, cool and fun. Unfortunately the soldiers don't do that much. Even though the entire environment looks like a war zone it doesn't feel like a war zone.

I've played frostpunk, it's a great resource management/strategy game, the player plays as the classic leader role. This war of mine though (dispite by the same dev team) is a similar type of game, but plays more from a perspective of an actual person in that situation. It's like a blend of RPG and strategy game and the game did that really well. For a matter of fact, I personally enjoyed the story part of this game more than the strategy part of the game.

Cons: The classic mode of the game consists of several scenarios with different characters and locations, even though some of them do stand out being more unique, the overall gaming experience are still very similar. It boils down to the key game loop of the game being a strategy game is quite repetitive. It's a very slow paced game and you have to be making guesses all the time. If you made a wrong choice, it will just set you back for another day in game time which means you do nothing but repetitive up keep. And I couldn't find a way to easily S/L in the game, it's all done automatically and you can only restart one day before. Unlike a traditional strategy game, you don't have many units to control, so a lot of the time you are just waiting on the character to finish what they are doing. There isn't as much strategy decisions you have to be constantly making either, there are strategies, but more like a few big ones to get on the right track or focus. As a result, I personally don't find the replay value of this game very high, definitely way lower than something like frostpunk. There is just not that many different strategies you could try in this game given the lack of resource. And to make the matter worse the slow paced repetitive gameplay doesn't help.

Pros: The game captured the war time atmosphere so well, even without an actual story or cut scene, the struggle is embedded in the gameplay, it's genious. The graphics is quite good especially considering how old the game is. It's like a 2.5D style so nothing fancy like AAA games, but I found it beautiful to look at and captures the warzone atmosphere nicely, maybe beautiful is the wrong word here. The story DLC for the game is highly recommended, I found them essential for the experience. This review will probably ends up being totally different if the story DLC didn't exist. The stories are so well written and told, I'm impressed by the way the tell stories in a platform-ish strategy game. They are the highlight of the game and I'd even say you can just play the stories and ignore the classic mode altogether. You will probably still get well over 10 hrs of gameplay. 

Overall, this game of mine with the story DLC is a must-try experience. It's more relevant than ever in today's time. It's really a civilian in warzone simulator disguised as a strategy game. If you are looking for a strategy game, this one is not for you. But for a gaming experience that captures the pain caused by war, this is probably the best that I've played. The cons in the game are more like design choices made by the dev team to put more emphasize on the experience of living with war going on. There are nuances and trail and errors in the gameplay. Just like our real life, nobody can guarantee what will happen if you made any choice, and there is no save and load in real life. The pace of the game is very slow. Just like real life, to scavenge in ashes or build a metal workshop with broken metals can not be easy and will surely take time. There are scenarios in the game that are just too hard and impossible to win. Just like our real life, a war is painful, and not everyone will survive.

P.S. Workshop and Mods are available for this game, so potentially the game could be modded to be a great strategy game, this review is just for the game as stock, and personally I feel the stock game communicates the message sent by the developers perfectly as is.

A resource managing strategy set in a country devastated by war. 

In This war of mine you control group of civilians who are trying to survive the war by any means necessary. 

The game is divided into day and night cycle. During day you are in your shelter, crafting, interacting with characters and npcs, and managing your resources. During night you can choose to stay in your shelter or go scavenging with one of your characters. You will have to choose what to bring back because your inventory is limited. Deciding if you need more crafting materials for your shelter, food for your starving people or weapon parts to craft weapons to defend against looters and soldiers, is the core part of the game.

During the game you will have to make hard choices, like giving a neighbour your medicine that will save their life or keeping it for later when you will need it yourself? Will you try to save another civilian when they are being attacked or staying quiet that you wont get hurt, possibly killed yourself? Every decision can make your game easier, your people happier, or go completely wrong and ending in lethaly wounded people who may get depressed and deciding that this life is not for them.

Overall, this is very well made game and experience that people should not miss.

This War Of Mine is a strategy/survival game which takes place in the fictional war-torn city of Pogoren.
You control a group of survivors, mostly everyday people with some exceptions, who are hiding in a shelter and the goal is to survive long enough for the war to end. You do so by scavenging for food, supplies and keeping the characters safe. I will further elaborate on this below in the Gameplay section. 

- Performance; Steam Deck: 
The game runs perfectly on any modern hardware. I've never had any crashes, frame dips or any technical issues whatsoever, even on my former PC many years ago, which is practically ancient by today's standards. There's even a port for iOS, so yeah, you get the idea.
Runs perfectly, out of the box on Valve's Steam Deck as well. You may need to adjust the right analog stick or the track pads to better simulate mouse movement for faster reactions during combat or time-sensitive base management, but 
other than that it's a smooth experience.

- Gameplay:
Before you begin, you are presented with the so-called scenarios. The game has like 15-20 of them. Each scenario has different characters with different skills, personalities and needs. The conditions are basically preset.

After picking a scenario, you start off at a shelter somewhere in the city, you meet the characters, you can check their backstories and start scavenging around the shelter for supplies. The gameplay is divided into two parts. During the day, you manage your shelter(build various tools, furniture, repair and upgrade the shelter, etc). The characters have moods, needs and traits, during the day you also have to maintain their moods, health, hunger and addictions(cigarettes, coffee; tied to their moods). You can build various things around the shelter, such as a workbench(for tools and base upgrades), metal workshop(for weapons and bullets), traps and vegetable gardens for food, etc.

Depending on the scenario(beginning, middle or towards the end), winter starts. Winter conditions increase the overall difficulty. You have to keep the shelter warm, some of the scavenging locations are blocked off due to the snow and the trader doesn't visit you as much as before. Also, since you'll be subjected to raids during the night, you might want to increase the shelter's defense.

You have a limited time to do the base management before the night begins. During the night, you can go to various locations, in order to scavenge for various supplies. Firstly, you choose which survivor to go scavenge, which one to sleep and which one to defend, since defending can decrease the chances of losing loot during raids.

The gameplay is a bit more different during the night, you have a combat option. Some characters are good combatants, so you should mostly use them if you decide to fight. The combat is not easy, especially at the beginning. If you want to face your enemies head-on, you need a firearm and armor, otherwise you're sending a survivor to the electric chair.
Stealth is the more viable option, if you have a crowbar or an axe, you can hide and take out enemies by surprise. It's not easy to master and you have to be very patient, because if you're spotted in an area with more than 1 enemy, you're basically dead.

You can also sneak around and loot without engaging in combat.

- Visuals: 
The game looks awesome, the visual style is very unique. It looks hand-drawn, gritty, sad, yet so comforting at the same time. Looks a bit like a graphic novel. Combined with some black and white photography, this contributes to a solid atmosphere. Just by looking at the shelter, you feel comfortable and safe. Just by looking at the pictures of the characters, you sympathize with them. The rest of the locations look bleak, inhospitable, dangerous and depressing, just as they should in a game with this setting. Honestly, the atmosphere alone make this one of my comfort games.

- Audio:
Another W. Audio quality is very high, do not play without headphones. The in-game sounds are clean, realistic and satisfying. Gun sounds are the highlight.
The soundtrack is just as good as it is fitting for the game's setting. Created by Piotr Musiał and Grzegorz Mazur. 
These guys knocked it out of the park. I find myself listening to certain songs on Youtube every now and then. Some people even record their own versions of the soundtrack. Game wouldn't be the same without it.

Audio is also important in gameplay. When you're scavenging during the night, you have to be careful with how much noise you make, otherwise the enemies will head your way to investigate the noise.

- Story:
Besides This War Of Mine Stories(more on that below), the base game does not have a story in the traditional sense.
Characters have backstories, each location has some kind of environmental storytelling, but there is no scripted story. Your actions, choices and events you experience are the story. You get a rundown at the end of each scenario and based on your decisions, the characters may or may not get a good outcome.

The Good:

- Atmosphere, visuals, audio. One of the most immersive games out there. One of a kind experience.

- Addicting and complex gameplay.

- Decent learning curve. Even after mastering the core gameplay mechanics, there are still many challenges.

- Replayability. Besides having 15-20 different scenarios, you can create a custom one and make it either easier for yourself or test your abilities. I already have like a 100 hours and I'm sure I'll do a 100 more in the future. 

- No handholding. Not everyone will like this, but the game counts on you experimenting, failing and dying, so that you can learn. You don't really know the outcome of a certain situation until you see for yourself.

The Bad:

- Sometimes you will get bad RNG, most specifically which scavenging locations are available. This can prove to be a challenge for the experienced player, but may often lead to frustration.

-Certain characters are not balanced very well. Some are very overpowered, while others are useless and a liability. I guess that may be intentional but sometimes it's just cheap. 

- My biggest complaint with the game is that there are certain scavenging locations, from which once you clear out of the enemies, you will get so many materials, guns, bullets, meds and food that it instantly breaks the game. You achieve endgame overnight and you will never have to worry about anything anymore until the ceasefire. People who have played will know which ones I'm referring to. Yes, this requires mastering the combat. Yes, this requires patience and game knowledge, but it should have been better balanced, at least the amount of bullets. Being able to fully progress feels very nice and rewarding towards the end of the game, but may break the experience during early game.

- Additional content (This War Of Mine Stories): 
The game also features 3 story scenarios, in the form of DLCs. 
Everything written above mostly applies here, with a few exceptions. For starters, they are a lot more story-driven. I really liked the storylines, I cared about the characters and there were some really heartbreaking moments. 

The stories also feature new characters, locations, game mechanics, choices and multiple endings.
The only complaint I can think of is that they're fairly linear in terms of gameplay. Almost always you have to play in a certain way in order to progress or you fail and have to restart.

Conclusion:
I love this game, it's an easy recommend from me and I find myself coming back to play a scenario or two every once in a while. If you can overcome the initial difficulty-related challenges until you learn how to play, you will keep coming back for more. I know that the devs are busy with Frostpunk 2 and The Alters, but I hope that eventually they'll roll out a sequel to this amazing game.

I've never quite liked wartime survival games. Was I sceptical, unaware or merely disinterested? Maybe. I always found it hard to kind of relate to characters in such milieu. After all, isn't it easier to put on the image of a hero, of a warrior, rather than of a haggard, starving civilian with a shivering, fading light of hope in his eyes?

I always loved the style of the game, the art - everything. With zero Rambos at your command, the characters seemed real but there was something too offputting for me. Impact of the events, morale issues, reactions... That aura of despair accompanied by the game's OST. It was just too disturbing for my liking.

However, my perception has changed. A war broke out in my country a couple years ago, which, I must admit, greatly impacted my sanity. It has only worsened after I've visited an actual warzone myself, lived under the artillery shelling for a couple weeks and has seen a portion of other in-game stuff IRL. I was afraid to launch this game after. Thought it might trigger newly acquired PTSD or just reduce me to tears.

But it actually went the other way around. Much to my surprise, I was able to find solace and consolation in this game. It compels you to go through hardships no matter what you're trying to do. Tries to mock your moral calculus. Duress you into something you don't want to do. But, startlingly, that's not negative. It's very soothing in fact. I adore it.

A dark, ruthless, and beautiful survival game. A game you won’t find anywhere else because it tells the story of ordinary civilians who must face the grim reality of a city ravaged by armed conflict.

[h1] [b] People with a Story and Their Traits. Survival Problems [/b] [/h1]

What I really like is the portrayal of war, which perfectly ties in with the game mechanics. We can get to know our characters a bit by reading their short and unique stories. One person’s wife is missing, another wants to find their grandfather, or an orphaned child is just looking for shelter. Each person specializes in something different, like running fast, making them perfect for resource gathering expeditions, being a good cook, which makes cooking meals more efficient, or being skilled in carpentry, which uses fewer materials for construction. Good management of people, day and night time, and our shelter is key to survival. Things like medicine, food, water, or ammunition will be scarce, and pretty much everything we can pick up will find its use. We’ll build beds for our group out of wood, create a stove from electrical parts to cook warm meals, and cigarettes, jewelry, and alcohol will be useful for bartering with traders. Other tired survivors can show up. We can help them by sending someone from our group to assist them, or share supplies. However, we won’t always have the chance to act altruistically, as we may need certain resources ourselves or one of us might not be physically able to go anywhere, either from exhaustion or injuries. I’ll also note that the game is not easy. It takes some time to learn how to efficiently use our resources or prioritize the most important ones we bring back after a night expedition. Once we master it, there’s a sense of satisfaction with each day we survive.

[h1] [b] Realism and the Consequences of Our Decisions [/b] [/h1]

This War of Mine is realistic, and you can really feel it. Every decision we make will eventually matter, depending on how we act - whether we think only of ourselves, steal the last possessions of others, or even go as far as to kill an innocent person. We have a free hand in how we gather the resources needed to survive, and the rest is a matter of our conscience. If we do commit murder, our companions will take note, which will affect their mood negatively, and the same happens if we help others - they’ll be happy. However, the worst situation is when one of our own dies. Aside from the obvious change in mood, our chances of survival will drastically decrease, so we really need to play carefully. As for more realistic aspects, we should also note that during the day, we can't stick our heads out. Hostile troops are particularly active then, andwe need to spend that time in our shelter. Only at night do we send one of our group members to explore nearby areas in search of useful items. However, we still need to watch out for obstacles like snipers or bandits.

[h1] [b] The Story [/b] [/h1]

The game offers several interesting and intriguing stories of many people. The endings vary and depend on our decisions, and some can really make us pause for a few minutes to think. As for the free play mode, we need to survive for about 42 days until our military comes to rescue us.

[h1] [b] The Atmosphere Does Its Job [/b] [/h1]

The graphics set a dark and heavy atmosphere. It fits perfectly into the war-torn environment. There is no such thing as color or brightness here. It gives a sense that luck or hope doesn’t exist, and the only thing that can save us is ourselves. The melancholic, unsettling, and sometimes uplifting soundtrack only reinforces this feeling.

[h1] [b] A Few Words from Me [/b] [/h1]

This War of Mine is not just a game that’s fun to play: it also opens your eyes to what ordinary people have to face in order to survive during wartime. Remember, you don’t have to kill anyone here. You can help every person you encounter and take in the lost souls you meet, but the most important thing is to survive. How far will you go to achieve this?

They fight for their lives by working together to defend their home, scavenging through debris for supplies, pooling their resources to fulfill each other's needs, and utilizing their knowledge to find solutions.

Gathering food and other items through looting is crucial, at least until you achieve self-sustainability. A stealthy approach yields better results in looting than direct combat, and not enough games do that. Decisions matter, so prioritize necessities and resource shortages, manage individuals' time, and make moral decisions, including handling emotional matters.

This is one of the few games where I found myself taking written notes about things like the type of "key" needed for a looter's house, type of aggression during attacks, trade opportunities, specific uncommon items required later on that I couldn't carry, and so forth which really added to the problem solving experience of it.

This is one of those games in my steam library that I've played a few hours of, got distracted by another shiny game, and just never looked back. Every time I sift through my library I see this game, have a moment of "oh, that was so much fun! I love that game," before scrolling on to the next one. If it wasn't sitting in my library I would probably never think about it.

It's a great story, the mechanics/game-play were unique to me at the time, and the available choices really make you stop and think. There's no going back, there's no obviously correct answer, only the brutal reality of futile attempts at survival. 

Personally though, it gets old after a minute. The decisions begin to feel like chores, as apathy grows in place of empathy. It's like choosing between a firing squad or a guillotine, either way you're getting put down. Eventually the mechanics lost their sparkle, since it's all novelty and little substance. 

I still like the game, and if I could play it for the first time over I would. There's just not a whole lot of replay value after a while, if I do pick up the game and play it again it'll likely just be for earning achievements. 

Overall, it is a great experience for getting a glimpse into what living in a war torn area might be like, and I'd recommend it to everybody the same way I'd recommend looking at the Starry Night or reading Watership Down. However, I'd also recommend waiting for it to go on sale, as it is an absolute steal at lower prices, and if you tend to get bored of repetitive games you'll still get a good value for it.

In the realm of video games, war has often been portrayed through the lens of heroic soldiers and epic battles. However, This War of Mine offers a starkly different perspective, placing players in the shoes of civilians struggling to survive amidst the chaos of a besieged city. The game is a captivating and emotionally resonant experience that challenges players to make difficult moral decisions in the face of unimaginable hardship.

A Gripping Narrative

This War of Mine is set in an unnamed city ravaged by war. Players take control of a group of civilians who have sought refuge in a dilapidated apartment building. The game unfolds in a day-night cycle, with each day dedicated to scavenging for supplies, crafting tools, and tending to the needs of the group.

The narrative of This War of Mine is told through a series of vignettes that focus on the individual stories of the characters. These vignettes reveal the deep psychological impact of war on civilians, as they grapple with grief, loss, and the constant threat of violence.

Moral Dilemmas and Tough Choices

At the heart of This War of Mine is the constant struggle for survival. Players must make difficult decisions about how to allocate scarce resources, such as food, medicine, and sleep. These decisions often have moral consequences, as players may have to choose between the well-being of their group and the ethical implications of their actions.

For example, players may find themselves in a situation where they must steal food from another group of civilians, or engage in dangerous scavenging missions that put the lives of their own people at risk. These tough choices add a layer of complexity and emotional depth to the game, forcing players to confront the ethical dilemmas inherent in war.

A Visually Stunning and Atmospheric Experience

The visual style of This War of Mine is intentionally muted and bleak, reflecting the harsh realities of the setting. The game's art direction masterfully conveys the desolation and despair of the war-torn city, while still managing to create moments of beauty and hope.

The sound design is equally impressive, with ambient noises and evocative music creating a palpable sense of tension and anxiety. The game's soundtrack is particularly noteworthy, as it features haunting melodies that perfectly capture the emotional turmoil of the characters.

A Must-Play for Fans of Thought-Provoking Games

This War of Mine is a powerful and thought-provoking game that offers a unique and insightful perspective on the human experience of war. The game's engaging gameplay, captivating narrative, and stunning visuals combine to create an unforgettable experience that will stay with players long after they have finished playing.

Overall, This War of Mine is a must-play for fans of thought-provoking games that challenge players to confront the complexities of war and the human condition.

Pros:

Gripping narrative with deep character development
Moral dilemmas and tough choices that add depth to the gameplay
Visually stunning and atmospheric art direction
Haunting and evocative soundtrack
Thought-provoking exploration of the human experience of war

Cons:

Can be emotionally taxing at times
Some may find the gameplay too slow and methodical
The game's open-ended nature may leave some players feeling frustrated or unfulfilled

Overall Rating: 5 out of 5 stars

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

So, the point overall of this game is to really drive home the difficulty of certain choices, and thematically with it's war-torn setting, I do think it really nails this concept. But I would argue that sometimes a player just...really needs a win, and this game just does not lend itself to success at all. It gets tiresome after awhile of working your ass off to keep people alive and semi-happy, and running into yet another random occurrence that throws that effort down the drain. It reaches a point where I would say it ruins the replay-ability of the game. If I know that at the end of the day no matter how careful I am or what choices I make that the outcome is going to be failure, then I personally find that a turn-off. It really is just one bad thing after the other. I get that futility is supposed to be the point in a way, which is why, again, it's still worth playing. Well, once at least. I guess in the end I think there needed to be a better solution to some of the outcomes or at least, a way to dig yourself out of the trouble you are in. 

I'm not sure what exactly the solution for this would entail, to be honest, because the theme of the game really is futility and tough choices. Because of that, would a lower difficulty setting that reduces certain encounters or slightly increases item availability solve this? Or would introducing something like that kind of ruin the point (as in...people in real war torn environments don't get to lower the difficulty setting)? I guess we can't say.

I'd argue that there probably needs to be a balance between 'making your point' and 'remembering that this is a game'.  I think the art, music and writing already do an amazing job at delivering the theme, and I just wish a few of the scenario outcomes lent themselves to making me want to come back and do it again and relive the story, or try out different things. As it stands, every time I think about re-downloading this, I remember how pointless it is and then proceed to not. I get the whole 'making it as real as possible' approach they went for, but I'd personally really love an ending where human resilience despite hardship is an option. Because like, that happens in real life too sometimes.
