[h1] THIS WAR OF MINE REVIEW [/h1]

[b]This War of Mine is a survival-themed strategy game where we control survivors inside the shelter. The setting is a besieged city (fictional of course) of Pogoren, Graznavia. The main theme is to stay alive and survive until ceasefire (which in this case is the endgame).

During my first couple of hours and days playing through the game, I have no idea what to do and my longest days of survival is just 5-10 days since they all died in different circumstances, such as survivors being starving, depressed, killed during scavenging, left the shelter and even committed suicides. It took a while for me to get used to the mechanics and what your job as a caretaker for this survivors let's say.

THE GENERAL CONTEXT:[/b]

- There are different types of characters with different quirks and abilities that can be an advantage in your daily playthrough. It can be seen via clicking their biography or just in top of their names [i](Ex. Katia = Bargaining Skills, Pavle = Fast Runner, Bruno = Good Cook, etc.).[/i]

- Each characters have general character states, we call them [b]Moods, Sleep, Wounds/Injuries and Hunger[/b] but each characters have unique [b]Sympathy Levels.[/b] Characters that you play varies degree of Sympathy [i](ranging from Lowest to Highest).[/i] Characters also have [b]Addictions[/b] as their way of coping during the war. These mechanics affects the characters' morale, overall gameplay and also affects the endings.

- You can build [b]Workshops[/b] and [b]Household Items[/b] and there are plenty of them and they cost [b]Materials, Parts and Components[/b]. They are necessary since characters have their needs and how you provide it to them also affects their morale and daily activities.

- There are plenty of locations to visit or interact that have [b]Food, Weapons, Medicines, Materials, Parts and Components[/b] but take note of their overviews. These overviews are following; [b]The Amount of Loot, Their Potentials and Their Danger Levels[/b]. It's up to you how to navigate the area and your methods on how to deal with them.

- There are certain events that will affect your gameplay. The canon events include [b]Normal Days, Outbreak of Crimes and Winter Season/ Snow.[/b] There are also certain events such as [b]Shortages, Increased Fighting, Band Of Looters, Area Cut-off, Bombings, etc.[/b] It can be monitored by having a [b]Radio[/b] in your shelter since it provides updates depending on the radio stations and their broadcasts.

- There will be visitors and neighbors that will come to your shelter. They either [b]Ask for Something (Help, Favor, Food, Medicine), Offer a Deal, Share Food, Trade, and etc[/b]. The way you interact with them will also affect the morale and status of your characters. Combine all those mechanics and there you have it, you can come up with ideas on how to manage your shelter to survive the war.

[b]MY THOUGHTS:[/b]

It's quite tricky at first like I said earlier. I didn't knew about those certain mechanics and factors. It's like diving into the pool and you don't know how to swim. I failed a lot of playthroughs and seen my characters die like a human being on war, it does get me when some characters have concerns and are in pain or something troubling them. You can metaphorically say that you're the guardian and you're overseeing people during the war. You get frustrated, angry, quite shocked and disappointed when something happens to your character.

The more you play, the more you gain. Not only seeing your characters progress in longer days but you tend to understand the current situation they're in. You can also understand the character's character. You make better judgement and decisions and cope up with strategies and methods how to deal with the current situation and having plans throughout towards the endgame.

I assume This War of Mine is inspired by the Yugoslav civil wars in the 1990s, and it delivers a compelling narrative ride befitting that heavy inspiration. They chose the quote: "In modern war, you will die like a dog for no good reason" in the splash screen, which set the tone quite grim from the outset, but fortunately it doesn't descend into some sort of over the top emotionally manipulative nonsense. It delivers a nice mix of highs and lows and as a result keeps you pretty invested for the duration of your playthrough, free of any invitations toward ironic detachment that might be typical for a game that went too far taking itself too seriously.

In terms of game play it's very much of a base building type except what you're building up is not a big settlement or city but just an ordinary safe house of sorts within a residential building, filled with plucky characters in the midst of a devastating conflict. You send people out to forage for supplies hoping they return, occasionally meet external characters at the door to make a tough decision or two and for the most part experience a slice of the sort of indoor suburban claustrophobia that was daily life for millions of people sometimes for years at a time throughout various 20th century conflicts from Spain to WW2 to Yugoslavia. Over time you build up a little stability and become more capable of caring for your basic needs, and the game a primal satisfaction in building a sense of security in place of chaos.

If you are a power gamer, you might have trouble accepting the fact you have to accept trade offs in This War of Mine. I think that was a deliberate design choice. You probably can't take on that military-base single-handed: you'll likely just die. If you think you'll survive by making friends with everyone and playing the nice guy, the game does a good job illustrating how weakness can and will be taken advantage of during a crisis. Importantly, however, the game offers up just enough of the best of humanity that playing the total sociopath can also land you in trouble before too long. In hard times you have to take kindness where you can get it while still avoiding getting taken advantage of and I think it's a great effort that the devs captured the reality of that nuance to the social human experience during a crisis. 

What I'm trying to say here is that it captures the atmosphere of its subject matter in a fairly value free way (well, relatively speaking anyway) insofar as that upstanding ethics, dubious ethics and sociopathy are all rewarded and punished in their own way at different times such that no strong value judgement is hitting you in the face constantly via the gameplay itself. This variability to what sort of ethical strategy is value optimal does an excellent job of capturing the capricious reality of civilian life during the tragedy of armed conflict. The multidimensional nature of life and the social human experience is characterised well and I think that was necessary to make an experience like this engaging and authentic. 

I must admit I went into this title with fairly low expectations, but I was pleasantly surprised by how deftly its subject matter was handled. [h1]Overview[/h1]
This game is one game that show you a tiny portions of how country at wars to civilians feels like. Sadness, depression, hopeless, shame, tense, etc. But if you think this game is base management game like fallout shelter, sheltered, or anything similar, you're completely wrong. This game more like action survival game. You only control these max 4 characters and they can't function autonomously except sick. So more characters, more difficult lol.
[h1]Pros[/h1]
+ The graphics wan't bad, and i liked the B & W stile of it for immersion into every dark things i mentioned in Overview
+ The gameplay is smooth and responsive, no overused animations wasting time and awkward combat
+ The surviving winter is hard but not impossible as long as you unlock hatchet quickly
+ Weapons also quickly not that scarce as long as you can toy with AI that wielding guns in stealth and having saw blades
+ The story missions can be more harder than regular mission lol since you follow events that forced you to stay at base or skipping few hours (Especially 3rd episodes)
[h1]Cons[/h1]
- Food in this game is really punishing, they grow at long time, you can only harvest meat with rat trap on base and there is a limit to it to eventualy run out. And in stove you can mostly produce 2 foods, no options to increase it to 4 for 4 players. Wasting day time and bcs there's no autonomy, it's really hard to maintain 4 player that basically 1-2 of them had a moment doing nothing. Also canned food even you dont need to cook it can't function as meat or into helping ingredients to make food. Kinda nonsensical lol. Plus why require vegetable and meat to make 2 portion? Not just 2 meat or 2 vegetable only?
- The lack of autonomy making the 3rd story mission hardest for me since the museum large AF, and one male characters never really go to well and always stay sick, wasting drugs/medicines.
- The quest in 3rd episode is robbing your firewood that essentials in early missions, but if you interact with them over and over is really annoying.
- Stacking of items in this game is your main enemy, you can only stack 2 woods and it occupy most of your inventory, making you keep repeatedly going over and over just to gather woods wasting nights that you only used barely 2 hours of it
- Explorations only at night and it was short AF. Include the punishing limit of stacking, i tend to get bored visiting same place over and over.
- Melee weapons except knife is your tools, and because of its ultra fast durability wear down. Sometimes its hard to fight enemies in early game. Until you found gun and understand bullet management. So stealth is highly encouraged.
- I know this might be sensitive, but why "balkan country devs" economy always so unfair lol!! Is that dire there to actually profit items in game? This is my personal issues anyway. This game remind me so much to Withcer economy. Merchant tent to rob you anyway.
- The last thing is theres no interim save, if you regret killing NPC, crafting/upgrading workbench or placing counters in room. You must repeat that day and if you do so much thing at that day, you basically f*cked.
- Sadly the mod community somehow died out in 2020 while the game keep updated in 2022, many mods get outdated to helping you around these problems.
[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is a good survival sidescroller adventure game, but after 10 hours playing it, you keep seeing the same places and scenario over and over and it tend to get you sick of it lol. So after completing one or two take a break. Maybe it freshen again later. Recommended? It's a good game but some things too punishing and unrealistic just to make our life harder lol,
I play it casually, it is hard to say that I enjoy it but it is definitely challenging and you will be surprised with the chapter conclusions. In my personal opinion it is worth the money.

This is a haunting game about civilians living through a besieged, war-torn city. There are various pressures to survive: getting enough food, medicine or bandages, patching up the house, heating up the house in winter. While this is a struggle, there are various avenues to the player -- the nightly scavenge to various locations around the house, trading materials with visitors, even getting some help from friendly neighbours. There are moral dilemmas about whether to steal, commit violence (whether against thugs or other civilians), who to feed or give medical help to, whether to help your neighbours. There are varied characters with their own special abilities, quirks and backstories - all of which help to flesh out the story of what is happening in the city. The game is about surviving, but it is also about the experience you are creating for your characters - including the moral trauma that they would have with them post-war. 

There are several fantastic expansions -- including the children pack, adding children to take care of, enabling the player to see the impact of war through children's eyes. The story packs are also varied and great, including a father searching for their child, a couple maintaining radio news, and a museum curator trying to protect treasures. 

I commend the game for the experience (have played many times across multiple platforms), showing the experience of war from civilians and common people, and supporting real-world charities (such as War Child).

This game makes you feel empathy for people in extreme situations who have to make some hard decisions. These decisions come up naturally in this game, with resources in safe places dwindling and more problems coming up.

Will you risk one of your own to scavenge for resources in a risky place? Will you rob helpless people to save your own? Will you let someone new join your group? Will you invest in expensive medicine if that knew someone got sick? or will you let them die to feed your original group? 

This game shows how games can be better tools for empathy than any other media in the right hands. It is you making those decisions naturally, without immersion-breaking boxes of text letting you know you are making a decision that might have consequences or text saying a character will remember something you did.

Fathers Promise 7/10

Fading Timbers 9.5/10

So the reason I wanna review this game is that there are no tutorials in the game. And its very important to know some things:

- It can be very frustrating when you dont understand what is going on in the beginning but just keep at it for 2-3 hours and you get the hang of it. There are a few easy short YouTube tutorials by helpful people to help you out in case it's still confusing.
- The main game doesn't really have a story. Its just a 'survive till the ceasefire' kind of run. If you want a proper story, play the dlcs.
- There is sometimes confusing dialogue like you'd be standing in front of a locked cabinet or door and your character would say 'glad I have the tool for this' but you wont actually have it. - The combat is most difficult to understand. Its best to see some YouTube videos for this. I found it best to kill by hiding one of the hiding places and waiting till the enemy walks past and icon shows up for you to press click or RT.
- Sometimes it gets very frustrating when you're just walking somewhere you didn't know will trigger people to become hostile and they'll kill you instantly. Which will waste your whole run. Well these are things I found that people needed to know. Other than that its a pretty addicting game. Hope you all enjoy it.

Alright, I was really on the fence about whether this game was worth it or not. Don't get me wrong, I had a lot of fun while it lasted and had a couple sleepless nights binging it. The thing is, 43 hours in, you get a pretty good picture of just about everything this game has to offer. I'm kind of left with a feeling of "that's it?" right now. There's more glaring fundamental issues from a game design perspective though that I wanna explain before I leave it at "not worth it".

1. Combat is reallly really bad. The main caveat about combat is how unresponsive the characters are to your commands. It's really janky trying to control your character, it's only mouse clicks and timing. The problem, especially for new players is apart from the fact there's no tutorial, there's no clear indication of when someone strikes or how long it will take to strike. 50% of your combat encounters will look like this:
- You have melee weapon, 
- enemy with weapon has back turned to you,
- you sneak up on enemy and strike him,
- his friends in the other room may or may not get alerted,
- enemy turns around,
- you spam strike on enemy and awkwardly shamble forward instead of striking him to get within strike distance
- you either get hit or you actually hit him before he does, it's never telegraphed, never in your control and neither is it intuitive,
- you can get stunlocked as a result and then die or blasted in the face and die anyway

Doesn't matter if you're a long time player, combat will forever be a janky system that can't be learned or mastered, You can cheese combat a bit by abusing AI behaviour (camping ladders, camping hiding places for ambushing etc.) but cheesing in almost any context and in any game is never fun. It's mainly done to circumvent grind or ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game design to get ahead in the game. You're going to savescum days many times just so you can retry a scavenging run again most likely. Savescumming? Yes, you heard right!

2. There's savescumming in this game. It happens often where in hardcore mode games, the automatic save system can be abused because it makes a checkpoint at an earlier point in time before a fight or a risky opportunity takes place and you can revert to that checkpoint if you quit the game. Dwarf Fortress, Slay the Spire, Caves of Qud, Neo Scavenger, to name a few games, are hardcore permadeath games with that flaw. My opinion on this is you either make the game save the world state at the moment you quit the game instead or just introduce a traditional manual saving system like in Skyrim. This in between save mechanic though is the worst of both worlds: it makes people who are either way going to cheat just go through the slog of repeating a day over and over again to get a new survivor to appear, to get a different outcome from a bandit raid or to just restart a scavenging run. I should also mention that you can Ctrl Alt Del the moment you see your character die during a scav run to just close the game and retry. This makes the game lose a giant portion of its intensity and grit, which is the consequence of choice. If you have the ability to cheat to get ahead, you probably will.

3. Last thing I want to expand on which I mentioned in the previous point. The game is a slog for the most part because of how time passes during day time at your base. You don't have much to do in your base in general apart from some menial tasks, or building things, but even then, you're only limited by the resources you have on hand to spend time crafting or eating. It's really boring and uninteresting having to spend time at your base. Your bases are always ugly, way too big to utilize the entire space anyway, are really annoying to navigate (especially because of ladders and ledge climbs) and you'll probably not want to even see your survivors living day to day. Whoever thought it was a good idea to have the daytime portion of the game interactable like it is now is; an idiot. It's another really bad design decision. It's a chore tbh. It's a real chore to see your surviors shuffle to their tasks, food, etc, waiting for crops to grow, water to get filtered and having to wait for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ timer to tick down from 6 A.M. to 8 P.M. This whole thing could have been replaced with a daily overlay action report where you get to choose actions to take on with 14 hours allotted time associated with each action (crafting, eating, sleeping etc), having the trader, survivors or neighbors show up on the daily report screen instead of waiting for them IRL to show up and for your survivors to walk to the door to talk to them. It really doesn't offer much to have the system the way it is now, it really isn't interesting because your survivors don't do many idle actions or interact with each other whatsoever. 

If you still wanna scratch the itch that TWOM gives you without the abuse, there's a really similar survival game called Rebuild 2. It's a flash game on Newgrounds (which means it's free cause it's a browser game) and I highly recommend it because it actually addresses all of the points I mentioned above:

1. Daily action report and allotted time for actions making it so much faster and easier to control what you're going to do from the beginning of the day

2. No save scumming. You don't get a different event for a day if you close the game and start again. Because it's implemented as a daily action overlay menu system, it just saves the game at the beginning of the day you left off BUT, the rng results which are the events of your actions (scavenging, clearing area, reclaiming area, defending fort) happen at the end of the next day and it's predetermined... so you can't change your choices

3. Combat is a predetermined event which happens at the end of the day defending the fort (much like raids in TWOM) based on some number factors and not implemented like the half assed combat system seen in TWOM

TL;DR: This game doesn't have in depth mechanics, it's really shallow with scripted areas and locations that can be memorized and repeated efficiently each time. Skill curve is really low, you'll master it too fast, it's not a fun kind of challenge but more annoying. This game is extremely unique, and extremely accessible compared to any genre it's related to. You will find no better take on the idea of being in a tense survival situation and having to make tough choices. This is a slow burn game - it isn't action-packed, and it's not about fighting, sacrificing, or painstakingly managing a base stressfully. It's about keeping your people alive, pure and simple.

Most importantly, every time something bad happens in the game, it is [b]your fault.[/b] Many games attempt to force you to adapt to incoming conditions in a way that feels oppressive. In this game, any difficulty you face (winter, crime uprising, etc) can be dealt with, WITHOUT risking the loss of your people, so long as you make the right choices and take it seriously. Your survivors feel like tough human beings, they do not stay injured for half a playthrough from a single bullet wound, they can recover from their tragedies. If your base is a well oiled machine which takes care of its residents, then you will do just fine. 

Resource management is extremely simple in this game. It is not about carting materials from one specific place to another and creating huge messes to sift thorugh- everything is dumped into a central inventory, and it is up to you to use the materials from there at crafting stations to make the stuff you need the most. There is no more material types than you need in the game. You will not be choosing from different tiers of food and parts constantly because everything has its use each day. The game knows what it wants to accomplish and did not go beyond that, and I really am happy with that.

Micro-management is extremely accessible. Survivors will need to be manually fed, manually medicated and get rest, however this is never an obstacle, and every day has a ton of time for you to get things done, never have I experienced a drastic loss in efficiency from running out of time. Just do your routine each day, and spend the rest of the day constructing and crafting whatever you'd like!

It's honestly blown me away how accessible this game is despite my previous playthroughs of other similar games. This game is extremely replayable and I am in love with it.

This War of Mine is a brilliant management/action game, that places its setting in a fictitious middle-european country, ravaged by war. About a year back when I got COVID-19 I played the ever-loving ♥♥♥♥ out of Frostpunk, and fell in love with 11 Bit Studios. After I couldn't get enough, I came back to This War of Mine, and I am extremely happy I did.

On my first several tries I treated the game for what I thought it was: a sacrifice-all kill-everything survival game. Instead what I got was an incredible, dark and gritty story seamlessly intertwined with minimalist yet extremely rewarding mechanics. In my 5th and successful run, I had an extremely comfortable playthrough (challenge wise) once I got past certain hurdles, yet it didn't feel like the game no longer had anything to offer me, just that I had been rewarded for smart tactics.

Does the game have a few bugs here and there? Sure.
Did I have to Alt+F4 a few times because I lost a character to clunky combat? Of course.

But I was never discouraged. This game has the beautiful incentive of perseverance, and the need to help your survivors reach the end of the unjust, unfair hell they find themselves in.

I am ecstatic to play the DLC for this game, and I am extremely excited for Frostpunk 2, Alters, and all of the other games 11 Bit Studios is cooking up. All in all, give this game a shot. A real shot. No matter what your first impression is.

[spoiler] Also, it is rewarding to infiltrate an entire outpost of soldiers and wipe them out like an extremely normal, mundane Solid Snake. [/spoiler]

There is no depth, no gripping story. You want tragedy? Read the Diary of Anne Frank. The book. In real life. There's infinitely more edification.

Basically you struggle to do the same things every day, while the game reminds you "real war is tough" even though this experience isn't very realistic. You'll have mastered the mechanics and gotten the hang of the systems within a week, and then your gameplay loop becomes trying not to mess up your resource management. I'm actually okay with this though, but I do wish more random events took place.
You have to choose what to take and leave behind when looting, but the looting locations remain untouched by other looters, or even the people living there. Loot doesn't respawn however, but if you actually pay attention to what you take and what you can trade for, you start to wonder why you'd even enter danger zones for loot unless you're playing a longer story. Once you understand how this works, you can even hoard all the loot to the entrance of an area to make it faster and safer the next time you show up, removing any sense of urgency getting supplies has. 
Your crew can craft moonshine distilleries, stoves, and fix shotguns with scrap metal, yet the concept of a backpack is beyond their understanding. So many locked slots, and not a single character can use them all.
The combat is my main gripe. It's dependent on real time RNG. That's right, no matter how smart you think you are, RNG can decide to end you at any time. Back stabs can only be done by specific characters (the game won't tell you which) as well. Stealth attacks are basically all you want to use, so avoid characters who can't backstab. If you're using guns, shoot and run. Leave if you have to, because a 1v3 shootout isn't in your interest.
The moral system is completely dependent on the characters hidden stats (wiki time). Your morals, survival instincts, and decisions do NOT matter when your crew decides that stealing from old people is the end of the world. Even your "bad" characters might decide that stealing and killing is wrong. Prepare to see characters constantly upset about the actions of other characters, only to not see the irony when they commit their own atrocities. 
The weather system also sucks. Had one character freeze to death in 66F weather. There was no warning that he was getting cold, no warning from the radio that the weather was changing, and no visual indication that it was winter. Just get the furnace and keep it above 70F. Wood is cheap anyway.
If you want to play this, I recommend starting outright with a modded playthrough. There are plenty of mods that add more inventory, weapons, increased loot tables, crafting options, and other quality of life improvements.

That said, real war sucks, but I think we all know it isn't fun and games. The intentions of the devs and the message they're are trying to convey is a good one. I just wish there was something that made the characters you're supposed to care about feel more like actual humans and less like sims.

The circumstances of the war in Ukraine make this perhaps a good time to write this review. I've been meaning to come to it for a long time but have never been able to find the right words. I think because I was trying to express it in the manner of a game review, which in this case is not really what I find most important.

I'll start by saying that this is one of the best games I've ever played. It's one of the most powerful pieces of art I've experienced. It's certainly one of the most important works I've come to.

Obviously it's impossible to truly grasp the experience of being in a warzone through a game, of being a refugee in your own land, fearful of what could happen to your livelihood, your life, your loved ones, everything and everyone you know. But it gives a powerful approximation of what people in Ukraine, in Syria, in Yemen, in Myanmar, etc... a few decades ago in Bosnia, which is the specific example this game is somewhat based on... have had to go through, and still go through. A well-realised and sometimes emotionally challenging survival game that impressed me a lot at first. I failed to keep my daughter healthy and it stung, and ended up killing some innocent people so that she could get medicine. Well worth playing through at least once, but what I find missing is a deeper layer of storytelling, emergent and/or scripted. Except for a few pieces of background information, dialogue is shared between all characters (except kids and adults have different lines), which quickly wears out the illusion of them having distinct personalities (particularly on your second and third runs). I would have loved to see more of both individual personalities and random traits that affect relationships between characters. A father playing a special game with his child, and a stranger playing another. The kid taking to one stranger but not another... stuff like that. It also suffers a bit from the "this is an emotional indie game so we don't need a good UI or QoL features" curse. You get punished a lot because you don't know the game mechanics (which mostly aren't explained to you), and not all of them make sense or are intuitive. So your first game you'll likely fail because you click the wrong thing or build something at the wrong time. Obviously, all games have a learning curve, but it feels particularly punishing in this game where the idea is to build an emotional experience. I still recommend the game for the feels and for a pretty good survival sim. It also made me check out Frostpunk, which so far seems like they've taken the lessons from this game to heart and built a survival game with more scope and a lot more personality.

The game is designed to show the struggle and horrors of a civil war from a civilian perspective, and while it succeeds in showcasing it's anti-war message, it's also a game I don't think is much fun as a result. 

One of the biggest issues is just that the game refuses to teach you anything about how to play it, other than the movement and action system. There's no explanation for any of the mechanics or conditions other than your survivors constant whining for food, sleep, smokes, or medicine. You get flavor hints and prompts; no numbers. You can guess at what the game wants you to do, but often enough your best guess might just kill a run because that's not how the game wants you to play it.

The wounding system in particular is very catty. In most games, giving the character a rest and a bandage will see them healed up. In This War of Mine, you need daily bandages (almost impossible to keep up), keep them fed to the brim, let them rest in bed for days and nights, and sometimes they'll still get worse. 

Sickness in cold weather is similar. The game offers you a heater, which one might assume would protect against the cold if you give it wood. Nope. You need multiple heaters. You also need to fill them to the brim, because that makes them hotter. No, it doesn't matter where they're placed. None of this is explained, and you'll be wondering why your survivors are freezing despite having a heater right next to them. 

It's easy to have a survivor freeze to death overnight when healthy, while you struggle to upgrade and construct multiple heaters, because you hadn't planned to need all these heaters, AND, every location is mysteriously out of parts.

It's very hard to recover from a downward spiral if you don't go on the wiki and KNOW where to go and what to do before it starts, because the game just doesn't convey anything.

I think my biggest gripe is the inventory system. You're given a grid with some locked squares, implying you can upgrade your inventory somehow, so surely you just need a high enough crafting bench right? Maybe make a backpack? Once you get that, everything will go smoothly in your scavenging, right? You'll be abl eto make up for all the spent parts on upgraded workstations, right? Wrong. It's a trap. Most survivors will have 10 slots for life. Deal with it. And items just don't stack past a small handful or 1 per slot. The entire system will have you leaving more goodies than not, which feels disappointing, rather than fun or rewarding. This is what most often causes the downward spiral. You need too many different things all the time and can't bring them home. You'll often have to burn trips by sending in a scav with armor/guns/tools/bullets which leaves no room for taking things back.

I think a lot of players might feel inclined to defend TWoM simply because it's stated goal is to simulate the miserable and desperate struggle of a group of civilians in a warzone. Sure. It succeeds at that. The game does simulate a desperate struggle, but it does this by obfuscating its mechanics and simultaneously punishing you for not knowing them. My best recommendation would be to get an inventory mod or a noob mod and be prepared to read a lot of wiki pages anyhow so you know what you're doing. Even with all of that though, I can't say the game is much fun. Once you learn all the mechanics and map the game out in your head, you'll feel like there isn't much left to see or do.

In a well structured experience, the game works with the player to determine satisfying exit points. For example, I might feel the need to stop after playing an hour or two of an intense horror game, or after feeling the satisfaction of finishing a curated six hour experience. In contrast, This War of Mine leaves me feeling like time has hardly passed after sessions where morning turns to night. It sucks hours out of my life like an unpleasantly bureaucratic vampire.

I love games that take us into places other than fun. I love that this war of mine takes us into places of loss, of grief, of suffering. However, ideally this pain should be chained to the experience. Losing a survivor after 6 hours of gameplay today had me feel real existential pain. It didn't make me think about war and loss, it made me think of the two thirds of the previous 6 hours that were spent micromanaging agonisingly slow timers and waiting. I will never get that time back.

The story of the game is based on the 1994 Balkans Conflict, particularly during the Siege of Sarajevo which lasted at least a year before broken and relief was sent to the people although in the game, the war would last around 30-60 days depending on the character set you start with.

Regarding the characters, barring one (Roman) they are civilians with different qualities, emotions, stories and strengths and you unlock more of their background story as the game progresses. You build your shelter in the day, you scavenge for supplies in the night.

The key to enjoying this game is not winning. Its surviving and as I've mentioned above, empathizing  with the soldiers, civilians, [b] even the thieves. [/b]

**The combat system is the worst aspect of this game.**
The character will often not react to your commands, just standing there, getting themselves killed. And you cannot save/load game at any time. So your character dies because the game decided not to listen to you, and then it saves the progress for you.

The game will also not teach/tell you when it's getting autosaved. If you think you've finished day in the game and decide to turn it off - oops, all day is lost, because it only saves at dawn. Try again.

Selecting characters works randomly. Sometimes, you click on a character and it gets selected. Sometimes you click on a character, and currently selected character goes to the location where you clicked. This hitbox problem seems to affect every interactive object.

You can basically win the game by going to 1 single location - the Garage. Trader's inventory gets replenished all the time, and once you traded with him, you can go to his basement to steal whatever you just traded in. And then repeat. Almost infinite items - you're limited only by your backpack capacity.
This "exploit" I noticed myself, but I read on a wiki about many more "exploits" like this.
It ruins the challenge.

There is no keyboard support in this game. You can't even look around with arrow keys.

The game does not remember my fullscreen setting - it always starts in windowed mode.

The game was made in Poland, yet the Polish localization is so bad (unnatural, mechanical), that I - being native Polish speaker - decided to play the game in English. Weird.
The English localization is perfect though.

The game begs for other improvements:
- Why can only 1 character go scavenging?
- Why does the character get tired if I finish scavenging in 1 hour?

No wonder the game is being sold so cheap - I suspect people would get frustrated if they paid more.
Well, I got frustrated enough to leave a comment.

For the past month or so there has been a great game drought so I’ve been playing through my back catalog of games.  I only bring this up because I've been sitting on this game for the better part of 6 years now.  I don’t even remember why I bought it to begin with because this is not my type of game.  Like, at all.  These survival sims just stress me out too much.  I play games to relax and wind down, not stress on whether my imaginary avatar can eat tomorrow or not.

That being said, this is one of the most thoughtful games I’ve played in a long time.  Let me be clear that, again, this is the type of game that actively repels me, and yet I made it through till the end of the war.  Sure I was left with one guy left and seeing the end screen of all the comrades I’d lost genuinely made me depressed. I still pulled through and finished.  And any game that makes a system so good that it keeps me invested despite my distaste for the genre is doing something right.

The struggles feel very genuine.  It’s hard knowing I left behind a friend who was so mentally unstable he would kill himself and still push on.  Having all my characters either sick or wounded and forcing them to scavenge for what little morsels could be scrounged up was sad and painful but also uplifting and so satisfying to find that one can of food I needed to make it to the next day.  The main struggles your characters naturally go through carries the game and alone is worth your time.

The only real problem I had with the game is the AI.  At the start you don’t really know how to deal with enemies so they are very challenging and will beat the snot out of you.  But by the end game I realized it takes them years to lock on to you so as long as you wait outside a door on a platform or something you can pick them off one by one pretty easily.  Then the ammo you scavenge from the dead replaces any ammo you lost.  It can really take away from that absolutely hopeless atmosphere.

Despite the AI I was still beaten and bruised by the game beyond repair.  By the end of the game I was on day 47 and would do anything to keep my last man, Bruno, alive.  I stole, murdered and forced my way through life.  I was raided everyday, they would steal my dwindling food supplies so I justified myself in stealing others possessions.  My mental state rapidly deteriorated as I was lost in endless cycle of blood and drinking just to stay alive.

Then the final screen played and I was reminded of all the sacrifices I had made.  All my friends were now dead, I was the shadow of my former self.  I had committed atrocities against my fellow man and tried to cover it up by helping some sick kids or a neighbor who’d been robbed.  Saying I was a good man at heart, forced to do bad by his surroundings.  But really I was a cancer.  Eating away at the fabric of society.  Plundering what wasn’t mine and leaving those with nothing to rot in the corpse of a dying city.

Few games have made me feel or brought up the same emotions as This War of Mine has done.

This War of Mine isn’t about winning a war — it’s about surviving one.

In this bleak, haunting game, you don’t play as a soldier on the frontlines, but as ordinary civilians trapped in the ruins of a besieged city. Every choice cuts deep: give your last scraps of food to a starving neighbor, or keep them so your own family doesn’t wither away. Steal medicine from the elderly, or risk watching your friends die from infection. There is no “good” choice — only the least terrible one you can live with.

You’ll watch strangers perish, powerless to help. You’ll do things you swore you never would, just to see tomorrow’s sunrise. And in the end, you’ll realize that for many, war is not glory — it is unrelenting hell.

This game doesn’t entertain. It reminds. And it hurts — exactly as it should.

NEWSFLASH, they were evil people trying to shoot me and they are dead now.

A fairly simple survival game with an emphasis on tactics and decision making. Though I'd be hesitant to buy this game at full price, it regularly goes on sale for $4, which I think is a great deal.

It took quite a few attempts for this to click with me...

It's bleak and gruelling, as you try to figure out what you're doing, but upon completion I have to say it's a really immersive, emotionally affecting, strategic survival/resource management platformer, which while not perfect, has a great deal to offer, the likes of which are few and far between.

As the game days go steadily by you become strangely attached to your people, such that any death, accident or illness feels genuinely urgent and tragic. As with 11-bit Studio's later masterpiece, Frostpunk, the early game punishes you mercilessly for getting a poor start, and there will come a point, if you're careful, where you can sit back, and take it easy. It's fail hard or win hard.

As the credits roll with Polaroids of the major events of your play-through, you realise what a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Hero Boris was, for the time he saved that girl in the abandoned bakery, and for the time he snuffed it in the siege of St. Mary's church, after which you don your helmet, tactical vest, automatic rifle, and avenge his honour. 

That's what this game will do to you. Just be prepared to take your time to learn the game, don't take unnecessary risks, and always keep a stash of 'high-quality roll-ups'.

 After all, in modern war, you will die like a dog for no good reason.

This game has been on my "to play" list for many years, alas, I believe I've come to the party a tad late. Back in 2014, when this game was released, the survival genre was in the middle of its renaissance. Games like Subnautica, Rust, Don't Starve, and Day Z, had all been released and were receiving great praise. Unfortunately, the variety of titles available at the time has relegated This War of Mine to the proverbial back seat. Now, 7 years later, is this game still good? 

Well... yes and no. 

If you love survival games, then yes, This War of Mine is for you; it's a paragon of the survival genre with a few unique mechanics that bring moments of tension and excitement. Unfortunately for me, these moments are too few and far between with the game relying too heavily on the tiresome crafting mechanics. So if you are returning to the survival genre, after a period of respite, expecting to re-ignite your love, then no, this game is not for you. Maybe in another 5 to 10 years, but not now.

I got back into this game a couple weeks back after not playing it much more after release. I'm not quite sure when I bought it, but around the time it came out i was still a kid in his mid teens. Played for a couple hours then quit because in all honesty I was complete trash at the game.

But coming back to it recently I found that being trash at the game is sort of part of the experience. In a good way, don't get me wrong. A fantastic way even. Your people will go through tons of struggles and hardships and you'll have to make important choices on what to focus on to keep people alive. Whether it be food, heating, general comfort, hell the game even takes into account psychological aspects where depending on your character, if they see or do something that would negatively impact a normal persons mental state, they can have full on anxiety attacks and such. Which you can treat over time by talking to them, or resort to cigarettes and booze to numb the pain... and then possibly get addicted to either of them.

I wish more games took their choices to the level that this game does. The phrase "choices matter" is an understatement here, and they don't always make it super obvious that you have a choice in some spots too. At which I'll say, sometimes if you see something messed up happening, think to yourself and wonder what the right thing to do would be, and if you have the balls to actually do it. As well as think about how it might negatively or positively effect your characters morale.

4$ is an absolute steal for this game and I sort of pray that something similar is in the works because I'd love to see a game like this be a bit bigger with more statuses and effects to manage. And to top all of that off, I noticed the sale and was recommending the game to a friend and went to buy the dlc. One of their DLC is pretty much just an opportunity to give a donation to charity. There are a lot of messed up situations in this game regarding children, and the fact that the developers even include that deserves a mad amount of respect.

The gameplay alone has a hell of a lot to enjoy. There's a strategic element to managing your time, your resources and your people, trading and scavenging, choosing infrastructure to build and maximising your opportunities. It's great fun.
However what really sets this game apart is the overall atmosphere of desperation and hard choices, it has moments of hope and tenderness set against an immensely bleak backdrop. This is a game that I have fallen in love with in a similar way I did with The Last of Us. IT has that gritty, hopeless theme and such a beautifully haunting art-style that adds so much to it. This is a game where the mechanics are simple but you really figure it all out for yourself. How to balance the needs of your people, with needing to find food or materials and keeping other people out, your morals even. It really is an interesting take on that whole theme of just trying to keep hope alive in the worst sort of situations - well depending on how you play.

So far anyway, I have enjoyed my time with the game and finding out more about my people and trying desperately to keep them all alive.

Something you've not really seen games do before, a true "survival" game and one that tries its best to counteract the usual video game wartime power fantasy. Some bits show their age these days, and it doesn't *fully* get away from that pull of letting you grab a gun and rambo your way through something, but the whole package is just an incredible ethos I haven't got out of anything else. You are made to feel like survival is barely at your fingertips every step of the way, deciding heavily on how your respond to arbitrary changes made by actors operating way beyond your level. You aren't the RTS godhand, nor the action RPG protagonist, you're living the life of one NPC who's just trying to not die of cholera in the background. And those survival mechanics actually work, and are actually really engaging.

This War of Mine doesn't pull any punches with how savage a modern day war siege can be and you can choose to be just as savage or try to maintain some humanity: the multiple endings of the game are connected to these decisions. In the side stories, compared to the main game they're a little weaker in that they are more linear with their progression but they are just as solid with their narrative. The additional DLC of the stories is a nice touch for something a little different from the main conflict shown in the base game and also well worth it. Overall this is an excellent game and well worth looking at for the survival management and strong stories.

This war of mine is a 2D game, its kinda side scrolling type of the game, but on the other hand it is made very intuitive, it has survival/crafting part of the game. The game is divided into 2 parts. 1st part is day, when you can go around house, build things, eat, rest or heal your survivors, trade if a trader comes around, or maybe help neighbours in some random encounter. 

The second part of the game is at night time, when you can choose one of your survivors and go out into town scavenging. There is a lot of different things, building materials, wood for heating, food, bullets, herbals, medicine and more. Your scavenger has limited space in his backpack, so I always chose the survivor that can carry the most items to go into scavenging missions.

First few locations for scavenging are easy, and you will make a lot of it. But as game moves towards mid-game, scavenging missions become harder, enemies carry weapons, and patrol around locations, and it is really not easy to survive. And game is kinda rogue-like, and once you ♥♥♥♥ up, there is no turning back, you need to start the game anew.

Progress in game is slow, but if you can every night bring maximum load of scavenged items, it will be a steady progress.

This game has beautiful art style. Add to that the somber music and desolate settings in which the game take place in, has a combination of hope and tension which affects the player. It would be huge if my characters could interact with each other in literally any fashion, rather than ignoring each other like mismatched college roommates. I'm not asking for BioWare-level banter or The Sims: Sarajevo Edition, but just the ability for survivors to chit-chat with each other would go a long way towards me perceiving these people as more than dolls in an usually grim dollhouse (it would also give me something to do for the 7 hours I have left after the day's chores of "listen to the radio" and "cook rat stew" are complete). It would also add some replayability: What happens when an elementary school principal, a militia deserter, and this country's equivalent of Anthony Bourdain have to survive together? I get that the developers don't want hijinks to get in the way of their very serious message, but I'm pretty sure human relationships don't cease to exist in wartime. If you want to tell a meaningful story, it helps to give me reason to care about these people.

As you can see, I have A LOT of hours in this game. I obviously find the core gameplay loop enjoyable (for what it's worth, it's a great "watching TV at the same time" game once you know the systems). But for a game whose marketing materials show people hugging, crying, having feelings, etc., that aspect of storytelling is bizarrely missing from the final product.

Well, I have only played 5 hours and restarted the game once. The concept is great, but with a huge flaw as far as I have seen - You can mostly scavange / loot items from other "people" in the city, with subsequent anguish and mental despair for your characters. This seems to be more or less unavoidable - Conflict is basically a part of the game and you will not be able to play this game "fair" if you are to succeed. This is maybe a part of the war, but I don't believe it is a necessity of war, where co-op is the key for long-term survival. So by doing the game-play narrowly in this direction, you can't really "win". You will always lose, even if you temporarily win. Some items that is a all out necessity is crucially hard to come by, even though in real life, it doesn't seem to be that big of an issue - for example bandages. There are so many other ways to make bandages, it is not really a difficult item in real life. Food is. I wished there were indicators, showing HOW tired, HOW hungry, HOW depressed they are, and what kind of things they need. For example, depression and sadness seems to be rampant, but no real solution to how to overcome this, even though I had both food, beds, sofa, radio and books. My guys were just not happy! The interface is ok, but overly simplified, few metrics as described, and more places to scavange where you actually don't steal from other people!

Lackluster verisimilitude undercuts what's good about this game. Characters lament not knowing where their next meal will come from while tending to the garden and help neighbours to the hospital only to return with their own wounds untreated. Cumulatively, this takes away from the sense that you're sharing a harrowing experience with your survivors as much as you are simply playing a game, fulfilling the mechanical needs of their meters. It seems to occupy an unfortunate middle ground of characterization, where the characters aren't blank enough slates that a personality can be suggested purely by their mechanical abilities but also the dialogue and flavour-text aren't strong enough that their crafted personalities are endearing.

I think games should allow for moments that are, in a classical sense, awesome. These moments are generally where the written narrative and the emergent ludonarrative suddenly interlock in a beautiful, transcendent whole. The AI of an enemy in XCOM 2 causing it to attack a soldier with a psychic shield for multiple turns, allowing them to have a drawn out energy-blade duel; the moment in Spec Ops: The Line when you choose how you respond to the lynch mob that just removed of one of your NPC helpers from play; Sans' judgement in Undertale. I found but one moment that even approached that in War of Mine, when a newcomer to my house was kind to my little girl character and was able to offer her a healing item since *he* was healthy enough to do a scavenging run instead of the other--injured--adults. It was touching, and fulfilling--but fleeting. And, for some reason, not what the game was build around or seemingly designed to reliably reproduce.

Sure, one can argue that the game is about feeling bad, not about awesome moments. But I would argue that if you're not being made to feel awesomely sad, you're not sad. You're merely recognizing that the aesthetics of the game are demanding sadness. That's the thing to say about a game like War of Mine because the alternative opens one up to accusations of sociopathy. Ah yes, when small sprites I'd told were old people on my screen said 'please don't!' as I took their digital food tokens, I was inflicted with much sympathy. I ace all my Voight-Kampffs! But the fact of the matter is that striking deep at real core emotions requires better design than what's on display here.

Basic premise is that you organise a group of refugees who've lost everything and are living in a bombed out house in a city warzone, all you have to do is keep them alive, scavange for what you need and just stay alive.

Where this game scores is not necessarily the technical issues but the characterisation. The individuals you look after are trying to deal with both the physical and mental issues of living in a warzone, hungry and tired and trying to come to terms with why they have to suffer when they never asked to be involved in a war they never started. It's heartbreaking to keep trying so hard and still seeing the people suffer, the hardest one for me was the one that starts off with a lone father and his daughter. It was hard to see how much stress and mental anguish the child suffered while the parent just muddled through. When another adult appeared you find yourself very suspicious of their motives, you have to decide if you're going to trust another adult to enter the group. Very clever way to play emotional games with you.

Yes, there are some technical things that could be improved, placing objects you made such as chairs and stoves can be a pain as you only have so much space and only allowed one type of object in a room at anytime. However it's not really about the technical prowess of the game, it's how it plays on your emotions and empathy for the suffering of other human beings.

It was very odd to play a game, they're just sprites but I really cared about the people especially the children, every time they wanted a hug or sat down and just cried, you felt you had to do something. So you're not only having to concern yourself with finding food, raw materials but also have to find ways to keep the character's morale going too.

The soundtrack is amazing, I paid extra to download that from Steam as MP3 and now have it on my permanently "quiet tracks playlist", incredible work there.

If you're not easily moved by a game's ability to tug at your emotions, you'll probably find this quite boring as it's really just a basic survival game at heart but if you're the kind of person who invests into a game's characters during game play then be prepared for a struggle to not give up on them and spend hours fighting to keep them alive, happy and healthy, I felt emotionally drained after a few hours of playing and needed time to calm down and cheer myself up.

Perhaps the same things that leads people to extinguish their environments gradually over time so throwing them into scarcity and panic. There must be answers to these questions.

Their movements are also quite predictable which I don't really mind, it does make stealth kills very easy but it's not the worst thing. I really wish the game would react more to you're scavenging or raiding. Instead every single location is heavily scripted which makes them loose any replay value pretty fast. 

When it comes to crafting the game tries to keep it "realistic" you're not going to craft a machine gun from nothing, or get medieval with a bow and arrow like this is minecraft. But it does have its share of nonsense, why do I need a filter to make Moonshine if the only ingredients are sugar and CLEAN water? Why do I need a filter for rain water, can't I just boil it? It's not the worst ever but I'm not above nitpicking moon logic in a game that wants to sell me a realistic war story.

I can't think of a good segway so lets talk about characters.
Each character has a unique ability which range from "unclear" to "worthless" and "game breaking cheese"
For an example, Pavle is just flat out faster at running than everyone. Not really that helpful is it.
But what do you do with a skill like "Good with kids"? 
Then there's Roman who has the game breaking "Combat trained" which means he can one shot melee, feels no guilt over murdering people by the dozens, and has way better aim and reloading speed.
Then there's Marko and his "Good cooking" which means his Moonshine takes half as many supplies to make but is worth just as much. No wonder they only let you carry one bottle per stack because Marko is the king of barter town. Combine him with Katia's "bartering skills" and you can buy basically anything. 

Each character can and will develop status effects as you play. A lot of which are at best unclear or at worst designed to just make you waste resources.
For example, still hungry means nothing. Don't waste food making sure everyone is stuffed unless they've got a status effect like wounded or depressed.
Same thing goes for slightly wounded. Just give them rest and regular food, don't bother filling their belly or giving them bandages.

However some statuses are just stupid. 
Depressed, Sad and Broken are dumb.
I don't want the game to TELL me how my character's feel. Especially because what triggers the statuses is basically "random". (In the sense they are so heavily scripted or character dependant it becomes impossible to find a pattern)
For example, robbing this one specific old couple will make who ever does it sad.
But robbing other random survivors? No emotional penalty unless you fail an invisible dice roll.
Killing random survivors is a great way to make your character depressed, but if the survivor is classed as a bandit (something you could only find out through wikipedia) then murder away! Who cares if they beg for mercy! Club 'em to death! Shoot them! Slit their throats when they ain't lookin! Their bandits! They have no souls!

The game wants to have its moral cake and eat it too. This is some Spec Ops the Line ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ where the game just gets really judgy on you for no good reason. 
Staying with that tangent for a moment and veering close to spoilers. The endings are dumb. 
Each character has 6: Death, Suicide, Leaving, Karma, Sad and Good.
Death and Suicide should be obvious.
Leaving means they left the party for whatever reason.
"Karma" happens when you survive till the cease fire or escape the city but kill too many people or steal too much. 
"Sad" happens when you do the same but you didn't steal enough or kill enough to get the Karma ending but you ALSO didn't do enough random side objectives to get the "Good" ending.
Good happens when you don't steal, don't kill, and give away free supplies whenever the game asks you to. 
Again the game is very judgemental, I wish that each character had fewer endings with more detail instead of stretching them to fill a bunch of arbitrary moral classifications. 

Also addictions, addictions are dumb. 
Some characters will suffer a mood penalty (making them more likely to become Sad, Depressed or Broken whenever the appropriate roll is made) if they don't get their one pure water and cup of coffee or 3 smokes a day. 
Also you can pound Moonshine back like its water and they will never get addicted which I think is funny for some reason. The game wants to tackle some very serious issues but doesn't want to look at maladaptive coping mechanisms. 
I wish I could use coffee or cigarettes to boost my character's morale, at the risk of them becoming addicted or having bad side effects instead of it just being an automatic thing decided on generation. Or at least make them random instead of fixed.

When it comes to taking care of your survivors, some actions are basically pointless.
For example building chairs does nothing, even if you have books characters will never read. They'll just sit around and do nothing. I know just HAVING them supposedly provides positive morale but the game doesn't give you any feed back on how much morale (if any) is gained from having a comfy house. Just cheap uninspired flavour text. 
Cooking is also pretty worthless sine it consumes more resources than just eating canned food or eating raw food twice. (Unless you have Bruno then cooking actually pays some return on investment) If you wanna play on GG-EZ mode just avoid eating all together until the second day of "Very Hungry" status. 

Also, I know part of the profits for every copy of this game go to/went to charity. But that doesn't justify rough experience like this. If you care that much about charity, donate to them directly. 

I do admit, I enjoy This War of Mine. But I don't think cackling with glee when Marko beats 3 gunmen to death with a shovel is the kind of enjoyment the devs want me to be having.

This War of Mine stands out for addressing the often avoided topic of the plight of civilians during armed conflicts. This is often ignored, not only in video games but media in general, likely because it's harder to glorify pointless suffering for propaganda purposes compared to conventional warfare and the current world superpower considers bombing civilian settlements a valid strategy they still practice to this day. This War of Mine seems to be inspired by the Breakup of Yugoslavia, but many may draw parallels to more recent Syrian Civil War which is still ongoing as of October of 2021.
The game starts somewhat promising, but it only takes a few hours for This War of Mine to become a regular survival game, and I can't help but think this goes against the original intent.
A lot of people mention different set pieces that elicited an emotional reaction from them, but I personally believe the game gets downright cheesy at times. The color palette is mostly comprised of different shades of grey and there's always sad music in the background, it feels forced rather than interactive.
Also, the cyclical nature of the gameplay plus the long duration of the campaign means that by the end of it most players will be thinking about moonshine economics rather than morality. You can only shank an NPC so many times until you become desensitized to it and I highly doubt that's the message they were going for because the sad atmosphere is maintained to the very end. 
However, I find it morbidly cool that your survivors can become so traumatized they basically become catatonic, now that feels like a worthy consequence for some of the awful acts you can commit.
To conclude, This War of Mine has a very interesting and provocative concept, but the execution is more conductive to a fun survival game than an emotional exploration of said concept. Still, it's a fun survival game and I believe that's pretty good too.

However, he soon becomes frightened by his next door neighbor, Old Man Marley, a supposed serial killer, as well as the "Wet Bandits", Henrik and Marko, a pair of burglars who have been breaking into other vacant houses in the neighborhood and have targeted the McCallisters' house. Pavle tricks them into thinking that his family is still home, forcing them to put their plans on hold.

Kate realizes mid-flight that Pavle was left behind, and upon arrival in Paris, the family discovers that all flights back to the United States for the next two days are booked. They ambush him and prepare to get their revenge, but Marley intervenes and knocks them unconscious with his snow shovel. On Christmas Day, Pavle is disappointed to find that his family is still gone. [h1]History lesson: The Kosovo War[/h1]

[Trigger warning: If you are offended by missing details, maybe to the detriment of your own side, please note that the following paragraph is intended to put the game in the right context. Therefore it is highly simplified. Anything else would go beyond the scope of a game review.
Update: I will now disable the comment function.]

Yugoslavia was a socialist satellite state of the former Soviet Union, patched together after World War 2 from Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, among others. After the collapse of the USSR, it fell into a bitter civil war. The Serbian military fought separatist rebels, and because of numerous crimes against the civilian population, the UN finally intervened. The 4-year siege of Sarajevo made particular headlines. This large city was occupied by rebels and besieged by the military. Snipers had almost all streets in view and bombs fell more or less regularly. Rebels, looters and soldiers fought each other, causing great suffering among the civilian people, including the then teenage game developers in whose situation the game throws us. We control a small group of civilians in the bombed city, without weapons, food or even beds.

[h1]Painfully realistic[/h1] 

At first glance, This War Of Mine is just one survival simulation among many. Like in Don't Starve, Rust or The Forest, the goal is to ensure the survival of a small group of characters. In contrast to the rather imaginative scenarios of other survival games, however, this one is about a real, brutal war. The protagonists are not knights in shining armor, but math teachers, TV cooks, warehouse workers, and yet this fight for survival is so much more than a DayZ. The gameplay is often tedious and repetitive. You have to cook food, eat, sleep and rest to be ready for the night. This hopeless cycle perfectly captures the grind of daily survival. Simple, taken-for-granted things like coffee or cigarettes are more valuable than diamonds. Days seem to last endlessly and mistakes are punished without mercy.  Death is permanent and every decision irreversible. If you take the risk of armed combat against other groups, a wounded character may die of his injuries days after. If you exchange valuable medicines for food, they might be missing only a short time later. The nightly raids demand fierce, sometimes immoral decisions and have harsh consequences on the group.

[h1]A simulation?[/h1]

Moreover, there are no fictional end times here that take away the burden of reality, no zombies and no aliens that you can beat up on without a guilty conscience and that make you believe that it won't come to that in reality. No, This War Of Mine has so already happened, it is happening right now and it will happen again. It's Yugoslavia. It's Ukraine, Syria, Gaza, Afghanistan. All over the world there are civilians experiencing exactly what the developers portray so painfully realistically. A war. Right on their doorstep. Right now. That's what makes This War of Mine stand out. It counters the smooth superhero warfare of shooter and strategy games with demoralizing suffering. It's unusual and guaranteed not to entertain. But that's exactly how it's supposed to be.

[h1]Welcome to Hell[/h1]

This War of Mine is a game about feeling powerless and lost. Every seemingly screwed up design element supports this. The incomplete information it reveals about the status of the game's characters creates uncertainty. The combat controls leave no room for finesse, making any exchange of blows with bandits or soldiers unpredictable and, most importantly, undesirable. If a tutorial window explained everything in a friendly way, then the moments when characters react so strongly to events, as in hardly any other game, would not be so shocking.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

It's heavy fare. Being good means having enough food for two days, instead of having to decide who stays hungry. In an interview, designer Pawel Miechhowski answers the question of whether This War of Mine is supposed to be fun: "No, it's supposed to be an experience." It is.
It's an unpleasant experience.
But one that is worth experiencing.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
[i]This War of Mine[/i] is a gritty story of survival and sacrifice of civilians in a war zone. If a dark and tragic story isn’t going to speak to you, give it a pass. The survival aspect is easy to learn, but challenging because of the number of resources you have to balance. Mastery of the game is possible, and it loses a bit of magic at that point. You get 4-6 runs before that happens, so it’s worth the price tag in my book. And then you can play the exceptional Stories DLC.
[hr][/hr]
If you’ve come to play [i]This War of Mine[/i], you should be here for the story. This game is somber, gritty, and a bit depressing, but it also reminds you that you are not alone. People thrown together by horrible circumstance work together and help each other…simply because it is the right thing to do. This touch of light was important, and kept the game from being too dark to be playable.

The War has stuffed your city into this handbasket, and you know where you are going. What will you need to do to survive? More importantly, what will you chose to do to survive? Will you steal from the old couple that doesn’t fight back? Will you steal from the bandit? Will you kill him if he catches you? What is the line that separates you from that bandit?

These questions are not just moral hyperbole. If you steal or kill, it can seriously hurt your character’s mental health. Surviving The War is just as much about spirits and morale as finding enough food.

You’re not here to win, you’re here to survive. Some people will struggle with this…I did. During one run, I was asked to make a small sacrifice in order to save the greater good. Even after 6 runs, I still thought “I could do it.” I didn’t make the sacrifice, and I got the worst ending (though the story made sense).

Combat is very dangerous and clunky, and your skill will not matter much. That is the point, though. Violence will be a split-second decision, and you might end up doing something you regret. Sometimes because you lost, sometimes because you won.

Because of these things, this game won’t be for everyone. Some people don’t like real life moral questions and darkness in their games/entertainment. While other people post about killing every bandit and soldier in every run…and I can’t help but feel sad. I feel like they missed the point. Not to mention, if you take morality out of the equation there are better survival/combat games.

In Classic mode, there is very little overarching plot. The story is driven by your characters, choices, and random events. Some events are small (help board your neighbor’s windows), while others change how you approach the game (starting during the dead of winter). Despite being driven by random events, the pieces come together very well, and I survived about 4 runs before I needed a more structured story.

[i]This War of Mine: Stories[/i] is what you are really here for. The stories are exceptional, and add a lot of life to the game. Stories adds some new twists and challenges, so make sure you can survive The War in Classic, before you try Stories.

[i]This War of Mine[/i] is also a surprisingly good survival game that requires to you balance a lot of factors. How do you manage your daytime get everyone food and rest, while maintaining and upgrading the house? Who goes scavenging and who gets some much-needed sleep…do you post a guard against raiders? Where do you scavenge? Sites with guards have better stuff, but require a lot of time sneaking, limiting what you can do…[i]if[/i] you don’t get caught. Do you use precious backpack slots to bring a weapon or lockpicks? Do you bring back food? Meds for your sick child? Electronics for your workbench? Jewelry (don’t knock the jewelry…you can trade a few useless baubles for an entire backpack full of lumber)? Each individual piece of the survival game is simple, but the number of things you constantly balance adds just the right amount of complexity.

I think the best praise I can give the survival game is that I enjoyed the process. When I played a Story and got an ending I didn’t like, I didn’t hesitate to fire up that story again because I enjoyed the process of playing the game.

The biggest weakness for me is that you can solve the game. Once you understand how all the pieces move, you can make “correct” choices that allow you to easily survive, get all your upgrades, and not have to make any tough choices. After that, the magic of the game was gone. The good news is that took about 6 runs, so I felt like I got a good value out of the game.
