This game provided me with a unique experience upon my first playthrough because, though I had played survival games before, I did not have to face the consequences of my characters actions. This War of Mine pits your survival skills against the desperate feel of a war-torn country, all the while balancing your characters health and mental suffering. Characters are a big element of the game and they will respond to events according to their personality traits. Further, characters each bring their own strengths and weaknesses to the table. Once you play through the game a few times, you will start to know which characters you love, and those you hate.

What's great about the game is that it gives you (until you play some of the harder scenarios) the option of being good survivors or bad survivors meaning you can either collect and obtain the foods and necessities you need without resorting to violence or you can become an outright bandit (I usually choose the ladder because I am sadistic like that haha). However, beware, the consequences of being a morally upright survivor has its pitfalls, for instance, its much harder to come across large stores of goods for your characters to live a comfortable existence during their time in the dilapidated war-torn city the game takes place in. That being said, there are weaknesses in taking the bandit route in that its much more hazardous and is mentally draining on many of your characters.

All-in-all, I loved the realism of This War of Mine and it is a very decent survival game. So if you like survival and are ready to face the harsh realities of war, try this game out because it will most likely tickle your fancy.

A very impressive and atmospheric game. It's not just a surviving game, but a war novel. My character was killed by bandits while looting for supplies and well, there is no second chance to replay the moment. It's the war.

Would I recommend this game?  --  YES!

Why? 

CONCEPT
Well, the concept is still a rare one in the gaming world. Showing the other side of war - the one of the civilians - the victims of aggression - is an important one, because as badass and cool usual war games might let someone feel himself, they are far away from the truth of war.

VISUALS - SOUND - ATMOSPHERE
The Artworks are beautiful (to me) and accelerate the immersion into the overall atmosphere. It's a fine line between creating a visual style that also characterizes the despair and tristesse of war without being repellent to the player. The devs did a really good job on that.
If you haven't done so, I recommend trying out the other visual mode ("Settings" -> "Pencil effect" -> "Soft" or "Sketchy") 

MUSIC
It's good enough to not having own songs played in the background yet also not at the league of AAA-Games. I dig the guitar songs (if the character can play it of course)

GAMEPLAY
While the interface being pretty simplistic the gameplay demands a certain task management and planning ahead (especially in the harder modes). It has a certain learning curve (which is extensive enough to be constantly learning for 30+ hours till you've "cracked the game"). Once it's reached though, the game has not very much new to offer, except trying out new strategies. Which is fine by me, replay value is still very high.

MAP
The Locations are manifold in style and encounters. While they're new to you it really is an adventure to getting to know the different encounter and loot possibilities. 
The map has quite some locations but after a few dozen hours of gameplay you've seen it all, know it all. That's one of the little downsides of the game in terms of long-term-playability. If the devs would decide to publish a Location DLC I'd happily and instantly would invest in it. (Yeah I know they stopped development)

SOCIAL ENGAGEMENT
11 bit studios proves, that being a profit oriented company and active engagement in social improvement doesn't exclude each other, but pair rather well. A certain amount of the profits for "This War Of Mine" and all DLC's has always been and always will be transferred to organizations that help children in areas of war.
If you want to contribute further you can buy the Art-DLC. It contains art regarding war and peace from artists around the globe which will be depicted ingame. 100% of the DLC-Profit goes to charity.

DEVS and PUBLISHER
I've got this game since quite a while (since before the first DLCs) and 11bit is a cool bunch of People. Their communication with the community is nice. The Prices of the games and DLCs are fair. They live social responsibility by heart. They had free major updates and content extensions. I never had that EA- or Paradox-Feeling with them. Here you got a team that is worth supporting.

DLCs
The DLCs are okay. Nice addition and good new content. I've played them once or twice (The Story-DLC), but mostly stick to the main game with some mods.
The best DLC to me is the "Little Ones" one. Having children in the house makes a huge impact and difference and the DLC adds tremendously to the gaming experience.

MODDING COMMUNITY
There was/is an active and productive community. Workshop is full of Mods, Skins, Items, Stories, Characters.
If the game starts to feel a bit repetitive, I recommend browsing a bit through the workshop content.
Whether you want the game to be more or less vanilla, add more items and crafting complexity or just want to play with custom characters (I know that there is even a John Cena Character downloadable, but I gotta admit, I haven't seen it yet),  the workshop got you!

CONCLUSION
If you like 2D-Style games, point and click, survival, looting, crafting, micro management, drawn visuals, dark atmosphere, emotional and ethical choices, many modding possibilities, devs that stick to creating good games rather than scamming their customers, then this is a must have game for you.

This might be the only game, that I recommend buying for the full price! It's worth it!

TL;DR: If you think that living as a citizen in a civil war is not fun, then don't buy it. Genuinely, not for everyone.

Before I list off the positives and negatives, let me explain.

Most of these negative reviews come with "boring and repetitive," or "rng dependent," or "seemingly pointless." If you are one of these people who can't stand being bored of doing the same thing over and over again and not getting a good enough reward, then it isn't for you, because this is what the developers intended.

The game isn't designed to be the most fun experience of you life. Who the hell thinks that living in a civil war and scavenging to survive is fun?

The game is supposed to put a spin on how you are supposed to see things as a survivor. It's supposed to simulate all of the terrible hardships that people endure. If you can't deal with it, that sucks, go cry to your mother and play Mario or something. I hardly imagine most people watching horror movies or shocking documentaries because they enjoy watching people suffer.

Positives:
- Pretty dang realistic
- Characters do have emotion, which is beneficial and detrimental
- Replay-ability
- Beautiful graphics
- Hits you in the feels
- Fairly impactful decisions

Negatives:
- Boring and repetitive
- Controls can be super annoying
- Combat is a little weird
- Frustrating losses
- Inconsistent with realism and gameplay balancing

Before the rant, I do have to say when starting out, somethings are a little inconsistent. It's difficult to balance fun and engaging gameplay with the entire concept of the game: living in war and poverty sucks.

Fun fact, that's not how life works. Especially in a circumstance like this game is presenting. Do you expect to get a tutorial for life? If you were in the middle of a civil war, surviving for as long as you can, do you expect to get a tutorial, someone to tell you how to survive? Do you expect that given any circumstance, that you will always survive because you made the most optimal decisions?

I totally understand every bit of what they are saying though, as a game, it can be very boring and repetitive. Tools are flimsy as hell and break and is honestly just not a fun game to play. But I hardly believe that this game should be played purely off of fun. TWoM if it didn't have any of it's original goal is frankly a subpar game at best. If you play this game and disregard what it means, which I would argue is most people, this game just sucks. 

If you cannot handle truly understanding the concept of this game, then just don't buy it. It's not worth your time.

Combat is an absolute joke (Snuck up on a thug with my athlete character, knifed him from behind while he was completely unaware, and it only took half his health. I completely understand the limits if your carrying just timber, but when I'm completely out of space from carrying scrap/teddy bears/tobacco/meds each items small stack is just ridiculous. An excellent outlook on the human condition during times of war. War is not a treat, revolutions destroy infrastructure and the ones who are the most affected are the civilians. The horror of atrocities is amplified for the ordinary soul. When we hear about conflicts on the news, it seems so distant. It's important to remember that war affects ordinary people in ordinary countries, we could all suddenly be affected by a war. It could happen to any country, there are very few countries that have never been in a war. War and human suffering are a few of the only constants throughout human civilisation. We are all human after all, other games have you control a group of nameless soldiers throughout a city in an attempt to conquer it. This game is all about the ones living in that city. The sacrifices they have to make. It forces you to empathise with unique people, they have their own quirks, needs, and stories. If and when one of your survivors die, you feel that death, the game makes you control almost anything and everything important about your survivors, you probably could've avoided that death. The game forces you to make hard choices and move on when you have a loss, you could call it a management game, but in all honesty, it's pretty much a simulation, of morality, and of the pain civilians go through in war. The true victims of any war are the people who live in those countries, the civilians who breathe the air.

It's not for everyone, and the gameplay/hyper-realism is a bit off-putting to me, but, it is a simulation of what it's like to be a civilian in a wartime city. Some of the elements aren't quite right, like the supply gathering and the forced interactions between people, but, I thought it was generally good and a meaningful experience.

This is a really good challenge the first few runs and after that you can use less useful survivors to keep the game tricky. A welcome change of perspective from most war games - be ready to follow a tragic story rather than a heroic one. A lot of replayability from randomly generated settings and a lot of character combinations.

This game is one of the most haunting and frustrating games I've ever played. 
You play as a group of civilians in an unnamed war (loosely based on the Balkans of the 90's) simply trying to survive the hell they have found themselves in. Each day is spent repairing and rebuilding, trying to shut out the horrors of the outside world and making life a bit more comfortable, and each night is spent venturing out into the dark to try to scavenge up a scrap of food to make it just one more day. You face other survivors trying to scrape by, realizing that your survival may be depending on their suffering. Some plead for you to help them, others fight back and can kill members of your party. 
Should a party member die, it resonates with the rest of the party and they become depressed, lessening their capacity to do work as they reflect on the loss of their friend. 
As someone who spends a lot of time reading about wars around the world, this game feels less like a game, and more like a human interest story on a blog or local paper. It leaves you with a sense of what sort of madness people will unleash on each other over things like race, resources, religion, or empire and how this madness plays out on the ground better than most war reporting you will read or hear. 
Is the game fun? Not really. Is the game full of meaning and challenging emotionally and mentally? Yes. 
Highly recommended.

I had high expectations because Frostpunk was one of the best games I've played. This War Of Mine is a more artistic game than anything else. Visuals are stunning, and the melancholic soundtrack gives a proper atmosphere and immersion. Unfortunately, it does not translate into the gameplay. The first clue that this might not be a good game is right at the start. You're thrown into the game without any tutorial, guide, explanation, without anything. Yes, the game is straightforward, so you'll learn it during the first thirty minutes. But there are many hidden mechanics and stats without any indication. For example, how is a character good at guarding or how good is he with weapons.

The game puts heavy emphasis on RNG. There are multiple location encounters with very different results. There are randomized events at the door of your base. And worst of all, your next character is also randomized. So in my playthrough, I got Cveta, who's trait is "Loving Children". I got her in the main story, where there are no children. She was a burden, nothing more. It would be fine if the game would be built around a bigger group of survivors, but in a scenario where you have only four, five of them? Nope.

UX is yet another flaw. I had the most problems in the scavenging phase. Switching between scavenging and combat is unintuitive, and I don't see a reason for it. Other persons are not highlighted, which was eventually a reason why my best survivor died. It was not due to some poor decision I made. I peeked through a door, didn't see any guard, entered a room, and got killed. How? A guard was sleeping on a bed, who I wake up by looting.

I could leave all the issues behind, if not for one critical mechanic: Karma (Morale). Basically, you're penalized for stealing or killing. A character gets depressed and eventually get a bad ending. Dishonored did something similar, but there are significant differences. Dishonored was build around both paragon and renegade playstyles and did not hinder your gaming experience. In This War Of Mine, I looted all neutral locations around day 30, and that's where the gaming experience ended for me. Since I didn't want to kill or steal private property, I broke up furniture with a hatchet for the next 15 days. My base was mostly sustainable, so I ended up trading crafted luxury goods for components, ammo, and crafting materials every two days a trader comes to visit. That not gaming, that's boredom. But what else can you do if you want a good ending?

This War Of Mine is for casual gamers, not experienced ones.

[b][i]"This War of Mine"[/i][/b] is a [b]anti-war 2D shelter survival game[/b], you follow a group of survivors as they try their best to [b]survive and scavenge resources in the midst of a war.[/b] During the day, you use materials and/or resources to [b]build and improve your base[/b]. During the night, you go out to spots marked on your map to [b]scavenge for resources[/b], these spots can range from harmless, to extremely dangerous with armed people who are [b]willing to kill you[/b].

I find surviving and scavenging the destroyed environments of the game [b]pretty captivating[/b]. You get bits of lore from abandoned notes, or written words on walls, making exploring the different areas of the game somewhat interesting. The [b]environment is also really well designed[/b], making this post-war world very believable. Exploring new areas, searching places and going back to base with an inventory full of stuff is [b]always satisfying[/b].

However, I feel that this game could have offered more in terms of gameplay, but [b]especially base building[/b]. The base building feels [b]very limited[/b], you are unable to rotate/flip directions of your furniture, and you're also limited to a grid by grid building layout. There is also a [b]lack of furniture [/b]and [b]overall base pieces[/b], you are also unable to destroy certain builds like the guitar once placed. This [b]really limits the base building aspect of this survival game[/b] and prevents you from really personalizing your home, I would have really preferred it if you [b]choose your starting house layouts[/b], or [b]expand/build your house from scratch [/b]with more furniture choices. But I digress, as since this is not a big focus of the game.

Gameplay-wise, the game is very easy to pick up, you do everything in the game by clicking; [i]moving your character, scavenging, attacking, trading[/i]—you get the point, [b]super general[/b]. Asides from that there's not really much to say, the gameplay is just scavenge materials at night, build base during the day, and [b]survive as long as you can or until the war is over[/b]. The only real challenge is surviving encounters with hostiles, and managing your group's condition ([i]hunger, tiredness, ect.[/i]).

The game also has this really fitting look for it, I especially loved the [b]sketchy-blurred look of rooms[/b] your player can't see, it makes scavenging new places a lot more [b]engaging[/b] as you can only hear footsteps/noises and can only [b]see your enemy if they see you[/b]. The game just has an overall look that [b]works[/b]! The designs, textures and models all fit the decrepit environment of a war-scarred city, and fits the atmosphere and setting of the game perfectly.

All in all, [b][i]"This War of Mine" [/i][/b]is really interesting survival game with [b]easy to learn mechanics[/b], [b]good and fitting graphics[/b], [b]interesting locations and events[/b], but a [b]lackluster base building system[/b].

It's late at night. I'm sneaking outside a ransacked supermarket because there may be food there and we're desperately short on it. I only have an old hatchet to chop up furniture for firewood or -if it comes to it- defend myself and chop people instead. I look through a keyhole and see a drunken soldier attempting to rape a young girl. Without thinking I open the door and bury the hatchet in his skull. He is dead before he hits the floor. I loot his body to get an assault rifle and ammunition. This accident turned out to be a godsent. Now we can defend our shelter and if need be, dish out some vigilante justice or simply fight for survival. The besieged city is truly a concrete jungle, only the ruthless and most intelligent survive here. Now I need to explain to my friends what happened. Will they be looking at me in shock and disgust or with awe instead? Did I do a good deed by killing that man? What if the girl had stolen something from him or was selling military rations under the table? It's too late for second guesses, he is dead, she is alive and so am I. We need to survive, one day at a time. Survive tomorrow and the day after that until the war either ends or we find a way to escape. Hopefully we can retain our sanity and not go mad. I tried playing this game. I like survival games that actually are gritty and more survival based, and I don't mind my people dying; things like that happen.... but good GRIEF is this game depressing. 

And yeah, I know it's supposed to be.  But there's a point where it goes from "Oh, that's so sad, but I need to press on" to "Okay, this is just too upsetting to continue." which I hit. So I'll admit, this isn't the game for me, and others will have a higher threshold then I did.

However, I play games as an escape, and one thing I hate both in movies and in games is a feeling of 'why bother'. Why bother fighting against zombies when humanity is doomed and there's no hope, just shoot yourself now and get it over with. And it's a very similar feeling to this. And again, I know it's supposed to be a feeling of war, and not knowing if it ever gets better.

The tipping point was where I overheard a soldier sexually assaulting a woman. And... I couldn't just do nothing. So I went in, and got gunned down by four soldiers. And.... I knew that was a bad idea. But. I still felt I had to. And afterwards, I just felt like there was no good options, and what was the point? And yes, I know these situations happen. It's realistic, gritty, and depressing. And it made me stop playing.

Now, everything I said is part of what makes this game what it is, and there's lots and lots of people who will say that, and it's my fault for not liking it. It is, I agree with that. And if what I said makes you interested in the game, great! I have no problem with other people liking this game, and I can understand why people WOULD like it.

But the bottom line is what *I* felt about this game, and whether I would personally recommend it. And I'm going to say no. I understand what it's going for, and I'm not going to fault it for being effective, but... I didn't enjoy it, I don't want to play more.

I appreciate the aesthetic and what the game tries to do. But the core gameplay loop is "crafting when you don't know the craft tree". So you either use a wiki or you use VERY limited resources to build something that you find out isn't especially useful at that point. That is fairly common in indie crafting games but This War Of Mine is all about ultra-tight resource limits, which is understandable given the set up. But it really ends up feeling like you spend much of the game just trying to memorize crafting trees so that on your NEXT play through you can execute things.

It is also a "long-form roguelike" by which I mean it is rogue-like with RNG and permadeath and whatnot. But a single playthrough can take hours. It can be frustrating to "play & fail to learn how to play" when that means dying two hours in the first time you encounter some new game element.

On top of that, there's a handful of annoyances. Selecting which character you control during the day is fussier than it should be. You can only tab between them, not select directly via hotkeys. There's lots of just waiting around -- skipping to the end of the day is very often sub-optimal. Which fits the theme but is pretty boring from a gamer perspective.

There are good things to say about This War of Mine. The music and artistic style are great and I appreciated the perspective it presented. My problem is with the game, itself. For starters, there's no introduction about how to play or how the controls work.  Right-click to run, left to sneak?  It also took me awhile to realize there's two different icons for "taking things" and "taking things from someone else." The day time requires micro-managing every character.  These people don't do anything for themselves except finding a chair to sit in. They'll complain about starving while standing in a kitchen with tons of food available.  There's no way to automate anything. Traps have to be built, baited, collected, and reset - manually.  Can't the trap just put food in my inventory and reset itself?  Oh, and there's a limit of two traps, but the game never tells you that. It doesn't even remove the option to build traps once you have the maximum two. Why can you make fuel at the stove, but not at the furnace? Why doesn't burning fuel at the stove heat the shelter? Why can you only melt snow on the stove? Why can't I use the furnace that's pumping out heat for the whole shelter? I mean, the shelter is 68-degrees, shouldn't the snow just melt on it's own? Oh, and after winter ends, why can't I melt the damn snow anymore?!

I micro-managed my way to the end of the war, but it was not fun.

It's a good game to sink time into, once you get the hang of it. Going to the same locations on different days can often surprise you.

While the inability to remove certain crafting stations after placing them is a downside, for the most part you can still customize the layout of your hideout. 

If I changed anything it would be the above-mentioned crafting station issue, and also how your survivors as a whole react to one of them having to kill hostile NPCs; while the reactions are realistic, it still bothers me a little bit to have a survivor called a murderer by ALL the others for (as an example) stopping the murder of an innocent by knifing a guy that the game itself has said is clearly deranged and twisted - or having to kill someone to defend yourself because they opened fire first and you couldn't run away fast enough.

But, that's nit-picking. The game is fun, as said. And if you want, you can even make your own survivor using your own irl photo for their portrait - or you can search the internet for a face you like and use that instead lol.

The game has this feature built in, so it can be done from the workshop screen in-game. You just need to make sure the portrait you want is .jpg format and is in the game's "portrait" folder.

The characters are barely written at all and I never really got attached, though I would get frustrated if 'good' characters (the ones with useful skills or stats) got sick or injured from random stuff I had no control over. Generally speaking that's rare though, and each scenario is short enough that even totally failing doesn't feel like a waste of time. I'd recommend this game for people who like survival stories/gameplay, and maybe for people who like stealth games (although the stealth here is very minimal and easy to master).

Now if you'll pardon me, gonna go fire up my PS1 and pick an RPG at random to reminisce about what story used to mean. Here's to hoping someone takes this game's format, addresses the shortfalls, and melds it the board game Dead Winter. Say what you want about zombie games, but THAT would be awesome.

Update: It's hard to say how long I've *actually* spent playing the game in total so far. As it is, TWoM is a faaaaaaaantastic restart/alt+F4 simulator due to an extreme number of design oversights or just plan bad design, the least of which is courtesy of RNGesus. I can't count the number of times I've had to restart an entire ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ day because 3 shots are deadlier to you with armor than 10 are to NPCs. Another obnoxious example of bad design - it seems that the number of bullets wasted during nightly raids even after being fully fortified scales with the number of firearms you have (haven't confirmed this due to how tedious experimentation is in this game, but the waste rate doubled immediately after making a second gun and has never dropped below 4 since, previous waste capped at 3 ~~~ Edit: Now confirmed - scales with available firearms), so be sure NEVER to have more than 1 gun on hand (doesn't matter what type) above whatever melee weapons. All in all, This War of Mine has great bones for anyone who wants to make a similar game, but be sure to be a little more sensible in your design, like having some way of recording when survivors have eaten last and having checkpoints after each gameplay section. Gets reeeeeeeeeally old redoing the same day's activities after RNGesus' shenanigans.

Make a mistake, initiate combat, and you'll be dealing with the consequences of a depressed, injured survivor for a week. The scenarios do offer some variation, but its picking your poison. For instance, in the heavy snow ones your survivors will never get warm enough, often get sick, and all wood is burned.

This was almost impossible to review as a game. As an examination of civilian survival under siege, it was extraordinarily effective. Anything that undermined conventional ideas of ‘fun’ or ‘balance’ did so deliberately, and correctly. You were [i]meant[/i] to feel rushed, tense, hungry, and exhausted. You were meant to feel miserable. That discomfort was the point, and it was handed out freely.

Systems that would normally be subject to criticism for friction or unfairness instead reinforced the theme. Scarcity, bad outcomes, and irreversible mistakes were not design flaws; they were the whole argument. Judged on its ability to communicate hardship rather than entertain, it succeeded completely.

Pursuing full completion was another matter entirely. Some achievements pushed the experience into deeply unpleasant territory, demanding actions that felt morally corrosive even within the game’s framework. For players inclined toward completionism, I hope you’re prepared to traumatize a child intentionally!

As an interactive work about war, it was powerful and unsparing. As a traditional game, it resisted being enjoyed, by design. That resistance was exactly what gave it weight.

This War of Mine is unlike any other war game out there. Instead of playing from perspective of a soldier or a leader of some sort, you get to play as ordinary citizens who find themselves trapped amidst a war. This game is basically divided into two major parts, the daytime and the night. During daytime you stay in your shelter and craft stuff, cook food and take care of the shelter and people in it while the night gives you a chance to go outside without being spotted by the snipers and scavenge stuff that you need for survival. The game allows you to steal and kill others but it comes with a price, if you steal or attack friendly people it will affect not only your character's mental state but also the mental state of others in your shelter whereas if you attack to help someone your character as well as others in shelter get a mental boost. 
There's a lot to talk about this game but I'll let you experience it yourself. If you want to experience what the ordinary civilians probably go through during times of war, this is the game for you.

There needs to be a label for reviews on steam where you can basically say, yeah there is a pandemic right now, sitting at home and playing a bunch of games I bought 600 years ago and filed away in my Steam library for the rainy day that never came.

This War of Mine was one of those games for me.  My reasoning for this was that the description and videos made me think it was gonna be really depressing. I was mostly wrong, it can get bleak occasionally but for the most part tragedy is avoidable (or, you can intentionally neglect some of your people if you want).

Its rough when you first start, there are a dozen things you need to craft in your home base from the very start but you can only scavenge so many materials each day, so you spend a lot of time juggling resources to best handle what your group of survivors need most at the time. 

When you scavenge (which you can only do at night, daytime is all about upgrading your base and taking care of your people), you sometimes run into situations where you can rob and kill innocents, and different player-characters react differently, some are appalled at unwarranted murder, others dont care, others still are glad to have more food/water/bullets at whatever cost. 

If one of your survivors gets mentally stressed enough, they can steal supplies and leave, or even commit suicide, but you have plenty of warning beforehand that you have an unhappy survivor and need to do something about it. Often, its just a matter of getting some cigarettes and coffee, or making sure they have a bed (that you have to craft) to sleep in.

A good game about resource and time management, it reminds me a lot of zombie-survival games, just without zombies.

It doesn't happen often that game captures the tough and hard situation of survival so well. 
The music only gives more strenght to this. 
This is a game that gives a whole new definition (for me) to war-themed games, and it's one my feelings weren't ready to discover. 
This games shows the terrible effects of war and that left a great impact.

I really want to like this game, I mean the atmosphere is fantastic, and I really like the idea, but I just can't. 

My major criticism is that the portrayal of the characters are not relatable nor realistic at all. As a fan of story-oriented games, this game sucks at this. They try really hard to make you feel bad, but I don't feel a thing at all because of the bad writing and lack of effort. Why can't I play as a psychopath who enjoys killing people? What's the point of "Good Cook" if it means one piece of resource can be saved every two days or so? The lack of variety is simply frustrating at times.

My second criticism is that the combat and inventory system SUCKS. Even though they attempted to make this game "realistic", but it doesn't mean you have to infuriate the players. Besides, what's realistic about using one type of ammo for shotgun, rifle, and pistol? It gets really boring after a while because people gets depressed so damn easily if they killed someone. But what's the point of combat system at all if the characters keep whining about it? The characters are not relatable in the first place, so it only frustrates me to see how ridiculous their reactions are.

The next criticism is that it seems they really don't get the point of this game when they made it. (which  improved a lot when they made Frostpunk). These so-called "moral dilemma" are plainly boring and stupid (again. bad writing). Fallout 1&2&New Vegas are infinitely superior than this game in this aspect. The writings are so bad and I'm like why tf would I want to care about these boring characters whom I know nothing about? Why tf would you want to portray the characters as either good or bad instead of delving into them and give them more depth? You can still see this in Frostpunk, where they only give you two choices: either be authoritarian or religious?? I don't know what to say anymore, and I definitely don't recommend this game.

[h1]Paradise Lost[/h1]
There’s a reason why war is among the most familiar backdrops in media. Within it, it’s easy to manage succinct objectives out of very complex situations, without tons of expository legwork. In video games we see war often. In real or fictional wars, war easily creates “good guys” and “bad guys” of us all. Everyone knows how devastating war can be, so using it can be an artificial way to manufacture empathy. An example would be Wolfenstein, a game in which you play as a Jewish-American solider in a Nazi-seized world. The premise, by itself, is probably enough to motivate most players through an entire narrative. You don’t need more. And you probably wouldn’t expect more. But in a way, that is kind of easy, isn’t it? Isn’t killing Nazis just a hall pass for murder?

Recently, what games have lacked in good narratives they’ve attempted to remedy with their imagery. For instance, anti-war messages in video games have existed for a long time. But since [i]Schindler’s List[/i] and [i]Casablanca[/i] don’t make good video games, it’s been extremely difficult for game creators to enforce anti-war messaging that doesn’t go one or two ways: (1) Portray the violence in the game so intensely that it makes you want to vomit, or (2) Display the psychological impact war has on the game’s protagonist. Both are valid and both have worked. 

But the irony in this sort of anti-war messaging is that those video games’ objectives almost always involve killing people. Anti-war, pro-murder.

That’s why This War of Mine is evolutionary. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2155859829

[h1]Anti-War and Anti-Murder?[/h1]
The story revolves around a group of survivors mixed up in a conflict coming to a neighborhood near you. The character Bruno, for instance, used to own his own restaurant before all this happened. Pavle, well, he used to be a star footballer. Katia, a reporter. And so on. The game - still being a game - notifies us of this for our survival purposes. So, the implication is that Bruno is probably a good cook, and Pavle is probably a fast runner. Katia’s interpersonal skills could make her a good bargainer. All of which will come in handy throughout this war of yours. 

Circumstances for this conflict vary wildly. The given scenario changes with each play-through, as does the cast you’ll control. Sometimes the war starts in winter. Sometimes not. Sometimes it lasts 25 days. Sometimes 50. Everyone is just stuck waiting, and praying, that one of the great militaries of the world will save these people from themselves. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2155860197

In the meantime, however, you need to survive. You’re going to need supplies, warmth, food, and weapons. And the true game is figuring out how to manage it all. And through the process of managing it, you’ll become hyper-aware of just how desperate these people are. Not just the player characters - the entire surrounding populace. Whether or not to risk your best scavenger’s life to save a woman from being ravaged by a solider, or to just keep walking, has a way of developing the characters and underlining the hell they’re in. It also brings a full-stop to any attempt of oversimplification. History is written by the victors, sure, but those people don’t exist yet. For now, it’s just a town of inhabitants, rolling around in the mud, fighting to exist.

[h1]Hell For Certain[/h1]
At first, when someone tries to kill you, you’re going to feel like you’re playing a game. “Good guys” and “bad guys” clearly defined. But when the time comes when YOU kill someone to survive, or steal from the sick to survive, or pour resources into your most valuable survivor first, to the peril of the rest - you begin to understand. There are no Nazis here. It’s demeaning, but thoughtful. Dehumanizing, but practical. In my game, if Pavle died - we all could. 

And he did. 

Some characters you meet reject the game’s experiment, forever convinced that looting is wrong, that killing is wrong. Others, however, are more understanding. Regardless of where the player falls on the spectrum, you’ll eventually have to face reality: Your characters are stuck here and help may not be coming. This means reevaluating previous lines you never thought you’d cross. Outside of this, Pavle played a kid’s game for a king’s ransom; inside of this, all that means is that he’s faster than most of his would-be murderers. 

[h1]Differing Priorities[/h1] 
The actual game mechanics are a Venn diagram of genres. It meshes survival horror, real-time strategy, with point-and-click adventure. Aside from its lofty concepts, the game is actually quite simple. If it’s cold, burn wood. When you’re hungry, cook food. At night, someone can scavenge for supplies to use or trade. Others stay to sleep or guard the base. The issue is that these decisions usually result in rather mundane gameplay - hours of watching someone sleep will do that. Prioritizing the day is what actually makes it interesting. The problem is that the safer you are (being safe is obviously the goal), the less fun there is to be had. Managing your base poorly, however, forces you to make more interesting choices. Choices like, Who gets to eat for the day? Playing the game well can result in a lot of sitting and waiting for one character to finish a nap so you can take yours. Not a triumph.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2155860997

At night, things change. This is when you scavenge for supplies. A beautiful cat-and-mouse game unfolds that perfectly balances risk and reward. Moral dilemmas constantly arise. As an example, you can donate to the hospital or steal from it. Maybe you need the supplies more? Maybe someone at base is dying? Do you value your lives above strangers? You’ll find yourself defending every hard choice, probably not unlike real survivors would in similar circumstances. Nothing is about what you want, it’s what you need. How do you judge someone that did what they had to do to survive?

While these characters are mostly silent in a story stuffed with game-y inventory management (like how everyone just happens to know how to build a radio, provided you have the parts), they still feel like genuine three-dimensional characters that I want to know more about. If they survive this hell, do they keep in touch? It’s that type of thinking that the game asks of the player, and is willing to sacrifice a lot the fun-factor for, in order to drive the points home. Does that make it a better game? No. Not really. But it is what makes it important and innovative. Sometimes that can be preferable. 

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
This War of Mine is, at times, a profound experience. It never really becomes a great game, but it is still a game I absolutely recommend. It’s not for everyone. But if you do decide to take the plunge, you’re going to find it more rewarding if you just let it wash over you. It’s not about the heroes with the highest body count. And while the game’s proposition is better than the game itself, rest assured there’s enough here to keep you interested long after a cease-fire arrives.

written review:

This War of Mine is a game where your objective is to survive the war. The war lasts for 20 to 50 in-game days. My first playthrough on Steam took me 7 hours with war concluding on day 32. The game is divided into day time, where you build, reinforce your shelter, decide what to do with visitors at your door if they come, talk with other survivors, eat, etc and nighttime where you go out scavenging for supplies. The smallest group of survivors that you can start with is 2 and the largest group that you can end up with is 4. 

Positives:

- great music and atmosphere. The game has very well designed sound and visuals. It is grim looking, but it never depressed me, the tune giving it more of a mellow vibe. 

- the game is fairly challenging. You will always lack supplies, I don't think I had many nights when I was sure that I had food for the next day. You also have a chance of being attacked and raided in the middle of the night. The war feels unfair, but at the same time it is definitely survivable. 

- engaging gameplay, I can't really say that I ever got bored. I always end up thinking "just one more night". 

Negatives:

- I would love a fast forward button for day time that doesn't just end the day. Often times I come to rely on mouse traps for food and it is random will the trap catch something, meaning I end up sitting the whole daytime together with my survivors staring at the trap, trying to figure out if we are getting anything to eat today or not. 

- sometimes it is very hard to figure out what will make people angry. Once I was gunned down for rummaging in the garbage bin outside the hospital. As the garbage bin didn't have "private property" all over it, I didn't think that the nearby people would mind, I mean it's a garbage bin! It seems that they did. 

- Dubious morals of my group - if ya'll going to judge me for stealing some food from a military base when we are all starving, then at the very least I would like to be able to not disclose the fact that I did steal food from a military base when we were all starving with you. 

- I sometimes would get stuck in the fridge when trying to talk to the child in my group. In order to avoid having my survivors be immobile for the whole day I would reload. Once you reload the outcome of that day can change, so a few times I ended up save scumming without intending to and undid a few raids on my shelter that I honestly could have lived with. 

Overall: 

This War of Mine is probably one of the only games that try to actively show you how bad a war is that I not only don't mind, but actively enjoy. It can feel unfair and can make me want to ragequit every single time when I lose a survivor, but it also keeps me coming back. I don't know would I buy This War of Mine full price, but it's on sale so often these days, that I got to say that if you catch it on sale, it's definitely worth your time to give it a go. If I had to put a numerical value on it, I would say that this game is easily an 8 out of 10.

Honestly I didn't expect much depth from this game when I first got it. I thought it would be your typical, small-scale strategy game with some minor base-building and resource management elements; the kind that you see from a lot of small indie studios that develop games as side projects or for fun and offer them for peanuts after a few years, or even for free.

Boy, was I wrong. The art style is fantastic, the gameplay is quite interesting, the storytelling is compelling and deep, and combined with the array of customizability for each playthrough (from characters, locations, special events, etc), there is an immense amount of potential replayability.

The premise of the game is to expose the player to the untold stories of war: the fractured families; the scared children; the lonely poor - all of whom are often forgotten amidst the chaos, and the greatest recognition they eventually receive is as a statistic, and nothing more. Stories like this are occasionally told in movies, in TV shows, even in cartoons, but in the medium of gaming all we tend to think of in a "war game" is soldiers and armies, but never the civilians fearing for their lives that are neither responsible for the conflict nor equipped to handle it, but are invariably caught in the thick of it. The setting the game bases off of - the 1992-1996 siege of Sarajevo - is also a living memory for many of us today, which adds a level of relatability, as opposed to the historical distance we see in most war games today.

The story is not narrated to the player through loads of cutscenes and exposition. Instead, the game prefers to let the player infer the story from the events that unfold naturally throughout each playthrough. Certain game mechanics, like listening to the radio every morning for news or eavesdropping on NPCs, will be key sources of information that will influence your decisions and supplant your understanding of your environment. [b]That[/b] is the story, and each playthrough will tell you a different one.

The core gameplay is quite simple and straightforward for the most part - you have resources which you need to survive, and you know of some means that could [i]potentially[/i] acquire you more. You can allot tasks to your survivors during the day to improve your dwelling, and at night you can send someone to search for resources around the city. However, that's pretty much all the game tells you, and that's all you need to know...at first. Eventually you will be surprised by special events that are influenced by your past actions, and you, as the player, will be just as equipped to handle them as the civilians you are playing as, making for a surprisingly immersive experience.

You learn and grow with your survivors, and you will learn to refine your plans and revise your expectations the more you play. For example, locations you are planning to visit in the coming days may be suddenly cordoned off by a military blockade or heavy snowfall, and if you have nowhere else to scavenge for resources, and nothing saved up, you're in for a tough few days until the situation eases up - and you don't know if/when that will even happen. This is where people get desperate, and you may have to turn to violence in order to ensure your survival. This is a reality of war, and the game presents this concept implicitly, but honestly.

Conversely, you may have shown kindness to someone in need earlier, and they may come to your aid later in the playthrough by offering you something you desperately need. Your actions have consequences - good, bad, and ugly - and the game reminds you of that universal truth throughout every playthrough, incorporating an impressive level of emotional depth too.

Arms and ammunition are valuable resources that present significant risk to their owners and their victims alike, and using them will instill a level of guilt in your group; you can't gun down every hostile character you see, and depending on the context, killing people will make your survivors sad. Your survivors possess empathy and will question the actions that [b]you[/b] as the player put them through, reasoning that the people they may have killed were just trying to protect themselves, and may even fall into depression if you don't find a way to stop that.

This is the reality of war. It's not always glory and action. It's not always black and white. It's not always us vs them. Sometimes it's loneliness and survival. Sometimes it's anger and guilt. Sometimes... it's us vs our own vices.

We do know one thing for certain though: It affects all of us. Everyone who has lived through a war has their own story to tell, that's why the title is This War of [b]Mine[/b]. That's the message I think this game is trying to tell, and that's the message I took away from my experience with it.

This War of Mine is a grimy game that will make you think about how your decisions will impact your survivors, and those within the world.

From choosing whether to kill or steal from a family for your own basic survival, to choosing to turn away those in need, the game will continually try to make you feel like a horrible person, and it does that exceedingly well within some arguably gorgeous locations, even if they're made to look like hell.
The combat and stealth mechanics in the game are done pretty well, and certainly don't detract from the game, causing you to have to decide whether to use what limited ammo you have in a fight, or to try and avoid it, at the risk of a civilian dying without your intervention.

I heavily recommend This War of Mine if it interests you at all.

This War of Mine takes a fresh and original concept of letting you play as the civilians instead of the military. The game however is marred by the fact that its almost unfun and just a chore to play.

The core gameplay is a rather simple survivalist/base building genre. This is all well and good but the issue is no matter what you do the game always seems to actively punish you. I'll explain, the game puts a massive emphasis on taking care of your survivors mental well being. Smokes and alcohol are huge in helping deal with this. This problem is made worse by the fact that both of these are luxury items and expensive and difficult to find. You can in fact craft them but it takes time to set up a Water purifier, Still, Herbal garden. This wouldn't be so bad if a key crafting material in the game, [b]wood[/b] ,didn't take up a whole inventory slot for every 2 of them you have. Most survivors have about a standard of 10 to 12 slots. Meaning at most from a single scavenging run you can make about 20 to 22 wood and a Herbal potted plant takes an absurd 30 wood for just one. This is made worse by the fact that if all of your survivors are smokers they will require an astonishing 9 smokes a day. It's bad enough that you have to manage food and security but having your own survivors a REQUIRE valuable commodity that the game itself describes as a valuable currency seems backwards.

Also to touch on moods the game will punish you for playing aggressively. Kill to many bandits? Depression. Get Raided to many times? Depression. Wait you fended them off everytime, doesn't matter depression. Only by helping certain other civilians can your mood for your survivors increase. Its compounded making it worse by the fact that many of these events are random chance outside scavenging missions. 

There's so many more things I could get into but I've tried to give this game a chance. If the inventory isssue was fixed or possibly made moods less brutal but you almost have to play the game a very specific way to avoid all this. Don't believe me go look at the wiki and guides for how your supposed to get set up in the first few days. There's not much room for error and its not much suggestion its more or less YOU HAVE TO HAVE THIS BY X DAY.

First day, I started with three survivors in an abandoned house, the first day was filled with stuff to do in the house. Second day, I have resources to craft some beds and a stove out of, as well as the ability to make a few meals. So I do that, and it takes up less than a quarter of the time I have available in the day, and there is nothing else I can do in the house without lockpicks. So I send everyone to sleep. Night comes, one person was still a bit sick so I send the scavenger out again and accidentally send the other two to sleep, and send the scavenger to the same house to get some important stuff they left behind before, and they return safely, but the house was robbed with no one on guard.

Third day, I got some building and trading resources, none of which I have a need for now. There is nothing for my survivors to do, so I send them to sleep. It stinks I couldn't keep them busy, but this night is going to be profitable with them all rested and ready! I can keep one on guard and send two to scavenge, twice the loot! I select them both and... wait one isn't selected, now the other one isn't selected.... I can't send multiple people to scavenge? Not just to separate locations, but I can't send them both to the same location? I wasted the day because I had nothing to do, now I have three healthy, fed, and rested survivors and I can't do anything extra during the night? 

This is where I threw in the towel. I was annoyed I had to waste the day. Seriously? They can't tear down the fence for wood? They can't read books to learn better survival techniques, they can't hang out and try and boost morale? They just have to sleep? And then I reach night, not needing ANYONE to sleep, and yet only one can scavenge? This is just with three survivors, I know this game goes up to at least 5. I can only use ONE person to get ALL my crafting resources, ALL my trading resources, ALL my food? No wonder the game puts you in a tough spot, it forces one character to do most of the work in keeping 3-5 people alive. I know it's a game, I know that the games goal is to put me in artificially tough spots, but the game also is responsible for making it believable, for getting me immersed in it's world. The world is supposed to be brutally like our own world (just post-apoc) and yet I can't have my survivors work as a team when it matters?

I want to send out two scavengers and keep one person on guard, have a great night looting, and find the person on guard injured or dead because he had no support. I want to give my scavenger backup when he tries to steal from another group of survivors, or the combined inventory space to make breaking into a heavily guarded compound worth it. 

I want the agency to be overly ambitious, to take bigger risks, and the chance to be rewarded for taking care of my survivors. Right now there is no reward, I knew I didn't have enough food, I knew it was going to get colder, and yet I couldn't do anything to prepare for it. Not because I was at my wits end, because my people were too busy. No. I had the time, I had the health, and the game wouldn't let me prepare for it. All I get to do is one-two guards, maybe one person sleeping, and one scavenger. That would be my war, that would be every night, that would be the game. The game, this game, wouldn't even give me the illusion of a chance, of agency over my future.

Short Version: Stop reading all other reviews; don't buy this game. 
Whole Review: This War of Mine is a side scrolling adventure game donning a very powerful theme of being a civilian during a military conflict/rebellion/etc in a fictitious country. You start the game with literally nothing and have to ransack an abandoned war-torn building, which becomes your base of operations, to recover from hunger and fatigue. To keep your civilian(s) alive and well, you must source food, medical supplies, water, eventually heat, firearms for defense, building materials to fortify the building. Challenges like armed thugs and physical obstacles which will require tools to be crafted can be expected from any game; This War of Mine keeps it interesting. Not every NPC is an “enemy” so your civilian(s) will react negatively to stealing from or killing other civilians. Inventory at the base is unlimited but in the field it’s pretty restrictive- downright minimal if you’re going out to scavenge while equipped with tools and weapons. The theme keeps what could be a simple game extremely engaging with the theme, music, and camera work.

The combat in this game is so poorly designed that it is literally unplayable. I can’t stress this enough: un-play-a-ble.

There is no tutorial on combat. You will die at the hands of your first armed assailant. You will Google it. You will be confused further. You will quit forever or start the game over.
If you power through it, you’ll figure out how to wield a melee weapon. You will die again while instructing your civ to attack someone who’s trying to murder you. The exact circumstance may vary, but you will be hammering away at your mouse/board/controller screaming YOU ARE BEING [attacked] AT STOP [adverb]ING AND [expletive]ING FIGHT BACK. Then you will die. Then you will press Alt+F4 (save points are at the end of night encounters).
If you repeat this process enough and don’t actually die in real life from your blood pressure spiking, you will identify that the action button does not initiate attacks and deduce that there must be a dedicated button. If you are quarantined due to an IRL global health concern, you will qualify what the attack button is and you will read something on the internet about ‘backstabbing’. If you are stubborn, you will fire the game back up and attempt to stealth your way upto an attacker.
If you succeed in stealthing your way up to and backstab an NPC, excellent. If you fail to backstab, you will just stab, and there’s actually a decent chance you’ll frantically repeatedly stab at your now-victim.
The fact that combat is such a crucial part of the game, and that it’s so poorly setup, makes this game something I can’t recommend.

This game absolutely fulfills its mission by living up to the theme text: "In modern war, you'll die like a dog for no good reason."

You have just enough power to influence the world a little bit for the better - and it actually feels impactful and satisfying. 

The art is great. The game mechanics are great. And I for one really like the UI. As much as you need UI to function in games, it's easy to let it get out of control and prevent the more thematic elements from drawing you in. It's hard to believe you're in a scary dungeon when there are neon green health bars everywhere. And many a game hath reminded us of mundanity by displaying micro-transaction options. 

This game has 0 micro-transactions - it's a truly story-driven, all-inclusive game. And despite being a strategic game (generally RTSs have the most intrusive UI) it still keeps the UI VERY minimal. You don't have a glaring "happiness" meter. You simply see that someone is "sad" or "depressed" etc. And you have to figure out how to cheer them up. 

This brings me to another highlight (imo): the game doesn't treat you like you're dumb. Granted, it's pretty harsh entering the world with NOTHING in the way of a tutorial and being told to figure it out or die - but honestly, that's the point of this game. It is genuinely not meant to glorify war. War is bad. You do NOT want to be there. That's the whole point.

As described, This War of Mine is a game about keeping normal, non-military people survive during a period of war in a fictional city.

The two phases to the gameplay are scavenging and survivor maintenance. During the day, you have to decide what your survivors will do with their current resources, whether it's maintaining their shelter, cooking food, growing food and even choosing who to help that shows up at your front door. During the night, you send a single scavenger out to get more resources. Sometimes, you must put this scavenger in danger to secure more valuable items such as better food or weapons.
 
What this game does really well is to keep the player on their toes. Every facet of survival is important, from sickness, to hunger, psychological stress and heat. Neglecting any of these at inopportune moments can have a major effect on the survival of the whole group. As such, the game is a little punishing as any bad mistakes such as missing a day of scavenging due to illness/injury/death can begin a downward spiral into a game over. There are ways to recover, but it usually involves making some tough choices. And yes, you'll feel the weight of very choice you make.

The game has some replay value, but once you've figured out how to handle the various situations, the game loses its tension. I found the first 30 hours or so very immersive as I was still learning how to optimize survival.

As far as the base game goes, it's very good and well worth your time. There's a learning curve but I don't think it's too steep. It was honestly kind of fun struggling to keep everyone alive, wondering whether the next day would be better than the last. Hmm, that sounds like the kind of experience the devs were going for...

This is a game where you have to make some difficult choices, and the dire mathematics of survival come to the fore. In this gritty zero sum game, your choices improve or reduce your characters' chances of surviving to the end of the war. 

Imagine The Sims, only instead being in an affluent consumist society they were concerned with stray bullets and plain survival. Who cares about a new pair of snickers or ice cream when you have to choose between using that thermostat in your hydroponic farm to grow your own increasingly scarce food, or the furnace to reduce the risk of someone in your group growing sick and/or dying overnight? Should you use your last antibiotics to try to prevent that companion from dying of acute pneumonia - or save the medicine for an easier case, incidentally improving the food situation for your other hungry dwellers? Are you willing to rob that old couple's house and sentence them to die, or can you afford not to do so? Will you duck and hide while a girl is raped in front of you, or risk fighting an armed soldier?

Adding complexity to the equation, children are a bright beam of hope; hopefully you'll manage keep them alive and as untraumatized as possible. Lead the characters too deeply into despair, though, and they might start getting into destructive drunken brawls, running away in the night, or giving up and offing themselves.

Should you think it needs rebalancing, there are mods to help make the game easier (or if you go overboard with them, make it too easy) or, conversely, turn an already hard game of hard choices into a living nightmare where you become glad that the developers balked at the idea of including cannibalism.

The experience and atmosphere in This War of Mine has been executed to perfection, perhaps because it's based so heavily on real-life events. Set in the fictional city of Pogoren in the equally fictional country of Graznavia, the game is based on the siege of Sarajevo, which lasted from 1992 to 1996. You play as defenceless civilians trapped in a war zone, and the reality of the situation is absolutely relentless. You don't play as any sort of soldier or fighter. Most of your survivors are wholly inexperienced in a fight, and can and will die. Even if you survive getting into a fight, wounds sustained can worsen without the help of difficult-to-obtain bandages, and condemn you to a slow death. 

This War of Mine is a testament to the unique properties of gaming as a storytelling medium, and if for no other reason, is a game that everyone should certainly play if possible.

This War of Mine is a unique survival game that, if expanded upon, could develop into its own sub-genre. You will get invested in the plight of your survivors.  You will be forced to make sacrifices between their health and their safety.  In the later stages of the game, the risk you impose on one survivor can mean the difference between whether or not the rest can survive.  Your decisions will affect what happens to the others that inhabit the game world.

But the game does more than that by setting the game inside an active warzone.  Many of us who play this game will never know what it is like to be trapped inside the city while a battle rages on the streets.  This War of Mine attempts to show us, vicariously, the plight of being powerless in the face of a great danger.  This War of Mine allows us to empathize with those less fortunate than us; from the starving child to the homeless war veteran.  

100% recommend.

Steam tells me I have played this game for 246 hours. That sounds insane (and maybe it is) but I consider every one of those hours well spent. I simply love this game. I have beaten every scenario, some multiple times. Everything from the atmosphere to the music to the crafting system to the difficulty of the combat system is flawlessly executed. 

I'll tell you the story of my first play through (no spoilers). On the very first night, one of my characters got shot but managed to escape. Over the next few days he existed in a badly injured limbo, trying to heal while my other characters cooked, cleared the shelter, and scavenged during night. On day 4, he died. My other characters were devastated. One left the shelter due to depression and the other died of starvation since she was the only one left (it’s hard to survive on your own). I think it was all over by around day 15.

 After “losing” (dying) I stared at the menu screen for a second. "Ugh," I thought to myself. "This is intense. I’m not sure I can play this thing." I quit the game. Over the next day or so however, I kept thinking about how compelling the game was, even though I had had a tough go of it. "If only my guy didn’t get shot, I think I could have found some food and I could have made it a bit longer," I thought. I decided to try again. I played the same scenario (The one with Pavel, Katia, and Bruno, FYI), and this time I was prepared. I had a pen and paper and I made a list every night before scavenging of the quantity of supplies I needed to craft the items vital for survival the next day. I avoided dangerous areas. I got smarter about which locations to visit and how to scavenge effectively. I got better at knowing what to craft at which stage in the game, and finally, I beat the first scenario. All three characters survived the war. I was HOOKED. I played another scenario. And another. And when The Little Ones came out, I snatched it right up and played all of those scenarios. I played every character and got to know each location and each characters’ stories. 

This game is brutally unforgiving. Give yourself some time to learn. Don’t be afraid to reset. You must be smart. you must plan. you must AVOID danger until you get the hang of how to survive. You will be rewarded in time. This game is mood AF; It’s dark and emotionally complex. War is dark and emotionally complex. Be the light in the dark. Help your neighbors. Don’t steal. Don’t kill innocent people. Or, see how it feels to steal to survive. Kill thugs and innocents alike. It’s up to you. I just hope you enjoy this game as much as I have, even if you don’t spend 246 hours on it.  

Hopefully I have done a shred of justice by convincing you to buy this masterpiece of a game. Playing makes me want to kiss my fingertips like an Italian chef, MUAH! It’s a gooda gamea!

[i]This War of Mine[/i] is an artistically beautiful [b]3D[/b] side-scrolling survival simulation. The gameplay is initially [u]very difficult[/u] and new players may find the lack of tutorial infuriating as they inefficiently craft and struggle with scavenging. Restarting two or three times in the first (game) week is not anything to be ashamed of and as such new players should strive to learn from their mistakes.

Upon the first successful completion of the campaign  (newly "veteran") players may fail to see the replay value; the lack of unique, repeat play-through achievements being their primary focus. I would encourage them to return to the campaign menu and to choose a new team, from there the focus should be on how they decide to play. Will you be a 'life-is-cruel' armed survivor, executing your enemies with practiced techniques? Will you remember your previous crafting mistakes? Trading for what you need and never stealing from the helpless and poor. The choices are many and as varied as your own individual tastes!

[i]This War of Mine's[/i] unique perspective on life in war is not something that should be so casually passed aside. There is real legitimate challenge for 'hardcore' gamers that are searching for that next trophy highlight. And for the casual player there is plenty to appreciate. I hope that this brief recommendation helps you to [b]add[/b] this wonderful game to your collection. Good luck, you'll need it... at least initially :D

This game is dark and more of a survival game than most others. There is also one hell of a difficulty curve. Its great to just get immersed into. There are some bugs but atmosphere and story far outweigh those minor issues. Unlike MANY RPG games, your choices actually have significant impact on your game. You doing the morally right thing actually may result in your death. For example:

I came across a small home with an elderly couple. I had some food to spare so i left them alone because what kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ takes from the helpless elderly? Well two or three days later i was out of food and one of my characters had been killed on another scavenging run trying to save a woman from a group of bandits. The remaining party members were tired, sick, and on low moral. I could only go somewhere easy, somewhere no one would fight. Low risk high reward. So i went back to that elderly couple, and took everything they had, including the medicine they had for the old man. I needed it to treat a sick member of my party. Those elderly people likely died after i left. They had no food or medicine to keep them going. It was me and mine or them. 

All that is just ONE story line. There are countless examples. Unlike most games where you are rewarded for doing the right thing, in this game doing the right thing can be a death sentence

This is definitely the best war game in history that shows how the situation is awful in the times of war. The game reminds me the documentaries I watched about Bosnia and Rwanda where similar things were happened in the year of 1994, the year I was born and sadly it is still happening in countries like Libya, Yemen and Syria after 25 years. Its realistic and depressing features makes the game even more deep. You are controlling few strangers in an abandoned building and trying to stay alive in an environment where other thugs are around to rob your shelter, while also every night one of your characters go to other places and find the things that can be useful. 

Also, it is the best survival action game I have ever played. It does not just force you to search and craft things to be alive, but also every character has his/her own personality and skills. They have their own understanding of morals and emotions which sometimes brought conflict with other characters when you decide an action for an example killing someone to take his/her food or helping other people. The moods of the characters always change according to your decisions and gameplay throughout the game and they affect your characters movement really. For an example, if your character has very low morale, s/he walks very slow and unwillingly.

The sad thing is the game starts to be repetitive after a time and the things that you can do becomes very limited, like the majority of sandbox survival games. However still, it has a very long campaign that add new stuffs almost every day and also stories, including the ones with children in DLC, are great too. Graphic design is also very great for a low budget game. 

Don't miss this painful but deep surviving experience.

I've played this game pretty much since it came out. It succeeds at the two things it attempts: it's a credible, thoughtful, well balanced resource-managing strategy game. Weighing up the decisions that need to be made to survive can pose some genuine conundrums. 
The second success is in presenting an engrossing, emotional and starkly immersive look at war through the eyes of desperate civilians. The emotional impact of making selfish or even murderous choices to get by can weight very heavily on the characters. Sometimes you have to just do whatever it takes to survive and live with the consequences because at least that entails living. Other times, a kinder, more altruistic choice will pay off and provide a morale boost or at least prevent an emotional catastrophy among the survivors.
The graphics and music are supremely engrossing, and the game-play is compelling and challenging. This is an astonishing experience, easily one of my favourite games of all time.

In war, there are only losers.

This game is simple, yet its message is profound. Too often we avert our eyes from the ugly truth, the horrors that war can inflict upon us. This game puts you into the shoes of ordinary civilians trapped in the crossfire, trying their best just to survive.  You will be able to feel their helplessness vividly, either through the lack of resources or the moral dilemmas that you will be presented with. What will you keep: Your moral code, or your group from starving?

You know, I really want to recommend this game. The concept is brilliant, the dark, oppressive theme is truly addicting to those who like dystopian settings. I've played it to death and keep going back to it.

So why do I not recommend this game? Easy. It's a buggy mess. 

Ever since the final version came out my sessions have been infuriatingly bugged. A well known woman in the church level causes the whole community to hunt you down because she goes hysterical for no reason. Items you have stored in one place on a level will just disappear. Now you *could* argue that this is something that would happen in the setting. People are naturally paranoid and hostile. Leave your supplies in one place and go back to them and it could be cleared out by someone else. Maybe we can forgive the game for those bugs which ruin your supply run or inexplicably get your character killed (remember it's permadeath too). However, then when the character you are playing starts acting out, that's where I had enough. I decided to brave a bandit-held building and tried to hide from one of them in the designated spot. However, she proceeded to glitch in and out of the hiding spot and not respond to any of my controls, proceeding to do the Harlem Shake in and out of cover as three guys casually surrounded her. Two shotgun blasts later, my character was dead by glitch, my only scavenger was dead, leaving an old man and his grandson to starve and freeze to death, and about two hours of my playtime wasted. This wouldn't be a problem if I could reload but you cannot. I understand the permadeath function in a game like this and I actually enjoy that. However, permadeath needs to have a stable game to work on. This game is not stable. 

The company seems to focus more on spewing out DLC than fixing their bugs, so I would suggest not bothering.

This game is truly one of the greatest games I have ever played. Each time you start a new save, its a different set of decisions and different strategies to get through. I love so many aspects of it but I will highlight a few of my favorites:

Decisions impact your characters!

If you choose to steal and kill, your characters will be sad, affected by how you are surviving the war. To me this is a welcome change to war game genres where you usually play a bloodthirsty murderer who has little conscience nor consideration of how you are affecting the world around you. For example, I stole some wooden planks on my most recent play through, and the characters were concerned about the people we stole from. Excellent. You also have to play off the strengths of the characters you have and look for the items that they may need to help keep them happy (e.g. cigarettes and coffee).

Characters and Trade

I enjoy that you can trade with many people, and that they have their resources renewed so I dont solely have to scavenge. 

SUGGESTIONS! Because even the greatest games have things they could improve on.

Scavenging...

I think this part is intriguing, although I would love it if we could get some sort of expanded backpack/carrying mechanism so i could carry more (e.g. a car, cart, wheelbarrow, or even easily as having two characters go to scavenge.)  

Food

I think if we are truly at the beginning of the war, or realtively close to it, it would be fun to have a wider variety of food you can find (e.g. chips) things that would have been hoarded but probably forgotten. I do enjoy how if you dont eat for two days, you still need two meals to make up for it.


All in all, I would highly recommend that you buy this game, play it, and enjoy it. It is an intense game and there is very little that I didn't love about it.

In my ongoing and likely futile effort to write a Steam review for every game in my library (#248 out of 558)... it's time for This War of Mine.

I'm a bit hesitant to throw around words like "overrated," but if I were to be completely honest here, I'd have to say that This War of Mine is far from the transcendental experience many in the games media portrayed it as being. It remains, however, an excellent Roguelike survival game with a unique setting that is very much worth your time if you're fond of the genre.

The basic premise is simple and compelling by nature of its uniqueness: you control a group of civilian survivors in a besieged town, scavenging for food and supplies while trying to keep safe from the battles occuring all around you as well as other, less scrupulous survivors. The actual mechanics are all fairly standard, and provide a solid if unimaginative difficulty curve of increasing desperation. Where This War of Mine shines is the occassional ethical quandrary forced upon you. Ultimately all of these dilemma boil down to the same problem: resources are finite. Will you sieze what you need by force, even if it means taking from others whose need might be greater? 

This layer of ethical consideration is what transforms This War of Mine from being a relatively bland roguelike survival game into something genuinely engaging and memorable. How far are you willing to compromise your morals to survive? And it's a theme that is only heightened by the game's roguelike nature, as you find yourself asking that question again and again and again. When you're sneaking through the apartment of an elderly couple, knowing that if you take their food, they will likely starve is a difficult problem to parse out by itself, but is even more powerful on the second, third, fourth and fifth time through -- because you know that without that food, your own ragtag group of survivors will very likely die instead.
