This War of Mine

This War of Mine is not your typical war game. Instead of charging through battlefields as a soldier, you control a group of civilians struggling to survive the horrors of a besieged city. This unique perspective, combined with its unflinching portrayal of war's brutality, has made it a critically acclaimed title. But is it a game for everyone?

Strengths:

- Hauntingly realistic: The game doesn't shy away from the harsh realities of war. Characters 
  deal with hunger, sickness, depression, and difficult moral choices. This creates a powerful 
  emotional impact that stays with you long after playing.
- Resource management: Scavenging for food, medicine, and crafting materials is a constant 
  challenge. Every decision feels weighty, forcing you to consider the needs of your group and 
  potential consequences.
- Moral dilemmas: The game presents difficult choices that have no easy answers. Stealing 
  from others, trading with armed factions, and even resorting to violence are all possible 
  actions, each with its own consequences. This forces players to confront the complexities of 
  wartime morality.
- Storytelling: While not a linear narrative, the game creates compelling stories through 
  character interactions and random events. Each playthrough feels unique, offering new 
  challenges and emotional moments.

Weaknesses:

- Repetitive gameplay loop: While the stories and scenarios change, the core gameplay loop 
  of scavenging, crafting, and managing resources can feel repetitive at times.

Overall:

This War of Mine is a powerful and thought-provoking experience that challenges players to think about the human cost of war. Its unflinching portrayal of hardship and moral dilemmas is not for the faint of heart, but for those seeking a unique and impactful game, it's a must-play. However, be prepared for its emotional weight and potential for repetitive gameplay.

Recommendation:
Highly recommended for players who enjoy resource management, challenging choices, and stories with emotional impact. Not recommended for those seeking a lighthearted experience or high replayability.

Additional notes:
The game is available on various platforms, including PC, consoles, and mobile devices.
There are several DLCs available that add new stories, characters, and locations.
If you're unsure if the game is right for you, you can watch gameplay videos or read reviews from other players.

This is a sombre, interesting game, with solid storylines and good game mechanics. You're drawn into a moral quagmire while trying to provide the basics to keep your people alive.
The controls can feel clumsy at times. Nonetheless, I have heartily enjoyed the hundreds of hours that I've put into this game.

Much of the game knowledge is supposed to be learned on the go, as if you really are a clueless city-dweller caught up in a war, unsure of how to survive when society is crumbling. But, here are several key pieces of advice that I think it is unfair of the game to withhold from you, and I would have been spared a lot of frustration if I'd known them before my first game:

1) When using a keyboard & mouse, you can select a survivor either by clicking on them or by clicking on their portrait in the bottom-right. As well as left-clicking to make them walk somewhere, you can right-click or double-click to make your survivor run there. I only discovered that last one after the first time that I tried to get through Sniper Junction; Sniper Junction without running went about as well as you'd expect.

2) You will never experience combat around your shelter. You are always safe during daytime; nobody will come to fight you during the day. At night, there is a random chance of your shelter getting attacked by bandits, but you don't directly control the defence.

3) You'll need to scavenge lots of basic materials to build up your base enough to survive. It's totally normal at the very start of the game to fill your scavenger's backpack with nothing but wood and components before returning home. If you see an item with unknown potential, then you can leave it for later in the game.

4) This is the most important piece of advice. When eating cooked food or canned food, survivors only need to eat once every 2 days. There is no benefit to serving them cooked/canned food once every day, you just deplete your food stocks twice as fast. So, if you build a stove from the outset, then you only need to feed your (original) survivors on odd-numbered days starting with day 3.

5) Once you've built a radio, you can turn the dial on it to change the frequency: there is more than one radio station!
Also, if there's no news since yesterday on a station, then it'll just show you yesterday's news story. No, that radio station doesn't really have 3 employees named Jovan who were all shot by snipers on consecutive days.

6) If a member of the public knocks on the door asking for help, and their spiel includes words like, "come with me," then responding, "Yes," will cause your survivor to immediately leave the shelter with them and not return until the next day. Make sure that you send a survivor with no more daily responsibilities to the door if you want to answer Yes!
Responding, "No," will make the petitioner never come back, responding, "Give me a minute," will make them hang around a bit longer, and responding, "Maybe later," will make them come back another day.

7) Your shelter starts out with various bits of non-interactable furniture that just look like background decoration; but once you get a hatchet, you discover that you can chop them up. You can quickly gather a big bounty of wood and fuel this way. Don't get confused and start chopping up your beds by mistake, though!

8) After improving your workbench, you are able to repair some of the breaches in your shelter's walls. It's a great way to improve your defences if you're struggling to get a gun.

9) Each unit of ammunition is one bullet or shotgun shell. Most of the time, one bullet isn't enough to kill somebody.

10) The game only saves at the start of the day. So, the best time to quit your game is right after the start of the day.

In terms of controls, the mouse and the gamepad are good for different things. The mouse-clicks tell survivors where the endpoint of their movement will be, while the gamepad gives specific instructions about how to move. So, I found that the mouse is better for the daytime (when you want to give tasks to multiple survivors concurrently), and the gamepad is better for the night-time (when you want to tell your survivor exactly how to get from point A to point B, because moving too slowly, moving too quickly, moving to the wrong place, or moving the wrong way around an obstacle can get you stabbed or shot).

If you've read all the way to the end, then I heartily recommend that you buy this game. You clearly have an attention span long enough to appreciate this game.

"This War of Mine" is like a doll-house for adults with the addition of a depressing and serious context (hint: it's in the title). Despite the management simulation aspects, the game is surprisingly compelling. You are never completely comfortable in your shelter and there will always be something that requires your attention - which makes it feel like there's constant challenge. Also you will want to know how your characters will manage to survive (or deal with somebody's death). 

The game's clunky controls unfortunately let it down in places. Sometimes you will swap characters by accident and send one in the wrong direction, and the combat system is not fully explained well enough - making it a risky propositon. Also the save system sucks with autosave only (I recommend killing the game's system process the second you make a fatal error) - and it's a LONG game. It's also fairly "easy" straightforward if you play sensibly and learn the game's dynamics - but there are enough different scenarios to play through, so the game has lots of replay value all the same.

If you've been playing games all your life, now it's time for you to do some serious responsible "adulting." This war of mine is real, so get to it.

This war of mine is kinda bittersweet. The first two playthroughs are truly magical with the unique setting and idea. However, after a certain number of playthroughs the cracks in the game start showing. The Final Cut version really took care of a lot of glitches but there are still some of them. They don't break the game but they lightly ruin the immersion. Also it gets repetetive quite fast. You're using the same characters through "different" scenarios and they have the same comments, reactions and so on. They never really interact with each other. Also after you visit a certain location enough times it's almost like a chore cause you know exactly what's gonna happen, who's there, how many thugs/soldiers/people there are. This War of Mine is a time-eater. The game requires you to invest a lot of time with only minimal payoffs. The game requires you to spend hours just plodding along.

Yes, that's sort of the point (the game's purpose is to replicate the feeling of being stuck in a wartime scenario). You're a civilian trying to get by while the city is on lock-down and resources are dwindling. (When you go out to get stuff, you're "scavenging," but outsiders are "invaders" or "looters.")

Game play alternates between day and night activities. Daytime in your shelter consists primarily of Resource Management skills: using meager supplies in the most advantageous ways. You'll assess what's available, how much you need, and how best to use it to build things like rat traps, water filters, beds, shelter reinforcements, medications, and so on. It's reminiscent of The Sims in that you have to take care of little people who walk around, get hungry, have health woes, and even emotional issues. 

At night, the game is a little like Thief (in 2-D) -- you sneak out to various locations and try to get more stuff. One of the game's big problems is that you are harshly punished if you don't figure out the interface in time. You will spend literally hours trying to accumulate stuff and stay alive, but if you click the wrong button on accident you lose all your progress, and the game won't let you rewind: If your character dies, that's it, he/she is dead. There's no save to go back to. 

Yes, "That's the way things are in war"  -- a combination of tedium and danger. Fine. But it stinks to play a game for 5 hours and then abruptly die because when you clicked "Run to Exit," the game made you go to an exit on THE OTHER SIDE OF THE SCREEN that you didn't know was there (and hadn't unlocked yet). That doesn't teach you about war -- that's clunky programming. This kind of unforgiving game-play is dumb and extremely frustrating.

Similarly, in the shelter portion of the game, there are game interface flaws that degrade the experience. For example, you can build an item and you can also chop that same item up to get firewood (for when it is deathly cold in the winter). One such item is the indoor garden -- which requires loads of precious resources to create. 

When you're using the garden, there is a single icon, but when it's finished (when your character has planted carrots or something), the single icon moves over and there are two icons, side-by-side, with one being the icon to chop up the whole gardening station and use it for firewood. Simply because of a program interface flaw, you might accidentally destroy your garden without meaning to! And guess what? There is no stopgap such as "Are you sure?" This would have been entirely programmable, if the creators had the foresight to realize the flaw of their interface.

The game is intriguing nonetheless. There are occasionally moral decisions to make -- usually a question of whether to steal from others. If you do, then your characters become depressed. You can let them play guitar or smoke cigarettes to feel better. Needless to say this is all a little shallow for a game attempting to replicate the horrors of wartime.

I played the whole thing through just to finally get to the end of the war. It is anti-climactic: the game abruptly ends and you see some scrolling images summarizing a few of the things that happened while you played. The real reward was having a good excuse to stop playing. I did find the experience different and involving for a while, though.

When the difficulty is just right, this game becomes a great medium for emergent storytelling. Why should I feel attached to a couple of generic civilian nobodies in a game? Because choices carry consequences. And that's something a lot of larger studios seem to forget these days.

Choices carry consequences.
That's probably the best way to sum this game up.

And i've gone back to replay this game with a new cast of poor souls at least once or twice a year.

Really well made polished little gem of a game. You take on the role of controlling the actions of a few people trying to survive through the war. During the days you need to do things like building beds, cook food, make water, fortify your shelter etc and at night you can send a single person out to scavenge and try bring back materials and food required to survive and build things during the day. You may also encounter traders at day and night who might be able to get you out of a pinch but at a cost. You also choose who you want to sleep or who you want to guard the shelter at night. There's an incredible attention to detail in what you do in this game. If you guard at night then that person becomes tired, but if you don't guard you could be raided. If you steal at night or kill then that person may become depressed. Everything you do has a purpose and can have a consequence which you must weigh up and decide what is best in order to survive through the war.
The atmosphere, music and graphics fit exactly with how the game is, very clever attention to detail and immersive. What a gem of a game, kudos to 11 bit studios. It's not overly complex or complicated, it's not trying to be something it’s not. It is just a very well made, highly polished, excellently designed game.
Definitely worth buying, especially with how cheap it goes in the sales!

The survival mechanics are good. It plays like a roguelike with base building and resource management. 

Notwithstanding there are problems with the stealing and the healing mechanic, making the game artificially hard.
When going to scavenge near places where someone lives, it's hard to figure if you steal from them or you're taking some random items that nobody bothered with anyway.
The game seems to recognize any type of search of objects as stealing like in Fallout 3, Oblivion, Skyrim, even if you put something that wasn't there. Or if you steal and put it back, it still counts as stealing if you quit the storage interface. It took me a while to understand that. The game also counts stealing even if you did not see the inhabitants, whom it might be your interest in not meeting, since some shoot on sight. It's very easy to see how such contradictory mechanics become redundant very quickly. 
Found some answers on the wiki, but this shows most of all the lack of a proper tutorial into the game mechanics: https://this-war-of-mine.fandom.com/wiki/Sympathy
Another thing to take note is that, it seems searching through rubbles of trash does not count as stealing, even if inside highly populated areas such as a hospital. If there is a hand over drawers, cupboards or there are just some items lying around - those belong to someone, especially if they are in the same room.
The other weak part is healing. The game conceives that the best treatment for wounds and sickness is pills/bandages and permanent bed-rest for a few days. In real life, people do not get better from constant bed-rest. If anything their muscles get atrophied. Movement is life. 

Another small issue is the lack of any fast forward option that seems to make the game feel more repetitive than needed.

I tested the game on 3 machines and I noticed that it's very resource intensive on computers with integrated processors. Intel Celerons and AMD suffer the most it seems. Keep that in mind if you want to play.

I'm not new to games, but a serious issue with this product is that it lacks a proper tutorial/introduction to base mechanics and this alienates many players.

In other words, the game has a steep learning curve. But the narrative and the music is real good, despite the tedious issues adding up eventually.

The game's lifespan could be increased if modding could bring new locations because there are only about 30 in total. Since the Final Cut already released almost all of the locations from DLC's users could help the game's popularity. Similarly to how Don't Starve became popular with endless user made content. Of course, true creativity would be unleashed if the game's source code would have been published. The decision belongs to developers. Anyone who would've wanted to support developers out of love, would just buy the game. Otherwise they'll pirate it, see that there's no tutorial no welcoming and leave.


On another note, the soundtrack is nice. The radio has classic music and some Polish rock. Although when trying to let the radio play in the shelter, there's the odd cutting out to the game's soundtrack which kind of hurts the game IMHO as one plays more.

Cons:
- The plot is locked behind DLC. The base game has no story. Instead it's just a loose series of small stories scattered across locations. The playable characters' stories are told through brief autobiographic extracts in the later days. But they don't change from scenario to scenario. All of this is more of a sandbox to explore as long as you like. There are some epilogues at the end if you survive/die but they leave more to desire for. The base game's story is very lite.
- No in-game tutorial/guide to explain basic mechanics such as stealing, sickness, wounds.
- Limited amount of locations and limited modding capabilites to add new locations. Modding is focused on custom scenarios/items/characters.
- Limited amount of random events.
- Game does not make use of the keyboard and does not allow to remap the keyboard settings. It could be useful to control the camera or the characters with the keyboard. Notwithstanding, the whole game is controlled with the mouse here. Clearly a result of not tweaking the game sufficiently for the PC. Only the TAB key is used for selecting in between characters.
- No option to fast forward speed when building inside the shelter. It becomes repetitive once you figure out what you need to get ahead - 1 rainwater collector, 2 beds, a stove, a metal workshop if you did not acquire weapons by day 2. The game does not explain what comes first, considering the apparent heavy reliance on crafting. However, crafting is rather optional unless you want to stay indoors - which you can if you have sufficient supplies to keep the cycle going. But this is usually an option in late game.

The best thing about [b]This War of Mine[/b] is that it's a right game at the right time. I mean, did you ever wondered why, even though we have a lot of wars going on all over the world, we don't have much people talking about peace nowadays? Back in the days, we had a lot of famous people, from [b]John Lennon[/b] to [b]Michael Jackson[/b], promoting the idea of peace. Nowadays? We only have those angry people screaming “[i]Kill 'em all![/i]”. And it looks like the guys from [b]11 Bit Studios[/b] (creators of the [b]Anomaly[/b] series) had enough of that. Because this game? Its entire purpose is to make people think about the true nature of war. Which is... hell. That's probably why everybody (both press and players) loved this game so much. It just feels like something that we all needed in our lives. It filled the gap in our hearts. Gameplay-wise, though... it's far from being a masterpiece.

Like all previous games from [b]11 Bit Studios[/b], [b]This War of Mine[/b] is a phones-oriented game. It looks like something that belongs on mobiles and, well, it feels that way too. Because the entire gameplay here revolves around you clicking the icons. Heck, even gamepad controls feel pretty bad (I totally recommend to either play this game with the mouse, or go for the mobile version). Don't get me wrong, though, it's a pretty nice experience for a mobile game, it's just... there's nothing special about it. Aside from what I've already said at the beginning of this review. It's a pretty charming survival game for mobiles. With the very deep atmosphere. But that's pretty much it.

I mean, when you see all those overwhelmingly positive reviews on all platforms, when you see both press and players loving it oh-so-much, you can't help but expect something special, right? The game that everybody should play. But the thing is... [b]This War of Mine[/b] is nothing like that. It's a really basic thing. A thing that comes in two phases. In the first one, you build up your living space with what you have, while trying to keep your characters fed and in a good health (which may be pretty tricky, since they really like to fall ill, especially if you won't keep your living space heated, which requires a lot of fuel). And the second phase is exploration, in which you'll collect materials by utilizing either stealth, or weapons. Or both. There's quite a lot of tricks you'll be able to use and there'll be quite a lot of tools to make and use, but overall idea is just that. You click the icons to collect the stuff and then you click more icons to build stuff from that stuff. That's the stuff. It's kind of fun for the first couple of hours, but, as usual with the survival games, it gets old pretty quick. Especially when you play it at home.

The game begins to shine with so-called season pass (which, unfortunately, will cost you another [b]$6.99[/b] in addition to the default price of [b]$19.99[/b]). See, the season pass is your only way to get the proper campaign. Three of them, actually, with totally different goals and conditions. And unlike the default game mode, those three story-oriented campaigns feel... awesome. Not only stories add more personal touch (it's almost impossible not to care about the characters there), they come with some really interesting and complicated choices and even offer multiple endings. Every “story” in season pass is different and provides you with something absolutely unique. You may expect at least one of such things to be included in the default game, but nope, won't happen. You want proper experience? You pay for [b]DLC[/b]. But, like I've said, when you'll get [b]DLC[/b], you'll begin to see this game's true potential. And after finishing with the stories? You can play the default mode up until you'll get enough. It's like our usual [b]DLC[/b] formula in reverse. I mean, usually, the video games provide you with the story mode and then add some extras. Like arenas, challenges and other stuff like that. This game? It does exactly the opposite. It gives you “the basic fun” in the main game and asks more money for the story. You want the full game? You get yourself a “complete edition”. No way around it.

Unfortunately, even though [b]DLC[/b] gives us much better and interesting experience, it also leaves us with the fact that to get the full game, we should pay [b]$27[/b]. For a pretty basic mobile game, because even interesting campaigns with the unique rules can't change that fact. Does it worth it? Well, the developers support charity, so... kind of. I mean, the game about victims of war that supports real victims of war? Isn't that [i]awesome?[/i] [b]This War of Mine[/b] is one of those games that don't make you feel bad about paying for them just because of that fact. You don't just buy the game, you actually do something good. But gameplay-wise? I don't think it's worth half of the price of the new [b]AAA[/b] title. Even though gameplay feels pretty solid and I totally love it how exploration feels in this game (even though the entire game is timed and usually I can't stand timed games), [b]This War of Mine[/b] is still a [b]100%[/b] mobile game to the bone. Up to the point where it actually feels better on go. Playing it at the café while enjoying your morning croissant? It actually feels better than playing it properly at home, while being able to play anything else on your huge [b]8K[/b] TV.

With a proper discount for the full version with all [b]DLC[/b] included, though? [b]This War of Mine[/b] is totally worth it just because of its incredible atmosphere and really touching stories that are impossible not to like. You don't just play this game. You [i]dive[/i] into it. And it's sure one of those games that you can't help but remember. So, yeah, it's an overpriced mobile game. But it's still one of the best games mobile market brought to us and its take on sad reality is pretty awesome.

I get that some people like the whole heavy, slow feeling, where the UI makes loading a game take 30 seconds (partly because of "cinematic" things like long, slow fade-ins designed to discouraging repeated "save scumming"), and permadeath and all that, but it just makes the game too heavy to enjoy -- and by heavy I'm referring to how long everything takes, the fact that one mistake at night means you have to repeat the whole day or suffer a significant loss, or even possibly a debilitating loss that pretty much means start the game over (like, say, getting your survivor killed trying to stop a soldier sexually assaulting a woman).

I'll be glad when this anti-savegame fad is over.  I have neither the time nor inclination to start over and over because of the game force-saving bad situations, or for repeating long sequences of play repeatedly because I had to alt-F4 and go through long load-in times to avoid that force-save.

Really would like to like the game, but it's just too tedious, irritating and discouraging.  Mission accomplished, devs?  You wanted to get across that war is awful, but you made the game too tedious to play through, at least for people like me.

Uninstalled after some 8 hours of playing.

This is a great game of survival.  It is cleverly designed to require careful decision-making on your part to succeed.  You control the actions of a small group of civilians struggling to survive in a city caught in the middle of a war zone.  There are about a dozen standard characters, each with their own personality, strengths, and weaknesses.  Some of the standard characters, for example, are a deserter, a teacher, a fireman, a cook, a music student, a lawyer, etc..  A few of these characters have banded together in an abandoned dwelling to survive until the conflict ends.  

You have to figure out how to deal with a multitude of problems in order to survive.  Your people need to get enough food, or they will starve.  Your people need to get enough sleep to function.  You need to deal with winter when it arrives so that your people don’t freeze to death.  You need to keep them happy, otherwise they can become depressed.  If unhappy, your characters may fight with each other, or leave your group, or get so depressed they stop doing anything.  They will tell you when something is bothering them so you do have warnings when your characters are upset.

You need to send one person out during the night to scavenge for food, supplies, and weapons.  You figure out who should scavenge, who should stand guard, and who gets to sleep.  During the day, the characters can perform actions like building needed items, or sleeping if they were up during the night. You decide what items they build with limited resources.  And finally, you need to deal with the almost nightly raids on your dwelling, which can steal resources or wound your people.  

These problems are not isolated, and you are usually trying to avoid disaster from multiple adversities simultaneously.  You usually just begin with a simple workbench and a chair.  The workbench lets you build simple things like beds, stoves, heaters, chairs, and kindling.  First you have to scavenge the dwelling for resources during the first day.  You want to find enough to build a metal working bench, which lets you build shovels, crowbars, and knives.  The first day, you want to build a workbench and a bed at least, and a shovel to help remove debris quickly.  Then at night, you send one of your characters out to scavenge one of the buildings nearby.  

One of the really nice features of this game is the variety of encounters your people have when they meet strangers when scavenging or who show up at the front door.  Some strangers will help, some are  army deserters, some are criminals, some are other civilians trying to survive, and some are military who may be friendly or unfriendly.  Figuring out how to deal with each type of encounter is one of the best features of the game.  The game auto-saves each morning, after the nightly scavenging and possible raid, so you are stuck with any bad choices you made during the night.

This is one of my very favorite games with great replay ability.  When you finally manage to get every standard character to survive, you can make up your own scenarios with additional characters.   

I highly recommend this game.  It’s one I still play even after having figured out how to deal with most (but not all) of the encounters my scavengers will meet.

Offering a unique perspective on the frequently over-glorified, man-made phenomenon we call "war", [b]This War of Mine[/b] puts you into the shoes of the average civilian, as they do their best - and their worst - to make do and survive in the harsh new reality they found themselves in. 

Your people act like real human beings in this game and will suffer mental and emotional consequences depending on what they are forced (by you) to do, whether it is to rob a poor elderly couple blind and basically leaving them with nothing to survive on, or being forced to murder someone who's just defending their home from intruders like you.

The game also has a "base building" aspect where you'll be able to unlock new crafting recipes by building new workstations and by upgrading them. Considering that resources can be a bit limited, some resource management is required here as well... and make sure to stock up well enough for winter! 

Although I've not tried it yet, the Stories DLCs even offers you brand-new stories to experience and each story supposedly will put you in even more morally dilemmatic scenarios. 

[h1]Overall[/h1]
This War of Mine can have a bit of a learning curve especially if you're new to the game, but once you get into the groove, you should be able to survive longer, and hence, experience more of the story and explore a whole lot more locations where you'll then get to interact with a host of new friends and enemies. At the end of the day, the game will open your eyes to the horrors of war from the perspective of the common folk but it also gives you hope that some people still retain their humanity and decency in the face of such adversity as war.

Heart-wrenching, thought-provoking and absolutely genius. The creators of this game should be praised for creating such a harrowing experience with such fleshed-out characters. The game is inspired by the poor living conditions and wartime atrocities that Bosnian civilians endured during the 1992–1996 Siege of Sarajevo, the longest city siege since World War II.

The game-play focuses on a small group of civilians trapped in a war torn city, their homes and neighborhood in shambles in the aftermath of shelling. With limited resources and the constant threat of danger, it will put you in scenarios where you become desperate to help your group survive... sometimes by any means necessary.

Will you loose all sense of morality and rob or kill without a second thought? Or will you do your part to help the people you come across? As the game description says, "during war, there are no good or bad decisions; there is only survival."

I highly recommend this game to anyone looking to be challenged. It is truly one of a kind!

Some games deeply resonate with the player, and leave a lasting impact. This War of Mine is a much-needed counterpoint to the focus games typically have on wars and warriors, and shows us what it would be like if most of us, ordinary people, actually found ourselves in war.

The gameplay itself is well-honed, and if you've played it before, the recently released final cut warrants another look. The resource management is complemented by the less-than-total control you have over your characters. They each have their personalities and quirks, and vices, and you can unexpectedly find your characters in a downward spiral if their needs aren't met.

Some of the best moments are when you only have one serving of food left, and you choose to feed Emilia, because she's sick, injured, and hungry, and Bruno, well, he's only slightly sick and hungry, so he'll just have to deal. Sometimes you can get into a sustainable loop where you aren't really worried about having enough resources to go around. Other times, a blizzard unexpectedly hits and closes off several areas - which just happen to be the safe(ish) areas you have not yet stripped of resources, forcing you to either go to the dangerous areas (littered with gangs that will shoot you on-sight), hit the soft targets (like an elderly couple who can't fight back if you steal from them), or simply going without - which could mean death for your own survivors. For me at least, I found these choices really tugged at my heartstrings, because sometimes, there are no right answers. Just like in war.

I could go on and write up a full essay extolling this game's virtues and why you should play it, but you'd be better served by just jumping into the game right now and experiencing it for yourself.

This War of Mine is a game that puts you in the shoes of civilians, rather than soldiers. While a civil war rages on, you have to ensure the survival of 1-4 civilians that got caught up in the fighting until the war ends. Food, medicine, wood and other materials are scarce, so you have to send someone outside to scavenge for supplies every night.

The game is divided into two segments: the day where all the fighting happens, and the night.

[h1]The Day[/h1]
During the day, your characters are stuck at their shelter, so they use this time to:
1) Craft items or furniture from the supplies you have scavanged/traded with to either satisfy needs, create tools for night segments, or produce goods for barter
2) Satisfy basic needs: sleep after a night guard/scavenge or eat food to avoid starvation, or treat wounds/diseases with bandages and medicine
3) Set up in-house resource production
4) Exchange items with passing traders
5) Interact with other survivors that come to your shelter with requests or offers (random events)
6) Trying to keep warm over winter

[h1]The Night[/h1]
The night is when it's relatively safe to actually leave the shelter. During this segment, you may pick one of your characters to go out to other locations to scavange/trade for supplies for your day activities and meeting basic character needs, while the remaining characters either take the time to get some sleep, or stand guard overnight against raiders.

The character that you send outside the shelter will visit a chosen location out of the ones that are randomly picked out for your session. The number of locations you can access increase over time, but certain locations may become temporarily unavailable either due to snow or fighting blocking them off. Each location in the game also has a couple of variations, where the same location may have different characters and events. For example, a school can be either home to some homeless people that don't pose any threat, or to a band of militia during different play sessions. However, the variations are limited in number (only like two or so per location) and most locations don't change over time during the same session. Some of these locations are entirely safe to visit, while some have armed men prowling the map who would fire at you on sight. 

Each character has a specific carrying capacity, meaning that there's only so much you can carry back home over one night, so you won't be able to sack everything over a single visit, since you only get one visit per night regardless of how fast you wrap things up during said visit. Items you can loot include building materials needed for crafting, food, medical supplies, weapons and other items. Some are out there in the open and can be looted easily, while other are blocked under locked doors/containers, debris, grates, or armed guards. Locks require crowbars or lockpicks (craftable at your shelter) to unlock, debris can be moved out of the way with time (made faster if you craft a shovel for it), grates can be removed with a consumable saw blade crafted at your shelter, while with guards you either have to sneak past them, or go in guns blazing.

The game does have a combat system that allows you to kill people, but killing people will affect your characters' mood and endings. Plus, unless you're well armed, your character can be killed quite quickly, so it's not the best idea to get into an open fight against people with assault rifles without suitable weapons of your own. Also, any injuries inflicted on your character will need to be treated with medical supplies and this will require some time, so you have to carefully weigh if getting into a fight is worth it. Though, if you do kill armed people, weapons you can loot from them can fetch a pretty price with traders...

Some locations are owned by innocent survivors just like your own. You can rob them if you're really desperate for supplies, but it will negatively impact your characters' mood and endings.

Once your character returns to the shelter, you will get a report on what happened at the shelter over night. Your shelter will occasionally be raided by other people, which may result in your characters getting injured or some of your supplies being stolen. The damages can be limited by putting more people on guard, having weapons in the shelter, and spending some supplies to bolster your defences and install alarms. Also, if the shelter isn't heated enough (especially a problem during winter), characters may become sick, which will require meds and bed treatment. Minor wounds and sickness may heal over time if you let the character sleep, but more serious ones will require both meds and bed time.

[h1]Impressions[/h1]
My first session was pretty hard, since I didn't even know how things worked and didn't know how to rationalise my resources, as well as what to prioritise on getting. So, I eventually ended up severely lacking food and meds with no safe place to get them... and ended up losing my characters while trying to scavenge stuff from a well armed place.

During my following sessions, I got the hang of how the game worked and didn't waste my resources needlessly (e.g., I learnt that characters become hungry every day, but this status degrades to a "very hungry" state only after three or so days, while a single meal is enough to overturn either state, so until you build up your shelter to produce food on its own, you can't feed everyone every single day). Ever since then, I was never really pressed for resources that much to need to take excessive risks or rob people... as long as I didn't screw up somewhere along the way.

It's nice that you get a randomised set of locations for each sessions and there are some random events and variations between locations so that each session feels somewhat different, but the variation is rather limited. Each location has about 2 variations or so. Also, few locations change over time, so if you've been to a place once, you don't need to expect any surprises the next time you come over for a visit. The only difference between the scenarios is what characters you get to play with (each character has some trait that allows them to do certain actions better), at what point in the game you get winter, and how long the war lasts. So, while you may find something new in a second or maybe even third playthrough, you will likely get bored soon enough and may need breaks between the scenarios if you want to still enjoy the game.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Likes:
+Get to see a war from the perspective of civilians who got caught up in it
+Decisions matter:
-->+Your resources are limited, so you have to pick wisely how you spend them
-->+Combat and stealing negatively affect your characters' mood, while good actions increase morale
-->+If your characters' morale hits rock bottom, they'll be rendered incapacitated
-->+Combat runs the risk of losing your characters for good... or at least putting them in bed and sucking up your meds... or death over time due to lack of medical treatment if you don't have any meds on hand...
-->+Helping other survivors may lead to them returning with gifts or other help
-->+Different endings for each character depending on how you played the session

Dislikes:
-The only real differences between the base game scenarios are what characters you get, the length of the war, and when winter comes down on you
-Few varieties of shelters with little difference between them
-Not much to do in your shelter after the first few days, but you may miss traders and random events if you skip this segment
-Most locations you can visit don't change over time and only have two variations at best
-No tutorial whatsoever; gotta learn how everything works on your own
-Only one save game slot

First thing:  I do recommend this game, with caveats.   But, given only a thumbs up or thumbs down review, I thought I should try to be objective.  I think you should know what you are getting into before purchasing this game - it could be thought of as "The Sims - Misery DLC."

The graphics are beautiful in the representation of miserable surroundings.  The characters are given enough personality for you to feel for their situation.  The game mechanics flow well.

Characters have bios and specific things they like.   A character may be a cigarette smoker and if you find cigarettes this may provide them a small respite from despair.  But, not too much.

You start out with three players in your hideout.  You can give them commands, such as scavenging, building objects, eating, healing or sleeping.  The days go by fast, make sure to get enough sleep.  Your players will quickly be on the verge of collapse.

War is hell.   This is a simulation of their day to day fight to stay alive when staying alive is all that matters.  The game play is in two parts - day and night.  

During the day you can build crude devices in your hideout to keep your players alive, such as a stove, heater, beds, weapons.  It looks like the standard building mechanics - you need enough of supply A to build part B to use in tool C.  If you don't have water, combustibles, a stove and food, you can't make soup.  A trader will usually come to the door and you can barter for things you need.  Be prepared to give away a lot to get very little in return.  I have not seen any leveling up, just a slow sad spiral into hunger, depression, exhaustion, sickness and injury until they are broken.  You can heal your players but it never lasts very long.  You never have enough supplies, your players will always be hungry, hurt, depressed and sick. 

At night, one of your players can go to other sites on the map and scavenge for food and supplies to keep yourself alive.  You control the scavenger while the others remain behind at your hideout.  Scavenging is a bit of stealth and can be a moral dilemma.  Will you rob the old couple in their house, or leave them alone?  Will you ignore the old man's pleas to leave his wife medicine, or steal it to heal your injured comrade?  Can you avoid the other occupants of other hideouts, or will you beat them to death and risk getting shot.  These decisions weigh on the conscience of the scavenger when s/he returns.   

When you return from scavenging, you are updated on what happened while you were out scavenging.  It may be a calm night, or raiders may have come and stolen supplies and injured your players that stayed behind to stand guard.  Your players that remained behind may have abandoned your hideout and do not come back.  If one of your players was sick or injured, they might have died.  If a player was depressed, they may have committed suicide.

I think the goal of the game is to survive until the armistice or ceasefire.  I haven't made it that far yet.   Maybe you can reach a point where you have enough food, supplies and weapons that you can barricade yourself in and ride it out.  I don't know.

At the end of the game, you are given a recap of every significant action taken in the game, such as players dying, robbing or killing others.  During one of my games, two players abandoned my hideout while the third died from his injuries.  On the final screen of the game, I found out that the two players that left the hideout were shot and died.  One was shot while trying to cross the border to get to his family, the other was shot when a trade deal went bad.

This is what you are getting into.  I would recommend this game to someone who understands what Cormac Mccarthy's "The Road" is.  Think of a Solzhenitsyn video game.   I would not call it "fun" game play and you will not be laughing while you play it.  I do not think this would be a good party game.  It's a misery simulator that can be addicting to play, just to see if can get them to survive another day, or figure out the game play to make the struggle easier.  The game itself masterpiece but I don't know if I would want to play this over and over again just because it such a melancholy game and the struggle seems too real.

So recommend it, sure.  But this is not The Sims or a fantasy RPG where you keep getting more powerful and magical healers cast spells to heal their crew or an FPS that lets you upgrade weapons to keep destroying all the demons the game can throw at you.   There is no conjuring or superpowers.  This War of Mine is gritty, depressing and probably not for everyone.  

Maybe everyone should play it.  The other side of this is that it all seems too real and this is not fantasy.  It has happened to humanity before, it is happening now and it will keep happening.  This is your chance to experience misery and hell on earth from the comfort of a computer game.

I'm generally not a big fan of survival games, although I keep trying different ones in the hopes that I'll find one I like. This War of Mine, however, is one I found some time ago and fell in love with! It's different from most of the "standard" survival games in almost every way, especially with it's art style and the effectiveness of the stories. It is, by all means, an incredible game.

If you've played Distrust (I only have recently), the gameplay mechanics are pretty similar, but Distrust didn't have the stories and the feels to grab my attention like This War of Mine did! It grabbed my attention, played with my emotions, ripped out my heart, urinated on my corpse, and brought me back to live as one giant, stinking mess of a man. Honestly though, while the game is pretty depressing, it's a true testament to the work 11 bit studios have done and really gives some horrific insight into how much war can effect the lives of civilians. The blend of story, gameplay, art, and music complement one another perfectly.

11 bit studios have also raised a load of money for War Child with the DLC sales for This War of Mine, a truly deserving charity in my eyes. This reflects, not only on how great the game is, but how great the company behind it are.

This is, by far, my favourite survival game, and one of my favourite games of all time. Never has a game left me with such feels. The fact it was released in 2014 and still had new DLC released this year is also awesome! Definitely recommend, even if you don't like survival games.

This is not just a game but a simulation about humanity and history of violence as well. It's highly atmospheric, immersive and overall heartbreaking to the point of being frustrating at times, and that's OK because it's supposed to be an uncomfortable experience. It's about war, it's about death, hunger, depression and struggle to survive. It's not simply about survival but HOW you will choose to do that. What is the cost of survival? Does it worth giving up on the part of your humanity, leave behind the values like compassion, kindness and empathy that has became a precious part of our civilized cultures? Will you choose steal from your neighbours or kill someone if you think you can get away with it at the end of the day?
I think the whole point of the game is to make you face tough survival situations like these, rise above all that crushing desperation and defeat but in the end make the kind decisions that when it's all over, ask if you can still live with yourself.

This War of Mine is a fantastic game to try out, it’s gritty, depressing and hauntingly beautiful. Like many reviewers had already stated, it’s not your typical war game, you don’t play a soldier, you play ordinary citizens, people whose life has change in an instant and are now trying to survive in this war torn city. 
The mechanics of this game are great, during the day you’re in your sheltered home, improving it bit by bit, during the night you scavenge, while the rest off the crew stays behind to guard your shelter and your supplies, which you’ll need to manage carefully.
The visuals are incredible, sure they are not your latest and greatest, but the style adds to the experience, simply put the visuals are as harsh and rough as the game itself. 
The characters you play feel like real people, each have different sets off morals, weaknesses and strengths. If you get the Little Ones dlc it gets even more depressing, with having children on your team, it’s fascinating to see how they react to the events and you will do anything to keep them as happy as you possibly can. Not only that but the kids can be really helpful around your home, after you teach them. 
This game is not for everyone, if you like strategy games, making snap decisions that can have some horrifying consequences and would like to experience the other, more depressing side off war, then you must try this game.

Bruno didn't expect the war, always thinking the situation would calm down before actual conflict arose, but when war did break out he found himself pinned down in the city, bunked with two complete strangers, Pavel and Katia. Over the course of three and a half week they survived, scraping by through catching rats, selling moonshine and burning various pieces of wood to stay warm in their shelter. 

However, almost immediately after the war broke out Bruno was hit by military sniper fire. Pavel rushed out to find meds the next night while Katia nursed him and over the next few days, he recovered. Through various over expeditions and mishaps the three of them slowly bonded as they continued to gather resources and scraps of food, however during the second week, Pavel left one night and never returned.

Word on the street said his body was found in the wake of a military expedition to a nearby construction site…

Now it was only the two of them, and in their desperation and hunger, Katia took all their remaining moonshine and set out to the nearby military outpost in search of food, they had been relying on Pavel to bring them some scraps but now they were on the verge of starvation.
She never returned. 

Finally broken, Bruno took their only rifle and set out for the outpost. Arriving he found Katia's body laying cold outside in the snowdrift, with a noticeable lack of moonshine.

In a fury Bruno spread the remainder of the night stalking the outpost, and by some miracle, silently slit the throats of every guard and solider he could sneak up on or out mauver. Returning home the next morning, depressed and tired, he slept. A furious rage still burning, he set out once more the next night.

Approaching the outpost, he silently passed through the building and was ambushed by a guard, prepared and waiting, who, fired three shots, one of which hit Bruno in the leg, wounding him. The returning volley was not so merciful to the soldier, For the remaining five hours, Burno played cat and mouse with the soldiers, avoiding and killing all until but the final two.

Hiding in the dark, Bruno waited for the alerted soldier to pass, a practice that was all to familiar now. Leaping out he quickly dealt with the solder, however, unbeknownst to him the last soldier noticed from above, firing his shotgun, once again wounding Bruno. Turing around, Burno fire three, three short bursts into the soldier. Broken and defeated he limped home, his thirst for vengeance quenched.

Finally making it home, Bruno lay down, as he had done weeks earlier, wounded and sick. He had managed to avenge his friends, having killed over seven soldiers, and closed his eyes for the last time.

This is how it feels; even though I didn't win, it’s the story, the choices that you make that makes the game so excellent. I even, when playing this run, genuinely feel, sad, angry, vengeful and finally content as all these events unfolded. I dislike using the word “experience” instead of “game”, which is so popular nowadays.

But here, in This War of Mine, it’s completely justified. Experiences change people, their thoughts and perspectives. This War of Mine does just that.

You’ve probably played countless war games, be it shooters, RTSes or some other kind. Universally almost, there were two sides: Us and Them. And yet, there is always a third side, the one stuck in between, the one suffering the most – the civilians. And now you get to play as them. There are no heroes here, just survival. No orders or objectives, only your moral compass. 

This game is only as good as your immersion into it. Sure, you can bludgeon everyone to death with a crowbar and loot whatever is left. You could steal from an elderly couple and let them starve to death.

But would you do that in real life, real situation? And even if, would you still be the same person after?

A different take on war entirely. This war of mine focuses on the unseen casualties of war, the civilian population. You'll have to make difficult choices that impact your survivors morale. Robbing elderly people who are helpless because you need materials for heat. Stealing food from armed survivors by hiding in the shadows and watching their movements or using brute force to take it. The eventual death of party members results in a very somber approach to war.

TWoM is absolutely one of the best games I've ever played, featuring a great emphasis on survival and management with tough situations and moral decisions. No tutorial, no guidance, and each mistake you make will cost you double, it's a game that shows the brutality of the war like no other.

As you start with just a few survivors, you'll struggle for everything. Food, water, meds, bandages, weapons, even the most basic materials, and your objective should not be to make it better, but rather to not make it worse. TWoM, despite being a survival-oriented strategy and management mix, offers a great replayability value, especially with all the paid and free content added across all those years, being a perfect game to pick up for people that enjoy survival-oriented strategy games. If you've enjoyed games like Frostpunk, Rimworld, 60 Seconds/Parsecs or Dead in Bermuda, you should enjoy this one as well.

TWoM is pretty much what defined 11 bit studios, and I'm very happy to be part of their success, as a happy player that has grabbed TWoM in their early days. The games that they're making are very unique, and TWoM is a perfect example of being one-of-a-kind game showing what a small studio made out of people with passion can deliver.

No charity campaigns for these victims, because they are brown and thus not as human as the ones the developers have supported in the past.

Civil war breaks out. Civilians are evacuated but some get stranded in the besieged city. They take refuge in an abandoned house. During the day, they fix it up, make some tools, build some rudimentary amenities. During the night, they scavenge other buildings, under cover of darkness. They trade with other survivors, fend off looters, try to survive until the city is liberated, one way or another. Maybe they will have to steal from others, maybe they will have to kill to keep each other fed and in good health. Maybe the war will change them,

This is a nifty side-scroller. Keeping your survivors fed and healthy with the shortages in food and medical supplies can be challenging. Limited scavenging inventory means hard choices may have to be made. Random events, like neighbors in distress, may make you question your humanity. Illness, injury, depression, and hunger may render your survivors unable to get out of bed. Caring for children under constant threat of bandit raids, food shortages, and the general depression of war may force you to re-evaluate your priorities. Escalating fighting and weather conditions may make certain parts of town inaccessible for scavenging. What will you do to survive? Will you steal from your neighbors? So it was late at night and I lacked a bunch of stuff at my home, and I went scavenging.

I packed some lockpicks and my trusty hatchet.

So I get into this old house where some people live that's been said to have some good stuff.

I pick the lock and easily get inside. It's late at night so I'm not expecting anyone awake.

Unfortunately, as I'm looting the place, I hear steps coming down from the second floor.

That never happened before, so I quickly hid in a tiny space between some walls.

It's an old man, he's seems to be armed and goes around saying "who's there?" and "what's that noise?".

As he comes nearer, my heart starts to pound faster and faster. The adrenaline overwhelms me.

Finally, I see him passing me. The shock and awe almost making me faint. But he goes straight by.

I feel relieved, and ready to race home...

But he turns around.

I thought he had seen me. I thought he was going to hurt me, and I didn't know what to do.

I panicked.

I emerged from my hiding place, hatchet above my head.

And I strike him down. Furiously. Blood sprays everywhere. My hand going up and down by itself.

I can't feel my arms. His screams are terrifying, but I can't seem to stop. 

When it finished, he was dead.

I turn to see what I did. A grisly scene. I would've have sat down and cried...

If it wasn't for another scream coming behind me.

His wife, standing there, at the door, looking at him.

My first thought was to immediately bail.

I ran as fast as I could.

When I got home, depression and guilt overcame me. All the material stuff was for naught.

I'll never forget that experience.

An atmospheric game that doubles as both a harrowing depiction of life during besiegement, and a challenging survival management sim. You have to make difficult choices every day, balancing hunger, illness, injury, and exhaustion, all in the hopes of taking your band of civilians through to the end of the war. It's not a game you win often, unless you're willing to save-scum, or download mods to make gameplay easier. This really helps illuminate how difficult and desperate these situations are, and makes for a game that you want to keep playing, in hopes of doing better next time. Once you start upgrading your workstations, growing and catching your own food, and have enough beds for everyone, things get a little easier - but there's always more to improve, and only so many resources with which to make those changes. The Stories mode is even more difficult, but also provides a compelling narrative and a greater feeling of satisfaction when you manage to do well, because the characters are developed and well-rounded, and more fleshed out than the handful of pre-made survivors the base game offers. I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for a challenging management sim, as this one provides a rather unique premise in its setting and character choices.

Its compelling, grueling, and unforgiving in all the right ways. It's wild to think such a game exists with core mechanics focused on resource management, looting, crafting, and decision-based storytelling. Every action has and equal and or greater reaction. Play cautiously or play ruthlessly. Finding enough time and resources day or night to last through the war, which could as short as a few weeks or stretched over a couple months, requires lots of skill and patience. Stakes are high and rewards are higher, but not as high as the unpredictable and auto-generated "wrenches" the game throws at you. You might get lucky and score big time with enough food and meds to last a few days and manage to survive another night without armed bandits attacking your shelter. Until suddenly, half your characters are severely ill and the others are falling into a bottomless hole of depression. Everybody but one character is incapacitated due to their status conditions. Meanwhile, there is a snowstorm blocking off everywhere but the places you've already picked clean and you don't have enough materials to make a heater to keep your survivors warm. You don't know how long this storm will last and when the war will end, and pray the trader stops by within the next few days. This game is a rollercoaster that is equal parts frustrating and gratifying. There is never enough time spent surviving in this war of mine.

[h1] This Is MY War, Not Yours [/h1]

This War of Mine is a survival game where you take control of some randos and try to survive a war-torn city until the war is over. During the day, you'll be using the materials you crafted to make new items and build new workstations to help you survive. Here, you'll also have to make sure that your survivors are fed, healthy, and get enough sleep as you manage your time limit. There aren't "meters" per se, rather the statuses decrease each day, except for sleep which can be increased during the day if they get enough time in as well. At night is where the game truly shines. Here, you'll take control of one of your survivors as you attempt to scavenge supplies from a set amount of locations. In these locations, you'll have to manage your time and use tools to get through various obstacles. Some of the locations have unique aspects about them, such as a lot of debris, hostile bandits, or friendly traders. When there are hostiles, using stealth can be incredibly intense as you have to worry about your time to make sure you get back, while also trying to get more supplies and avoid the enemies. 

There are a few special events during the day, such as giving medicine to children, helping out neighbors (or ratting them out), or trading opportunities. This adds to this "morale" mechanic, which, when it actually shows, can be very interesting. Depending on how things are going, your survivors will react to your actions (technically the survivor's actions) and their mood may even be effected. Killing innocents, having your survivors die, or things generally not going well can lead to depressed moods and may even have dire consequences, and each survivor has different feelings about something (such as some being okay with the occasional murder). The crafting options are fairly limited and are largely situational, and even after so many hours I found myself not using certain ones because they felt useless. Even with that though, when you're scavenging you have to decide one what you want to bring with you because your inventory is incredibly limited. Will you grab the alcohol that's worth a lot of money, or extra wood so you can build that greenhouse? The game advertises itself as being very emotional and difficult, but I don't know if it's because I'm used to these kinds of games, but I never really found myself having a "hard" time except when I wasn't getting resources simply because of bad R&G. Overall, if you want a pretty standard survival game, with a more personal touch, this is probably for you.

I RECOMMEND it only when ON SALE for those who like light survival games. The reasons are below.

Important to note that I have only played the survival mode but I own the complete edition.

1. It is relatively EASY, or so I have found, and I am not even a harcore survival game player. (Example I have played Rimworld and Don't Starve, none of which I have ever managed to finish.) I have done two plays: Even in the first I almost survived until the end, though I had no clue of the mechanics and what was worth to build. In the second I survived without much trouble, and ended the game with a huge store of food and meds. In the last two weeks before the game ends I have been more or less just waiting for the time to pass, and I would have been able to craft all the work stations if I wanted to... or if I needed to, but I didn't. I was not pressed to do so.

2. REPETITIVE. Between my two plays the majority of the explorable locations were the same, only the situation was different in those places. For those who are not familiar with the game during night you sneak around these locations, pick up stuff until the bag of your scavanger is full (perhaps dispatch some inhabitants) then return home. During the day you build and craft, which there are a lot to do in the begining. From around the second half of the game most of my activity consisted of: checking the news in the radio, feeding my guys if anyone was hungry, waiting a bit to see if anyone comes to the door, if not then press the end of day button, ergo not much to do.

3. NO HARD DECISIONS (not enough at least in my second play when I had some idea what I was in to) I felt I had to make them only in the begining when deciding the building order of the most vital items, and what materials to pick up for those. Once my cart started rolling there was hardly a pressure. And again, in the end I could afford to build all station, if I needed to. As to making life-and-death decisions, I didn't feel I had to make many if any. Perhaps I just started out so well that I could afford to help everyone who stumbled to my door.

4. NOT as GRIPPING as I have expected. 
and
5. CHARACTERS DON'T HAVE ENOUGH PERSONALITY. These two are connected for me because the latter is the cause for the former. The look and sound of the game managed to deliver the depressing atmosphere, but a lot of other things fall flat for me. First of all characters don't interact with each other during day time. You can only make them talk to eachother when someone has low enough morale or if it is a child. Secondly, everyone has the same few lines, there is no individuality. The characters' personality seem only comes through their diaries, which only gets updated once in a while, and some characters seem to be more prone to do something (or perhaps it is just random). Example in my second play one of my survivors repeatedly argued with the others, but this only came up as a notification in the summary of the last night, never getting any more deeper than this. I feel it is a missed opportunity to let us learn more about our characters and possibly getting more attached to them.

6. BUGS and GLITCHES: I have only found one gamebreaking bug, but it happened more than once. When someone was on low morale, and I sent another survivor to talk to them, I lost control of all my characters. I couldn't issue any orders to the others, I couldn't make the talkers stop, everyone was just standing there, so I had to just end the day. There are graphical glitches, such as: characters spinning around when getting up from a bed when someone wants to talk to them, closing a door then walking through it two times, etc.

7. SHORT, which may be a good if we consider the repetitiveness. My second play, when I managed to survive, took me around 12 hours, and I am even considered a slow player. So altogetherly I have spent around 22 hours (the rest I was AFK) and I feel I have seen everything the gameh as to offer.

All in all I had fun in the begining but unfortunately the second half of the game became more of a chore because there was nothing new or challenging happening, and so I was just looking forward to the ending. I am glad I bought it on sale.

[h1]This War Of Mine[/h1]
[u]In war, not everyone is a soldier[/u]

This is a fantastic game inspired by the 1992–96 Siege of Sarajevo during the Bosnian War.

As it paints a picture of war from the other side, its dark, gritty, raw, bleak, sad and at times straight up depressing and despite that its a fantastic game. It makes you care about your characters and the decisions you have to make to keep them alive.

Your actions matter. Kill or rob an innocent and your morale will suffer, with characters even turning on the group if bad choices were made. Turning away or helping people in need has consequences but at the same time you must remember if you help someone how does that affect your own situation.

You get the real feeling of struggle as you battle hostile scavengers, bandits, illness, hunger, injury, tiredness, soldiers and even the cold all while trying to keep your parties morale up.

Each character has their own backstory, personality and abilities and this really helps on further play through's. They have their own unique thing I.E: Smoker, Coffee Drinker etc. 

There are a bunch of preset stories to play through but then you have the option to make a custom game or even download a scenario via Steam workshop.

The crafting and scavenging mechanic is very enjoyable. As you search for basic raw materials to patch up holes in walls and build rat traps for food etc.

The addition of the War Child and Little Ones DLC further expanded on this. By adding children characters who are struggling to survive and come to terms with the horrors of war. This add's another level of sadness as you try to protect and innocent child.

Also nice touch all money from the war child DLC goes to charity.

The art style is fantastic almost like a hand drawn effect. The music and atmosphere are perfect for the setting.

I have the season pass but will leave individual reviews for each story.

So basically this game was on my wishlist since the day it was released. I just never felt like buying it somehow, and boy oh boy how much I regret that It took me 5 years to finally experience this gem of a game. I've just played This War of Mine for 8 hours straight and I'm in love. Let me explain to you why;

The beginning is a bit rough; there's no explanation about what to do while you're also immediatly being thrown in the middle of a group of survivors during a war. After a few minutes their basic needs start to kick in; they get hungry, sick, tired or sad. The job is to keep them fit and happy for as long as possible but this is where things get interesting because: how far are you willing to go to secure the wellbeing of your group? The first playthrough, I ended up at an elderly couple their house but (because the game isn't telling you clearly wat you can or can't do) I accidently scared them to sh*t while walking into their house because they thought I was gonna rob them blind. I was only in need of one bandage so when I found it, I left the house and all the other loot. Appearently my character felt so bad about it that he ended up in a depression while believing that taking that one bandage caused the death of this couple.
 I felt bad about this specific event (and the character went way deeper into a state of being 'broken') that I decided to do another playthrough while paying a lot of attention to what the people I encouter are saying before i act (this so I won't accidently steal and later 'cause death'). All of this went pretty good for a while untill other problems pop up like; being raided, the cold, walking a little bit too far into a building resulting in being lethally shot, death of group-mates causing depression upon other mates, group mates just leaving and taking food with them etc. This is where the game got real and interesting for me because something inside me changed. Where in the first playthrough I still had a decent amount of freedom in making choices, here I found myself forced to go back to that same eldery couple and rob them blind to guarantee the survival of my group (which were all wounded, depressed and hungry). I even took a knife with me to put them out of their misery.
This is exactly what the game is asking the player; what remains of your human side when you're forced into situations like this. what is the morally right thing to do. When things like playing the guitar, listening radio, reading a book all fail and you're left with the bare choice of survival; what kind of human do you choose to be? When killing the couple and leaving the house with the right loot that I needed I thought about the quote from the Joker in The Dark Knight: "As you know, madness is like gravity...all it takes is a little push''. The thing is; This War of Mine gives you a lot of these pushes and it's your choice how to deal with them. 
I know I will invest a lot more hours into this game because I keep on making choices I regret in the end and there's a lot more to discover for sure (also about myself). I strongly recommend everyone to buy this game, especially while it's in sale. It's a great experience which you won't forget.

A heartbreaking horror story with high replayability options (a variety of: situations for locations, locations themselves, characters, minor and major events.) As someone who plays a lot of shooters and strategy war games, I was intrigued by this game: a different perspective on war. As I was playing, I realised that the name "Progoren" (of the fictional besieged city in which this game takes place), could have easily been replaced by "Aleppo". 

It is a brutal slap of reality that this game could easily represent what people in a besieged city experience, in real life. That is no doubt also the message that War Child wanted to bring across with this masterpiece, in an innovative attempt to educate people what children in war go through, and that they require serious attention afterward to rehabilitate from the warped reality of daily life that they grew up in.


That is the purpose of the game. But now on to the game itself:

- This is a game with loads of possibilities for replayability. Available locations, situations for locations, playable characters, minor events, major events; all of the above are variable. Replayability: 10/10
- The artwork and design is interesting, strangely simplistic and yet it manages to pull you into this dark, harsh, reality. I can't think of any cons to it. Design: 10/10
- Mechanically, the game is quite intricate. Each character is truly a different person, with their own skills and flaws, biography, and based on that, reactions to certain situations. The survival is unforgiving, morale is flexible and paramount, and every action has its consequence. A mistake in the use of resources or in the picking of a location to scavenge at night can be a devastating blow to your playthrough. Caution is advised at all times. Combat and stealth are well executed. Mechanics: 10/10

In my opinion these are all the aspects of a game that matter. I honestly cannot think of anything I could improve or give feedback on.

When I first played it, I thought "This is like the Sims, if your Sims could commit suicide or die of starvation." I say this because of similar design elements. However, as you can see from the 150+ hrs logged, my completionist butt stuck with it. Once you log that much time into it, it does start to get boring, but mostly because there aren't fast forward buttons (like in the sims) for when your characters are involved in tedious tasks.

All that said, it's an engaging game that makes you need to strategize without being incredibly difficult. It accurately depicts the horrors of war, locations change after you visit (i.e. the hospital being shelled), and your choices do matter (if you attack a soldier intent on raping a civilian, it increases moral vs if you attack a defenseless old couple, your party becomes sad). Similarly, soldiers and rebels can be cruel to the average civilian. 

If you have a tendency to get attached to your characters, it's going to be rough at first. Before you figure out the game, party members will die from starvation, wounds from bandits or scavenging forays, sickness, or even by their own hand, if you cannot fulfill all their needs-- and often times you can't. Plus, the ending comes abruptly and with little feeling of accomplishment (if you're playing for hours, finally feel like maybe you're getting ahead, then 'the war is over'). However, this all feels very intentional to me, and leaves a resounding message-- there is no real winner in war. 

Overall, a good concept, with maybe a few things to be improved, but definitely worth a play through-- ESPECIALLY if you're only playing military-aggrandizing FPSs. Many scenarios and characters, all with different strengths and weaknesses, and their own individual backstory that unravels the longer you play. Wait for it to be on sale and buy it in a bundle, or with with DLC.

You know, a lot of gaming focuses on simulated combat and warfare - because it's attention grabbing and, in a decontextualised environment, fun. 

That's all good and well, but it truly takes masterful game design to create games that let you engage in these fantasy environments, while grounding you in reflection on what war actually means, and in many cases, how un-fun real war is.

By that measure, This War of Mine slots along classics such as the Metal Gear Solid franchise, in giving you a game which has great gameplay and a memorable storyline, but also enough to chew on philosophically and ethically as you play.

Highly recommended.

It's full of thorny problems, and that just makes your small gains all the sweeter. As things begin to go wrong, the choices get harder. Do you intervene when you see a soldier assaulting a woman in a ruined supermarket, or do you keep your head down? Do you shoot a medicine you can’t afford? These questions don't have right answers. But posing them, and putting the moral issues in sharp relief alongside the physical ones, is what makes This War of Mine one of the year's most thoughtful games.
