The first time I tried This War of Mine, I started at 10 am and played straight through until 6 or 7 at night, stopping only to eat and assure my girlfriend that I was still breathing. I haven't felt this sunk-in to a game since XCOM.

It's not because the game is overly complex - although there is no tutorial, and the first time you play, it just throws you into the deep end without knowing what you are doing, almost ensuring you will screw yourself over without realizing it. But that's kind of a good thing. It shows you what the game is about.

The basic structure is this: you control a group of 2-4 citizens trying to survive in a city gripped in a open conflict between government forces and armed rebels. (It's basically set in the mid-90's siege of Sarajevo, but the names have been changed.) You will have to survive this scenario for a certain number of Days, at which time NATO forces liberate the city, and any of your characters still surviving are able to escape.

Each day consists 12 hours of daylight and 12 hours of night. You will have many tasks that need to be accomplished: repairing the shell holes in your building's roof; cooking food; cobbling together beds, tools, and weapons; boiling water; much much more.

You can use the daylight hours for these tasks, but the problem is that you usually need to spend these hours sleeping. You can't sleep at night, because thugs and scavengers will attack your building when it's dark and steal your possessions or hurt your characters. So at night, some characters need to stand guard, and you also need to send someone out scavenging yourself, or you will run out of materials and food.

You end up sleeping in shifts in order to maximize your time management. It's basically a worker placement/resource management game. Assign your characters to tasks, and try to figure out the most efficient way to turn resources into other resources that give you an advantage, or just keep you alive. Each character has an index for Hunger, Morale, Sleep, and some other stats. You need to eat, or you'll starve. You need to keep warm, or you'll get sick. You need to sleep, or you'll stop being able to function. You can choose to scavenge, or trade, or even steal from (or kill) other characters you come across; but harming others and stealing will drop a character's Morale, and going low enough can result in fights with other characters, depression, or even suicide.

It's incredibly immersive. You come to know and care about your characters, as they each have different skills and personalities. One might be a handyman who's great at building things, while another is a hardened ex-soldier who doesn't lose any sleep over murdering someone to take their Vegetables.

The first time I played through (light spoilers), Marko (the guy I was scavenging with most nights) came across some armed thugs. I would have been able to steal from these guys without feeling bad (because they're not good people), so I tried. But they were armed, and Marko got killed trying to escape. When he never returned, Bruno and Pavle (already depressed) became despondent and stopped doing any work or eating. Then Zlata showed up at the door. Her special skill was "Bolster Spirits" - exactly what my ailing fellows needed! And it started to work, I tasked her with cheering them up, and she spent hours talking to them, bringing them out of their darkness.

Then winter came.

As we got colder and colder, with too few materials to build a stove, the depression came back. Eventually Bruno broke. He beat up Zlata and left, stealing the few remaining supplies we had when he did. Pavle went catatonic, and soon died of exposure. Crushed, I ended the game knowing that Zlata could not survive on her own.


I have now put MANY hours into the game and beaten it with each different group of survivors. Each playthrough tells its own story, although they are all similar, they are never exactly the same. Events happen and locations differ, forcing you to pick different strategies to solve the same problems. Some minor nitpicks of mine that don't ruin the game, but do need fixing in my opinion.

- I understand game time needs to flow faster than real time, but it moves so fast it takes a character like 30 minutes to move from one side of a small house to the other when it would really only take 30 seconds or less in real life. It's really frustrating when you have an hour left to leave a scavenging location before the night ends and you can't reach the exit in time even when you run when it shouldn't really take more than a couple minutes max to reach the exit. Or when you wait until the last hour to feed a character in the day time in order to stretch out your food supply but your character doesn't even make it to the kitchen in time to eat, let alone have enough time to eat. This would be an easy fix with a mod, but I have no programming experience and I don't know of any mod that addresses this issue.

- Some of the inventory stacking doesn't make much sense. Like why does one bottle of moonshine take up a whole inventory slot when you can have 10 bottles of water in a single slot? or 1 knife vs 2 pieces of lumber? This needs to be addressed, and again I haven't found a mod that fixes this. Most of the inventory mods have reviews that say they don't work properly, so I haven't bothered trying them.

- When you have the element of surprise, bullet damage should increase tenfold. It shouldn't take 12+ rounds to kill a man with body armor and a helmet on if you get your first shots off without him knowing you're even there. I know for certain I could bring him down myself with 1-3 well placed rounds. While I am a former combat infantryman, it's really not hard to aim a gun even for a civilian (especially one like my character who already had 30+ in game days of scavenging and killing experience). This little incident caused the death of my most valuable scavenger because I quickly ran out of ammunition and didn't have enough to eliminate his two buddies even though I was carrying around 25 rounds.
*There is however a workaround if stupid things like this happen to you, as soon as your scavenger dies you can press control-alt-delete and bring up the task manager to minimize the game window where you can then close the game on your taskbar. The game autosaves every in-game day. So when you open the game again you'll be able to replay that day and night to fix any silly mistakes you made.

- Near the end of my first play through, a woman came to my door asking for help. I had previously helped her board up the windows of the house her and her daughter were staying in, so we were on good terms and naturally she came to me again when she needed us. She said she had noticed men watching her house during the day and was worried about them raiding her house at night and harming her and her daughter, so she asked me to send one person to protect her that night using her deceased husband's shotgun. At that point I had enough resources for her and her daughter to stay with me instead and be safe. I had my house completely boarded up with a reinforced door and alarm system, I had 3 military rifles, one scoped rifle, 2 shotguns, 2 pistols, 3 knives, an ax, almost 200 rounds of ammunition, and I had enough food to feed my 4 people as well as her and her daughter for 1-2 weeks. I just wanted to ask her to stay with us instead, but the game would not allow that (rather frustrating). I had to either let her and her daughter potentially get raided and harmed, or sacrifice one of my own people for the night to potentially be harmed. The only character I was willing to lose for the night was sleeping because he was on guard duty the previous night, so I was planning on sending him with her as soon as he was well rested, but she got upset and left without giving me the chance to help her. This resulted in all of my characters getting depressed because we just left her to potentially die with her daughter.

At a certain point some gameplay felt reminiscent of the zombie flash game The Last Stand/Last Stand 2/Union City with the searching locations, albeit far more detailed and with a real-world basis rather than a fully fictional world basis.  This isn't a negative comparison, just a comparison.

The gameplay mechanics are a matter of learning what works well and utilizing it.  There will always be setbacks, but on my first playthrough I found there were developments and aspects of survival in the game that I utterly neglected because I didn't even know they were available, nor did I know how the crafting and development trees integrated.  The game doesn't show you how they develop, you just have to intuit it (or look it up elsewhere).

This makes for a harsh, harsh learning curve.  If you play it blind, subsequent games will improve massively.

Time and resource management become critical, as well as sleep, food, and morale.  It's an excellent game, though not always a fun one - it's frequently bittersweet, which makes for a very challenging, different game.

This War of Mine is a meticulously crafted experience to force you into a difficult position. The lack of tutorials, or "help, how do I do this?" menus only strengthens the deep feeling of hopelessness that you find yourself into. Did something and now you regret? Well, too bad! That is life, you gotta live with it! This War of Mine succeeds where so many other titles failed: It forces you into a complex situation where you need to show your true colors. It makes you take a deep breath and consider deeply the possible consequences of your actions. And there are no indicators, no counters, no User Interface telling you what is best or what is happening after. It makes your choices meaningful and important. It makes you cry for being helpless, for being unable to fend for yourself and your loved ones. 
On top of a beautiful soundtrack This War of Mine is a unique experience that can truly open your eyes and help you sympathize with people in tough situations. It can also help you find that humanity in you that might have been lost in midst of brainless shooters. But to get there, you will need to get through it first. [b]While I truly highly recommend this game, use your best judgment for when is the best time for you to play it.[/b]

OK, now time for the serious review. At $20, I can recommend it. 

My biggest complaint with this game was the controls using a gamepad are pretty garbage. Games with stealth elements that have less than perfect controls are always frustrating, and the GAMEPAD controls in this game are literally broken. Your action button stops working if NPCs are taking nearby! Ah, the quirks of PC gaming...

So I went online to find a fix, and I was surprised this started out as a mobile game. Intended for point and click controls, no gamepad or keyboard. Lo and behold, all my problems with controlling the game were gone when I started using my mouse to control the game. I highly recommend everyone reading this do the same: Just use a mouse to control the game.  

A little frustrating not having a tutorial, a little frustrating not having control over save points. But I get it and it adds to the atmosphere. You are controlling a house of refugees in wartime. They didn't get a walkthrough before war broke out. 

Not being able to load the latest save point really pissed me off when I didn't have full control of the game using a gamepad, but once I had full control with a mouse, it made the game more exciting. If you do something risky, its on you, not the mechanics when you get capped. Risky actions have can have immediate and dire consequences in this world. 

FYI, if a character dies, don't sweat it. Someone else will show up before too long to join your motley crew. But if you REALLY do not want to lose a character, press ALT+F4 to crash out real fast after you die. It an unintended hack, but it works.

Basically the game asks you the question; What would you do in a desperate situation with no good options.

The story seems to be inspired by real events due to the feeling of desolation and real horrors like starvation and people dying from trying to get a piece of bread then being shot by a sniper 200 miles away.

Another plus for this game is that all resources are all useful and you´ll need all of em i.e water, food, wood, medicine, dildos whatever and you are always on the brink where everything is still needed. 
Also i would like to commend 11bit studios for the economical trading system where certain items are worth more than others like coffee or medicine due to low supplies i.e just like in real war times which indicates real good design.
Bravo.

It's jammed, but Anton says he can fix it with some supplies I can get from the supermarket on the way back.

[h1]This War of Mine is a deeply atmospheric and evocative new experience of war, as it is told from the perspective of the civilians just trying to avoid becoming 'collateral damage.' Scavenge. Make Tough Choices. Build. Kill. Survive.[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
During the day, you may craft, reinforce your shelter, and tend to the physical and mental conditions of your survivors. At night, one of them must leave the relative safety of the shelter to scavenge for much needed supplies like food, medicine and supplies.  Do you sneak through the rubble of the city around you? Or do you fight the other survivors, bandits and corrupt military you encounter? CHOOSE!

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Art and Atmosphere[/u][/b]: The game features a dark, scratchy, inked art-style that made it feel as though you were playing in a haze. It really gave the game a surreal quality despite the horrors unfolding around you. Which, presumably, would be how a person living in a war-torn, bombed out city would might feel. The sound effects, the game visualizations (ex: for sounds) and character biography cards all add to the sense of dread, tension and the faint hope of rescue.  

[*][b][u]Combat/Stealth Mechanics[/u][/b]: As I mentioned above, the game does a good job of adding a level of stealthiness to the night time encounters. Combat is usually brief and brutal. All contributing to the sense that these are not heroes or trained combatants, but rather desperate everyday people. 

[*][b][u]Compelling Survival Mechanics[/u][/b]: Your survivors need to eat and sleep. They need to be kept warm and healthy. They need to be able to recover their calm after traumatic events. And they need to be kept armed if they are to survive the night. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Clumsy Controls[/u][/b]: I'm not sure if this was intentional (to add to the atmosphere of desperation) but the controls in combat are a bit on the cumbersome side. All actions (including combat actions) are done by clicking buttons that appear contextually, depending on the situation and whether your character is in "scavenge" or "combat" mode. It is not quick or intuitive.  And when the command to "attack" is a mere millimeter away from the "run towards that bandit with a shotgun" button, mistakes will be made. OFTEN.

[*][b][u]Awkward Save Game Mechanics[/u][/b]: The game only saves your progress immediately after a night mission. That means that if you have to close the game after performing all your daytime upkeep activities but before the night mission, the game does NOT save AND the randomized morning events will be re-randomized. Also, if your character dies on a night mission, the game saves IMMEDIATELY. There are no save slots and no quicksaves. You are locked in. Probably done to contribute to the atmosphere.

[*][b][u]Severely Limited Inventory Space[/u][/b]: Your survivors have inventory space between 8 and 17, I think? Items tend to not stack higher than 5 and your equipped items also take up that same space. This makes prioritizing salvaged supplies paramount since you'll likely have to make several trips back to each location to collect everything. It also makes it irritating to trade with other survivors. 
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall, I'd say the game is definitely worth a look on sale. I recall my first successful play through as being compelling and moving. However, I feel like too much was sacrificed in the name of curating a particular experience. The implementation choices for the controls, save mechanics and limited inventory space were frustrating enough that it spoiled my desire to purchase later DLCs.

Not really for me. This game is one where you have to enjoy failing constantly and restarting to learn from your mistakes, but since a lot of the scenarios are randomized, you can't really prepare properly. I may keep playing, but until then it really isn't for me.

One of my favourite games on Steam as it is very unique. So much so, I find myself coming back to it again and again.

The setting is a modern Slavic war zone, where you get to play as the civilians trying to survive till the end of the war. The DLC does add a story element to the game, but for the most part, you are creating your own narrative as you go. You really have to balance whether to help those in need or yourself in order to make it through the war. Which sets a great backdrop for the game play.

Even though it seems like a 2d plat-former at first glance, it plays more like a point and click adventure/strategy game. * (mostly-similar mechanics) Rebuild 3 - Zombie survival, base management and strategic combat, rpg'sque, crafting, some characters ideal to combat, some to crafting, etc..
* (slightly-similar mechanics) Gunpoint - Stealth/forward combat styles on a 2d plane.

But This War of Mine is different in several ways:

* "Don't even have food planned for tomorrow (for months)"-level of difficulty as normal.
* Amazing beautiful and atmospheric backgrounds, well defined effects (to indicate sound, unseen-areas, etc.).
* Chilling atmospheric sounds.
* Gripping atmospheric dialogues.
* 3d. (yeah, current-implementations of this type-of-game were unfortunately shockwave/flash games, and were unjustly derided as such)
* Gripping and luring plotline.

Very worth-while.  Go to it and remember the imperative to live.

I'll go against the grain here and won't recommend this game. Reading other reviews, a lot of people liked this game because it is allegedly so gritty, realistic and unusual. But it just isn't a good game, in my opinion. 


[h1]First, the story.[/h1] 

There isn't one besides that you are stuck in a city ravaged by a civil war and it sucks. Instead, the game just constantly hammers its message home: war is bad and innocent people get hurt. Who knew? It's not even subtle. In the hospital, you find a note that the pediatric wing was hit the hardest in a shelling and most kids died. In the supermarket, a soldier is sexually assaulting a woman and there's nothing you can do about it. Kids are begging for meds for their mother. That kind of thing. And in case you somehow miss all that, there're a few F... the war graffiti around. But luckily, the greatest problem your guys have is that they're out of coffee or cigarettes.


[h1]But more importantly, the gameplay is not very good, either.[/h1] 

Over day you're stuck in a house where you can do some crafting and your guys can eat and sleep. Occasionally, a trader or people looking for help come around. At night, one of you goes out scavenging. 
The days are absolutely tedious. Every day, you have to scan the radio, make firewood, cook food, make water, tell your guys to eat and sleep, and take care of your other crafting. It's completely repetitive. And you have to do all that by point & click if you play with mouse and keyboard (don't know how it works with controller). There isn't even the option to speed time up, you have to wait until they veeerry slooowly finish what they are crafting before you can send them to the next task. 
The nights aren't much better. Try to sneak through the different locations, grab all the stuff, go home when your backpack is full. In some locations, you can trade but you have to bring whatever you plan to trade and since neither "prices" are fixed nor the trader's inventory, it's almost impossible to predict what you'll need.
Combat is basically spamming your mouse button and hope for the best.
There's no RPG element whatsoever, so you don't get better at combat, sneaking or trading, you can't even craft a bigger backpack - there's no change, no progression, it all stays the same.

All in all, I was pretty disappointed. I like base-building games. I like strategy games. I like stealth games. In theory, this game is right up my alley. But the only strategy involved here is the sequence in which you build/upgrade additional crafting benches and finding enough supplies to do that takes several days of scavenging. There's a couple of options to generate food but they are pretty useless and take a lot of supplies, a lot of time, or both. The stealth part isn't that great, either. If anyone is moving close by, you wait until they went elsewhere or take a different route. Basically, everything in this game is tedious and takes too long and there's absolutely nothing that makes up for it. 

So, I recommend this game for people who like being bored and depressed. The rest should maybe give Sheltered or Mark of the Ninja (if you like stealth) a try instead.

Base management-stealth hybrid, set in a warzone where you play as civilians trying to survive the everyday realities of a war torned city.
During the day you build your  base and manage your group of survivors, making sure they're eating, sleeping, healthy etc., and by night you raid a location in the city, getting supplies by way of scavenging, stealing, or trading.
Despite several badly designed mechanics in my opinion, I highly recommend this game to anyone that likes base management and/or serious games.

It's not a very bad game, but it's not a good one either, and it's definitely, horribly overrated.

You control a small group of civilians who try to survive while there's a war going on. For some reason, you never leave your house during the day, and you are able to go to one single location, with one single character, for looting, during the night.
The whole game consists in gathering materials and crafting stuff, except for the looting missions at night where you also have some time-limited exploration/stealth/combat (but still focused on gathering materials). I think I killed maybe 8-10 people in my playthrough, all in self-defense, including some people who were friendly one night but aggressive the night after for some reason :s

Prositive:
+ As another reviewer said, "realistic war simulation from a civilian perspective" (I wouldn't say realistic, but that's still an original perspective with some tough survival elements)
+ Nice art and ambiance (although globally depressing - not a fun game !)

Negative:
- No manual save, and autosave only once a day (when the night ends)
- Boring days at the house: after the initial ransacking of the house and equipment-building, my days were basically "put wood in the heaters, listen to all radio stations, press End Day".
- No control over time (can't speed it up, you can only end the day but not fast forward a few hours). I'm pretty sure I missed a bunch of daily events because I couldn't be bothered to wait a whole day after doing the tiny things I had to do in the morning.
- While the day is unnecessarily long, the night is punishingly short: night exploration is very time-constrained, and if you don't leave the area before the time limit (which is never announced, you'll just find about it the first time you reach it), your looter may get in trouble on the way back home.
- Painful combat mechanisms/UX. Good thing combat isn't too common.
- So many DLCs

It has been long since a game grabbed hold of me and pulled me deeply into its world, and longer still since a game stayed with me long after the ending credits.  I can't even remember the last time I watched the credits on a game, but as I triumphantly stepped out into the sunlight as news of the cease-fire called out from my tiny radio, and the credits began to roll, I watched them, sort of numb inside from the experiences I had witnessed, the things I'd done, things I'd had to do, just to survive...

The characters are only roughly fleshed out, but that only means that you can come up with your own stories.  For example, I got a stong vibe that Katia and Pavle would have had lots of unwashed, desperate wartime sex if not for gloomy, sullen Bruno incessantly thwarting their romantic endeavors due to his secret and perverted lust for Katia, but they had to deny their feelings and sacrifice their shared need to cling to each other for what?  So Bruno could lurk in the kitchen, using his culinary gifts to stretch their meagre resources into few extra meals?  War is hell.

If I have one regret, it is that I didn't kill Bruno off the day before the war ended.  I wish I could have seen the look on that miserable, selfish, whining coward's face as he lay clawing for breath in a trash-filled gutter, see the realization set in that he'll never get to go back to his restaurant, or see the mysterious 'friend' he kept nattering on about.  Then I'd check in on Katia and Pavle, watch them both pretend to be sad at Bruno's passing, neither willing to admit what the other is thinking:  "If he hadn't been such a good cook, I'd have beat him to death with a crowbar myself WEEKS AGO!  Tobacco is worth its weight in gold to the trader, we never would have gone hungry without that fat wanker smoking all the time!  He might as well have been burning MONEY!"  

This game is billed as being replayable, but the thought of stepping back into that world so quickly after stumbling out of it gives me pause.  This is a solid game, unique and gripping, but also severely depressing.  I highly recommend it, but if you're looking for a game you can play over and over, look elsewhere.  I may revisit it in a year or two, but one can only immerse oneself in such a bleak and unforgiving world for so long.

From Cook to Killer - Bruno's Story.  

Who would have thought Bruno had it in him?  He started off with Marko and Pavle - a rag tag bunch of survivors - and seemed by far the meekest of the group.  They were stumbling along, hard day after hard day, dangerous night after dangerous night, slowly and patiently gathering supplies, reinforcing their shelter, creating basic infestructure and trading.  In a word - surviving.  The group shunned violence and even went out of their way to help those in need when they could.  Then Roman joined up and suddenly everything changed.  It was as if his violent past and bad karma had caught up with him and cast an evil eye over the rest of them.  One the 14th night, Marko was killed at the church while looking for supplies. Then in short succession, both Roman and Pavle were killed.  Bruno was left all alone.  

Partly out of pure desperation, and partly driven by vengence, he picked up a weapon for the first time in his life, and visited the places where his comarades had fallen.  When the deed was done, he took the supplies.  Eventually it became easier - or did he get better at it?  The awkward clumsy cook turned cold blooded killer.  Eventually Zlata joined up, and Bruno sent her off for her initiation - her first blood.  She paid a visit to the elderly couple in the suburbs, who were trying to live a normal life in a world gone mad.  It didn't take long.  And like Bruno, Zlata got over it.  

Over time the two made a comfortable life.  They were able to trap their own food, make water, make moonshine, refine it into pure alcohol, grow herbs, and make medicine.  They were able to trade booze and medicine for the indispensible basics needed to run their small manufacturing operation.  They survived the winter.  One could even say they were thriving.    

With news on the radio speculating about the imminent arrival of peace-keeping forces, Bruno decided he had one last mission.  A bit of unfinished business.  One dark night he slipped away wearing a battered helmet and balistic vest - and armed with his trusty hatchet and sawed-off shotgun.  He paid a visit to the church where seemingly a lifetime ago, armed thugs killed the priest before turning on Marko.  He returned before dawn, slightly wounded, but 3 bodies laid on the stone floor of the church - human wreckage in the wake of his path of vengence.  Zlata returned for several nights, reaping the plentiful bounty of loot.  

And then just like that, the war was over.  

Zlata left her homeland and settled in Canada.  Bruno stayed behind and tried piecing back his life.  The two never spoke again.

At its core, This War of Mine, is a 2D side-on crafting-survival game.  The bleak setting is a civil war in a fictional eastern european country, where you must survive as a small group of civilans (two to four) living in a bombed out house.

Gameplay has 2 phases; each day you build up your home, crafting tools and equipment, and deal with occassional vistors wanting help or offering trade.  At night you scavenge for resources in various war-torn locations, where you can encounter various people, mostly harmless nobodies, some traders, and some hostile.

It's at night when most of the action happens, you could be shot at by unseen snipers, get into a fight with soldiers or thugs, or steal from other survivors if you get desperate enough.  As usual, combat can lead to injuries that need treating.  Not so usual is the depression that can occur if you steal from innocent survivors, that will also need treating.  At the end of each night you return to find discover whether your friends were injured during a robbery or slept peacefully.

The atmosphere is already depressing and gets even worse when things start going wrong.  Your people can starve, die from sickness or injury, commit suicide, or run off in the middle of the night.

If you let it, this game can really draw you into the story unfolding for your survivors, feeling all the ups and downs they go through.  The recent story additions play on this, giving you more narrative beats and difficult decisions, in what feels like a more tailored experience.  I found The Last Broadcast story particularly moving and look forward to playing it again.

The story is excellent and the decisions that you do require some forethought and multitasking. Take heed with what you do in the game and any mismanagement with your resources and fellow survivors will result in terrible consequences. During certain parts of the game, you must be able to compromise and not be enthusiastic in taking everything there is in the area but rather be stealthy and take down any threats that may hinder you.

tl;dr:
I (still) like the core gameplay, but can't recommend at full price, mostly due to my experience with bugs and limited replay value.
[b]Don't read any guides, this or any review, etc. Try the game on PC, or don't.
The less you know beforehand, the better the game experience. You have been warned.[/b]

Gameplay:
[spoiler]The game core is good, but your most enjoyable run will propably be the first one while you don't know what to do.
That's the whole idea - a couple of [b]clueless[/b] civilians trying to survive.

Once you know the game mechanics well, it degrades into economy/base management.
You'll know what to build, what stuff to get, which tools and characters to use, which locations to visit, what exactly to expect there.
Instead of "Danger... I'll better shy away from that one" you'll read "zOMG, phat l00t on day 2!".
Ultimately you can make it without any major troubles in any scenario, the immersion and challenge is gone and it becomes a repetitive "wait out until the end".

Some game design choices force boredom upon you, e.g. skipping to the end of day when nothing else to do may cause your heater to run ot of fuel in the skipped time.

The Little Ones DLC is a waste. It does not enrich the gameplay, due to children's limited options. They can't even interact with other children visiting you. It is basically "lock away and feed".

Some achievements are poorly designed, because you'll only get them for doing exceptionally bad in the first place.
[/spoiler]

Technical/Support:
- Never ever even think about getting console versions. Controls are atrocious.
- 11-bit does a bad job maintaining it. Sure, graphics got polished and locations added, but... after years, there are still major bugs. [spoiler]E.g.: Interaction with with kids may frequently cause lock-ups of involved items and characters, forcing a restart at the last auto-save. Or the bug when no neighbours show up at all, which has been solved on Steam, but not in DRM-free versions. You can neither update, nor downgrade to a working patch. This basically forces you to re-buy on Steam because half of the game is missing.[/spoiler]
- New content is frequently bugged, and new bugs appeared in old content with new patches.
- Load times went up significantly compared to older versions.
- Pathfinding became worse compared to older versions. [spoiler]E.g. characters are running way past the neighbours they're supposed to interact with, then walk back. I also had characters stopping working to make [b]positive[/b] remarks like "We're gonna make it".[/spoiler]

This is not the glorified experience of a super soldier wielding more guns than the average man can carry. It’s the plight and suffering of the common man who is a victim of circumstances entirely outside of your control. You are not meant to enjoy this game or in any way feel that you have the tools to succeed. But it will certainly push you to try nevertheless—obsessively so—likely because it is so terribly difficult and depressing when you inevitably die…slowly, one day at a time. And remember, this was created by the company whose reasoning goes, “Not sad enough? Let’s add children. Let’s add children with PTSD.”

[quote][i]My first experience, years ago, ended with Bruno crying on the ground. Katia was too wounded to get out of bed, Pavle had been killed trying to get us food, and now all Bruno had to do was boil some water so we could finally eat. But he was too broken to get up anymore. He sat there, weeping, until he froze to death on the ground.

That’s kind of how I felt.[/i][/quote]

At least we do have second chances in this game. There’s no reloads or retries while the game is still going—unless you’re quick on the ol’ alt+F4. But you can start over. So people saying that this game is exactly like war are not entirely honest. You still get to sit in your comfy chair when winter comes. But you’ll get pretty close to understanding just how soul-wounding it is to be an unwilling tenant of ‘conflict areas.’

[h1]Difficulty [/h1]

You can pretty much assume you’re going to fail your first scenario. Not just because the game is hard—but because it’s hard due to the fact that you have no idea what you’re doing. The game doesn’t really have an assist for this (despite the clear and elegant interface). Protection against predators is important—but how? You figure these things out through failure. And then through the Wiki. Eventually you will learn the things you should know: who runs like a pregnant yak, what’s a teddy for, where do I find an axe, when do I take the medicine, why would I give food to starving children when I am starving myself, how many people do I leave to guard, and just how essential is a chair? Don’t axe the chair.

This becomes a lesson of priorities. Namely, don’t die. Don’t charge people with your fists. Remember you basic needs: shelter, water, food—and about in that order—closely followed by anti-depressants, which in this case means cigarettes and booze. Also, take notes. You’ll be sad when you can’t remember where you left that stack of components because your bags were too full of wood and they didn’t seem needful at the time.

But even after mastering the mysteries, there’s still plenty of challenges to keep veterans occupied, for instance: Marko Solo runs, and ending on a ‘content’ note rather than just alive-but-not-quite-standing.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

One criticism is that this is not a fast game. You move at the pace of a sickly, wounded, sufferer of depression. And yet, I’ll still get sweaty palms when creeping around a neighbor’s house—slowly—wondering if I’ll get a shotgun to the face. This is the only game where I’m afraid of rats because you just don’t know if they’re rats. It’s also the only game where I’m afraid of parishioners and homeless people. Tension and dismay abound with only brief respite when you have too few materials to do anything but sit and play a melancholy guitar as you starve. But watching your characters sleep for five hours somehow seems to build anxiety when you know you have yet to barricade the windows before the raiders return, and they are coming tonight. But there’s no fast-forward either; just slow, stifling, patience as you’re bleeding out.

A second criticism is how easy it is to die a death of panicked clicking. For example, 'I had a gun, so why did I run up and try to punch this guy’s face to death? Err…to my death.' Yes, learning to kill appropriately (and quietly) is definitely a basic need. And yes, going on a murderous rampage through the neighborhood is the easiest path to victory (so long as you’re equipped with a couple sociopaths), and yet it is not the optimal route, as Zleta will tell you. But I do recommend YouTubing the proper use of crowbars nevertheless.

Crafting also seems a little off to me, being difficult to make a profit off hard work—but then, that’s probably intentional. 

[h1]Story[/h1] 

There isn’t much in the way of story other than: you’re in a war-zone. But there is plenty of mood and ambience to convince you of this despair from the gloomy, ashy colors to the skyline on fire. It’s a modern setting but often feels like a black and white docudrama directed by Spielberg; it’s hard to believe that people do actually live like this. 

The characters however are believable: ugly, troubled, but realistic with mundane backstories. I never feel particularly happy with them, or that I relate well to them. I have no special hero. They’re just people. There’s a slight disconnect, though I’m not sure if that was intentional—perhaps because of the multi-character managing view, or because there’s a kind of emotional self-preservational sense of detachment, the way you’d feel about someone else’s diseased and discarded puppy that you’re pretty sure is going to die. 

But, beyond the war-zone, there is a deep realism that’s more than “if I don’t have enough kindling, I can’t make clean water.” It’s “if I don’t stash the booze, Roman might get drunk and start beating up his housemates.” I think it is that attention to the details and ultra-realism that makes hacking a person to death with a hatchet absolutely hair-raising. Especially since they were probably your neighbor. Especially since you’re probably killing them over a can of corned beef. It’s brutal.

[quote][i]After four years of surviving this war, I was equipped with Roman, the one man army, who had pretty much single handedly brought the war to a close and cleaned the streets. His entire household was warm and content, thanks to him, thriving in cigarette-rolled capitalism. It was going to be my first perfect run. One night Roman went snooping in what I thought was an innocent household. He wasn’t going to steal anything—didn’t need it. He tried to sneak past a sleeping woman, but she woke up and came at him with a knife. The door to escape was barred. He had a weapon; he could have easily killed her. But she was just a civilian. He tried to punch her to frighten her off, but she stabbed him in the ribs. Roman never saw the end of the war that came two days later. [/i][/quote]

[h1]Recommendation[/h1]

It’s a good game if you’re depressed—or if you want to be depressed—or just be grateful for things like…tomatoes. If you want a game with a challenge, I recommend it. But more philosophically, if you don’t want to forget what kind of world you really live in, this one will make you grateful, but also horrified that charities like War Child are still needed today.

This is a game with a strong focus on the narrative and your decisions. 
The gameplay is divided into in game days, during which you are setting your survivors with various tasks. 
The food and water supplies are sparse, there’s no basic furniture and the shelter is a collapsed ruin – so you have to choose each action very carefully. 
Each encounter offers something new and all your choices will have a long lasting consequences for the rest of the game.  Most of them will hurt like hell, so don't expect an easy learning curve. 

There are random events that happen when you least expect it, and at least from my experience, luck will always play a major factor - whether you start during the summer and you dont need a stove, or if you start in late autumn and the stove will be your first priority. 

Advice: Keep special attention to food and hunger states, since this was for me by far the hardest thing to manage.

The game is hard at first, but also very rewarding once you manage to get through the war without neither killing nor stealing, even helping all neighbors and other civilians on the way. Depending on your decisions you get different endings for your characters. It’s fun for me to bring each character towards a better future as mentally and physically healthy as possible.
I also love that the developers already offer quite some bonus content, from a charity DLC to the free anniversary update to the children DLC - and they are still adding content to the game (in form of DLC), even now 4 years after release!
Definite recommendation.

For three or four days now, I have played nothing but "This War of Mine". I am a veteran of Iraq and I remember all too well the hardships it brought upon the civilians, especially in the beginning of the war. I remember being heartbroken at the sight of children crying and begging for food on the side of the road.

This "game" puts you square in the middle of the experiences of those civilians. It is a brutal, kill or be killed world - where an act of unimaginable violence may let you live another day, but it can also break your heart and soul. Some days, you are offered a chance at compassion - and if you take that chance, risking your own safety and resources for others, you may find you feel a bit better about yourself.

Then there are the times where you are stuck between a rock and a hard place. You are unarmed, scavenging for anything to save your friends, and you peep through a keyhole and see a soldier brutally beating - and possible worse - a woman. He has an AK-47, you have a lockpick and a rumbling stomach. So you sit there and watch - afraid that any noise may turn his violent attention upon you. When it is all done, you hide until he leaves and then, shamefully, pick over the bloodied body of the woman for anything she may have scavenged before the soldier got to her.

This is "This War of Mine" - a dark, beautiful, haunting, exhilerating, and horrible tale.

What's that tagline, "The first casualty of war is innocence"? It applies here - in a way you would have never imagined coming from a computer game.

Inspired by the Bosnian War, This War of Mine is a survival strategy game that explores the horrors of war by putting you in the shoes of the civilians. You spend your days taking care of your survivors and your shelter, and send people out scavenging for materials at night, which can take the form of straight trading, looting or actual thieving. All along, the game throws you moral choices, be it in the form of taking new people in when you don't have the food, helping out your neighbors in need when you need the medicine for yourself or putting yourself in danger of physical harm to save others.. Moral choices aside, the game is extremely hard. I beat it first time without too many casualties but was hanging on by a thread for most of it. I've heard people complain about replay value but I'm three playthroughs in and still enjoying it tons. Every playthrough brings new possibilities, you explore more of the mechanics, meet new characters... I almost got a unlocked an alternate ending too! This is a pretty good game. Very interesting concept that works great.

During a day the player controls a group of survivors, keeps an eye on them, decides what should they do (making new things, collecting items, sleeping, melting snow into water, cooking...etc..) and helps them survive in a decaying building. 

On the other side, every night the same question appears - what now? One of us should sleep. One of us should go out and scavenge. And one of us should guard the house to make sure nobody will steal anything from us during the night. This is where the real fun starts - scavenging means exploring (usually) hostile areas and stealing items. At first it's ok - stealing some things from an abandoned building... no problem. Stealing from a house full of thugs... no problem. But what next? Abandoned building have nothing to offer because people took everything already. What now? Should we steal from hospital full of injured people or from two old and almost deaf people? Let's focus on these old people. Eh.. they have a son.. who has a shotgun? What now? It's either kill or be killed. Steal or die.

This War of Mine soon becomes a game full of moral and uneasy choices. It excels at illustration of the horrors and hard choices of war from a new point of view. This game will make you a bad person. This game will find the evil buried somewhere in you and forces you to use it to survive. TWoM greatly captures what war makes from us - only the strongest survive, you can feel as a good person but when it comes to surviving we are all bastards.

This War of Mine is a strategic survival game where you must find food, find supplies by either scavenging, looting or stealing. Well worth its price as the game has high replayability. It does frequently go on sale which is a nice bonus.

[b]Story - 8/10[/b]

The goal is to survive the war in the fiction city of Pogoren, Graznavia. You can craft your own story by choosing if you want to steal, kill or just barter with the NPCs.

Liked: The story is shaped by your own decisions and you could lose characters just because you wanted to go steal one night. The scene after you survive showing all your actions and story of characters after the war.

Disliked: Simple story with no major twists or turns unless you choose to do so.

[b]Characters - 9/10[/b]

Liked: There's a variety of characters to play as, so a new playthrough always gives you a different situation to deal with. Each character gets their own traits and you can have up to 4 in your shelter at one time. They all have their own story too and if you keep them around you can learn more about them.

Disliked: Some characters ability wise can be dead weight for your team, you may even want to purposely get them killed so you get a better ally.

[b]Gameplay - 9/10[/b]

Gameplay revolves around a Day and Night cycle. During the day you spend your time crafting and taking care of the characters needs. During the night you choose which characters go to sleep, guard and scavenge. During scavenge you explore different places to collect supplies and more places will open up to you providing you with more options and more loot. This is where you can lose your character if you take risks or are not prepared. If you do not leave the area in time your character may not come back to the shelter. After the character returns or does not return there might be a raid in your shelter. This could involve your characters getting injured or loss of supplies if you did not prepare well enough during the day.

There is also special events that can happen ranging from an increase in crime, winter or bartering. 

Liked: Variety of crafting but easy to learn, taking care of characters needs will be difficult at first, loads of places to explore, combat is simple but rewarding, Franko saves lives.

Disliked: Winter can be easy if you know what you are doing. 

[b]Art - 10/10[/b]

Liked: Characters look real and the environment looks broken. This shows what war is about.

Disliked: I had no problems with the Art.

[b]Soundtrack - 6/10[/b]

Liked: Guitar tracks can be nice and other tracks are atmospheric. Sound effects were good all around.

Disliked: Short soundtrack, not much variety, can be repetitive.

[b]Overall - 8/10[/b]

First of all, I feel it's important to mention that this is the first game I've bothered to take the time to review on Steam. It impressed me so much that I felt the need to praise the developers on a review forum rather than just speaking its praises to my friends (and anyone else that will listen, because I do!).

I thought of it as Fallout Shelter's community-survival gameplay mixed with oldschool Metal Gear (not MGS, just MG...) stealth combat. During the day you take control of all shelter inhabitants, directing them what to do and what to craft with your limited resources. During the night you take direct control of one inhabitant you designate for a scavenging mission. All scavenging locations are different and provide different challenges--some are empty of people but require you bypass locks or boarded-up doors via crafted items, some might be filled with other civilians just trying to survive, some were chock-full of armed thugs who shoot-first-ask-questions-later. When dealing with civilians you must choose between acting benevolent or malevolent--you could either help them and trade items which they desperately need, or rob them blind (and then trade the stolen items that they need back to them!). All of which has positive and negative effects on everyone in your group. Some survivors appreciate someone willing to get their hands dirty (with blood) for the benefit of the group, others become depressed at the fact that they needed to resort to criminal activity to survive. Sadness, injury, and sickness all require time and resources to cure (comforting from other survivors, bandages, medicine respectively), meanwhile you need to make sure the shelter is secure and everyone is fed.

The replayability with the different starting scenarios (and the option for a randomized scenario!!!!) is absolutely amazing. I bought this game (along with several others that really interested me) about a week ago as part of a huge sale, because I'm rather frugal when it comes to video games. I just managed to complete my first scenario. Upon finishing the first scenario, I actually regret not purchasing all of the DLC while it too was on sale.... but it won't stop me! This game impressed me that much, that I refrained from buying the base game until it was on sale but now but now after playing it I am willing to pay full price for DLC to extend its life.

If you’re a fan of story-driven games where your choices matter and really have an impact on the ending of the game, then I highly recommend This War Of Mine. Not only was it incredibly entertaining (especially for the non-sale price!), but it’s also one of the only war games out there that doesn’t put you in the shoes of a super soldier running killing everyone and everything that looks at you. The combat is difficult but rewarding, the survival aspects aren’t ground-breaking but certainly keep you entertained and thinking between scavenging missions, and the game as a whole is just amazing. Oh and the fact that the hatchet’s tooltip says “used for chopping up furniture….. or people” is just the icing on the cake; especially since you actually chop people up when stealth killing with the hatchet. And then your character either feels good about it (if they were violent looters/thugs) or terrible (if they were civilians).

I was not interested to play this game based on the advertisements, but I randomly purchased it at a low cost and it totally surprised me.  You will be scavenging and creating a base for a group of survivors.  You have to manage operations in your base daily and at night you send one survivor to scavenge. You will have to ensure that your shelter is warm and your survivors have access to medicines, food and other basic necessities. You can get better off in the game by bartering. You can produce goods in your base (e.g. tobacco, alcohol or so forth) and exchange them for basic necessities. 

This game is hard in the beginning and you will fail many times in the beginning, but it is totally worth it! If your character gets injured and you ran out of medicines or bandages - you can take them to the hospital. The doctors will medicate and bandage your character for free. Do this before they get too sick or injured as the extremely depressed and deeply injured characters are unable to leave house at night. 

Depression is a dangerous killer: 
- Your characters may get depressed if you kill civilians or make poor choices.
- Alcohol can lower it and turn depression into sadness. Listening to songs on radio and playing an instrument can lower depression and prevent it. 
- Talk to a depressed character. 
-  Make your survivors to work in shifts to ensure that they are well rested. Overworking leads to depression. 
- You can  lower the risk of depression by helping people out in the game. 
- Depression prevention is very important, because sometimes depression is very hard to cure. The depressed character is unable to take care of his duties. As a result rest of the survivors may become overworked and they are in a risk of depression as well. 

Increase security of your shelter asap, because otherwise your characters will get severely injured in nightly raids. Get guns. You can buy guns. You can barter alcohol, tobacco or medicines to purchased guns and bullets. There are locations where you can discover guns, but it is good to have more than one for nightly base defense. I sometimes craft guns in the end-game to exchange them for other necessities. You should leave at least two good guns to base always when you go out raiding at night, because availability of guns reduces the risk of your survivors becoming injured in raids and theft. 

This game is not for you if you want to be a rambo. The combat mechanics have been made purposely slightly unpredictable. I usually kill NPCs by sneaking behind them or surprising them. I prefer to avoid direct combat, because it is not possible to be sure of outcome and characters end up dead easily in armed confrontation.

It's a decent game, but it has significant problems. The setting is interesting, focusing on the survival of ordinary civilians during a city under siege, inspired by real life Sarajevo, if I understand it correctly. The game is kinda bleak, but I didn't really find it depressing, it's rather you managing to make a cozy little shelter in a rough place, at least once you've figured out the mechanics. My favourite feeling was managing the temperature at a decent 16 degrees during the cold wave.

The presentation works well, they sell the bleak setting with simple but pretty graphics. The story of each character is kinda basic and didn't quite grab me, though.

The place where the game falls apart is in the mechanics. The game is a survival game with crafting and rougelite elements: The core gameplay loop is you building stuff during the day, and sending one person to scavenge during the night. You can't reload earlier saves (I mean, I'm sure you can do some save file shenanigans, but it's not the intended way to play) and the game randomizes content. You manage the usual survival aspects: mental and physical health, hunger, thirst, sleep, temperature. All good stuff.

There are some merits to the survival mechanics, usually I find that there are way too much focus on managing a huge number of bars, here it feels a bit more relaxed. However, the game falls apart a bit in the execution. I won't spoil the specifics, but there is definitely a best way to play, where you basically can ignore any real randomness and do more or less the same thing each time. This defeats the core principles of a good rougelite, where the challenge is doing the best with the assets you're dealt, and makes the gameplay similar, and offering little reason to replay it. And since the developers obviously intend you to replay it, giving you different starting characters to unlock, it must be seen as a bit of a failure on their part. 

Other issues is the game length, once your shelter is up and running, there is little incentive to do much more than play it safe and wait out the siege, and so the final part of the game feels tedious, and winning a foregone conclusion, and while I haven't clocked it, I would say that this part streches for easily an hour, maybe more. 

But before you've figured out the optimal strategy the game is a lot more interesting, and unless you look at a faq, it might take a while to find it. So if this game seems interesting to you, feel free to give it a try. I don't regret my purchase at all, so my "thumbs down" should be more seen as "read up on it before you buy" than "avoid".

[h1]Lackluster RNG game[/h1]

This game shields on the fact that its theme is war, and that it is giving us an insight on how cruel it can be, to be a very low effort game, which explains the very positive reviews with people moved and praising the game, but also complaining about mechanics. There are 5 main issues: RNG, Character morale management, the saving system, the fighting system (or lack of one) and bugs.

RNG: This war of mine is a *very difficult* game, which is always nice but the difficulty is achieved through RNG (random) mechanics like the loot spawned on the places that you visit (ex: the same place containing plenty or no food, unpredictably), the random chance at night of your survivors being injured or getting sick (this can happen even with good defenses and heating, and can be alleviated, through having the resources only, which are RNG-dependent), the random chance of the trader giving you the items you really need in vast amounts or carrying nothing of use, the random chance of getting new survivors and who they'll be (some useful, some not), and all kinds of random events requiring your resources and punishing morale if you can't meet the requirements...

Saving system: Gameplay-wise this game is completely infuriating, more after buying the "the little ones" DLC, where you grow more attached to the little characters and want to see them live.. A good way to avoid the RNG unfairness is to brave the most dangerous locations, but for that you will need to retry many nights in order to learn the patterns of the NPCs that will run you off or kill you if they detect you, or alternatively lose the night once you're found, which can easily derail your game and end in the death/disappearance of at least one character, which in turn tends to spiral into the death of everyone. You just can't afford even a single bad loot run, your situation is always desperate. If you retry a night which is a necessity for the most part, it means that you will also have to repeat the day, on which the same 20-ish minutes will need to be repeated "craft, sleep, trade...", a saving system (which is nonexistent, the game saves automatically once day and that's it) could alleviate this issue. 

Next, the combat is very unstable: one of the worst issues in this game, there's no skill involved, it comes down to who can stun-lock the other first, I've been in many fights and it's pure luck if you don't get stun locked and killed, even if you ambush someone things can go badly because after the ambush the other guy can retaliate and stun-lock you into a flurry of hits until you're dead or terminally wounded, so you'll need to pray to the RNG gods and maybe retry the night a couple times in order to not get killed, you can avoid fights but sometimes they're necessary to avoid depression (maybe you have the option to defend someone) or to get vital loot like a gun. There's also lots of optional fights that you can take for the loot, but they're so unfair and dangerous that your best bet is to avoid them, although you may not be able to afford that luxury. 

There are also the raids that may happen when you're away, you have no control over what happens other than leaving guards, but the results vary wildly, I've tested this loading the same day a few times after a raid (the raid intensity won't change even if you load) and things changed from everyone running them off using a lot of ammo, to the same but wasting way less ammo, to someone getting minor injuries, or even someone getting major injuries, this happened leaving 3 strong, healthy, well-rested and well armed guards with the house holes patched up, but it seems that the stronger raids always carry a lot of danger, there's always room for defense RNG shenanigans despite your best efforts.

Morale: Your characters get depressed easily, if there's someone in need at your door and you couldn't afford to help them, everyone gets sad, if they reach a threshold they may not respond to your commands and could run off alone with vital supplies or injure other characters. Stealing from innocent people and killing "innocents" also results in this, even if those innocent people were chasing you off their property and cornered you into a fight to the death. Luckily there are characters that suffer no morale impact after stealing or killing, so you can use them to do the dirty work in loot runs, however the game for some reason will impact the morale of everyone in the base if you do something immoral, even if they weren't on the loot run, making your depression-resistant characters useless.

-This War of Mine

First of all, I loved this oppressive, tense, honest and heart-breaking game. I give it 9 helpful shovels out of 10. For classification purposes, this is a resource-management survival game where you Sim-like control a group of survivors in a war-torn city. Unlike the Sims, the BEST I could consistently do for my survivors was: Hungry, Tired and Sad. Those were the good days and the little victories like sleeping in a bed were immeasurable. 

[Possible spoilers follow?]

As in life, there is no tutorial so your learning curve may vary; the uncertainty adds to the this-is-chaos-and-I’m-no-expert immersion. You’re a normal person, out of their element, balancing unknowns in a rapidly shifting situation. Learning by doing makes mechanics like combat wildly terrifying. My shovel/fist flailing and frantic running almost killed someone once… and then, later, did. Unless you restart, there are no take-backs but there are plenty of consequences. Most war games glorify and justify but This War of Mine has stark remorse, guilt, and worse - hopelessness. There are times when both you as the player and your survivor characters are both quietly saying, “I don’t think we’re going to make it.” 
I was worrying about my pseudo-Slavic victims of war even when I wasn’t playing. “How can I help them get through this? I hope it doesn’t get cold tomorrow… How can I get medicine for Pavle without getting shot at? We can’t afford both bandages and water...” You have some moral decisions to make: steal or starve, help others or horde for yourselves, intervene in horrors or stay unseen and safe. When you’re the normal video game war-hero there are obvious, shining, righteous answers but when you’re sick, wounded and starving your actions may more closely match the grey, gritty charcoal style of the game’s art. 

It’s harrowing. 

And what makes this game important is that you feel it. The tension of waiting for a good news report on the radio… every… single… day, the monotony of scavenging, guarding, and trying to sleep, and the desperation of bartering away things you really need for something you’ll die without. I’m pretty proud that one of my characters lived until the end of the game on my first try. It was touch and go. When the cease-fire news came, I had just told my character to eat the last of the rat bait, buying him one more day alive but ensuring starvation afterward. It didn’t feel like a victory – more a long, sad sigh of relief. Rewarding but haunting. Which is why this game is different and awesome; it’s an exercise in empathy. I almost can’t recommend This War of Mine because of how dark and human it is but that’s also the exact reason you should play it.

There's a lot of customizability and variability to give This War of Mine good replayability. The challenging game play makes success very rewarding. The music, characters, and environments are immersive. Aspects of the game are repetitive, but not to the extent that it hurts the game play. The stories and individualized characters and character comments keep the repetitive aspects of the game secondary. Players who enjoy survival themes will particularly enjoy This War of Mine.

As a game, this is a stellar resource-management survival simulator with atmospheric storylines. As a work of art, this is a deep empathetic tableau – and it has a message for any player with enough emotional intelligence to listen. Deviating from the normal strain of “super-soldier-fighting-baddies” games, you are a band of civilians stranded in a bombed-out house during the onset of civil war. Social infrastructure has broken down, and you’re on your own.

During nightfall, you’ll scavenge for scraps; each night presenting moral dilemmas and glimpses into the theater of wartime horrors. During the day, you’ll make tough decisions in resources management: as your characters’ bodies and spirits wear down, you'll begin to vacillate between prioritizing food, heat, safety, or mental well-being.

The interplay between the night and day game mechanics are what makes This War of Mine a unique triumph. Moral choices made during the night will influence your resource management decisions during the day. Go ahead, steal from your elderly neighbors, you’ll hate yourself in the morning - [i]literally[/i]. How clean can your hands stay when the temperatures drop, and your child is fever-stricken? People get sad through doing bad things. We all feel sad when we need to *stab people as they walk through doors or up stairwells*. 

The need for requiring one plank of wood to fuel a fire can mean survival or disaster. Where Rimworld (great game) had you hankering for a general skillset, This War of Mine will have you grieving for the loss of a character.

This War of Mine is a very interesting experience, it shows a side of warfare that remains hidden to most of us, the lives of the civilians caught in the crossfire. Its depressive atmosphere and dark realism are fundamental in generating empathy and sadness in the player, who will start caring very much for his/her ragtag group of survivors. However, the sentimental setting of the game shifts attention from another important aspect, the mediocre gameplay. Your main tool of survival in This War of Mine is Stealth, a genre I know very well, which is very poorly implemented in the game, fixed hiding spots, useless takedowns and poor character response time and speed all make for quite a frustrating experience, in addition, the NPCs field of view is very buggy or poorly done because I can never tell when one is looking at me or not, hiding spots become useless once you’re spotted, they only work the NPCs don’t enter the same room you are in. Your character scavenging is a civilian, he is also completely stupid. I understand the intent of showing the difference between soldier and civilian, but I don't understand how the survivors can't perform basic actions like: hiding behind objects, open a door while in cover, kick a door down, efficiently run from danger and carry a reasonable number of items (the vanilla game is completely flawed, mods recommended). The combat system is another negative aspect of the game, enemies (even other civilians) have a very clear advantage over you, they perform much better in combat and by perform better I mean that they have a higher chance of landing a hit or counter attacking than you do, you cannot scavenge in groups (which is terrible) and you have 0 control over the defense of your home (even if you choose to stay instead of scavenging). Guns are completely unbalanced and random, sometimes they one shot someone and others they take 1/4 of health, you never know. I shot a man in the back, point blank, with a shotgun and he just turned around and shot me with a rifle and killed me (even though I had a vest and a helmet). I personally believe that the positive reviews that this game has come from the setting, which I give a 10/10 for its superb atmosphere and representation of war, but gameplay wise this game comes forth as uninspiring and frustrating. I respect and love the message it transmits, but the gameplay itself isn't very impressive. IMO videogames have several “areas” in which to develop and, while This War of Mine nailed atmosphere, crafting and story, it dropped the ball in gameplay. Overall 7.5/10

You don’t really care what it’s about or why, and neither do the survivors you’re responsible for keeping alive. The game has two phases, day and night. During the day you stay at home and regroup, rest, eat, etc. At night, you go out into the city to scavenge, trade, and explore. Most people would be like, “Yeah easy enough.” And ♥♥♥♥, with the world the way it is, I wouldn’t be surprised if some of the people playing this game are aces from real life. But even these survivors have yet to face the long winter of This War of Mine.

[b]PROS[/b]

+ A genuinely sensational soundtrack. It’s gloomy, it bares down on you, and perfectly matches the mood the devs successfully set. Besides the score, music can be played on a guitar by a survivor or over the radio. These take priority over the score and are made to imminate from their relative location, it’s pretty neato and adds to the atmosphere. In fact, the sound in this game is fantastic all-around.

+ They executed the timing in this game brilliantly. Days can drag on forever when you have nothing to do (you can always end the day manually) but when you’re rushing-around trying to harvest rainwater or distill alcohol it goes by in a flash and you can never quite get everything done. Night is the same way, and if you get caught by the dawn your survivor could be in serious danger.

+ Excellent writing and dialogue. There’s just enough to immerse you without becoming burdensome or annoying in length.

+ Nails the difficulty. You can’t adjust the difficulty outside of making winter come earlier and last longer, and that’s important. It means that no matter how much you stockpile or how healthy you are, you’re one bad night away from losing a survivor to the cold or a bullet.

+ Makes you really consider your choices. “Good and evil” are totally irrelevant when you’re starving or your kid is sick. You gotta do what you gotta do, whether or not it’s “right” isn’t what this game asks you to answer. The question this game asks of you is, “can you live with yourself?” Sometimes, it’s a tough question to answer.

+ Become a survivor! Upload a picture of yourself into the game, add some stats, select an avatar, and you can watch yourself die a slow, cold, hungry death!

[b]NEUTRALS[/b]

0 Can become repetitive quickly in the late game. The fact of the matter is that surviving is a grind, and so is life for that matter, so this isn’t the game’s fault per se. It’s just that sometimes you’re doing so well that literally no one can stop you, and sometimes all your survivors are sick or wounded and there’s nothing you can do but wait.

0 While the map does have many different locations that can change-up and add/subtract these locations, it’s always the same city, and once you’ve played enough, you pretty much maintain a fundamental and generally unchanging strategy, but not always.

[b]CONS[/b]

- No multiplayer. I feel that this game would benefit a great deal with multiplayer. Co-op would be obviously nice, but so would competitive.

- You have to control every survivor, and they RARELY take any action on their own, which can become extremely annoying.

- No sense of purpose beyond surviving. This is a small complaint and barely a con, but I would love to see more than just “don’t die”, you know?

[b]T.L.;D.R./CONCLUSION[/b]

The thing I learned from This War of Mine is that what makes for a compelling statement doesn't always make for a compelling game. I loved the idea the moment I watched the trailer and I don't think I would change anything about the game itself, as every element is designed to convey an important message about war. Games have a long history of glorifying armed conflicts and there are seemingly infinite titles with the word "war" in them, and yet even the ones that try to show war for what it is (essentially a rather awful business) sooner or later boil down to action-packed shootouts where every enemy skull cracked open with with a bullet is a little adrenaline-inducing triumph with little time for moral considerations.

This War of Mine is different. It's a tale about trying to survive in inhumane circumstances while retaining some shreds of humanity. Your enemies here are not minions of a ruthless dictator or followers of a murderous ideology that can be lethally dispatched without breaking the comfort of moral superiority. Your enemies here are mundane and impersonal, slowly and inevitably creeping at the characters under your control: hunger, cold, disease and mental breakdown. You also have to fight other human beings, but it's hard to think of them as enemies, as they're also just trying to survive and protect their friends and loved ones, sometimes even at the cost of compromising their morals. And it becomes harder to judge them for it, as the longer you play this game, the more moral compromises will you be forced to make as well, up to the point of making you wonder if you're still one of the good guys.

And this is how a video game becomes a powerful medium for an important message. War is not guns and glory. War is a set of circumstance that turns people against each other, making moral principles a liability that puts individuals who follow them at a disadvantage. Over time, only those willing to break them get to live another day and condemn another settlement to freezing and starvation by robbing them of vital supplies.

So, why can't I recommend it? Because, while I find every aspect of the game superbly executed, I also find it too overwhelmingly depressing to play. I heard opinions like this before I tried it and it literally couldn't be a better recommendation for me, yet after playing it for just a few hours, I was done with it forever. I know it's not supposed to be fun or exciting, as that would make it just another glorification of war, but the resulting experience is just too offputting for me. No matter how hard you try to get all the supplies you need, your characters are always on the verge of breaking down. No matter how hard you try to be a good guy, at some point the game will make you choose between that and staying alive. And then, as if the game wasn't painfully gut-wrenching enough, the devs added children to it, for crying out loud. I'm sorry, I just can't enjoy it in any way or capacity.

This game teaches you how to budget.

It also teaches you why and how economies work.  One day you need bandages because everyone's wounded, and all you have is a ton of useless meds.  The next day, you need a lot of meds because everyone's sick and all you have is bunch of useless bandages.  Monetary value is simply a reflection on how much you need something at any given time, and value doesn't have to be expressed in dollars.  Sometimes its expressed in canned food as your friends and you are starving to death.

This game also made me realize how easy it is to rationalize theft.  It is hard to play this game without being tempted to kill for food, and when you personally experience that little hamster running in your brain that says [i] "You need it more than they do," [/i] you understand why others would kill you for food.  It's a weird feeling when you arrive back at your camp after a night of scavenging and stealing, maybe even murduring, to find that others just did the same to your group.

This game will change you.

I personally feel like the "omg so difficult!!1!11!" aspect of the game is overplayed a little. I think the difficulty is good - challenging, but not overwhelming. With no gameplay knowledge, walkthroughs, wikis, or prior experience, I succeeded on my first playthrough but with some losses.

I'm also not huge on how much people say "omg so war!11!1" about this. To me it felt more like a general "society broken down" situation rather than a warzone, although obviously there is heavy crossover between the two.

Echoing others: don't look up gameplay videos or wiki information or anything like that before you've played it. Figuring it out under the pressure of the game's hostile environment is how it's supposed to be done, and I think knowing how things work makes it significantly less fun. The game is designed to give you enough leeway that while you're learning things you don't get dumpstered for not knowing them, so it's not as though you'll be overwhelmed. You'll be just the right amount of whelmed.

One tip if I may though: try to have enough real-life time on your hands that you don't need to have any large breaks (more than a day or two) between sessions for your first play through. I'm not saying do a marathon session, but it's much more immersive (and enjoyable!) when you don't forget most of what's going on between sittings.
