This War of Mine is a Survival/Resource Management game inspired in the Bosnian War, that focus on the civilian side of the struggle, a great and fresh premise for a game.

The game takes place in a Eastern European country amidst a civil war between the government supported soldiers and a rebel faction called the Vyseni liberation uprising. Our characters (which we can chose from a different bunch) are caught in the middle just like everyone else that didn't manage to flee the country. The job of the player is to make sure that his characters are taken care of until an halt is put to this situation.

The game is divided in two phases, the morning phase that takes place in the shelter, which is the only phase where you can control all your characters. In the shelter you can craft items, make improvements, feed your characters, take care of their medical needs, brew moonshine among other things. Every now and again an event will happen, either someone wanting to barter, or anyone needing your help where you can decide to help or not. These events are very interesting since they have different rewards for different outcomes and the fact that most of the times your choices will be made based on the amount of resources you have or not, bring out your survival instincts which will probably bother you sometimes, but then again that is great for such a scenario.

The second phase takes place during the night where you gotta decide which of your characters will guard the shelter, which character get to sleep and (and this is my first issue with the game) which single character will you take to scavenge, and yes unfortunately you heard right, you can only go scavenge with one character, which means less resources, and also means no backup in case of a bad situation, might be for balancing reasons, yet feels like it could be way better.
During these scavenges you can be faced with different struggles, like the lack of equipment to reach the place you want, some encounters that are interesting like saving the girl at the supermarket and risk getting killed or just turn a blind eye, you can also find random military searches or thugs which can turn your life into hell, since one day without loot might mean a exponentially difficult task to keep everyone healthy.

Into the mechanics, the one I enjoyed the most was the noise circle, really makes stealth scavenging feel like its in your control and at the same time fun and nerve-wrecking really well accomplished. A mechanic I didn't enjoy as much was the combat, even though it looked really cool sometimes like melee attack into shotgun shot, more often than not it felt clunky and really unresponsive, sometimes when i was in close range, the game struggled to understand if i wanted to shoot my shotgun or to melee attack, since it doesn't allow me to pick ranged weapon only, and that was really bothersome. Maybe a turn-based combat would turn out better.

In the arts department the aesthetics of the game looked lovely with that sketchy background and the great 2D models. The soundtrack, although limited, helped set the mood really well.

I found this game to be a breath of fresh air, but I still feel like it could be so much more, although there are a considerable number of events their number isn't that great per playthrough, after day 20 I had so many resources that every scavenge run was only for exploring purposes and to try to trigger events. I also expected that places disappeared after X days to give room to other locations so there could be more stuff per playthrough or that NPC's looted places as well so we'd have to make more decisions regarding where to go first according to what items we needed the most, unfortunately that wasn't the case.

Overall it is a solid experience and I'd love to play more games like this, however after having a successful start the game can really start to drag, and that's not what you want for a game that takes 10 hours to finish.

+ Addictive game;
+ Great setup;
+ Amazing Atmosphere;

- Clunky Mechanics;
- Lack of more events per playthrough.

[h1]The Other Side of War[/h1]

"This War of Mine" is a well-executed survival sim/resource management game. It immerses you in the environment, and allows you to make choices as a civilian in a war zone. I recommend it. 

Where this game shines the most is in the gameplay, and the nuances therein. You always have to choose how you're going to approach a playthrough, and each character has strengths that determine how you play. You also choose between various scenarios with differing condition/starting resources, which adds replay value once you've mastered it, which doesn't take long. 

Another thing I like about this game is that you can be down, but not out. Certainly there are situations where you find that everything is working against you, but craftiness can still get you through the playthrough. 

One thing the game lacks: Movement using WASD. You do have controller support, which is nice, but I feel like if you choose to play with kb/m, or simply can't afford a controller, playing simply by pointing and clicking with the mouse works but is [i]somewhat[/i] restricting. If the mouse focused directly on the camera and carrying out actions while you also moved with WASD, it would provide the optimal experience. 

Time is of the essence in this game. You start every day at 6 a.m. and time runs in 10-minute increments. Some days you have more tasks to manage than others (you have to cook, make structures for your shelter, etc.) I find that playing with the mouse is nice because you can set each member to do tasks concurrently, making for maximum efficiency. You can play with the controller, and there are aspects to playing with the controller that make it easier, but it hampers efficiency. WASD would make it even more efficient and smooth, which is also beneficial when you're in a hostile area and absolutely, positively must click the right icon to survive, rather than cycling through all the icons nearest to your character using the controller's D-pad. Doesn't sound like much on paper, but in the moment it makes all the difference.

I suppose it is nice that you can play the game with just a mouse - just a touch clunky for my tastes. Having a choice between both would be great. I will take time to mention that there is heavy mod support, so maybe this will get modded into the game, which would be great. Would be nice to have it from the jump. 


[u]Pros:[/u]
[list]
[*]Choices matter, impacting progress and the story
[*]Learning curve is just right - you'll know how to play this game after a few attempts, especially veterans of resource management games
[*]Resources are appropriately scaled
[*]Active devs and community modders
[*]Nice people on the community discussion board (which does speak to the integrity of the game, imo)
[/list]

[u]Cons:[/u]
[*]No movement via WASD
[*]Great story, but can be depressing if you don't have the heart for it
[*]No ability to save (the game autosaves at the end of every day, but I suppose being able to save all the time could break the game
[/list]

If you find this game on sale and enjoy resource management, get this game. You won't regret it. It's a great game that isn't a AAA title. And replayabilty gives you your money's worth. 

[b]Final score[/b]: 8/10

Controls are very simple and intuitive, allowing the challenge to come from how you manage resources and respond to events. My chief complaint toward this phenomenal game is that it can be too slow at times, making me wish there were a fast forward button.

A couple tips: Don't spoil the experience by looking up guides until completing at least one playthrough on your own; overcoming adversity is part of the fun. Alt+Tab consistently crashed the game for me, test it on your system after the start of a new day (when saves occur).

[u][i]Full review:[/i][/u]
Like a microcosm of the split, warring factions of the city, the civilians have also fractured into small, wary, tribe-like groups. Some are willing to trade with you while others will shoot you on sight. The small group that you watch over consists of one to four people depending on which scenario you play. These are drawn from a modest collection of realistic characters. Each has a backstory and reason for being in the city when the fighting began. Don't mistake this for a heavily text driven narrative kind of game. It uses just enough text to set the stage and then lets you experience and create your own stories.

There is a realistic but sometimes burdensome level of variation in how useful each character is. They all have one unique talent that they excel at as well as some hidden general competency statistics. The imbalance among them can make some playthroughs significantly tougher than others. Overall, the game will test you mightily as you learn the ropes but actually became too easy once I had discovered enough ways to boost my efficiency.

Playing as nonviolently as I could limited my combat experience but when I did fight, I found it to be awkward. It is largely dependent on your equipment and whether you get the drop on your opponent, rather than any player skill.

One cool tool that the developers use to feed you information without breaking immersion is the radio. It can give you updates on the war's status, tips on what goods are able to be bartered at a higher price due to scarcity, weather forecasts and more. Winter is the most brutal period to make it through and you will want to know when it is coming.

This game's muted color palate and heavy use of black is what I would call subtly beautiful. It effectively communicates the grimness of the setting. A sketchy, pencil-like visual effect lends a hand drawn quality to its 3D animation. I'd also like to highlight the differences in how each character moves and holds themselves. Their personalities are imbued into their movements in a way that I don't recall seeing very often in video games.

Adding to the atmosphere is a mostly downbeat soundtrack reminiscent of The Last of Us. It has character without becoming too busy for the mood it is trying to set. I like the music, but there are few enough tracks that repetition eventually began to wear on me. The soundtrack is included as a free DLC.

I would like to encourage anyone who buys and likes the game to pick up the War Child Charity DLC. It only adds a little artwork to the game but 100% of the proceeds go to charity. You can choose to pay 1$, 10$ or 20$ for it. I skipped The Little Ones DLC but its recent price drop makes it more enticing.

A final note on game length: My first playthrough took 13.5 hours, the second lasted 11.5 hours, and my final two took a combined 10.8 hours. The final one was a custom scenario designed to be shortened by the optional Anniversary Edition ending attached to the "Epilogue: Exodus" achievement (an annoyingly difficult to accomplish task during regular play, but still fun to experience once).

I have always wanted to make/play a game that shows the horrors of war, where one must struggle psychologically against the constant barrage of fear, guilt, and despair.

This game goes further than that. It tells a story, that you write, of characters in a war zone whose lives you control. It's a game about survival. Survival that includes securing food, shelter, medicine, and most importantly of all, psychological well being. In this game, fear and depression are just as dangerous to your characters as disease and armed bandits. 

Combat plays a role, but this is not the point of the game. As is the case in real life, all combat is extremely risky, quick, and often deadly. Killing people carries consequences, and getting killed carries even more. Death is permanent, there are no-reloads, and you feel a genuine sense of grief and anguish over the lives lost. It has devestating consequences to the rest of your characters. Also, the combat mehanics are deliberately simplistic and clunky. If you want a game with cool combat, look elsewhere, because in This War of Mine, killing is not a game--it's the problem. 

The game goes a step further by including difficult moral choices. Do you offer help and valuable resources to those less fortunate than you? Do you steal? If so, from whom, and how far are you willing to go? 

The first few times you play through this game, you will lose, badly. And it will be depressing. But don't despair. After the first couple playthroughs, you'll get the hang of it, and the game won't feel as hopeless. Give it a chance, and see where it takes you. You won't regret it.

Pavle was a man.
Pavle was a father.
Pavle was a killer.
Pavle was a hero.

On day 5, Pavle robbed an elderly couple. They just stood there and watched as he searched through their house, looking for supplies to feed his friends.

On day 8, Children came to our house begging us to take their mother to the hospital. Pavle volunteered, saving her life.

On day 13, Pavle killed two hobos with his bare hands. He stole their box, they came after him with knives. He had no choice.

Pavle was never the same. He returned with supplies. His friends would live. But he couldn't live with himself. He killed two people the other night. And for what? Carrots and bandages? 

He sat there, depressed.
A former football star.
Breaking down.
Crying. 
He couldn't live with himself. 
He hated what he had done.

"No more blood on my hands"
He swore as his friend Katia went over to console him.
He took a well-earned drink of moonshine and went to bed.
Pavle. A man. A human. Acting the way a human should act when they kill another human.

Pavle went out a few nights later, robbing various places. He robbed thugs, he robbed soldiers, he robbed defenseless civilians. He did whatever he could to keep his friends Katia, Anton, and Bruno alive.

But he wouldn't kill. Ever again.

Day 17: Pavle couldn't sleep.

Day 18: No one could sleep. Pavle's sobbing was too loud, too painful to hear.

This went on for several days.

Day 37: Armed men came to our base. Our neighbors robbed them. They offered a reward if we helped them find the culprits.

We would never rat out our neighbors.
They were nice to us.
They gave us food when we had none.
We told them we knew nothing.

"We're in this hell together" Pavle said to himself, regaining hope.

Two days later, we were attacked by viscious thugs. This wasn't a raid, they wanted to kill us.

We all survived.

Anton was wounded.
Anton was dying.
He needed bandages.

Day 39: Pavle went out to steal bandages so Anton could live.

Day 40: It hit Everyone hard. Katia was hit the hardest. She wanted revenge. Anton told her it would do nothing. She wasn't a killer. She had seen what taking another life did to Pavle, it broke him. But Anton's wounds were getting worse, she needed to go back.

Day 41: Katia returned. Anton recovered. Bruno was just standing by, watching everything unfold. Unable to change it.

Day 45: The war was over. Supply crates were sent, medics rushed in, people were rescued.

Katia.
Bruno.
Anton.
A mother and her children.

It was the actions of one brave man that they all lived.

No one had risked more than Pavle.
No one had been through more than Pavle.
No one sacrificed as much as Pavle.

Pavle the man.
Pavle the father.
Pavle the murderer.
Pavle the Hero.

10/10 
R.I.P. Pavle.

[spoiler]the achievement itself is about bringing a child from a 'broken' emotional state, back to normal, which in itself is a good thing ... but of course, in order to do that, you first have to put the child into a 'broken' state ... which means ... treating them really horribly, which includes: making them sleep on the floor, starving them, deprieve them of meds when they get sick, ignore them when they're upset, or in short, complete and utter neglect of the child's well-being.

First, I want to get two things out of the way. Do not expect the game to be easy and hold your hand. And even though that is a fact it still is a masterpiece for what it does.


This game plays in a fictional war in our modern world. You play as a group of survivors living in their shelter in the times of war. That means, that the fear of being killed is not only quite big but also ever present. They want to survive and see the ones they loved or simply try and get out of the city and leave it all behind. And that means that its up to you to help them to reach that goal. On your first day in the Shelter you are able to loot most if not all of the items in said shelter. It will take a while but once you have done it, you wont have to worry about it again. From here it is all building and upgrading your shelter.


From one simple station you craft various other stations or even upgrades for your own shelter, as well as items you need to upgrade other stations or the one you are working with right now. But those are not the most important things. In fact, nothing is extremely important as everything is important. You need every little thing you can get. And that means you have to manage with the things you gathered in your house. But now you used it all up, so what now? Well, its about to get real as the night falls. Now you choose who gets to guard the shelter, who gets to sleep (either on the floor or in a nice comfy bed) and who goes out to scavenge. And this has effects on your group. Over the night, everyone gets hungry. If you let them eat that can be dealt with but if they dont eat in 2 days they get very hungry and you have to deal with theit hunger. Everyone as well gets tired if they wont sleep. This means that they have to sleep over the day, if a bed is available, or have to rest on the night. If they wont do it for one night or day, they will get very tired and this has to be dealt with as well. And why put up a guard that needs to sleep over the day? Well, it isnt all that safe over the night. You send out your own scanvenger after all and most likely into buildings that are not abandoned. And the same will happen to your own shelter. People will try to break in and steal your ressources which you have to guard to keep them. And this can lead to not only hand on hand combat but also guns being used later on. Injuries from the event have to be dealt with over day and night. Let the person rest most of the time and of course bandage them if you can. But it wont be the only thing affecting your survivors. The worse they feel, the more depressed they get which can basically leads to them running away if you wont deal with their needs. This can be delayed if you let your characters talk to each other when such an event occurs.


But now back to scavenging. You need some more ressources after all to build up your shelter and weapons to defend yourself with. But sadly you cant take everything you want with you. You only have limited amount of space and sometimes are needed to take tools with you, like the shovel, bonesaw or lockpicks. Sometimes you even have to take a weapon with you to take out the dangerous bandits in your way. And sometimes the people you think, are bandits are not even bandits but survivors just like you.


On my first time playing the game, not knowing anything, I wanted to try my best not to kill people if I didnt have to. I would kill bandits as I didnt see them as other survivors. They simply stole for their own good and didnt care about the lifes of others, after all. And then I got into the church where the description told me that the people living their wouldnt be all too friendly, but I didnt know that this was focused on what lied behind the church and not below. So I went downstairs and killed the first man in cold blood. Another comes in, as he heard the noise and I dispatch of him just as quick. Two more people come running in and instead of running towards me, they run away and all I can read is that they try to get away from the murderer and that they are looking for help from others. I realised at that moment that it wasnt them who were the bad people. It was me who turned into a bandit simply because I didnt even considered that these people might be more friendly than it told me. I stopped playing the game for about 2 weeks after that, having to think about it constantly. The game made me feel extremely bad about that decision and after I began to play again, I tried my best to check before I go for the kill. As that was my initial intention after all.


The longer the game gets, the further it progresses in the story of the war. Winter comes and so does the time of crime. Two events to keep you on your toes. In the time of crime you are being raided almost every night and the people who do it are not your normal survivors who steal things. They own guns and armor and try their best to get to your stuff. And the winter is probably when it comes to that, the lesser of two evils. The winter is simply another condition added ontop of the challenges you have to deal with already. This game makes you think. It makes you feel. Before you hit the menu screen you see a quote that reflects the reality of war. "In modern war, you die like a dog for no good reason." In your first gameplay, this doesn't mean much. But after your first, second, even third, it starts making more sense. It starts stinging—like pouring salt on an open wound. This quote by Hemingway epitomises the heart of the game. As you lead a group of survivors—from two to four depending on which ones you choose—you must scavenge for items, build survival aids such as traps for small animals and heaters for winter, bartering with other survivors for goods and defending yourself from thieves, you feel like you're starting to get the hang of it. Sometimes you must do the unthinkable, which is depriving other survivors from the little they have, in order to save your own survivors... for a couple of days. Stealing is oftentimes accompanied by murder. And even if you have everything you need to survive, sometimes everyone just dies. No leads or reasons. Everything you did; scavenging, stealing, killing... it all seems pointless, for nothing. 

On my first gameplay, I survived eighteen days. Hardest eighteen days of my life in a game. I had to steal and kill. Survivors died from illness, famine, and suicide. Every time I seemed to have everything I needed, a harsh night came and thieves stole everything from me. This depressed my survivors, and on my second and third gameplays this made them fight with each other, to the extent of injuries. And since our medication had been stolen, there was no way I could help them. Some of my survivors would run away with some of our supplies, resulting in even bigger shortages. This hurt and infuriated me. Why did bandits have to steal from me and ruin everything? I kept asking myself this until I realised that I was a bandit myself. Because no one is safe from war—war is unforgiving, and when bandits steal from you, you realise that every time you scavenge and steal from others (with the alibi that it's in the name of survivability), you're doing the same as them. 

You're a bandit, the person that makes others die the same way bandits make your survivors die. I survived until the war ended on my third gameplay, but I still felt bitter. I realised that the only reason I survived towards the end was because I had to steal medicine from others. Defenseless elderly couples. Surviving the war without compromising your morals is so difficult, just like real war. No matter how much you want to help others who come to you asking for help, whether it’s because they need help boarding their shelter or getting a wounded family member to safety, sometimes you mustn’t. You have your own problems to worry about, but this puts emotional strain in your survivors, and that’s where things measure up and start going downhill. This game truly shows the horrors of war. While “Call of Duty” and “Battlefield” portray war in an entertaining way (though you could argue COD’s emotional moments also portray the destruction of war), “This War of Mine” renders the horrors of it and how it affects citizens. This is a painful, enlightening game. Please support the developers and buy it, get a small glimpse of how war affects civilians.

Imagine you are a normal citizen of a slavic country that had just erupted into war on the streets you grew up on. With no options, you seek shelter from the bitter weather with two complete strangers and decide to work together to survive. You have no idea how to do anything. You are already wounded, and with very little supplies to go on, all you can do is hold on. You scavenge up what you can and try to scrape by for just one more night so that your new friends might scavenge up some bandages for you. You live in fear every night because the guards you left might not be enough to repel the looters. You are constantly given the choice to help those in need and maintain your humanity, or devolve into a heartless survivalist and raid the homes of the innocent for much needed supplies. When you encounter more dangerous groups of survivors, you must learn to fight on your feet because any wrong move in the heat of things could spell the end for you. Even when you return with a good haul, you have a growing sense of dread that your group might not all make it.

My advice is if you think you'd like a game that is emotionally harrowing and mechanically very simple, don't hesitate to get This War of Mine. Don't look up any guides, don't watch any playthroughs, just jump in. 

This game is best enjoyed when you know nothing about it going in. The story that you weave in the way you choose to approach tough decisions will be a great reflection of yourself. I highly recommend asking what This War of Mine was like for your friends, because you'll be surprised how many different ways you can play this game.

I bought this game hoping for something different and interesting more than something I expected to get a lot of joy out of.  The theme is a bit dark to expect joy from after all.  My expectations were fairly low going in.  They needed to be a lot lower.

Technically, the game works fine.  I didn't encounter any bugs that I noticed, and it looks good.  You can almost forget its 2D at times thanks to the art.

Unfortunately, that's where my appreciation has to end.  The developers have made so many choices, clearly deliberate choices, that simply ruin any enjoyment I might otherwise get from the game.  The first one I noticed was that I can only ever send one guy out scavenging.  I couldn't understand that decision for the life of me, but I could deal with it.

The bigger problem (for me) hit me soon after.  Crafting.  Crafting in this game is nonsensical.  The same materials make crowbars and water filters.  The sorts and amounts of materials you need for doing most anything are... seemingly random.  They don't change or anything, they just don't make sense.  

The crafting materials themselves don't make much sense either.  They clearly wanted to make things simple, and streamlined, and as some one who has actually made most of the things you can “make” in this game... just no.  Much of it is actually harder to “make” in game than it is to actually make (looking at you water filters) while other things (crowbar, for example) are far to easy to make... and break so quickly that they're clearly crude approximations of their namesakes, but work far too well for such.  I suppose that's par for the survival game course, but I still find it jarring.

Crafting baffles me again with it's prerequisites.  You need to upgrade your workbench before you can... board up the gaping holes in the wall.  Uh.... no.  A rock (a rock tied to a stick is much less injury prone), and some nails you fished out of the ashes after burning some reclaimed wood will work.  It isn't fun, but it does function, so long as the nails aren't too rusted away.  (Yeah, I've done this too.  Hammer's are awesome.)

So, the crafting was just too gamey for me.  If that won't bother you, then it won't bother you.

Another gamey thing is how fast plants grow.  Even radishes don't grow that fast.  Maybe bean sprouts?  If so, where did the beans come from, and why didn't you just eat them?

Then there's the fact that you can just start a fire, whenever... somehow.  The only way that makes sense is if you have Bruno, the compulsive smoker.  I figure he had a lighter (major currency item in under siege Sarajevo btw).  Otherwise, well, I find it hard to believe that the characters in game were all that good with a bow drill, or a sun lens, or even know what char cloth is.

My biggest issue with the game was the characters.  The game asks you “how far will you go to protect the people you care about?”  I quickly realized that I didn't care about any of these characters, at all.  Maybe there was some hidden info to make you more invested in them that I missed.  If there is, well, that sort of thing probably shouldn't be hidden.

With some exceptions, the characters in this game are... well, they're sort of people I moved to the middle of the woods to get away from.  They don't know anything useful. They get upset about things that make no sense, and they care more about their addictions now than having food tomorrow.  I've known six year old children that would be more useful in a survival situation than some of these characters.

I do find these characters believable.  I also find myself uninterested in their plight.  In a game that asks me to care, and to do things because I care... well.. it's a bridge too far, on top of the wonky crafting, miracle gardens, and solitary hero salvage runs.

In the end, I just don't care, and that just kills the game, for me at any rate.

During my school years i was going through the library when i stumbled upon a book called "i remember Beirut" by Zeina Abirached. it was a comic book about the authors childhood living in Lebanon during a civil war, which sadly goes on today. I never even heard of Lebanon and every person at school i talked to about it never heard of the country as well. I even attempted to talk about it in one of my history projects, but then i realized i couldn't and had to go on about Gallipoli that the school system thought was so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ important to learn the third time. There are so many places in the world that are strife with war that should been talked about in the news, but the only countries the news wants to show are Jerusalem and Syria, which sadly many people might know the country because of the conflict.

"This war of mine" is a form of justice that the developers wanted to show to the world, about a subject that is not looked up to a lot in gaming, hell even most media. I always like my fast paced action games such as "F.E.A.R", and even sometimes implemented humor like "Postal 2". But sometimes you just have to come back to earth and look at the harsh realities of human nature that has gone haywire. Its a game that doesn't shy away from mature themes on war and even if it doesn't have a spectacular combat system it makes up for on how it's presented.

[u]gameplay[/u]
the controls of the game is fully mouse use and works well for the most part. you do everything with it, from moving to selecting to placing to attacking to all that sort of stuff. the reason for this could be for the fact you play as an entire group. you have two cycles, one where you manage your group and  you shelter in the day, and one where your desperately scavenge a selected location during the night.

the day time cycle is when you have to manage your stats of your survivors and possibly improve your shelter, you can make various crafting stations and miscellaneous stuff such as chairs. sometimes people come to your shelter to exchange goods or to ask for help for possibly goods in return. Even the characters you have all have unique stats and personality. some like to smoke and others like coffee, you don't have to do their needs and their happy to help out. you only have a certain amount of time during the day and your constantly rushing to do the basic necessities to survive the next day. it a little bit funny how the music is so calming when your constantly rushing the survivors, but that is little comfort where the biggest problems come from scavenging

You can only scavenge at night and have a limited amount of time like daytime, the character you choose can depend on how much they can carry and its a very big factor in this game. you only have a limited amount of slots and how much you have can carry can depend on life and death. but the areas that are safe from hostile are finite, and soon you will have to be robbing bandits or military outposts, or worst of all, other survivors.

now the combat in this game also works well and there are various areas where you can hide and take cover. the combat it even more intense with a permadeath system that if you one of your survivors die, they die for good. the combat isn't really hard once you get the hang of it but that is not the worse of it.

the game has a built in mood mechanic that changes if the characters do something heroic or evil. now keep in mind you do control your characters and not their personality, if you get them to kill a bandit or soldier or save someones life, they'll be happy or care very little. But if you get them to kill or rob a survivor, sometimes they'll become depressed to the point that they will start crying or worse, commit suicide. their mood can depend on what they will do and if they are content, they will be really hard to depress unless its extreme scenarios, if they are their movement is lowered and their actions take longer. it's a very well implemented mechanic that is very fitting for the game tone.

[u]artificial intelligence[/u]
the npc have their own personalities and reactions to the presence of the controlled survivor when your spotted by them. there are ones that will just ignore you, or threaten you to leave if they are survivors or sometimes soldiers. then there are ones that will kill you on site which are bandits and mostly soldiers. the game has a health bar and if their health is really low, sometimes they will beg for mercy, or run if you killed most of their team. If your not spotted and watch them, they have their own idle animation, like reading a book or going to sleep.

[u]atmosphere[/u]
the game itself is as depressing as the trailer said it would be. you will be constantly having to get needs that shouldn't be hard to get in our time, like food, water medicine, and a lot of other problems that are death threatening. even the beginning of the game when you first start has no other button in the menu, except the word "survive".The background also sets the tone for the rest of the game like a pair of shackles with a man and a child holding hands and looking out to the distance of smoke and decay, with a dilapidated wall saying "♥♥♥♥ the war". you start it up and here you go, a group of survivors and a little backstory of these poor people, and the rest is up to you. I did manage to survive on my first run but was the worst play in my life which i didn't want to do. one survivor died, and another with post traumatic stress disorder.

there is no hand holding in this game, there is even no tutorial, because it wants you to push you to the limits. its a look into the cries of people that have never been heard or given a lot of justice. your group is no superhero, they are like you and even feel remorse from the pain of others. you can go through the game without killing outright good people, but you still won't save everyone. 

the game isn't bleak and depressing, you can help others in times of needs like giving medicine to children. It will give you a massive smile on your face when you get as many people out of this alive and still pure to themselves, i sure did.

[u]negatives[/u] 
the placement of stuff can be an ass, especially where the buttons are placed. putting the "end day" button next to "our stuff" has led to many days where i couldn't finished my tasks because i tried to look at our inventory. now you can exit and reload the save, but it goes back to the beginning of the day and then you have to do it all over again.

the ai in combat is also thick as well, here's a scenario.

two soldiers kill a rebel, i'm hiding and when one of them falls down the hole i kill a soldier, i though he would leg it but my survivor can hear him climbing the ladder to where i am and i wait for him with the shotgun, then i kill him. what im saying is that if i was somewhere where there was one entrance. every armed enemy will come rushing at you one by one. a little bit more thought into the characters ai would have made for an engrossing experience.

[u]conclusion[/u]
the whole game is set in a make believe country of Poregon and even that it makes a good impression to be one of my favorite games. It's a game where every single problem you experienced is because of war. there is nothing good coming from it for any good person. it works well as a game that conveys its message. this is a game that manages to help people understand the struggles of refuges.

Characters sad? Stop looting and try honest barter. Not enough materials? Go on a killing spree. It doesn't necessarily mean you'll succeed; I'm talkig about the [i]feeling[/i] of never being in a truly desperate situation.

Which is truly an awesome feat of game design... but isn't it supposed to be the opposite?

I guess the thing is, This War of Mine expects you to play with your own head, making the conscience of the player a mechanic on its own. When characters complain and suffer, you're supposed to feel bad, even if there are no straightforward penalties.

Do you? That probably depends on the player. I'd say on consecutive walkthroughs the chances are slimmer, while the unrestricted fun of gathering resources never goes away.

Still, it's great that this game exists.

1999 Game of the Year! Oh wait... its 2017?! Yep, here I am reviewing a 2014 2.5D sidescroller in 2017. Whats more peculiar is a name that pops up in the production credits... Alienware?! What is a powerhouse of advanced modern gaming doing even promoting a sidescrolling rpg in 2014? Read on. 

This game was released in 2014, but its development took place before that, around 2010. Prince of Persia (latest remake) was released in 2008 and got fairly solid reviews. I believe this game was conceived with significant inspiration from this title.

The gameplay is a conglomeration of several games. The game is primarily divided into two modes, Day and Night. In the Day you can modify, craft, and ransack your home shelter for materials, as well as maintain your survivors' homeostasis. This part of the game is a mix of The Sims, and Fallout 1 & 2. 

5 seconds real-time is 10 min in-game. When the clock strikes 8pm, its officially Night, and you must decide if you will be sending someone out to scavenge that night. The scavenging/combat side of things is a mix of Prince of Persia and Jagged Edge.

If you are old enough to have enjoyed The Sims, Fallout 1 & 2, Prince of Persia series, and Jagged Edge, then I'm pretty sure you're gonna be blown away by this game. There is no tutorial. Not even some obscure 'Help" menu or option. Seems like this was done intentionally. There is no Difficulty modification setting. You're just dropped into the story, and figure it out.

So I'm going to give you guys a short list of Pro's and Con's for this game from my perspective...

Pro's:
- Brilliant realism and immersive story development
- Nostalgic gameplay dynamics
- The graphics actually look good

Con's:
- Finite playable character set and instance generation options
- End of game is randomly determined, but is not long enough in any case IMHO
- Combat is cumbersome, with a 2D environment but pseudo-3D depth elements such as move to cover, or move to shadows options
- Combat can be glitchy at times, requiring a well-timed click in real-time to utilize any of the depth element objects
- Game deserves to have a LOT more content than it actually has

In Conclusion:

This is probably the only survival game where it is IMPOSSIBLE to win on your first play through. You will be messing around with the game dynamics trying to figure out what your priorities and needs are, and how to consistently address them with minimum struggle. The first time I actually completed the game was probably my fourth or fifth play through. Game ended at 45 days. I was relieved, but also a bit disappointed. My two remaining survivors had overcome unbelievable adversity, a cold winter, the loss of our best scavenger, followed by the loss of his replacement a combat trained individual, countless raider attacks- but by now we had reached full survival security. Shotguns, plenty of ammo, dew collectors and animal traps kept us in a surplus of potable water and food. We honestly could have survived for at least another 45 days the way things were going. 

Great game, but needs to be picked up and ran with on the independent mod workshop scene to improve replayability. I still recommend it as is.

Now, plenty of the reviews have already discussed the beautiful, heartbreaking meaning this game holds. "This War of Mine" is a game about the civillians in a wartorn city--the side that CoD never talks about.

But, there are plenty of reviews about the amazing range of emotions this game makes you feel, so I'm going to talk game mechanics for those who care.

The game is seperated into days and nights. Days, where you rest up, eat, and recover from injuries or sickness while upgrading your base with furniture to make it feel more "homey" and tools to help you survive. Nights are where you scavenge for supplies to use during the day. You travel to one location a night and loot all available objects--rubble piles, closets, fridges, the like. Sometimes, a location will have people inhabiting it and you will have to decide whether they are a threat or a non-issue. If they are a threat, you decide whether or not to avoid them and sneak around, or to kill them. Every choice that you make has implications, and that isn't even counting the decisions you make when another civillian ends up on your doorstep.

The game uses point-and-click mechanics effectively. You click on the character you'd like to do a task, you click the task, they're off. It simplifies the actual controls to further shine a spotlight on the emotional toll this game takes on you and your characters. You spend less time learning complicated tutorials, and more time experiencing the game. There's actually no time spent on tutorials, the game throws you right in, and I personally think that's a good thing (though I'm sure others will disagree). I like that you're just thrown in to a game where the people you're trying to guide to safety were also just thrown in to a situation. It puts you on an even playing field from the very start and gives you something in common, though subtle. 

After you complete your first playthrough, you gain the option to create your own custom story, with your own custom group of people and map. I like that the game forces you, on your first playthrough, to play in a non-sugar coated, completely unexpected, randomly-generated circumstance. It ensures that your first playthrough will start with confusion, then you learn throug trial and error, then become a hardened survivor (or die in the process). It makes sure that everyone that buys this game experiences the story this game was supposed to tell before letting you mess with it, but still allows customization after. 

All in all, I'd say this game is a solid 9. It uses game mechanics masterfully in tandem with the emotionally heavy story this game sets out to tell to draw you in despite the simplicity. I'd say it's a must buy, even when not on sale.

Excerpts from a war diary:

Day 1: My name is Bruno. I was a chef once. Had a cooking show. It was a good life. Doesn't matter now, here in the middle of a war. Now it's just me and a couple people I've met, trying to survive together in this hellscape. Katia, a former reporter, and Pavle, a football star, or so he says. They seem like good people, at least.

Day 2: We've established ourselves in an abandoned house. Found some useful things, made ourselves as comfortable as possible. We have decided to take sleeping, guarding, and scavenging in turns. Maybe we can make it through this.

Day 4: Had a visitor today; someone desperate for help. Apparently a shell hit a tenement nearby, buried some people in the rubble. Pavle ran off to help. He's a good man; we'll do without him for a day.

Day 7: Pavle went on a scavenging run to the super market last night, but didn't return. We're worried. Katia has volunteered to go look for him tonight. I hope nothing has happened to him...

Day 8: Pavle is dead. Katia found his body last night at the super market. He apparently went down fighting, crowbar in hand; but he'd been shot. A woman Katia found there told of a girl who'd been saved from an assault by a soldier the night before. It seems Pavle jumped in to save the girl. She got away; he died a hero. We weren't together long, but we'll miss him.

Day 10: It's difficult with one fewer person to help, but it's also one less mouth to feed, at least. And Katia managed to salvage a good bit from the store. But it's already running low.

Day 11: A girl came to the house today looking for somewhere to stay. Her name is Zlata. She's cute, and she's got a lot of positive energy. We let her join us. Should help bring things back up after losing Pavle. Katia and I have been pretty depressed since he died.

Day 13: Zlata has been great. She somehow knows just what to say to make us feel better. Though we are all a bit hungry from lack of food. Hopefully we can find some more soon.

Day 15: As if the hunger wasn't bad enough, the looters make it intollerable. They've been hitting us relentlessly the last few nights. We've lost a lot, and have gotten a few scratches for our trouble. Katia says it's time to go for a sure thing. She plans on going out to rob a quiet neighborhood to the north tonight. It's not ideal, but we're getting more and more desperate. I just hope we can live with ourselves when this is all over...

Day 16: Katia got some good food and meds from a house last night. She said she stole them from an older couple. She's pretty torn up about it. Said the old man pleaded for her to leave them alone. She took as much as she could bear to take from them. Tried to leave them some food and medicine. This war is no good for anyone!

Day 18: Katia came back from a scavenging run with some serious knife wounds! We knew the area she went was dangerous - she took our knife with her - but apparently this city is full of psychos now! She said she got the jump on this guy, but he still messed her up before he went down. But she managed to save someone from them. We've patched her up as well as we can and she's sleeping it off. I'm not sure she's going to make it without better care though...

Day 20: Zlata is gone. She went out last night to look for more medical supplies for Katia, but she hasn't come back. She's gone, like Pavle before her. Katia is still in bad shape, and looters hit me last night too, so now I'm not much better off. What a miserable month it's been. No sign of improvement either. I'm beginning to wonder why we are still trying...

Day 21: Katia finally gave in last night. She was a fighter, surviving as long as she did with those wounds. I'm alone now. No food, only a few meds left by some idiot who thought I'd hold them for someone else. Doesn't matter. No one is making it out of this mess. Going to head to the construction site in town tonight. I hear there may be good supplies there; but more likely a faster death than bleeding out from my wounds. It's been three weeks since this hell began. I'm ready for it to be over anyway... So I guess this is goodbye.

this is a really hard game to sell to someone until they experience it; This is such an overlooked game its not funny. Given steam's 2 hr refund window you cant go wrong giving this a shot, its just an great game. you start out in a house and your first day is clear debris and looting everything of value inside, plus building a few initial structures like beds and a workbench for tools to make things easier. this home phase of the game always occurs during the day, time continuously goes at a decent pace and at 8pm every day the game goes to its 2nd phase of night supply runs. basically you decide if 1 person is gonna go out into the city to a bunch of different locations (each playthrough the locations available can vary), while the other party members either sleep or guard against getting raided. but the part you control is the guy/girl who goes on supply runs, every location on the map will give you a vague idea of what to expect, like danger, possible trade, what kind of loot etc. 

everything is played via a 2d map, the loot is random, you sneak around and loot whatever you need most. most character have around 10-12 inventory slots, the lowest being 8 and the max being 17. each item you loot in the game has a stacking limit, which really adds crucial planning of what you have banked up and what you need to build the next item or structure in your home to help you survive. this is not a loot game where you get rares/epics/legendary, you are digging in rubble and deciding which junk is more valuable than others. im talking components, wood, gears, electrical, cigarettes, books (for morale/fuel), weapon parts, broken guns, whole bullets and just gun powder/shells, raw meat, veggies, bandages, meds etc. nothing is glamorous here, if a party members is sick and you find some partially effective herbs as meds you feel like you won the lottery. 

towards the late game you can be well set up and self sufficient, but one wrong run and someone dies and things can drastically go from safe and great to horrible. there isnt save scumming to save you, the game continuously single saves periodically. you can play however you want, be the good guy and only loot what’s freely available (the game clearly tells you what is private property, ie stealing), or you can rob defenseless people and murder everyone. there are consequences, certain party members will look down at murder/stealing and will get depressed to the point the mentally give up, they can even abandon the group and leave you. there are stages for morale, hunger, sleep, wounded, sick. so you can always turn things around through clear actions, but if things are left untreated they can get worse and people can leave, or even die; not to mention they will be slower and less productive when tasked to do something. 

There are 2 season in the game, winter and not winter (insert whatever other season you want here). the game changes drastically during winter, and fyi you can start a new game in winter. wood into fuel for your heater is essential to avoid sickness. Travel to certain locations at night can be restricted from snow or simple fighting. combat can be fast and unforgiving, you can insta kill enemies from behind or guns quickly kill you or the enemy. personal health is made very clear after your first playthrough. if someone got sick and i didnt have meds they slept sometimes for days slowly getting better, meds and bandages are no joke when needed; the idea that... oh they are tough its a video game, nope, taking care of your health is vital or things can spiral out of control. 

Eventually you will reach the end of the game where a ceasefire occurs and you get to see a post game timeline of your story and how it unfolded and what the final outcome for your characters were. 
Highly recommended.

It's been a while since I've played, and I didn't play for long when I did. There's a reason for that. I don't want to trivialize what happened.

I started an average game with an average cast. Of them, one stands out in my memory: a soccer player who could run a bit faster than everyone else and who could carry a decent amount, too. He was my first pick for forays outside. Me and him, we were able to dart in and out of places easy, make deals with other survivors, and come back home safe.

That was, until one fateful night.

We went to what we thought was an abandoned house. Bit out of sorts, shelled, but still standing nonetheless. I walked up to the front door, thinking I'd greet any survivors and possibly work out a deal with them. In retrospect, I should've been more understanding when they pursued me, and I should've ran away instead of further into the map. Hell, at the end, I drew a knife I found on them and tried to defend myself. But their shotgun blew my soccer player away.

The man I had relied on was dead.

In my mind, there was only one thing left to do: retrieve his body and bring justice to those who murdered him. I returned to a shop I had been to earlier. They sold handgun parts, but I couldn't afford them, so I killed them. I killed a man's son in front of him while he cried for me to stop. Then I killed him. [i]Rest for the weary,[/i] I thought. [i]He was going to die soon without that medicine the man was trading for, anyways.[/i]

Of course, the young man I killed would've lived longer, but I omitted that.

I started omitting a lot of things, honestly.

After going back and systematically killing every member of the offending family that murdered my soccer player, I felt I had carried out justice. But that wasn't the end to this "justice". I went to a supermarket and found dirty raiders, looters, and bandits. [i]They're improper folk,[/i] I mused. [i]The world'd be much better off without such bastard children.[/i] 

And so they died, too. For justice. 

As time went on, lives ended, and round after round was chambered, this perversion of justice came to a climax. I was down to one man. All the others had died in combat, including during raids on my home carried out by the families of those I killed. Honorable deaths, all of them. None of them like my soccer player. I armed my one man with an AK and stormed a hotel that was being used as a distribution hub for human trafficking. Many died. So did I. 


I could have started another playthrough. I did, actually. But not far in I realized that I had already taken all I needed to learn from this game, and that playing it further would be - pardon the expression - an [i]injustice[/i] to what I had learned.

It was at the end that I realized what this game was getting at: humans can rationalize a lot. Sure, I was detached from it all. I wasn't seeing through my eyes and smelling their blood and feces. But the decisions I made - for "justice" - were inherently flawed. In putting down what i thought to be monsters, I became one myself. And to uphold a moral, I broke it beyond recognition.

This War of Mine infuses story into its very mechanics, and for that it should be (and is) lauded. The immersion ran deep as I was learning the game: a risky attempt at theft would leave a character wounded, with bandages only to be found in dangerous areas. I listened behind a door as a soldier offered a woman food for sex. When she refused, he became violent, but not before I burst through the door and provided egress for the woman, risking my own head as he shot at us both. I had to make the hard choice to rob an elderly couple in their home. The man followed me around but never attacked, just begged me to stop. When I returned a few days later, they had both vanished. I understood that I killed them by raiding their food and medicine stores.

As I played more and became more comfortable with the game, it became easier and the strife seemed less real, even on the hardest difficulty. I never found justification to build an herbal workshop. What’s interesting, though, is that I may have built differently depending on the cast I chose to start with.

That’s because of how much goes into the characters you play as: varying available inventory slots make them better or worse at scavenging, most characters are addicted to a certain product such as coffee or cigs, and each has an ability or special reason to use them. Bruno is a terrible scavenger but a good cook, using less resources to prepare our food. He’s also a sensitive prat and he’s no good at making others feel better. Katia is a reporter who’s expert at trading, rewarding me for bringing the right items to the right people. (a huge early-game bonus can be had for trading meds with the son and his sick father) Pavle’s a fast runner and someone else is very strong, or sneaky; that particular sneaky character makes quick work of a house of hostiles. On the subject, it’s also an optional-violence game, so that’s great to see.

There’s even an option to import pictures and create characters of your own; I recently finished a rewarding run using some of my closest friends.

This game really doesn't have much behind the shiny coat of paint it dons. Stripping it away reveals an overly simplistic inventory management game with rudimentary stealth and combat mechanics.

And don't get me wrong, I love inventory management. But this game is bogged down by so many annoyances that add up, resulting in a game that is extremely tedious and boring to play. Some problems could've been avoided by adding a timer speed up, some could have been avoided with some balancing. Why do I have to watch a character dig a pile of rubble for two minutes and have nothing to do meanwhile? The shelter management is a joke, it could've probably been a text-based screen and it would've been much better. It is RIDICULOUSLY easy if you survive after the first few days. You will be drowning in expensive resources after you learn to prioritize what to loot. Trading is balanced poorly - why would you ever waste your time travelling to a trader when you can just scavenge meanwhile and sell/buy the junk you need from the trader that comes to your house every 3-4 days?

And as much as the theme and atmosphere of this game is praised, most of it falls flat because of bad game mechanics, and the other times is just so obnoxiously ham-fisted. You can loot an elderly couples house of all food and medical supplies and replace it with wood blocks, yet they will somehow manage to live happily until the end of the war. The game just tells you to feel bad without actually showing anything happening due to your actions, save for a few rare exceptions.

I can only recommend getting this during a sale, for a touch device preferably. Expecting an interesting narrative or captivating gameplay will leave you disappointed otherwise.

I wouldn’t say that you become devastated because the game tells you that Marko’s wife and kids won’t see them again… If that sort of thing does it for you, awesome. This game will not appeal to everyone...it is a very dark, gloomy environment, with very simple graphics.  But it's a very different game...much different than what most are use to seeing/playing.  

The point of the game is to have your group survive in a bombed out city...you may have to steal from others, possibly hurt or kill others, and all your choices will have consequences.  Your choices will affect the mental and emotional states of the individuals in your group...and because you can make different choices on other play-throughs, this game can be played multiple times, with varying changes based on your decisions.

Key word to remember is that your group is trying to "survive" -- does not mean there will be rainbows and sparkles.  It is gloomy, and sad, and thought provoking...and many will try it and decide they do not like it right away.  

But I think it is worth giving it a try -- if you can get it on sale (I just bought the game for $3.99 USD), what do you really have to lose other than the time you put into playing the game?

Update:  Day 44 of my first play-through, and lost a member of the group (shot/killed by bandits)...once they are dead you can't get a "do over", (unless you quit the game and start a new game). This game had been on my wishlist for a while, and I just got it and it hasn't disappointed yet. I've racked up almost 23 hours in four days of owning it, because it's that good.

[i]This War Of Mine[/i] has a fairly unique concept, in this age of first-person shooters that immerse the player in the experience of combat. It focuses on the civilians affected by war, rather than the people actually fighting the war, and it does it really, REALLY well. You play a group of 3-4 civilians who have come together for survival, and while it's not entirely like managing Sims, it's a similar sort of time management during the days (and honestly could benefit from the time speed controls like Sims has, but that's neither here nor there). Crafting stations can be constructed with parts, so that you can collect rainwater for use in cooking, for example, or turn collected herbs into medicine or cigarettes. At night, you have the option of keeping everyone there to guard (because there's a high chance of being raided at night, with serious injury or theft if there isn't at least one guard), or leaving guards while sending someone out to scavenge for supplies. Some of the characters have better skills for scavenging than others; more inventory slots, quiet sneaking, or skill in combat that can help in the event that your scavenger encounters hostile people while out.

It's not a [i]happy[/i] game, or even fun, but it [i]is[/i] highly engaging, and a time-sink, clearly. I did spend some of the days with a book open in my non-mouse hand, because I had nothing to do but wait for people to finish sleeping (about five minutes), but that's not a bad thing. It's a game about time and resource management, knowing how to build up your shelter and keep everyone fed and rested, and what things to hold onto and which things you can let go when trading with friendly people. You have to weigh the risks of letting one of your people go to help others get people out of a collapsed building, or sending your scavenger into an area known to have military personnel or territorial homeless people. It's a lot like Oregon Trail, actually. You can seriously mess up, but it's hard to. A big bonus is that the Steam Workshop is full of great mods, which don't affect your ability to get achievements; things that modify the item stack size are a HUGE help, because trust me, the default of having a stack of [i]two[/i] boards at a time gets old and inconvenient really fast when you have a severely limited number of slots for carrying things back.

So far the DLC is great too, introducing kids into the mix. Keeping a kid happy and healthy is difficult at the best of times, but in wartime it's much harder, as it would be in real life, I imagine. The child or children that you have to manage along with your adults have the limitation of not being able to do much to help out, although you can have an adult teach them how to things like make fuel for heating and cooking, or start a new filter in the rainwater collector. Toys can be made for them, but they still get antsy about not being able to see their friends, go to school, or play outside. They need reassurance and interaction from the adults periodically.

This game is absolutely worth the purchase price, and getting it on discount is even better. Like I said, it's not a happy fun game, but it's a really amazing game that's really well done, and it's definitely easy to get sucked in and go "oh I'll just do one more day, it won't take long".

"Katia," Bruno called from the kitchen. As she approached the doorway he held out a bowl of soup, "you haven't eaten since yesterday." Katia gave a smile that barely masked the feeling of concern that she was feeling.

"Neither have you," she said. "Will there be enough when Roman get's back?"

"There will, the rest is his. I already ate a can of tuna fish this morning." Bruno's eyes darted to the clock, it was nearly 4pm. "He'll be back soon."

Katia took a long sip of the broth and they shared an uneasy glance. "I'll go-"

"I'm going," Bruno said, cutting her off. "I'm sure Roman's fine, his time in the military made him tougher than all of us, but if he's not, we at least need to know what happened to his rifle and body armour. We went through hell to find that stuff. You stay awake and use the handgun to guard our stores. We can sleep through the day tomorrow."

"Okay, one condition," said Katia. "You take the gun."

Bruno gave her a weak smile.

-----

When the sun rose the next morning, Katia was bleary eyed, staring at the light as it crept under the front door, kitchen knife clung firmly in her hand. The house creaked as the sun warmed the wood and a gentle warm breeze blew into the lobby from the patchwork around the repaired wall.

They weren't coming. Neither of them were coming back and Katia knew it. She could sleep safely now, the curfew was over and the military would be roaming the streets. Nobody in their right mind looted during the day. Katia collapsed into her bed emotions overwhelming her. Sadness, lonliness, rage. Tonight she'd be going there alone, to find her friends.

-----

She awoke only hours before sunset. Enough time to prepare her backpack and eat what was left of Roman's cold soup from the kitchen stove. Roman had taken the rifle, Bruno the pistol, all that she was left with was a household kitchen knife a spare rifle magazine and some bullets. Not that it would matter, if the guns hadn't saved Roman and Bruno, they wouldn't be any help to her. 

-----

At first glance, the ruined villa looked almost empty. Katia knew better; at least two of her friends hadn't returned from this place. She moved carefully and observed for almost a full hour when she noticed the two soldiers patrolling. Following them carefully back along their patrol route, she found her friends.

Bruno was slouched against the back of a couch, looking back at her through an open doorway when the soldiers stepped over his splayed legs. His spectacles sat crooked on his face, blood trailing down from multiple bullet holes that punctured his chest. His once white shirt was now stained with red in at least three places.

Katia struggled to keep her throat from choking shut. Roman was a less grotesque site. Deeper into the room, she recognised his kahki military issue pants. He was still face down on the floor in a pool of his own blood. His sandy blonde hair was matted in dried blood against the back of his head.

The soldiers had exited at the other side of the room without a second glance at her fallen comrades. When she approached Bruno's body emotions surging within her, his pistol was still in Bruno's hand untouched. She tucked it in the back of her jeans and moved over the Roman, rolling him over.

His wounds were far more disturbing up close, he had been shot in the neck and bled to death face down in his blood. The front of his armour was still wet from the blood he'd been laying in and his rifle was picked clean.

Katia rolled over the corpse of her fallen friend and unstrapped the armour. She'd helped Roman with it before, so the buckles and straps came away easily. She strapped it onto herself and tucked the rifle over her shoulder. It wasn't a noiseless process, and that was totally fine with her. This war had taken it's toll on her for the last time.

Loading the rifle with the magazine from her backpack, she stalked her prey through the rooms ahead of her. The soldier that turned around when she entered was the first to go down. The first shot deafened her, but tore her target straight apart. In the first spray the target looked defeated. With the next, he collapsed. She saw the white of his partners eyes as he spun around and raised his rifle. She didn't feel ready for mercy.

Katia shot in his direction, but he caught only one of the bullets in his left arm as he dived behind a cabinet. Katia swung backwards out the doorway, planting her back against the wall for cover. She could hear yells and footsteps running around the rooms above and below her. From the cover of the doorway she shot at the first movement she saw inside the room, just like she'd seen in the movies. An animalistic yell from the man indicated that she'd at least found her target once more. Through the wall, a sting caught her in the back of the body armour. 

From behind her, footsteps came running up the stairs. She drew her pistol and shot wildly at the man that came up the stairs. She emptied Bruno's pistol into the man on the stairs before he'd emerged and he tumbled away into the darkness. Spinning back into the doorway, she shot into and around the cover catching the soldier in the face as he peeked out to get his bearings. The last man found his way into the room moments too late. Katia squared her aim and fired, one last shot hitting him square in the chest. But it was too late, her magazine was empty.

Without time to reload, Katia ran at him as he raised his weapon. Rifle shots slammed into her chest like she was being repeatedly punched, but she was already running with too much intertia to stop and she dug her kitchen knife into his chest. And then his face. And then his neck.

The first stab made him yell. The second made him scream. After the third, he slipped away in a gurgling mess.

-----

Katia weakly pushed open the front door to her home and dropped her backpack in the foyer, cans of food and ammunition spilled out onto the ground. The door had been left open. That meant that looters had come in the night. She was alone. Her friends were dead. She slammed the door and collapsed onto the floor. The day passed in a haze, she had nothing now. Someone had come to the door, banging, begging for help. For a place to stay. By the time she realized what it was they'd already left.

That night Katia went to bed unfed and without anyone to help her bandage her wound, bled to death gently in her sleep.

There are many war games, and many survival games. This War of Mine takes the best elements of both genres and creates a beautiful, haunting, disturbing, terrifying story that is as hard to play as it is to stop playing.

This little game might seem inconspicuous at first with its limited color palette and even the premise which is far different from the majority of games revolving around the topic of war. In This War of Mine, instead of playing as a soldier, you join a group of civilians (though solo scenarios are also an option) in their struggles to survive in a besieged city of Pogoren. They're no fighters, they have no belongings, and they seek shelter in an abandoned ruin somewhere within the city. It is up to the player to make sure they make the best of what little they have. You need to make sure they don't starve, don't become depressed, don't freeze to death or get sick during colder days. Nightly bandit raids aren't making things any easier because each raid means that your survivors can potentially get hurt and your resources get stolen. And resources is something you will need desperately for everything from building and upgrading different facilities around your hideout to crafting weapons, medicine, and items for barter. The main way to get resources, and the one you [b]will[/b] have to resolve to if you want to survive, is to scavenge at night which can actually be pretty difficult at times, depending on the area and the physical/mental state of your characters. If your character is sick or wounded, depressed or simply not cut for scavenging/combat, your nightly resource hunts become more challenging. And it's quite easy for your survivors to fall victim to different ailments that can (and will) hinder your progress. It's also fairly easy in this game, especially in the beginning when you're still learning it, to drive yourself into a corner where the pool of your choices becomes very limited. Scenarios in which you have to send your starving character to find some bandages because your other character is too wounded or sick to move become very possible and it's exactly then when the game becomes a real depression simulator. You start making rash and desperate decisions which result in your characters going on stealing and killing sprees, slaughtering innocents and taking every last bit of other poor souls' food or medicine. Things get dicey, but I think it's exactly this constant sense of danger and unpredictability that makes this game, or at least the first few runs, an unforgettable experience. But then, once the war is over, you start to wonder... You survived, but for what price? And are we really that much different from our oppressors?

This game touches a subject that most games don't: the lives of civilians during war. And I have to say, it does the work brilliantly. You'll feel the bleakness of the atmosphere and the despair of your survivors. And more often than not you're forced to take meaningful moral choices: when you really need supplies, do you try to sneak around a warehouse full of patrolling bandits and risk getting shot, or do you barge in a small house owned by an elderly couple and rob them blind? Whatever you choose, the game won't blatantly tell you if you're right or wrong, but your characters (and you) will remember your actions.

One of the best parts about this game is the survivors. Each of them has their own story and personality, so they feel like real, believable people instead of machines. You'll [i]want[/i] them to survive, and you'll feel terrible if one of them dies for whatever reasons. In addition, the endings for your survivors are cleverly built in as well. Even when you've survived the war, you may find that you just haven't won at all, as your people fail to find their families and friends, live an unhappy life, or even commit suicide out of guilt. The moment when each of your characters earns their happy ending is the most heartwarming moment ever.

Even when I've completely mastered this game, I still found myself coming back to it over and over again. I'm not exaggerating; this is a game that everyone should play at least once.

There's much annoyance in the game (e.g. in the winter you have to keep your heater full of wood, so you can't end the day early even if you have nothing else to do - the temperature will drop and people will get sick). The stories that intend to be more difficult (only one survivor, or two really bad ones) achieve this by being even more annoying. 

You can't go for any kind of sustainability, cause everything is tied to components (or otherwise arbitrarily limited, like you can only have two traps) - which take a lot of carrying space when scavenging and are otherwise very limited when trading. I always have enough goods to buy more components, I always want more components, there's never enough components. It's not just for building, it's for everything. To grow food you need water. To prepare food you need water. How do you get water? With a filter made with components. And it serves no real purpose, since there's only one production chain (so you can't adapt by switching what you were doing) and there's nothing else to do (so you just sit on your ass and wait for more components). On the other hand, even with unlimited components, just feeding that one silly chain would be tedious and boring.

Speaking of arbitrary restrictions, you can't have more than one person scavenging. Apparently the city is not big enough (although I've had a bug once, where the game claimed two people brought supplies from scavenging).

Amazing game with tear inducing elements. My nomination for the '.... just something in my eye award'.

The graphically style is, IMO, absolutely gorgeous. It's also perfectly matched to the style of the game.
Same goes for the music - while limited, it is beautifully written and evokes just the right feeling.

The gameplay itself is fantastic because: 

Difficulty can range from an easy story/achievement mode to a brutal swear and prayer fest. 
It suits both casual and hardcore players alike as well as anyone in between.

Both exploration and combat mehanics are easy to pick up. The stealth based combat can take a little bit to master and when mixed with character permadeath can lead to some heart pounding moments (although you can just Alt + F4 before the day xx screen to restart from the last day if you want to be cheap). 

The characters are emotive, varied and most importantly, real. 
It allows the player to experience a vast array of reactions to living in a city ravaged by war. For example:

You can murder a sick father and his protective son and steal all their supplies - most characters will be greatly depressed by this; requiring hours of talking or booze and sleep to feel better.
Roman won't give a ♥♥♥♥.
Or - you can trade the son some medicine, getting a really good trade rate on his supplies because he's desperate,  making most characters slightly happier.
Roman won't give a ♥♥♥♥.

This leads me to the story aspects:

Each character has their own unique story, which is gradually revealed to you as you progress. They are also all affected differently by various actions you take in the game. The stories are, to me, well crafted and interesting.

If you have any sensitivity to you at all there will be several tear inducing or depressing moments throughout each playthrough. I've seen a few reviews / comments saying this game is a "depression simulator".... well, yes, the game can be sad. However: the way that the game evokes sadness by making players think about the real consequences of war is exceptionally well done. The fact that people feel connected enough to feel depressed is, in itself, strong praise to the writing.

And in terms of replayability:

There are 21 characters (including the children and additions from The Little Ones DLC) who all have different skills and bonuses to different areas. Storywise replayabilty is there - but:

Gameplaywise the mechanics don't change much through each playthrough - you will always need the same resources to build / upgrade the same items to get you the things you need to survive. 

There are slight variations, such as: easily created custom story mode and custom characters, varied character abilties / locations to visit and different scenarios at some locations, which, depending on your patience and how much you enjoy the mechanics, should get you through 5 or 6 playthroughs.

Other stuff:

 - ALL of the profits from one of the DLCs goes straight to an NGO helping children affected by war. I *think* some of the profits from the rest of the game did too. 

 - Not one bug that I experienced. Not a single one.

 - Good price including DLC: ~ $30 or ~$10 on sale (more if you choose to pay more for charity DLC)

 - You can CHOOSE from 3 options how much you want / can afford to donate to charity. How effing cool is that?

Can't think of ANY other developer who managed all those points.



TL;DR / Overall:

Fantastic gameplay with gorgeous graphics, beautiful music, great writing, easy customisation and moderate replayabilty. 

Support charity for kids by buying a videogame.

All at a good price.

What more could you ask for?
