We were used to games like Call of Duty and Battlefield, which glorify war and make it out to be "cool", and "always for the betterment of mankind". I feel like this game is so important because it reminded us all the war is not something to be taken lightly. War is a horrible thing, and often started for horrible reasons. And I feel like the thing we needed to remember the most is that the people who suffer the most in war are the civilians caught in the crossfire. 
     I feel like everyone should play this game. Not necessarily for the gameplay, even though that by itself makes the game worth it in my opinion. We owe it to ourselves and to our fellow man to understand what exactly war entails, lest we learn to crave it.

This War of Mine is like a pendulum that swings from pain to boredom.

Day time is boredom: everything you do in daytime is repetitive and monotonous. You literally spend minutes each day passively watching you characters do the same things: cooking, building, cheering each other up. There is nothing positive to say about daytime. You just struggle to keep everyone alive, repair stuff that got broken during the night and various routine. Note that in daytime you can't even go out of the house and the occasional traders or npc interactions are completely useless because your team will be to broke/tired to do anything.

Night time is pain: you finally get to play the game, but it's so badly designed and implemented it will just result in failure. First of all, the location descriptions is completely flawed, and in most places you'll only find useless gears or wood, even if it says food and meds. Second, you are supposed to kill people (I guess?) But the combat system is so badly implemented you basically have no control on the outcome of the fight. Not only that, but if you actually end up killing someone your dude will get depressed and just lie in bed. Finally, my favourite part, while you have to deal with all this ♥♥♥♥, the npc's can just shoot you on sight and instakill you no question asked, even if you went bare handed. I also find it ridiculous that the game gives you zero explanation of the basic mechanics so that you can ♥♥♥♥ up a multi-hour long run just because you didn't know a particular interactio  (remember that you cant save...), it just feels like an artificial way to inflate playtime.

I normally do not get side scrolling games.  I did that in my youth playing NES games like Contra and Castlvania.  "This War of Mine" catch my eye for its visual artwork and story.  Your characters are placed against nearly impossible odds: survive life as a civilian in a war torn city.  You are given a collection of individuals that have their own distinctive abilities and emotional levels.  Some are the good people, and others just have no emotions (the war removed them?). 

Each day is broken into two phrases: Day and Night.  During the day, your chracters try to eat food, drink water, make repairs on the house and other tasks.  At night, one of them goes out to scavange anything you can find.  Danger lurks around every area.  Making the wrong decision can be very costly.  As the game unfolds, you learn more about each character's past and how they came to be in this spot and time.  In all the gloom and dreary, its a fantastic game to play through.  There is even a cooperative board game being produced of this game (for 1-6 players) on Kickstarter.

This game is an emotional trip.  It balances perfectly the need of the characters (and the player) to maintain their sense of humanity and the consequences of trying to be the good guy in war.  It took me five separate runs before I even made it to day 20, not to even mention completing a single run.  When I did complete it, I had to resort to murder and theft to survive.  This War of Mine is not a game that gives you a "feel good" ending, but the ending isn't a kick in the balls either.  It doesn't make you feel good, but you certainly feel different after playing it.  Play the game if you want to see what I mean (it's a steal on sale).
My first complaint I have with the game is with the controls.  Combat is very hard relying on only the mouse, so I didn't use it after my first few runs and just used stealth.  You could argue that the developers wanted to reward the patience of stealth over running and gunning, but I feel that it should be easier to kill one person by spraying a Kalashnikov at them than by stabbing them repeatedly.  Still, this is balanced with the enemies who take quite a long time to aim and some survivors (here's looking at you, Pavle) can often run faster than a soldier can aim.
My last complaint is that I feel the game could have a bit more variance.  By the time I finished my first run, I figured out most of the locations and their alternate events and how to effectively manage the shelter.  Different characters change a little bit of the strategy (playing using only Cvete and Anton for example is God awful), but overall I wouldn't change it far too much in subsequent runs (though most of the beauty of each character is in discovering who he was before the war and watching him develop).  I think the game would be better with more locations, more unique shelters and more unique improvements for each.  Overall, however, I think the game is absolutely phenomenal and should definitely be bought on sale.

First off, any game which actively contributes to helping other peoples lives (as TWOM does via portions of their proceeds going to War Child) is pretty amazing. On top of that, the game is actually really solid and does a lot of things really well. It tells the compelling stories of survivors/victims of war and outlines the horrors/struggles they might face together. This extends beyond simply managing food/water/first aid-medicine but also into securing your residence to prevent (or more accurately help to defend against) being raided by looters, building amenities like a furnace and stove to keep warm and cook food, finding ways to encourage your survivors to keep fighting before they are broken by depression, etc. What I liked most about the game is that it forces you to think outside of what you may be used to in these types of games. You are not an overpowered badass breaming with weapons; what weapons you might find or construct are better used for defensive purposes because you're simply not strong enough to take on an entire war-torn city on your own (you will be out-numbered and out-gunned 95% of the time), but the game DOES give you opportunites to fight back (ie. jumping/killing a lone soldier before he assaults/rapes a young scavenger, etc.). Everything seemingly has consequences as well (not on a world-altering level); deciding to rob/steal or murder an innocent survivor like yourself might cause your household to disapprove and fall into depression; donate food to another (less fortunate) survivor and have your household grow content as a result.

If you're even a little bit interested in this game pick it up. At the very least, you're helping a good cause! But I assure you, there IS a solid game here to enjoy as well!

To try and put a simply binary good or bad on this game is do do it a great injustice. Simply put, This War of Mine is a poignant, dark, and depressing take on war through the eyes of the victims of war. It's loosely based on the Seige of Sarajevo during the Bosnian War and subsequent genocide during the unstable period in the Balkans in the 1990's. Echos of this appear throughout the game from military snipers indiscriminately shooting civilians to subtle details like a radio station broadcasting the discovery of a mass grave outside the city. My first thoughts on this had me questioning how tasteful the of the theme of the game was and made me uncomfortable to say the least. However, war child does nothing to glorify anything about this war.

The controls are simple and the mechanics work. Survival is difficult. Winter is cold and wood for burning in the heater of your shelter becomes scarce. If you use all your wood for burning, you might not have enough to forify your shelter which makes you suseptible to looters who can injure the survivors and steal valuable resources. Food is scarce, medicine is even scarcer and the player will have to make some hard decisions regarding their resource management. Do I trade this bottle of antibiotics for these tools or should I hold on to them just in case? Do I help the neighbors with this canned food or do I hang on to it incase we run out of meat? These are the questions you'll have to ask yourself frequently. Conditions aren't just static in the city either. For example, snow or fighting between rebels and government forces can block of previously accessable locations for looting, forcing you to wait until it clears up which can be anywhere from a couple days to a week or two in-game time.

To top it all off, the survivors are all pretty frail compared to their contemporaries in other games. Some more than others. This isn't any old game where you can wrap up a wound in a field dressing and treat a wound imediately. Getting shot two or three times will kill your survivor. If your survivor lucky enough to get away, you'll have to scramble to find enough rare and expensive bandages to dress the wounded for days while they basically take bed rest. You'll be short staffed for awhile while they heal and if it gets cold and they happen to fall ill while recovering it could very well spell the end that person. While falling ill, getting wounded, and starving to death are certainly all risk, the psychological aspect is powerful and emotional in this game. Characters have mental health and are effected by the actions of other survivors, their own actions, their physical state, addictions, and by how safe they feel depending on their individual personality. The stress and sadness of survival is real to them.

These mechanics and a narrative from each survivor that unfolds throughout the conflict really create great atmosphere. Despite almost no background narrative, each character is done so well that you'll find their decisions seperating from yours to an extent. The emotional rollercoaster of this game is watching your characters feel guilt over things that both you and they felt were necessary, but are morally damning. As a player, the attachment you feel to these characters makes them seem so much more than just simple scripts and textures. 

The few issues with this game are really just the replay value, which is not as infinite as it seems and the occasionally silly AI movement mechanics. Other than that, This War of Mine takes the often ignored perspective of conflict and creates a stellar, emotional, and difficult survival title out of it. If War Child suceeded in one thing it is creating the theme and atmosphere that there is no black and white, but only progressively murkier and questionable shades of grey.

Even before you hit the menu screen, you've seen that same Hemingway quote so often trotted out by the Call of Duty series: "In modern war you die like a dog for no good reason." Except in This War of Mine, that quote really is a guiding principle. As you try to lead a group of survivors during an unnamed conflict, by scavenging for items, jury-rigging survival aids like heaters and vegetable gardens, and bartering with other survivors for goods, you might occasionally feel like you're getting the hang of wartime survival. But then This War of Mine reminds you, in shockingly effective and heartbreaking fashion, that war doesn't follow predictable rules. Sometimes everyone just dies, with no rhyme or reason.

One of my first games of This War of Mine turned out to be one my easiest, but I had no idea how well I was doing until later runs, when I struggled to regain the same ground. This time, my three survivors — Bruno, Pavle, and Marko — had almost everything they needed. I watched over them from the 2D, cutaway view of their shelter as fresh water came via a rain trap I'd built from assembled raw materials, and fresh meat came in from the homemade animal trap in the basement. They had a series of small workshops where they could build new furniture and appliances, plus an herbal workshop where they could create fresh bandages and homemade medicine.

By night, Bruno usually slept in one of the homemade beds while Pavle stood watch over the apartment with a knife, protecting it from looters, and Marko went scavenging in the city. Every morning my game auto-saved, ensuring that I couldn't undo any nighttime disasters.

The scavenging phase plays out as a tense, atmospheric 2D stealth game. While some abandoned locations are looters' playgrounds, the war-torn city features a lot of other unsavory types. Soldiers and militia might be willing to trade with you or simply ignore you, but they can turn on you in a heartbeat. Other survivors might shoot you on sight. Rummaging through a pile of rubble sends sound waves far into the distance, alerting people to your presence. Get spotted in a place where you shouldn't be, and you'll have a choice: run, hide, fight, or die.

Very different, and successfully so. 
Decisions will have a real impact most of the time and the mood is somber, but don't be fooled by the graphics, this game will suck you in.

On the one hand, the game itself is really good. Set in the middle of a war, it's your job to help the people in your group survive. Doing jobs during the day like building items, upgrading others and answering the door to strangers. Come the night time, you select one of the team to go out scavaging around town, that's where the game really shines.

Once out and about, you sneak into building, which may be empty or not, and take as many thing as you can. If people own the items, they're not going to be happy about this of course, so you may end up in a fight and ultimately killing them, or worse, being killed yourself. 

If you make it back, the items your collected, parts, wood, food etc. can then all be used by the group during the day. Rinse and repeat. It's not as repetative as it sounds though as there's a lot to do during the day time and each location at night is interesting enough for you to want to explore them all.

The main problem with the game is ... it's depressing. It's supposed to be though I think. It's set during a war and bad things are going to happen. On my latest playthrough, two of my team were killed by people at a location they were scavaging in and the third member killed himself after the death of his mates.

When the game finished I felt deflated, but I did want another go, so it's not all doom and gloom. 

I've yet to make it to the end of the war, so I've no idea what happens, but I suppose that would cheer you up no-end.

Anyway, great graphics, haunting music and interesting mechanics make this one to play, at least a few times. If you can take the weight of the groups troubles on your shoulders that is.

For such a simple game, it captures interest easily and effortlessly. The game challenges you to live on less and to make tough choices in what you are willing to live without. 

You can feel the seige through the screen, you can feel the enemy tighten it's grip on the city adding to your sense of urgency and uncertainty. Venture out at night through the cold ruins of what was one the place you called home. This War Of Mine takes you to this place and you have a hard time stepping back to your normal life behind the screen.  

I give it high marks for its atmosphere but it doesn't fall short on game play either. It might look like a game that doesn't need a whole lot of attention, something rather casual, but this would be a wrong first impression. As I said, the choices are real and have genuine consequences, and trust me it hurts when you lose a member of your group weeks into the ordeal.

It was definitely worth the money when I picked it up a couple years ago and one I don't regret not gettting on sale.

In "This war of mine" you help a group of people survive in a half destroyed building. They build stuff to improve their home at day and search the town for supplies during the night.
This is harder than one might think. The game is quite unforgiving and one bad decision can kill your characters easily. I lost three of them in battles with other survivors. Fortunatelly the game kept sending me new ones to fill the ranks - for a while.

The fourth one was the lawyer Emilia. She already arrived wounded and even though I tried my best to keep her alive, raiders kept attacking us at night, wounding her more and more. After a few days she passed away, despite all the efforts, medicine and bandages. That was actually a bit sad.
I give the game credit for being so immersive. Whether it's a trusted companion who dies or a neighbour and their children who ask for help/food, it makes you feel affected.

In the end poor Bruno was sitting all alone in a fortified house full of food, supplies, weapons and ammo. The raiders were going crazy. Every night they attacked. So he stood guard during the night and slept in the day. It was an intense week but finally he survived the war and could bury his 4 friends.

I had a great time and many memorable moments.

This game forces you to make tough decisions and when you lose a character not only do you lose usefulness in surviving, but you for a second you feel angry, sad--and the other characters who've been living alongside them feel the same. [h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
To me this game is deeply flawed, even though most people seem to like this game.  Starting off, it isn't conducive to being played blind, unless you want to learn from trial and error.  It'd be one thing if the game was a rogue-like experience, but characters dying is a great disadvantage and can quickly lead to a game over.  So, unless you choose to look up guides or mod the game to rebalance it, you're quite likely to waste time playing through unwinnable situations, since you don't know enough about managing your precious resources.  Making matters worse, I find the gameplay to be very lackluster, with aesthetics that seem to intentionally take advantage of a post-apocalyptic scenario to be grim and unpolished.  I seem to be one of the rare ones who's at war with this game, even when it was first released, so I can't say it only improved after it was patched.    


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	Many resources are included in this survival game, such as alcohol, medicine, food, water, wood, ammunition, etc.
•	Though the specific details aren't clear, the situation and way people respond seems appropriately dour.  


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
•	The gameplay and how you control characters is uninteresting, whether you're doing mundane tasks or out scavenging.  Every action you take is done by moving your mouse over objects and clicking on them.  You then watch a circle fill up over the character's head to show progress is happening.  I'd think searching for resources would be more novel, but all that's different is having to navigate unexplored areas and deal with blind spots.  This is normally where survival games pick up, but it's not the boost of action I'd have hoped for.  
•	The story isn't gripping.  Despite personality traits and histories being written into my party, they don't feel like real people who are depressed and fighting to survive.  When one of my characters died in combat, I wasn't on the edge of my seat, I wasn't upset the rest of the survivors would be grief-stricken (one of them wasn't, funny enough), I was annoyed because I didn't get the stuff they scavenged.  A character dying wasn't emotionally stirring, it was just a hassle.
•	I find the choice to make the entire game in grayscale to be done more out of laziness than an artistic style.  The imagery is very rough, so adding color would only emphasize how unrefined the graphics are.  Personally, I find a pixilated game with color more aesthetically pleasing.  Or creative and purposeful use of limited color could have had an interesting impact, but the only thing you have to look at is shades of black and white.  
•	You do get into fights with NPCs, but all you do is pick a weapon and then click on the enemy.  I'm surprised it doesn't show a white circle over the enemy's head as you idly watch them duke it out.  It's half-full, they're almost unconscious!
•	If it weren't for the backdrop of a war going on, this would be a mind-numbingly boring game.  Filter water, cook food, and wait for items to craft as you shuffle characters around.  


 [h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
When I played this game originally, I was doing fairly well my first playthrough.  However, some mistakes I had made early on due to ignorance about the utility of certain resources was leading me to lose ground and have trouble keeping up my inventory.  I decided to try nodding the game with player made content to increase my stack size, so I could scavenge more items and craft some necessary resources. This wound up being nigh impossible due to developer patches being released and the DLC complicating matters, so nothing seemed to work consistently.  Even the developers were struggling to make things work properly (vests and bags), so there were clearly issues with the coding.  As a whole, with me and others struggling to get the game to work and load right, I'm perplexed as to how this game's rating is 90+.  I might give this game another shot some day, to see if some much needed patches and improvements were made, but I don't think this game is for me regardless.  I just happen to be in the minority on this one, but I still wanted to express my own battle with This War of Mine.

It takes a lot for a game to feel like reverting to text to describe dramatic events, charater interactions and major plot points wasn't just done out of convenience, lack of resources or laziness. Here it is implemented tastefully without any compromise on the immersion and gritty, depressing (yet cut with a fair dose of ironically peaceful moments), ugly and sombre atmosphere this game pushes upon you so well. 

Morally ambiguous decisions don't just leave you feeling as though you made a ♥♥♥♥ move, which would be a significant mark that many games try and fail to hit in the first place, but rather they go one further and place upon you the cognitive dissonance and weird pain that comes with genuinely conflicted choices that couldn't simply be lumped into 'good' or 'bad'.

Difficulty scales nicely too, and there are options to make things easier or more difficult for yourself. The game subtley encourages you to be extremely crafty about many of its gameplay mechanics like scavenging. 

There are a few rough edges I feel with fluctuating trade values and a few of the mechanics exclude you from having to use some of the in built features. As a matter of refinement and elegance, this could perhaps be balanced slightly better in future versions, but it's not anything significant that makes it not worth playing. It can feel a bit frustrating how repetitive it can be having to scavange and re-grind so many places because of your tiny inventory size, leading to lots of repitition which can be quite time consuming; or waiting many days to trade/craft something where you're missing 1 item but have 50000 broken weapon parts. But neither of these things ruin the experience, rather encouraging you to make wiser decisions and keep an eye of what you do and don't need.

One more thing, the sound track gets 11/10, perfectly complements the atmosphere and is really enjoyable.

This War of Mine (TWOM) is a survival platformer game developed and published by 11 Bit Studios. It was released in November 2014. TWOM is based on the city of Pogoren, inspired by various civil wars in Eastern Europe. You play as a group of civilians from various backgrounds that need to survive until the end of the war. This review will cover the campaign, the gameplay, the soundtrack, and the negatives.

[h1] [b] Campaign, Gameplay [/b] [/h1]
TWOM features one mode, the campaign. It is incredibly dark and gloomy. It is harsh, emotional, and unforgiving. All of your characters actions have consequences, whether it may be good or bad, the bad mostly outweighs the good throughout the campaign. The primary aim is to reach the ceasefire point, which is around 45 days. TWOM is a very well-structured game because consequences vary. For instance, one character may be more susceptible to innocent killings whereas one may not be, and this affects their mental health. The game's structure revolves around day and night counterparts and survival and crafting are main features of TWOM. Day time allows your characters to craft things, interact with others, cook, and so forth. Night time allows one of your characters to scavenge different places in Pugoren, while the rest either sleep or guard the base. Day and night are solid contrasts because one focuses on survival through defending and the other focuses on survival through attacking.

The other main features are scavenging and crafting. At night time, you can choose one character to scavenge. This character will have between 10-17 inventory slots depending on their background, which is how much they can scavenge. Characters can take any item from their base, so weapons, goods for trade, and so forth, which is beneficial because most places you will encounter enemies and some places you can trade your items for others. During day time, crafting is a core component of surviving. The resources you scavenge or trade allow you to build various equipment, weapons, and structures to help improve your home capabilities. For instance, you can build an animal trap and to operate the trap you will need bait through either 1 canned food, which is rare and not encouraged, 1 fertiliser, or 1 chicken. You can then gain two chicken when you catch a rat in which you can cook with a constructed stove. For note, TWOM does not have varying difficulties so in general the game is difficult. I played three walk throughs and on the third attempt I managed to create a sustainable home food economy, but at the trade-off of a lack of weapons, meaning I could not scavenge because I had a knife compared to others guns. Therefore, these mechanics create interesting situations in which you have to deal with scarce resources and adapt to the changing needs of the environment.

I will provide a quick snapshot of certain events in my game that capture the emotional intensity of TWOM. On one occasion, I travelled to the church and sneaked into the house behind. A guard attacked me and I killed him. I return to the church the following day and the priest attacks me, I had to unfortunately do the same. I did the same to the last guard down in the basement and before I finish him, he says ''don't do this man'', but I seal his fate. I do this in front of three children of theirs who are crying and loudly yelling ''Patrik, please wake up'' and ''Why did you have to do this''. I want to share this with because this captures the entire experience of This War of Mine. You are civilians trying to survive and not harm one another, rather help each other, but over the duration of the game you become desperate to survive and turn into someone you don't want to be, a thug or a bandit. Your characters experience the emotional trauma of wanting to end the war, but you need to survive and make these uneasy decisions. Later in the game, I experienced another haunting event - raiding an elderly house and attacking them both because I needed resources or my characters would not survive another week. The grandma begs me ''Please don't hurt me, please take whatever you need'', which haunted my characters for the next week. But the question raises of ''was it worth it?'', but you will confront these situations in the game, which is why I describe it as a dark and gloomy game because it really captures the anguish of someone in that type of situation and the consequences of actions.

[h1] [b] Soundtrack [/b] [/h1]
TWOM features a great soundtrack that complements the atmosphere and setting. It features beautiful instrumentals that fit each situation. For instance, a darker song when you are scavenging or a lighter guitar song when your day begins.

[h1] [b] Negatives [/b] [/h1]
I will list my negatives here because I emphasis certain points in my other paragraphs. First, there was no tutorial. I didn't like this because it is a tough game and there are a variety of components to understand so I would have liked even a simple tutorial. Second, I did not like the combat system. It felt unbalanced, particularly the enemy mostly outmatching your abilities, resulting in you mostly losing close-combat fights. Lastly, the game crashed on me twice when minimising, but this did not hurt my experience of TWOM.

[h1] [b] Conclusion [/b] [/h1]
TWOM is an intense and brutal game. It features an excellent atmosphere that complements the war-torn city of Pugoren. It incorporates a crafting system that allows you to build equipment, weapons, and structures for your base. It's primary selling point is the relationship between characters and their decisions and their overall wellbeing through these decisions and their consequences. TWOM creates situations that showcase the need to survive and the need for your characters to make uneasy decisions for the best of your group. Note, I did not try the DLC yet. At USD$19.99, I highly recommend this game. 

[h1] [b] Rating [/b] [/h1]
9/10

[h1] [b] Pros [/b] [/h1]
	- Characters decisions and their consequences and how it affected the game.
	- Environment.
	- Crafting and scavenging system.
	- Day and night system.

[h1] [b] Cons [/b] [/h1]
	- Combat system.
	- Lack of tutorials.

This is a 2D survival game. You play 3 characters (picked at random from a pool of 12) in a house during civil war. Time passes (accelerated) and the objective of the game is to survive until the war is declared over, which happens at a random time so some playthroughs last longer than others.

[h1]Sound & Vision[/h1]

Graphics are stylish but deliberately dark and colourless. Whether at home or out scavenging, the game takes place within the 2D rooms of a building which is slightly larger than the screen so you can drag the mouse to pan the camera around and see all the rooms, or zoom in and out. Doorways and hidden items are marked by icons and you left-click anything you want to interact with - presumably the single-click is geared towards the Mac mouse.

There's a melancholy tune accompanied by the sound of explosions and gunfire in the distance. Some additional music can be found on the radio which you can craft early in the game but in general the ambience is naturally downbeat.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

There are 4 aspects you have to maintain to keep your characters alive: health (injury, sickness); sleep; food; morale. You give instructions to each character during the daytime (craft stuff, sleep, help/barter with the visitor etc) in order to improve these 4 factors, for example build a bed or cook some food. At night you send out one character to scavenge from other buildings while the others sleep or stand guard. As in-game time progresses more and more buildings become available for scavenging. They are graded as safe, risky or dangerous - if you're attacked and injured it can be catastrophic (as I found to my cost). You can also choose to attack others using weapons you've crafted or taken from victims, but this will affect the morale of your whole group so you have to consider it carefully. It's possible (and even advisable) to play the entire game without any conflict.

Each of your characters has his/her own strengths and weaknesses which are described in their Bio. You have to learn and exploit these traits in order to maximise your group's survival capability. For example, some have a larger carrying capacity so are better at scavenging; one is good at cooking and uses fewer resources to produce food; some smoke or drink coffee so you have to provide enough so they don't get depressed.

Through the course of the game you're subjected to extra challenges such as winter time and an outbreak of crime during which your scavenging becomes restricted. The severity of these events can be pre-set at the start of the game, essentially the level of difficulty. You can also choose your characters instead of random selection.

Once you reach the end of the game (either surviving or not) you see the story of what happened to your characters after the war. In the case of my playthrough they all died in various ways.

[h1]My Experience[/h1]

I knew what type of game this was going into it so I was prepared to make important decisions in reaction to an ever changing environment, and the slick graphics looked nice in the screenshots. The reality of it was not as interesting as I'd hoped and as for the graphics, it hadn't occurred to me that I'd be looking at the same thing throughout most of the game. The store page shows what looks like a cutscene but no such thing exists in-game so I found that a bit misleading.

You don't really feel like you're making big decisions, it's just endless scavenging/crafting grind. You're always looking at the same 3 characters walking slowly around a 2D house becoming relentlessly sicker/sadder/more tired so you're always on the back foot trying to keep up, like in a bad dream. The decisions you have to make don't feel proactive. You have a list of items to craft and you have to decide which ones you want, which raw items to scavenge to make them and which buildings to scavenge from. The whole game entails clicking items and occasionally deciding whether or not to help someone or barter with them. It becomes stale. In a Point & Click adventure game you have an interesting storyline, changing scenery and cutscenes. This is just the clicking without much else.

Yes yes, I understand the drudgery is the whole point, but when all is said and done this is a game and therefore should be enjoyable and something to look forward to. I had a review to write but when I found myself procrastinating, thinking of this game as a chore and doing 'displacement activities', as my mother used to say (ie. anything else to avoid having to play it) then I came to the realisation that this game is not for me.

I don't disagree with the many other reviewers who have given this an 'Overwhelmingly Positive' rating. I totally get it. It is a professional, complex game with a powerful message, but I personally did not enjoy it. It teaches about the hardships of war from non-combatants' points of view, but dare I say a book or the daily news might be a more appropriate avenue than a game? Just putting it out there.

Another aspect of the game I found frustrating and unnecessary is the fact that you have no save options whatsoever and if you want to change the level of difficulty mid-game (as I did), too bad, you can't. Any devastating event or bad decision is permanent. You can't revert to a previous save because there are none. Perhaps this is deliberate, in order to force the player to face the consequences of their actions, but to me it's arrogant of the devs to withhold this basic function from the player, as if to say they can't be trusted to play the game as-is.

[h1]Linux Issues[/h1]

The resource requirements of the game appear modest. It's a 2D static environment with only 3 slowly moving characters. So why does it make my i7 CPU run at 100% with the fans screaming like a jet engine, even on the main menu before I start the game, and sometimes freezes or crashes to desktop? It's not just me, others have complained of this. The situation was so bad that I feared for the health of my hardware and decided to play in Windows instead (which doesn't seem to suffer as much), but this further dampened my already sour mood with the game in general.

[h1]Difficulty[/h1]

For my coup de grâce I'm now going to explain how this game is fundamentally flawed.

The first time you play you have no idea what lies ahead so you're flailing around aimlessly crafting whatever you can for no real reason. There can be no informed decisions about anything, it's all just blind guesswork. At this point the difficulty is impossible/unfair. You will not survive.

The way you eventually survive is by knowing what's going to happen (the events always follow the same pattern) and therefore which items to scavenge/craft. So in other words you just have to keep repeating the same game until you can predict the future and click the necessary items. Does that seem like a challenge to you?

[h1]Value[/h1]

I'd say there's more than enough content to warrant the midrange pricing, if you like this sort of thing. Replay value is compulsory.

[h1]Steam[/h1]

It has everything: 30 achievements; 6 trading cards; Steam Cloud; Workshop, even DLC.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

There is (intentionally) no fun or sense of achievement in this game, until the brief moment right at the end IF you finally survive. It's a point-and-click struggle against the environment which is out to get you. Winning involves learning the situations the game has to throw at you (by repetition) and clicking the right items to keep your head above water. Ratings show that many people enjoy this and you may well agree with them. As a non-Steam-purchase key activation I'm glad that my downvote doesn't affect the overall rating of the game but I can't recommend it with a clear conscience.

This is not a fun game.  This is not meant to be fun.  Don't misunderstand, it is definitely enjoyable, and worth the time put in, but more enjoyable like 'Things Fall Apart', or 'Crime and Punishment', or 'Heart of Darkness', or 'The Grapes of Wrath.'  This is an adult game that asks, "What is it like to survive in a war zone?", but instead of just telling you about it, like a novel, it sets up an experiment.  Here is the city.  Here are the people in the house.  Here is the story you make.  You must make them survive, make them get through.  Your reward is a roller coaster of the heart, as you are forced to make impossible decisions, challenged between altruism and selfish survival.  And your reward is a combination of knowledge of yourself, learning more of these people's lives, and maybe, just maybe, making it out the other side.  You only get a small snippet of what happens to everyone after the war, but at the same time, it is less important than the choices you made, how you tried to stretch out the food and medicine, how you tried to make your home more safe, and who you decided had to go to make your group survive.
Or, if you get the DLC, your family.  And the DLC really does expand in a grand way on this, mostly by showing children in the most realistic way I have seen in any game to date.  As smaller, weaker humans with less experience.  They will make you make hard choices.  They will then make you question your choices.  And even though you need to help them not be afraid of the very real monsters in the dark, they will help you not be afraid of the real monsters in your soul.
Also, pro parenting tip from the game... if you train kids in how to do household chores, they can help around the house.  Although, they still want to spend some time playing.

- That gaming side tends to take you out of the game a bit learning ways to 'game the system' - how best to do what the game wants more than relating to the situation depicted.

But that last point isn't as bad as it sounds. The game does well mostly at those gameplay elements, despicting issues and other people in the game, and providing options for different playstyles.

It's not a game I really feel warm and fuzzy about returning to, and I don't really look forward to parts like the combat side. But I think it's a great experience worth trying.

Sweet game. It's a Zombie-survival rogue-like game without the zombies. This review is just about the points that stood out the most and make this game unique.  You could play to trade and survive or scavenge and conquer (kill those who stand in your way). I started with the first but then moved on to the second strategy after I learned the controls and could raid a house of army deserters who had kidnapped the owner and starved him to death. I have not yet finished the game so I don't know how that approach will affect the outcome.

Pros:
-Atmosphere and realism: You're constantly reminded that you're in a war and you're caught in the middle of it trying to make do whichever way you can (creating traps for rats, having to trade in order get more materials/components/things that you need and not just scavenge for them).
-Gameplay: Sneaking and fighting crudely resemble Mark of the Ninja in footstep sounds, hiding spots, stealth, and stealthy kills.
-Thrill: Because of the rogue-like mechanic and the gameplay mentioned above I really felt that I had to do my best to not get killed in every scavenge attempt. I had my heart-pumping every time I was sneaking in behind a shotgun-wielding thug while I was hoping he wouldn't turn around so that I could get to that room to see what it had.


Cons:
-Controls: They just suck. You have to use the left D-pad's left and right to choose which action you want and often these actions are not in order so you have to cycle through until you get it right. It's no problem in the shelter but during combat it's life or death (I'm looking at you, Cover). The game dev's should have prioritized the most-common sense options depending on the situation... but they didn't. 

Neutral:
-No friend-foe distinction: You don't know whether killing that person who wants you to leave will not affect your scavenger guy until after you do it. And that's part of war... but the devs could've made some sort of distinguishing
-No load save: Adds to the realism of life (only one go), especially in a war. But sometimes the controls get you killed and you don't know how those controls will respond unless you try them...

Recommendation:
Overall, this is a good game to buy.  It's fun, thrilling, and memorable despite its cons. My recommendation is to have a try-run where you can experiment with the controls (especially in a fire-fight).

Contrary to some of the reviews posted recently, this game does offer a fair amount of replay value.  Each team of survivors have strengths and weaknesses that should be used to tailor your strategy.  Some are good at bartering, some at crafting, or fighting etc.  So you can focus your playthrough on a bartering strategy, scavenging, sneak-thieving, or straight up murdering people for the supplies you need.  

The scavenging locations that are available to you are selected from a pool at the beginning of the game and gradually open up as you progress.  So you will rarely have access to the same locations at the beginning from game to game. There are also random events that have a huge affect on the decisions you'll have to make.  Sometimes winter will come early, forcing you to build a furnace quickly and to focus on securing fuel and components before other scavengers pick them clean.  Other times, a crime wave will sweep over the city, making it essential to shore up your hideout's defenses and on securing weapons and leaving multiple guards at night.  Each game offers something like this to force you to make tough decisions.

Taking all of the above into account, I'd say that you can easily get 10+ playthroughs before you start to routinely encounter the same stuff again.  Certainly better than the one or two playthrough reviews I've seen recently.

This War of Mine is an incredibly well-made game. Every time I play, I tell myself I’ll just spend a few minutes on it, but before I know it, hours have flown by.

This is an excellent survival and resource management game, especially in terms of atmosphere. It captures the essence of war better than any other game out there. The storyline in both the main game and the DLCs is well done, and while the gameplay is basic, it has depth and detail. The game is challenging and quite difficult, but also highly engaging and enjoyable, with great replay value. It feels like revisiting a book or movie about the hardships and devastation brought by war. I highly recommend it.

The gameplay is deceptively simple—you can control everything with just a mouse. But don’t let that simplicity fool you. This game is tough—really tough. In fact, it feels almost impossible to complete the game without losing any of your starting characters. Resource management is challenging and rewarding, with every decision carrying significant weight. Each playthrough is unique, thanks to randomized events, supplies, and characters. Only a few specific locations tied to story events remain consistent. When scavenging, you’re constantly balancing risk and reward: play it safe for fewer supplies, or take bigger risks for bigger rewards—but at the cost of your characters’ fragile lives. And then there’s the emotional toll—watching your characters grapple with guilt and despair after killing someone or stealing supplies. It’s a stressful experience, but in the best way possible.

Your decisions always have consequences. You’ll need to carefully weigh your choices, as the morality of your actions deeply affects your characters’ mental states. The game doesn’t shy away from making you question your ethics, adding a layer of complexity and emotional depth.

The DLCs are absolutely worth it, introducing new stories, characters, events, and locations. I highly recommend getting the Complete Edition—it’s well worth the investment and elevates the overall experience.

But the true standout feature of this game is its atmosphere. The depiction of war is so immersive and haunting that it pulls you in completely. The choices you face feel agonizingly real. Even with its minimalist 2.5D graphics, lack of character voiceovers, and no deep, overarching narrative, you’ll find yourself deeply caring about your characters. You’ll even feel a surprising sense of empathy for random NPCs you meet along the way.

This War of Mine takes an unforgiving look at the lives of a group of civilians trying to survive in a war torn city. At its core it's a 2.5D survival and resource management game, but when your first night comes, you'll realize the scope of this game unfolds tenfold. In the morning you'll spend your time keeping your survivors alive till the next day, fighting things like hunger, injury, sickness, and depression, building up your home while trying to keep it safe from raiders. You'll be visited by other survivors, and it's up to you to decide if you'd like to help them or turn them away. When night falls, the game takes a new direction, as you scavenge different sections of the city for resources and materials to help your group. You'll be faced with raiders, survivors, and others just trying to live out their life as peaceful as possible. You'll be forced to make snap judgments, like killing others who may threaten you, or leave them alone; steal from other survivors for your own encampment, or let them keep their possessions, risking your own future of well-being in the process. You can't be careless of what action you take, either, as every decision you make, your people will have to live with the physical, mental, and emotional consequences. Every death feels real, and every loss hurts deeply. This War of Mine is not your average survival game, it's a difficult, bleak, depressing, heart-breaking, yet beautiful experience.

You can play the good guy and help everyone, which generally gives you useful rewards down the line.
or
You can play the bad guy, kill everyone and steal their stuff. You easily and quickly end up with stockpiles of so many supplies you don't know what to do with it all, which makes the game MUCH easier to complete with zero repurcussions... except perhaps the epilogue at the end when you find out what happens to your survivors. 

Addictive for awhile until you learn how to manage your inventory supply, then after 30 days (in game, not realy life, obviously...) when you get the hang of it, it just sort of drags on and becomes repetitive because the story doesn't really go anywhere. If they threw in some scripted missions that you were forced to complete instead of choosing random locations to loot I think that would keep people a lot more interested to continue. I did an 80 day story and I probably would have stopped after about 50 days if I wasn't curious about how the game ends, which to me felt arbitrary and sudden.

To sum up...
PROS: Great gameplay mechanics, amazing atmosphere/vibe, decent backstory, good visuals
CONS: Choices are irrelevant as long as 1 survivor makes it to the end, would have been nice to send groups to scavenge instead of 1 person, during winter survivors are a bunch of babies who get sick way too easy in none-freezing temps, story ends abruptly, little to no replay value

Overall I'd give a solid 4/5 stars. It kept me hooked but left me disappointed with the ending.

I gave this game various tries in the last few years, and I see one major problem, the meta. Simply put, the fact that the game is quite challenging almost forces a player to do a set of very specific things to survive and complete the stories (leaving aside various mechanics and options). The problems with the "meta" are twofold. Based on pure trial and error, it will take a LOT of time and repetitions for a person to finally develop such a playstyle, which can be extremely frustrating. The second option that an average player has is to read guides and follow them as closely as possible, which makes the game very repetitive and by extension tedious af - that coupled with the game's depressive mood - leaves an experience hard to call enjoyable in any way.

To be clear, I truly get the idea of the game, it's not about being enjoyable, but rather portrait war in an alternative tough manner, and I do appreciate it. However, I feel that focusing on cruelty and darkness at such extents misses a huge opportunity. I strongly believe that this game would've had much bigger success if the devs had tried to make it more accessible (by reducing the difficulty, having a more satisfactory sense of progression, and improving the overall feeling of the game, among many others). Ultimately, doing so would've helped spread awareness of how terrible war is to many more players, which should've been the main objective behind this project, IMO.

For these reasons, I cannot recommend this game to most players. A good idea, but poorly executed.

In my case, my character decided to run upstairs, which got me lost in the building and ultimately ended up in my frustratingly awkward demise as I had to manually tell my character to run back down the stairs and past the shotgun wielding thugs.

b) I stay to defend, and never leave: I run out of supplies.

On the surface, This War of Mine is a survival strategy/simulation game. You rebuild and improve an abandoned house in the daytime, and at night you scavenge for supplies. The mechanics are simple – certain supplies are required for certain improvements. You need wood to build a bed, weapon parts to build a saw, water and meat to cook, and bait to set traps. At night, you sneak around different areas in varying states of destruction – a field hospital set up in the ruins of an old one, a flophouse for the lowest vagrants, the home of an old husband and wife just trying to hold on – sneaking around, avoiding conflict, and grabbing as many supplies as you can carry. The controls are simple. It’s quite literally point and click.

The gameplay, however, is almost unimportant, except that it forces you to make choices, hard, brutal choices. Food is always scarce, and when I played through the game, my characters were always starving. I saw them complaining every day about their empty stomachs. I could either let my characters starve, or rob an old couple blind. I took everything from them as they watched, helpless, begging for me to leave them something. It put a knot in the pit of my stomach. When I picked the game up again, my characters were horrified at what they had done.

The most chilling moment was when I had a character kill a man. It was the first time I encountered another person, and I didn’t know how they would react. I didn’t want to lose, didn’t want my character to die. So before the vagrant I ran into could do anything, I beat him to death with a shovel. In the next room, there were even more vagrants who all simply ignored me. When I returned home, the character who killed the vagrant was depressed. She was wracked with guilt.

This is the success of This War of Mine. It puts you into the mind of the starving, the dispossessed and the desperate. It shows you that survival is not easy, that the truest victims of war are not fallen soldiers but the innocents left behind. This War of Mine isn’t just a reaction to the endless stream of war-glorifying shooters, it is a response to all war and anti-war art that focuses on combatants as the sole recipients of horror. Wilfred Owen, Kurt Vonnegut, Tim O’Brien, all hallowed names in the annals of war literature and criticism. Yet they all focused on the burdens borne by the soldiers and overlooked, as many do, the civilians stuck in the boot-churned mud. This War of Mine challenges literature’s view on war and in doing so become literature itself. It is so rare that games become art, but the sickening feeling in my stomach every time I see one virtual character mourn another tells me that this one is, in fact, a work of art. e

Ok, so, this is a tricky review to write because i'm not a completely sociopathic person and i do understand human suffering and that war is a terrible thing.  But that's rather the point, i do know that already and i wanted a game not a never-ending stream of "War is bad mmmm-Kay" with - and this is the main point of this rant - very little game attached.

Daytime - there is essentially feck all to do in this section of the game. 2 minutes of cooking and eating and maybe build a thing, and then you have to sit through the rest of the day so all of your little dudes/dudettes can have a go at sleeping. Because there's no way to queue actions and no fast forward time button. And no way to check what materials something needs without one of your very very slow little people walking to the damn workbench to look. And why the heck can't i upgrade the damn stove just because there's a pot of food sitting on it? Just move it to the damn fridge little man...  And if you do make a lovely, well-equipped house for the little people are they happy? No, it's "a brief respite from the horrors that surround us" because god forbid there might be a second where we aren't reminded that War is Bad.

So we come to Nighttime - that's gonna be more fun, we'll be sneaking about on perilous, action-packed escapades! Oh. For starters, it won't be "we" because for some completely non-explained reason no matter how desperate we are for resources only one of my little people is allowed out at night. The others will sit on their arses and whine about being hungry and even starve and still a second person may never leave. Presumably something to do with War being Bad. But ok. at least my one little dude who is a "Skilled Scavenger" will do something exciting! Hmm, well, actually it turns out i don't have a sawblade so i can't get in to the room with the shiny stuff (apparently my "Skilled Scavenger" can't just use that pile of metal scrap that's right there to knock a hole in the wall of the completely abandoned. shelled house) - guess i'll go clear this rubble so i can get at that interesting looking cupboard. Oh Christ. I'm going to have to sit and watch him spend most of the night scraping some rocks. Because there's no fast forward time button. I guess if there was I might not have as much time to sit and think about how War is Bad.

And a final note on that, you know one of the ways that people deal with War being Bad? Humour. And there is not a drop of it to be found in this game anywhere.

So is there anything good about this game? Yes.  The artwork is awesome, it's certainly atmospheric (if rather one-dimensionally so), and it is in a strange way somewhat compelling - otherwise i wouldn't have spent so many hours on a very annoying game.  Unfortunately, none of that can make up for gameplay and interface being borderline terrible.

I do recommend this game. It's filled with tough decisions and an immersive environment. I can't, though, recommend its DLC "The Little Ones". Not because of its content, but because of its price. It's unacceptable that a DLC would cost $6 less than the original game. At this moment, during a sale, it managed to be more expensive than the game itself.

I have well over 300 hours logged on this game and it remains a favorite of mine. I paid full price for it, if you see a sale then do not hesitate to pick it up. 

You do play as civillians however some characters do have fighting in their backgrounds which can be both useful to the group, or detrimental as the game progresses and character stress increases. Some in the group seem more prone to fighting each other if left together at the shelter while the scavenger goes out. People will leave on their own, often stealing valuable supplies, if things get bad enough. 

The addition of the Little Ones expansion provides new challenges as it can be very difficult to maintain the shelter and keep the child happy. Just like the adults, the child can become depressed and their mind broken. If the child gets sick and stays sick for too long, you may come home to find that one of the other adults just leaves with the child to get help. You do not find out their fate until end game. 

As for scavenging, there are a few hidden events at locations that require you to fully search to find, some require multiple visits to complete the area. Group morale will rise or drop depending on who you have in your group at the time when your scavenger has to kill/steal to survive, so you always have to be aware of that when you get into an altercation. What seems to be a self defense move now might find you a highly depressed group member unable to function when you arrive back home. 

One of the negative reviews claims that you cannot build things in time to survive on any mode but easy. This is not true. You can build in time, but the point is WHAT to build and when it is safe to upgrade. Certain group members can be essential to this, as one lowers the needed materials, or utilizes raw food more to cook better meals using less. You find more people the more scenarios you complete. There are crucial items for the shelter to build, there are more casual items. It's your job as the player to decide what those items are, and yes the wrong choices do lead to failure. Ideally, you want to build to have resources that keeps everyone full and happy. Realistically? Your group will be half starved, slightly sick, and barely hanging on in some modes/group combos. No one said survival is pretty. Each group member has an individual end game rating based on your choices. You may only get the A ending for one and C or worse endings for others. 

I like that there is the workshop for this game that lets you create your own scenarios. I am still playing through one that has the "pretty little liars" tv show characters as your 'civillians.' 


In the future, I would possibly like to see animals put in the game as dangerous encounters as well as a pet you can have at base or to take with you to scavenge. I'd also like to be able to trap the rats at certain locations for food, or have the rats as more than background and capable of biting and making one sick.

No matter what i did (uninstall, re-install, turned off cloud-syncing etc), I couldn't progress past Day42. Even asked the developers for help, but all they said is that it will be fixed in an upcoming patch, which never solved my problem.

Update (Jan 2019): Think I finally found a solution to this problem. Deleted all save game directories (user/appdata/roaming/11bitstudios) and (steam/userdata/xxxxxxxx/282070). Then un-selected steam cloud synchronisation in game's steam options and installed the game on a completely different PC. I have since played right through a campaign to the end of the war and even got a bunch of achievements in the process. I still think that developers should have looked into this problem more and provided the solution, as I was not the only one to experience it at the time.

The two main points in this game is managing your home with up to four or less survivors and then scanvenging in other areas nearby your home.

The first part, managing your home, requires directing your men/women around.  Making a water catcher to collect water needed to cook food, building beds to sleep in, getting sleep, building a heater and then keeping it lit to keep your home warm.  Also, tending to whatever ailments your characters may be suffering.  Maybe they were attacked at night and one of them is injured.  Either make him/her sleep it off to recover or bandage him/her up.  If ill, give him/her some herbal medicine or actually medication.

The second part is scavenging.  After you have chosen your one man/woman to go to a location, he/she will have to dig through designated spots he/she comes across to collect needed material.  Some of it material to help build things in the home, other is useful items, like bandages, food, and medicine.  There is a limit on how much to carry so deciding what to take and what to leave is important.  Also, there are areas in these locations you visit that cannot be accessed unless you use a tool like a saw blade or a lockpick.  Often they will help you find useful items or give you a better route to take, either to save time or bypass hostiles in the area you visit (if they are there).
Caution while moving while scavenging is important.  There are times when running is needed to save time or to get away from hostile characters, while walking is need in other areas so you are not heard.  One problem I have with avoiding characters in this game is they sometimes will not move.  I had a character one time hide out from an enemy who kept raiding the same medicine cabinet I was next to.  
Frustrating to know the enemy is bugging out because there is a time limit to complete your scavenging or else your character gets stuck in that zone. [b]This War of Mine[/b] is essentially a survival-sim with a rogue-like flair. It is not a bad game. It has a good foundation that has significant design flaws that prevent it from achieving a recommendation.

It has all the usual features of a survival game. Build up your house / dwelling with materials from the outside, feed and warm yourself, and stave off bad guys and intruders. There's nothing novel about the game play here, but the setting — a civil war in a non-descript Eastern European country — is at least unique and humanises the gameplay more than most sims would. You will have to make difficult decisions to steal from your elderly neighbour for food, or steal from the less-kindly bandits and risk getting shot. It's these decisions and the overall oppressive, gloomy atmosphere where This War of Mine thrives.

Where it suffers are some bizarre gameplay decisions. As a rogue-like there is no saving. Well, not really. I don't have many concerns with this except it also offers you no tutorial. You have to learn everything on the fly. Not sure how combat works and got yourself killed 10 days in? Back to start you go. You haven't learn how to stealth kill people? Dead again. Didn't know that some guys with guns will shoot you on sight and others just want to trade? You guessed it. 

Be prepared to play the first 2-3 days over and over again needlessly to learn what should be in a tutorial. Or how about the inconspicuous hatchet, which is actually the most important item in the game. From the description, it seems only useful for destroying your own household for scrap. But it also destroys worthless items in your starting house for a good deal of wood, a critical early resource. It's also the most powerful melee weapon in the game.

It doesn't help that a random number generator is lurking behind the scenes to determine if someone will get sick, whether you'll get attacked in the night, or even whether that knife strike will hit. 

And yet once you have figured all this out, the game doesn't offer much else. It's fairly easy to eventually become self sufficient and you're just hitting end turn until you 'win' after a  (of course) random number of days. While each play through is a bit different depending on your starting crew and scavenging areas, you will essentially have to build the same items in the roughly the same order: Hatchet, Beds, Stove, Traps, Rain Collector, Vegetable Garden. Few other build orders will give as much success as this. As such longevity does suffer here. A modding community may help this to a degree but as far as the base game goes I was exhausted after one game with no desire to replay it. The fact that I finished it at all however is a testament to what the game does right, which just isn't quite enough to get a thumb up.

When [b][i]This War of Mine[/i][/b] starts, the game delivers unto you three lost souls who've banded together to try and survive the Eastern European civil war that surrounds them. They're civilians—not survival-trained, battle-hardened soldiers—and ill-equipped to suddenly live without running water, heat or readily available food. During the daytime, you manage their actions inside a cracked, multilevel structure. It's barely livable at the onset, with holes in the walls and piles of rubble obstructing part of the building. Command them to dig through rubble and you'll open up more space and start finding organic and scrap materials that will help them scrape by day to day.

Your initial trio of survivors start off hungry, tired or wounded and, no matter how much scavenging, bartering or crafting as you do, those states of being are never too far away. Just to make your shelter moderately livable, you'll have to have them patch walls, build beds, grow vegetables, filter rainwater, bait and catch small animals for food.

The game is hard and sometimes disturbing because it makes you feel the grief of war. Make life-and-death decisions driven by your conscience. Try to protect everybody from your shelter or sacrifice some of them for longer-term survival.

Key Features:

- Inspired by real-life events
- Control your survivors and manage your shelter
- Craft weapons, alcohol, beds or stoves – anything that helps you survive
- Make decisions - an often unforgiving and emotionally difficult experience
- Randomized world and characters every time you start a new game
- Charcoal-stylized aesthetics to complement the game's theme

[b][u]THE GOOD[/u][/b]
- Distinct, dismal pencil art style
- Powerful examination of civilian life in wartime
- Complicated & challenging morality

[b][u]THE BAD[/u][/b]
- Becomes monotonous after a time
- Autosaves only
- Some systems are a bit too easily exploited

There's a lot to like about TWoM, the gripes I have are mostly minor. You run a group of scavengers in a warzone trying not to get killed, managing your base by day and looting/stealing at night to survive. Neat concept, though I think it could have been executed better. Note that my playtime noted here is way below actual.

PROS
* It's easy to get absorbed in the dark atmosphere. Shells going off in the background, a slow acoustic that invokes deep sadness and loss, art/graphics that heighten the mood (if it can be called "heightened"), it's a beautifully sad production.
* Has decent replay value, starting with different survivors every play-through, locations and the events tied to some locations are randomized, and now you can even tweak all the details of your play-through--who you start with, what events are where, how long until ceasefire, and to top it off, it's even Workshop compatible now. I didn't tinker at all, but that's really cool.
* Nicely written backgrounds for each of the characters, as well as building personalities for each of them (which serve a purpose in gameplay). 

NEUTRAL
* In light of that last pro, the actual dialogue leaves a lot to be desired. It mostly consists of "I need this" or "I wish I had this" or "glad I have this book" or "I wish we didn't kill that guy" or something very humdrum. I put this as neutral because it does serve as a gameplay reminder that said person needs or dislikes or approves of something, sort of like playing Sims.

CONS
* Probably my biggest gripe is that you have to click-drag to move the camera around the map, and there's really no excuse 

for this. Considering the "WASD" keys and even the arrow keys are all unmapped, why couldn't they be used to move the camera? It's entirely point-and-click. You get used to it after a while I guess, but c'mon.
* "Combat" as it is, is a clunk-fest, and will almost invariably wind up with your scavenger dead.
* Speaking of which, let's talk about inventory space--okay, fine, you wanna limit my scavenger to around 12 slots? 

Realistic I suppose. What's not realistic is that A) there is no way to increase inventory space (though it looks like there should be according to the UI), and B) you can only scavenge with one person. On one hand, this heightens the whole survival element, because you have to make agonizing decisions about what to use said inventory slots for--cool, I get that. What I don't get is how other scavenging parties consist of multiple people. Not to mention, how when you're managing your base in daytime, you're controlling multiple people--the gameplay is implemented, it's right there--so how come we can't do that when scavenging? I've got one guy fully-rested with a shotgun at the ready, lemme take my other scavengers out that aren't doing anything, so I can imagine some elderly Russian dude sitting in a chair on our porch downing a bottle of our finest alcohol with a lit cigarette nearby yelling "GET OFF MAH LAWN" as he threateningly readies his gun, while we're out actually getting a decent amount of materials.


Overall though, decent game for the price, definitely worth having in the library for a rainy day. Never know when you'll need that dose of heart-breaking war survival depression.

This War of Mine is a sidescrolling survival game where you take the role of several "noncombatants" in a shelter. From optimistic musicians to world weary thieves and soldiers, you must guide them through the last month of the siege by scavenging, crafting and outright murdering the odd bandit or civilian for precious resources.

This game as it says does not make you play a skilled soldier, you play as civilians who have never fought in a war. The survivor have unique perks that helps them get through the shelter a little easier with strengths and weaknesses. Some survivors may be good at combat but terrible at scavenging while others are useful in the shelter but will have trouble braving the dangers in the warzone. With a limited inventory of what you can bring back from a night's scavenging, decisions must be made to decide what does the shelter needs. Do you take several cans of food over the stash of components that will let you expand your shelter. Do you have your exhausted survivor pull a double shift because the other survivor is slightly ill and you want to save the medication for others in need or to sell for supplies

Aside from day to day needs, scavenging brings danger in the form of snipers which wastes precious time you can spend trading with others. Or hostile bandits greedily protecting their stashes, to launching your own raids against other shelters. Sure you may sleep easy killing bandits but just stealing from others will make your survivors feel guilty and outright killing them will push them slowly towards despair as they become no better than the military. The game capture the wellspring of emotions one may make, do they become partisans out survival to grab what they can to survive or do they attempt to avoid conflict except as a desperate last resort? To some it's easy, to others it's not.

The game is certainly not Anne Frank Simulator but it does pull your heartstrings as a war survival game.

This War of Mine is a huge balancing act to keep all of your survivors alive in an unforgiving mid-war city inspired by real events in the Bosnian war. Instead of playing as mundane soldiers, you have to scavenge for food, water, medicine, keep your survivors warm and safe from bandits and raiders for as long as possible.

During the day you have to manage each of your people, keeping them well fed, healthy and well slept. Other survivors may come to your not-so-safe-house to trade with you, or others may come to seek shelter do you accept them into your care? Maybe... if you do you have enough food and accommodation to keep everyone alive?

During the night one survivor may venture out to scavenge for food and crafting materials, outside it's either robbing from a poor, innocent, dying family or trading for scraps of food with the last of what you can grab from the ruins of a war torn hell-hole. Not everyone outside is looking to kill or steal, many are survivors just like you.

This War of Mine isn’t a "You must have feels now!" kind of game. The Last of Us is an example of great story telling but it doesn't come close to This War of Mine’s feel factor, The Last of Us had a sad opening, but it never made you feel guilty about your own actions. TWoM doesn't tell you when you've done wrong, your survivors aren't just robots there for you to babysit, each survivor has a name, a personality I was always attached to my 3 main characters and I felt like, even though they don't have voiced dialog, that they were part of me trying to desperately keep them all alive, never taking risks. They'll react differently to situations, if you kill an innocent person or rob from a sick elderly couple it's reflected upon you but also your survivors, they'll become depressed and maybe even commit suicide if you don’t have some Moonshine on hand, even then the memories linger on.

But how long can you survive by not stealing or killing anyone? You need food and supplies! The large crafting system allows for the bits and pieces that you either scavenge or trade to be crafted into, traps, rain catchers and other things, but even sustaining up to 3 people is very hard with just a few small contraptions to feed and comfort. And this is all within the first week.

I think 'This War of Mine' an important game to talk about, because it approaches a topic no other games do - being a civilian in a war zone. The problem is, to me, that it's not a great game.

I love the game for it's idea to give you a feeling of being stuck in a war as a civilian and how it tries to convey the hardship you would have to endure.
Sadly it does it technically in such a bad, unnecessarily tedious way (like being able to scavenge only at night + only 1 person at a time) that it ends up scewing the whole experience.

Furthermore the game is also very unrealistic. For example, a human can survive for about 30-40 days without food (if hydrated, and you would die around 45 - 60 days). Yet in the game, after two days of (still) eating a littlebit, they seem to begin to starve.
Also water, unless there's a chemical or radioactive fallout, it's pretty safe to drink rainwater. You don't need to construct a filter every day to use it, you can just boil it to be on the safe side. Not to mention you can just put a pot in the open to collect rainwater, why the need to build a complicated machine for it?

Furthermore the graphics. I get it that the Developer wanted to convey a bleak feeling, but if you watch footage of the war in the Ukraine, Iraq, Nigeria, or Syria, it's not all dark, grey and muddy. 
Sometimes the days look really beautiful and peaceful, like nothing as happened. That is what is so surreal about war, the cruelty and destruction thrown against the beautiful environment of a once thriving life - which is now crumbling under it's horrors.


To me it seems that the Developer didn't do much research on life and survival in a war zone, and instead just did what he thought people would do in such a situation, and what it would be like. 
Honestly, a lot feels forced and arbitrary to me. Like the Dev had to limit your possibilities to make you feel how hard war is. Which to me is a really bad choice, because it makes it feel unrealistic and like a "game", and not like a real experience.

Instead make things meaningful - for example the limit of scavenging with only 1 person; Allow more than one to scavenge, but that would increase the risk of being overwhelmed in a raid. See? No artificial limitation and you immediately have a stronger impact of your gameplay choices, and a stronger experience of the hard choices to be made in a conflict.


What I really like about the game though is how some of the AI families react if you kill one of them. This is really well done.

.

So overall I think, if the game was better designed - and more realistic, the emotional impact would have been much stronger and probably made people think about war much more.
Now it's just an okay building / survival game with a war background. And if it hadn't that, I am sure the overall rating would be much lower.

I praise the Developer for trying, and for how it got people to talk about war (well, did it? How many of you actually did research furthermore into armed conflicts after playing the game?). Yet I just can't recommend it. I wish there was a "neutral" option for reviews.

So my suggestion is to watch actual footage from armed conflicts, and donate the money directly to charities instead (like Doctors without Borders). Believe me, it will make you feel and think much more.
