[h1]This War of Mine is a point and click survival game. [/h1]

Let's start off with the gameplay.
Gameplay is quite basic. [b]It plays like your everyday point 'n click adventure game.[/b] You point and click where you want to go or what you want your selected character to do. You can control up to four characters and you switch between them by clicking on their portrait pictures. [b]The entire game is played using only your mouse.[/b] You literally point 'n click till the end. 
So the core gameplay is pretty basic. [b]The difficult part is making choices.[/b] It's basically a base building survival game. A bit of strategy is involved. You have to choose what to build, when to build. What to upgrade first if upgrade at all. At times people might ask you for favors. You can either choose to help them or not. You can even betray them. You can trade with other NPCs, rob them or even kill them. All this also affects your characters. They might get depressed, sad, cold...or get killed by other NPCs. Yes, your characters can get cold and die from frostbite. They can die from hunger, just leave the shelter or get gunned down.
This might sound all too complicated but it really isn't. You will lose 1-2 party members in your first playthrough but after that you should understand how the game works and your 2nd playthrough should be alright...If not perfect. [b]The game ain't actually hard.[/b]

Now i said "playthrough" back there. [b]There is no story.[/b] Don't let the game and people fool you. [b]It's basically a glorified survival mode.[/b] There is no replay value here. It's true that i've played "through" it 4 times but just because i wanted to do a perfect run with the hardest settings (harsh winter, 80 days of survival).
Every time you start a game it's pretty much the same thing. It's a survival mode. Nothing more. It's not a bad game. It's very fun, addicting and will keep you playing for at least 2 "playthroughs" or till you get a perfect run or get bored. I'd say it is worth the full price if you don't mind point 'click games but don't expect a deep story. There's none. You're just a civilian during a wartime who is trying to survive by looting junk and stealing from elderly people.

[b]Definitely a unique take on war[/b] but far from being a masterpiece people claim it to be. In it's core it's still just a simple survival mode.

[b]The game also uses cheap techniques to get you killed.[/b] People seem unarmed before they start shooting at you and that's very unfair. One of my characters died from frostbite when she was sleeping next to the furnace and it was +18 in the house. How the hell did she die from frostbite?! This is the reason I had to do 4 runs. I HAD to get a perfect run but the game used cheap tricks to get me killed. I never died 'cus the game was hard. The resource management is rather simple and straightforward.

Of course the central mechanic of this game is decision making, and you'll be facing a lot of tough ones all throughout, as the game does a really good job at testing your morality: 

[i]Are you willing to give away useful bandages to a wounded mother? 
Will you rob people for their medications to help your dying friends? 
Are you going to kill innocents for their valueable supplies?[/i] 

These are just a few of the many questions you'll be asking yourself while playing. You have to be very thoughtful about what you choose to do as your characters will face the mental consequences of your decisions (ex. becoming depressed, start to fight with each other)

This War of Mine transcends from being a game to a harrowing experience as you become acquainted with your little group of survivors, empathize with them, and mourn for them. The monotone visuals and ambient sounds really capture the bleakness of the environment and drips with atmosphere as you fight off raids, steal from others, and consume food from dubious sources. The pace is manageable yet does a good job of keeping pressure on you as you try to last just one more day.

What I like best about the game however, are the little touches the developer puts into it. There are a lot of very subtle mechanics at work which you don't see in many games, from the sophistication of NPC AI right down to the branching of individual stories you help forge, you can tell they put a lot of love into it. 

Almost every decision you make feels weighted and as things escalate, eventually becomes less and less about what's right or wrong but rather what's most efficient enough to push you past the next day.

As with other survival games, you learn from multiple playthroughs(or scour the wikipedia pages). The only very minor gripes I have with this game is that some interactions are hard to see since everything is monotone, you're unable to queue tasks and some descriptions of items and their mechanics while flavorful tend to be pretty vague.

All in all, if you're someone who enjoys the survival genre, forethought, patience and are intrigued by the premise, This War of Mine is definitely worth getting. Two thumbs up.

3.	The game is difficult and it can be really frustrating at times. It wouldn't be so bad if there were a lot of different ways you could do those things, or some ways you could do them well or poorly, some variety, some challenge, but there's really not.  Most actions are accomplished at the push of one or two buttons, with no challenge in them whatsoever.  What matters in whether you succeed or not is whether you've managed to scrounge up the necessary materials in your scavanging attempts at night, and that's mostly a matter of luck, not skill -- though I suppose there's a little bit of skill involved, in that you have to avoid getting caught.  But other than that, it's all up to the random number generator, as to what junk will be available for you to scavange.

The rest of the game is mostly just applying common sense, like eat when you're hungry, sleep when you're tired, take meds when you're sick, etc.

Ocassionally there's a moral dillema such as: should you give away your very scarce and valuable meds to some kids who come begging for them to save their sick mother? This is a strategy and item management game set during war. You start out with 3 or more characters and you have to cater their needs by collecting and crafting items such as wood in order to make beds, food and gas in order to make cooked food etc. 

As someone who has a hard time with learning curves, I found this game fairly easy to pick up and learn. The game is a challenge though because you need to cater all of the needs for your character which can be a lot to manage. In order to collect items, you have to send one person you are managing out to scavenge. You do this by choosing a location and searching there. Each location has different items and danger threats. You have to be stealthy here and the game will sometimes test your morality. For example, I once broke in to a house which was presumably empty, but it turned out that there were some old people living there, who were completely defenceless and couldn't do anything about me stealing their stuff, so unless you are completely heartless, you will find moments like this very depressing. This also has an effect on a sadness mechanic which, if it gets really bad, will require you to cheer up the person by either getting another character to talk to them, or by getting them drunk!

There are a lot more mechanics to worry about as well. You will need to collect water and fuel in order to cook food, as if you don't cook it then multiple food will be required for each person in order to fill them up properly to check off their hunger status. Some characters also smoke meaning you will require tobacco, and other characters will have other traits such as "good cook" and "fast runner". Different characters have different item limits on what they can carry from scavenging as well. The game is actually VERY stressful and isn't exactly fun in the traditional sense. However it is very compelling to play despite the stress and sad moments. 

The game also has a mode where you can create your own scenarios. E.G. How rough the war is, how many characters you want to start with, how rough the winter time (which brings a load of other weather effects making the game EVEN HARDER), and also how many days it will take before the war ends. So if you want a challenge, this game delivers. 

PERSONALLY, I found the game far too stressful to play for too long, which is why I have only put in a few hours in to the game. I feel like if I could manage the stress in the game, I would play it a lot more, because this game is VERY compelling, will really poke at your emotions and overall is an enjoyable time, despite being very stressful and depressing. Honestly I am actually pretty sad that I can't play this more.

The FPS is one of the most popular game format, usually with you playing some decked out commando who just murders people left and right. On top of that, you also have to manage the emotional state of the group.  Cross one too many lines and some characters may break down altogether for days at a time, sometimes never recovering.

What really makes this game great, aside from the brilliantly depressing atmosphere, is how the tides of the game can change just in one night.  One night you're feeling really hopeful that you'll make it through the war this time and then crime breaks loose and your camp is hit hard.  You struggle for the next week to find food, making tough decisions about who gets to eat and who goes hungry until you're able to make it out to scavenge for the supplies needed to replenish your stockpiles.

Ultimately a great game that really highlights how terrible war is, not just for those fighting in it, but also for those unfortunate enough to get stuck in the crossfire.

I have recommended this game due to unique, thought provoking style. However you really need to be right kind of player and in the right mind set to enjoy this.

To start with this game is well polished, well written and really does have a sense of what it's like to survive as a civilian in war. The constant lack of of resources, the day-to-day struggle of survival, the constant fear of being robbed and the hated you have for those that steal from your precious supplies, even though that's what you have done to get them in the first place. 

The game shows the other side of war not normally shown, however this is biggest problem of the game. Although it is very thought provoking and in some ways educational, it kind of fails as a game. By its very definition is just not fun, and why would it be. 

The major problem is the way the save game system works. If you fail there is no way to load an earlier save. This game has essentially no difficulty level, it's permanently in 'Iron Man' mode. 

Only one survivor is able to go out and scavenge and this is very limiting, but I guess it's balanced to be just like that. Also there is no direct control on what happens during a raid. You can’t use any sort of tactics to kill or rob intruders so it's just done via a random number generator which makes you feel cheated. There is very little feedback on how your rather limited choices affects the results of a raid. 

Therefore you start to work out ways to limit the risks, as you would in real life, but this generally involves cheating. Things like cooked food is never stolen and doesn’t spoil. Therefore it’s best to cook all food and not leave any raw food. Also the starting stockpiles and cupboards in the house can’t be used once they have been emptied. You can cheat the game by keeping at least one item in one of these and before going out each night drop all your hard earned items into it. The raiders don’t steal from these. 

I would certainly recommend this game as it's a great look at the hardships of war, however it just not fun. It kind of fails as a game because it tries to ram the point of “War is hell” down your throat and it loses its entertainment value pretty quickly. As you need to restart and try the game again from Day 1 and you know all you’ll be doing is cooking food, purifying water, making furniture and sneaky around trying to scavenge, it kind of has very little replayability. The interesting stuff doesn’t happen to around day 20 or more and that's when you start getting weapons. However to get there you need to play though the first 20 days again and that's just boring. 

So if you want a thought provoking game and you don’t mind hard core games and repetive game play then this is an ideal game for you. If you want something fun and entertaining and you don’t like “**** You” gameplay then stay clear.

What is it?

This War of Mine is a third-person survival game, based loosely on the events of the Siege of Sarajevo, during the Bosnian Civil War.

The game has you control a series of unique civilian characters with the sole purpose of outlasting the war. The odds are pitted against you, as the weather, aggressive bandits and a scarcity of resources all conspire to kill you.

What works?

This game is incredibly successful in translating the atmosphere of a warzone. The gameplay elements help to drive home both the depressing nature of war and the central theme of the game; the battle to survive in a world of scarce resources.

Two elements in particular are worth focusing on…

Weather:

The weather system is brutal, and once the Eastern European winter swarms in, the ceaseless fight to stay warm and healthy begins. Temperatures quickly drop below freezing and your characters’ only hope is to focus all their energy on staying warm. Should you fail to keep your shelter warm, your characters will get sick, and this sets into motion a whole range of trade-off decisions trying to heal your sick.

Medication is not easy to come by and far too expensive to buy through trade. This then leaves you with two options. First, set out at night into the dangerous inner city, littered with trigger happy snipers and hope like hell that you scavenge some medication from the rubble of fallen houses. Second, divert all your resources you were using in keeping your healthy survivors warm, to set up a herbal factory and produce the medication yourself. This is incredibly time-consuming though and your quest in healing one member of your shelter may result in the death of all the others anyway.

Bandits:

As the battle to survive intensifies, bandits emerge and aggressively invade your shelter in the hope of stealing your precious resources. These resources must then be spent in shoring up your shelter with a series of makeshift fortifications to keep future bandits out. Fail to do this and you will return home with your supply store looted. You can always put somebody on guard, but leave him without a weapon to defend himself, and he will suffer an injury, leaving you with another mission of trying to keep one member of your team from dying while simultaneously not jeopardizing the lives of the rest.

In both these situations each choice becomes an exercise in compromise; a tradeoff. Do you try save the sick/injured and potentially jeopardize the chances of survival of all other members, or do you allow the one member to die and risk sending the remaining characters into severe bouts of survivor’s guilt and depression?

A quick word on aesthetics:

I found the music to be monotonous and bland, but although it is not spectacular, it rather ironically helps reinforce the atmosphere of the game, the feeling of a bleak, endless war.

There is obviously no multi-million budget for the game, and as such, no next-gen physics were used to deliver the game’s graphics.

This didn’t result in poor visuals though. Instead the game is delivered through a sereis of beautiful pencil sketches which helps reinforce the theme of resourcefulness; taking what you have available and making something worthwhile out of it.

Where it fell short:

This game does drag on at times and there is no way of speeding it up. An option to speed up gameplay or even to pause and strategize without the game screen blurring would be great! The option to minimize the game to your desktop without having to completely exit the game also seems like an intuitive feature missing.

In Sum:

The successful creation of a warzone atmosphere, the attention to resourcefulness and strategy, right down to the extreme difficulty of the gameplay, combine to make this game one of the most successful l’ve ever played, at achieving its core, thematic goals.

I would highly recommend this game at 8 out of 10.

During the day you are in your shelter, building things, prepping, answering the door etc. At night one of you goes out to scavenge for food and risks being murdered or having to murder. It sounds so simple but damn, this game will rip your soul out and stamp on it.

The game isn't preachy or anything. It is your own empathy that punishes you for the things you do. The game gets into your head to the point you are really invested in these characters. It takes a long time to progress so you get really invested in the survival of these characters and caught in a difficult situation.
You must scavenge, you need to look after your family, but at what cost? You have the options to kill and steal, but doing so will mean intense guilt tripping.Your characters aren't killers, they're firefighters, students, normal people caught in a terrible situation. The masterful A.I. in this game means each character is not a generic badguy but a real person. Maybe you kill a woman who was going to alert the gunman in the house, only to find the gunman doesn't shoot you, he breaks down crying and ignores you as you loot his house. And as you loot you find a note and realized you just killed the light of his life and that your actions will probably cause this man to take his own life.

Perhaps you get cornered and your only choice is to fight your way out, you limp back to your house and discover that your actions have caused an elderly couple to be left defenceless to raiders. Maybe this game convinces you not to steal and murder and so you let you characters get sick and die because you don't want to hurt anyone... That's the sort of game this is. We wont see the mainstream media talk about a game like this, because it brings out the best in us, in the worst of situations.

1.	Game lacks some "good production money" - like for example Walking dead. I love characters in that game from the first minute and you can really tell what their personality is. In this game, everything you got is one photo and few sentences. There is no voices, no facial animation etc.
2.	Game mechanics. I'm simply not in the mood to find out if I should build a chair or a bed with given wood. Do I have enough wood to build everything? Should I choose wisely? Do I really need a bed? Should I build water dispenser first or oven is more important? In real life, there is so much more possibilities and you will know what you really need. In this game you have to learn (in hour? in 2? 5 hours?) just to "please the game" to move forward. I suppose that bad decision will result in sooner end (in fewer days). Should it evoke reality? Nah – in real life you will not decide between 5 actions. You will use all possibilities to survive. For example - when your character is hungry, there is the text "hungry" by his name. No – this game do not give you this possibility.

This War of Mine is one of those games that just grips you tightly in its cold, desperate fingers and refuses to let go.
Nevermind food, water or taking a rest - your survivors need you.

You think about the impact of every action, even positive ones like giving medicine to others who need it.
Should you have kept it for yourself? Would my survivor perhaps have been saved if we had stockpiled bandages?

At this point in time, I've played 20 hours of TWOM in the span of two days.
Each and every hour was deathly boring, yet somehow kept me going through it.
The interface is as simple as it gets; just point and click whatever you want to do.
The experience of playing it...that's where the kick in the gut comes.

Every action my survivors take.
Every injury. 
Every illness.
Every theft, robbery and murder.
Was I right?
Was it justified?
Did I need those supplies more than them?

Really?

This is the kind of game that keeps me up at night, lying sleepless in my bed as I think about what I've done and who I've done them to.

9/10 would get depressed again.
(But will need to take a break...maybe a week before starting a new story.)

Survival game with no zombies or any other radiation mutated monsters. Well made, atmospheric, worth the money. It includes a scenario editor.

It's a war and you live in shelter waiting for end of war. You control some characters directly by ordering them what they should do. Each of them has its own specific bonuses. Someone is good for scavenging, meaning he can grab more stuff, someone is good in cooking, meaning he saves ingredient during process, someone has nothing. Someone is smoker so he will p...make you angry by constantly begging for some cigars.

Each day has two phases - a daytime where you are in your shelter, controlling characters, cooking meal, crafting tools like device to catch rain drops for water, mouse traps for additional source of food or even trading with someone ho came into your home. Someone can ask you for help. A night is scavenging time because it provides more cover than daylight so you don't get shot by a sniper. Choose a scavenger to go outside, choose the destination and explore other places for supplies. Some of those places are guarded, somewhere you can find people willing to trade. Be careful, during night time someone may rob your own shelter if it is not guarded.

Each of your action evaluates the mood of your group. Someone needs your help and you don't? Your characters will be sad. If you help, they will be happy that you are still humane even in this situation. But you take risk of a trap or getting shot. Also if you will rob someone too much, your characters will feel shame.

If you finish the game, you may repeat it with completely different conditions. Within this game is a scenario editor where you may prepare new conditions, new characters (even with your photos) and share it with other people. The game is well made and deserve all the money it costs.

The four arrive in an abandoned house, setting up shelter until the war ends.

Everyone is sad.
Supplies are scarce.

Zlata, in despetartion, kills an elderly couple for resources.

Everyone gets sadder.

In order to redeem herself, Zlata helps a man get medication to his ailing father. She also helps some neighbors dig out trapped citizens from under a collapsed building.

Things are looking up, until Anton, who is an elderly man, develops a severe illness.

Then while on a scavenging trip, Zlata is gunned down by some thugs.

Cyeta goes to investigate, discovering that these thugs have prisoners locked up. She frees one. Cyeta comes by the corpse of Zlata. While mourning her friend, Cyeta takes a bullet to the head when another thug sneaks up on her.

Only Anton is left.

Anton stealthily sneaks into the building and quietly takes out two guards. He grabs a gun from one of them as well as some ammo. He guns down the rest of the thugs. They didn't even know what hit them.

For the next week, Anton survives by hinself by taking food and medication from the now empty hotel. However, Anton is still saddened over the loss of his friends.

Things then take a turn for the worse. Returning from scavenging one night, Anton dicovers that his supplies had been raided. 

He has nothing now.

And then the cold of winter arrives.

Anton freezes to death. Alone.

The game lets you play with characters of your own creation. Excited by this, I made myself, my wife, and my friend.

It started off well enough. But then winter came.  The cold made us sick.  And then my wife went on a mission one night because my friend and I were too tired to leave.  She was badly wounded.  She got horribly sick during the next couple of days.  But she had to keep limping to the hospital night after night because my friend and I were too sick.  Then my friend's character got better and my wife came close to death. I we needed more medicine. More than the hospital could trade to us.  And my wife was almost out of time.

I knew, however, of a place that had lots of medicine.  Another band of survivors.  I had traded with them before.  But I was low on all my supplies now save for water and some firewood.  I took these to trade when I sent my friend on a  mission.  But I also had him take a shotgun and ammo.

I went to trade. They wouldn't give me any medicine for the food and water.  And they only would give me one bottle of pill for the shotgun.  Not even close to enough. I knew my character would die. But worse, my wife would die.  

I wouldn't let her die.  

My friend's character took the gun and killed the survivors. All of them. He grabbed all the medicine and food he could and came back.  

Because of the medicine, my wife recovered.  My character recovered.  But my friend's character...he never did.

A week later, he just left. No words. Nothing.  He had been fighting depression ever since the killing.  We tried to reassure him. But it stayed with him.  And we never saw him again.

Two days later the war ended.  My wife's character and mine escaped back to their lives.  And part of me likes to think my friend's character did too. 

None of this happened, truly. It was nothing but pixels on a screen in a video game.  But that play through hit me harder than any other game I have ever played.  Every choice you maker, from helping a sick mother down the street to killing for supplies stays with you. And part of the reason I haven’t played the game since is because I don't want to ride that emotional roller coaster again.

So if you play, and I VERY much think you should play, do yourself a favor and don't put your loved ones or friends in  it. It's amazing how it becomes deeply personal when you do.

This weekend I’ve been playing This War of Mine, which is made by the Polish development company 11 bit studios. (And I here thought CDProject was the only big development studio in Poland!) With the gaming market overflowing with war games whose main objective is to shoot your way to victory, this one focuses on the victims of wars: The civilian who are stuck in the war zone with no way of getting out.

This War of Mine is a strategy game with major RPG elements. The gameplay is divided into two major parts. During daytime, you stay with your group of 3-4 survivors. They have taken refuge in a house and you need to make sure they have the beds, heating, food, reinforcements, and other comforts they need. If they aren’t taken care of they will fall sick or depressed. You also need to make sure to pay attention to the radio so that you are updated on what is happening in the war, or if there is any other special precautions you need to take in order to survive…

The most important part in this game is managing your resources. They are very limited and you will need to make some difficult decisions on where to spend them. I never had enough resources during my playthrough so there was a constant feeling of “just getting by” which really added to that desperate survival mood. There is quite an interesting crafting system connected to all of this and you will notice quickly that this is where the core of the gameplay is found.

During nighttime, when darkness falls, you can send one survivor on an expedition to collect more resources. I loved how this part was made, as I had some very preconceived notions on how the game would work. I am seldom surprised by games and can usually predict what to expect but this was a refreshing exception. Without going into details; I thought my survivors would behave like CoD-players, meeting other CoD-players, fighting senselessly. But this was something different.

In short, your gameplay depends on your own morale and level of desperation. This means that you can always find the kind of experience you are looking for. The important thing however is that you return before daylight, when the shooting starts again. This means you need to make quick decisions and be methodic during your expeditions.

The people you meet during your trips are interesting, deadly, clever, caring. The AI is well made so if you decide to go out stealing you will find that you need brains to succeed – people are not stupid.

In the end, I loved this game. It ticked all my boxes: Strategy resource management, house building sim, RPG, (moderately) scary exploration, scavenging for goods and living on what can be found, appealing design choices… There is a high chance I’ll play it again and it’s made so that you will want to: With each playthrough you can play with new survivors and go to different areas.

There is also a newly-released expansion which I haven’t tried. (Titled "This War of Mine: The Little Ones". Watch the trailer, it’s gripping!)

So in short: Everyone should play this game. It will make an impact.

This game is a unique perspective on what almost every major action movie/game glorifies: War.

Don't get me wrong, those are part of my usual diet, but this served a sorely needed pinch of salt.

Civillians, soldiers, deserters, rapists, psychopaths... all feature in this brilliant experience as it tries to show you what people in war torn countries go through to survive. It doesn't do so in a weepy close up of the protagonist suddenly feeling disillusioned and crying and then going on to butcher people anyway (while hating it... growth!), but rather forces you to take the place of people from the faceless masses that feature in the war montages that come in the opening sequences of any war related media to set the tone.

You can play how you like, the "Karma" at the end of the game doesn't affect the gameplay in any way. You can kill, steal and turn a blind eye to others' plights and survive Post-Apocalypse style... or you could refuse to add to the already piling corpses, try not to let it change you and cling to the humanity that is so easy to tout when things are fine.

It IS just a game, and I hope I'll never be forced to actually make the decisions I had to in my first playthrough. Because the game constantly forces morality to go up against the will to live - in a very grey area kind of way.

What are you willing to do to survive? How far will you stoop?

What a little gem of a game... "This War of Mine" is a 2D survival simulator, that depicts the lives of a small group of civilians in the ruins of a city, torn apart by war. You will start the game with your characters taking shelter in a decrepit building, and will, right from the start, have to address security issues, fight hunger, cold and psycologic depression. Your characters will need to scavenge around the city for food and useful materials, during the night. During the day, they will need to use these materials to improve their shelter, patch up holes in the walls, build some basic furniture, cook food, burn wood for warmth etc... 

Survival will be a brutal business, and you will be faced with harsh moral dilemmas. A helpless child turns up at your door, in a cold winter morning, asking medicine for his sick mother? You take pitty of the child, give him the last of your medicine... BUT... remember that character of yours, who caught a nasty flu a few days ago (because you had no more fuel for heating...)? Now his chances of surviving the winter have become very slim. His sickness quickly becomes debilitating, and he is forced to stay in bed. The other 2 characters have to do everything they can to keep him alive. They pass many sleepless nights, scavenging around, desperate for food and medicine. Very soon, they become depressed and, one morning, one of them simply disappears. He has had enough, could not take it anymore, and  decided to abandon the shelter. Now you are left with just two characters, one of them severely depresssed, and the other one sick, forced to bed. Very soon, the depressed guy commits suicide. The lone survivor also meets a miserable death a few days later, sick, hungry and depressed. Game over.

This is just one of the possible scenarios, a grim and sad one. There are many others. If you are efficient, if you pay attention to each character's strenghts and needs, and if you make the right decisions, there wiil be hope. The game offers you the possibility to play with a variety of characters, in a variety of settings, with different starting conditions. So, a fair number of different playthroughs is possible. 

Combine all these decent gameplay features with some beautiful 2D art and some haunting, atmospheric music and you get yourself a trully unique experience, unlike anything else you have played until this day. This title will really make you realise what a privilige it is to enjoy freedom in real life, have food on your table everyday, have free time and money to enjoy your hobbies (like gaming for example). But it will also teach you that there is always  hope, even in the most desperate situations. And that people need not only food and shelter to survive, but also solidarity, kind words and support from other human beings.

Tldr: "This War of Mine" has been one of the most memorable experiences in my (long) gaming life, and I recommend it without reservations.

This War is Mine is a fresh and generally good survival game with some minor flaws. The game takes place in a fictional city ravaged by a civil war. At the start, you take over an abandoned shelter with 1 to 4 survivors. The government has demanded that civilians leave the city and, assuming that anyone remaining is a rebel supporter, has snipers shooting people on sight. As a result, you can only leave the shelter at night.

During the day you tend to tasks around the house: building furniture, cooking food, crafting, sleeping, dealing with neighbors, etc. At night, you choose one survivor to scavenge for supplies. The other survivors can either sleep or stand guard against looters, who occasionally attack. Survivors differ in carrying capacity, combat training, mental fortitude, health, and empathy, and each survivor has a unique trait that helps in a (usually) significant way. You have to manage food, water, and mental and physical health. Many survivors have addictions too, to either nicotine or coffee.

Within a few days you'll be forced to scavenge from places where other people are, and this presents you with moral dilemmas. Should you steal from people? Should you risk your life to help others? Should you barter? Or take what you need by force? These choices are what make the game fresh and interesting, but unfortunately the developers didn't take them as far as they should have. Breaking into a house and stealing all the food or fuel doesn't result in anyone starving or freezing unless it's scripted that way, which it usually isn't. Similarly, if you beat someone nearly to death, they won't die of their wounds later. Choices would matter a lot more if you saw people suffering and dying as a result of your actions, but you mostly don't. The people who seem to suffer most are your own survivors, who may be wracked by guilt. Each character gets his own ending, based on the choices you had him make.

As supplies go, the game is pretty well-balanced. You'll feel constantly starved for supplies, and survivors can't carry much, but if you're not careless there's enough to survive. There are some semi-random scripted events that affect the city by increasing or decreasing raids on your settlement, causing shortages of certain supplies, or blocking travel, and then there's winter to deal with. Combat in the game is clumsy, but I feel that it's fitting. Your survivors aren't trained soldiers, just regular people thrown into a chaotic situation. It includes a fairly satisfying stealth mechanic. There is an annoying pathfinding problem that can get you killed, though, so move carefully around enemies. The daytime scenes often get boring, which is another flaw in the game. When you're waiting four game-hours for water to collect or for people to sleep or for a neighbor to come over, it's frustrating. I don't need more to do during the day; I just really wish the game had a way to speed up time or advance to the next daytime event.

The game lets you customize a lot of parameters at start, such as which survivors you start with, how long the war lasts, how many hostiles there are, how long winter is and when it arrives, which areas are available to scavenge in, etc. You can also customize the survivors to a limited extent. And you can take the set of starting parameters, add a bit of flavor text, and share it with others as a custom "story". The graphics and sound are good enough. The game has gamepad support but it's pretty bad; it's much better to play with a mouse. Each standard playthrough should last about 12 hours (assuming you survive), and the game has a good 2-4 playthroughs in it if you want to try playing different styles.

All in all, I recommend this game. But I also recommend that you avoid the DLC that lets you have children. The developers were cowards in developing it, because despite this being a grim survival game, your children can never die. In a game about the horrors of war, about the inhumanity of man, about making hard choices and facing the consequences, having invincible children is stupid and really doesn't fit the game.

The game is fun, but repetitive. The graphics are nice, it takes some strategy, and it's personally got me hooked. On the other hand, it's really repetitive and it's frustrating. Overall, I got to give probs. to 11 bit studios for making a great game, but it could use more place the player can go to.

For anyone looking to buy this game, I highly recommend it. TWoM has been one of the most moving games for me that I have played in a long time. As great as this game is, I personally can only play it one session at a time, generally up to months apart. It's not because its a bad game or anything, if it was i would be writing a negitive review. The story and situations can get pretty dark at times and just end up weighing down on me. To further explain what I mean by that, I will be telling the grand tale of my very first playthrough. So grab your popcorn, grab your loved ones, and grab your tissues. 

Our story begins with the 3 characters I was lucky enough to start with: Pavle, Bruno and Marko. Before the war, Pavle was a football player, he has the fastest movement speed of the survivors. This automatically made him my main man for scavenging, especially in areas where I knew other survivors would be. Bruno was a chef, who I made stay at home almost the whole game. He spent plenty of time cooking meals for our group. And Lastly, Marko, the fireman. He has a larger backback and loots faster. This made him my number 2 man for getting supplies.

The game started off quite well, as within the first week I was able to build plently of workstations, beds, furnature, etc. We had a large supply of food, water and meds from the very start. We even had plenty of sellable goods for when we came across a trader. Everything was fantastic and the future was looking bright.

Then I made the first mistake. I decided to go shopping.

In need of even more supplies, I decided to send Pavle to the supermarket to see what i could get. As we were looting the place I realized there were people in the next room. I peeked in through the keyhole and saw a soldier and a woman talking. She was in need of food, and the soldier was offering her some in exchange for a "favor". He offered to help her if she came back to his place. Clearly not interested she declined, however things got violent. He attacked her and held her at gunpoint, saying if she doesn't go with him she will be shot. As she was being taken by gunpoint, it happened.

I made my second mistake.

Sitting by watching this, I felt sick to my stomach, and I knew i couldn't just let this happen. Pavle sprinted into the room and suckerpunched the soldier knocking him off balance. This gave the woman just enough time to run away. However, doing this didn't exactly please the soldier, and i recieved a bullet to the stomach. He was kind enough to let me live and Pavle stumbled back home.

Upon returning home, we discovered that there was a break in. Luckily we didn't lose anything other than basic supplies, but everyone was shaken up. For the next few days I kept Pavle in bed, giving him medical attention. However, Pavles wounds ended up getting worse, and on top of that he became ill. At one point we ran out of Meds, but then we lucked out and a trader shown up. We ended up selling the rest of our basic supplies along with out valuables to get more pills and bandages for him. After a few days he started recovering and we started to get a glimmer of hope back for the future.

It was at this point that the ♥♥♥♥ storm began.

Right when Pavle was almost fully healed, we got raided. During this raid, we lost a large portion of food along with the last of our medical supplies. And if that weren't bad enough, one of the raiders found it nessisary to attack Pavle. With no medical supplies, we would have to go out at get more. It was also at this point that our dear friend Marko started his long trail of depression.

After days of scavenging for resources, trying to keep pavle alive, the trader returned. Once again we were able to buy meds and more food. Unfortunatly we recently made a weapon for self defense we had to sell for the supplies, since we didn't have anything else to trade. But in the end it was worth it, we got pavle more meds to heal him up and foor to keep us alive. Once again everything was starting to look up.

Then we got raided.

Again.

And guess who got hurt?

Yes, Pavle.

Again. 

At this point Pavles survival was looking grim. Markos depression had gotten worse and Bruno was exausted. Unfortunatly, Bruno was the only one fit for gathering. I sent him to loot, and due to my fantastic luck, he was attacked. While scavenging, Bruno was spotted and was shot on his way out. Unfortunatly for him, although his wounds were bad, Pavles were worse. And they couldn't share the meds.

Bruno died the next night.

Marko was devestated. He was broken. He completly shut down. Neither he or Pavle would be able to go out for supplies. Things were looking bad for Pavle. Without meds and bandages he would end up dying.

But then, for once in our lives a miracle happened. There was a knock on the door.

Her name was Cveta.

She came by, looking for shelter and a place to stay. We may have just lost Bruno, but in the most dire situation, we found someone to help us. That night, we sent her out to help our dear friend Pavle.

For the short time that we knew her, Cveta had been a saint. She was willing to go into the more dangerous parts of the city in search of medical aid. But children, remember, this is a sad tale. And in such a sad tale, there is no room for hope or happiness. There are no such things as miracles.

Because that same night, she was shot clean though the forehead by a sniper.

Luckily for us, however, Pavle had recovered slightly. He was able to leave the bed for the first time in weeks. Unfortunatly for him he still needed help and Marko was completly unresponsive. Pavle tried talking to him, to cheer him up and give him hope. But it was of no use.

That night, the near death Pavle had to go out himself in order to save his own life. But after a whole night of searching, there wasn't a single roll of gauze to be found. And to make matters worse...

His wounds reopened.

He died later that night, after fighting for weeks to live, watching his friends, his family fall apart in a desperate attempt to save him. That same night, Marko, with nothing left to live for, hung himself in the room upstairs.



The End

DEUTSCH: 
This war of mine: Review & Spieletipps, inkl. DLC "The little ones" 

Ich schätze und empfehle Euch "This war of mine". Das sage ich, da ich ansonsten immer Spiele vermeide, welche in Richtung Ego-Shooter oder zu  realitätsnahe Kriegsspiele gehen. 
Ich mag Aufbauspiele, eine gute Geschichte, Mittelalterliches – und, wenn etwas strategischer oder Mann-zu-Mann Kampf integriert ist in der Geschichte, dann ist dies in Ordnung. 
Nun, abgesehen vom Mittelalterlichen, sind diese Dinge alle in "This war of mine" enthalten. 
Aber Achtung und siehe – da ist viel mehr!
Nicht nur aufgrund der Spende, die man beim Kauf des DLCs integriert hat, geht dieses Spiel teilweise tief in die Moral hinein – und wie diese vom Krieg Schaden nimmt oder darauf Auswirkungen hat. Es geht einem nahe! Es ist nur ein Spiel – eigentlich – aber wenn man einen kleinen Schritt weiter geht, wie man sich während des Spiels fühlt, dann sagt es Dir eine Menge über Dich selbst, aktuelle Ereignisse und über Leid. 

Zusammenfassend: 
Es ist ein gutes Spiel und wenn Du möchtest, wird Dich dieses Spiel nachdenklich machen über Werte und wo Du, - ja ich meine Du selbst! - heute stehst!

Einige Spieletipps:

Als Erstes zur Information, es ist ein Side-Scroller. 
Bezüglich des DLCs "The little ones": soweit ich dies bis jetzt testen /anspielen konnte:
Kinder involviert zu haben macht es sehr viel schwerer über die Runden zu kommen:
man muss sich mehr kümmern, man muss eine Person mehr ernähren und macht sich um diese Sorgen – und diese Person kann nichts tun, um Dir zu helfen. Aber ich habe gerade erst angefangen und noch nicht bis zum Ende gespielt. 

Ich empfehle während des Spielens sehr:
ein Depot / Handzeichen am Anfang eines jeden Ortes zum Plündern anzulegen. Einerseits kann man Zeit sparen, wenn man zurückkommt und nach mehr sucht, andererseits kann man, wenn der Ort gefährlich ist, auch untalentierte Personen hinschicken, wenn der Rest der Gruppe verletzt oder müde ist.
Auf einem Zettel Notizen zu machen. So weiß man, für was man zurückkehrt, nachdem man - das Spiel für heute beendet hat:
- was ist wo in Deinem Depot.
- wo braucht man welchen Gegenstand oder welches Werkzeug um etwas zu bekommen, 
z. B. Dietrich oder Axt um eine Tür zu öffnen, etc. 
- wo es Gefahren gibt. 

Übrigens, als ich das Spiel anfing, hat es mich irritiert, dass es keine Speicher-Option gibt. Wenn man das Spiel verlässt, speichtert das Spiel immer an dem Punkt, wenn der Plünderer in ihre / seine Haustür tritt.

This War of Mine is a story of civilian survival in a war torn city.

The core mechanics of the game essentially come down to resource management. 

The basic resource categories you need to manage come down to these broad groups:

1. Food (ex. raw meat)
2. Building Materials (ex. wood)
3. Weapons/Utilities (ex. lock picks)
4. Happiness (ex. cigarettes)
5. Healing (ex. medication)
6. Bartering (ex. diamonds)

The game uses a cycle of two times: night and day.

During the day you will do things like:

1. Cook food
2. Distill alcohol
3. Sleep
4. Set mouse traps
5. Grow vegetables 
etc.

During the NIGHT you will go out and SCAVENGE.

The night is the more interactive part of the game. During the night you will look at your map and determine where you would like to scavenge in the city. Some locations (such as the Garage) will be relatively safe and have people for you to barter with. Other locations (such as the Construction Site) may not be safe. You may need to bring a weapon or be prepared to not be seen. The entire goal of scavenging is to bring back food, materials, medications, etc. for your party back at base camp. 

Criticisms:

Overall, I feel like the game becomes very grindy. The fact that you can only carry a limited amount of resources with you while scavenging is realistic yet tedious. You will have to spend multiple nights scavenging the same location in order to loot all of it. While this feels realistic and reasonable, in practice it just becomes monotonous and repetitive. 

Day time phase is a bit of a hassle and simply becomes a routine. You will make water every day. You will put tired people in beds every day. You will cook every day/every few days. Basically day time is just a monotonous time sync as you go through the motions of keeping everyone healthy. And that's honestly what day time is - going through the motions. It's not fun, it's not interactive, and you do the same thing nearly every time. It's disappointing. 

What I enjoy about the game:

I absolutely love the concept - it's clever and I have to give the studio props on originality. It's fresh and something I have never seen before. I like the resource management concept of the game - unfortunately I just didn't care for the way it was executed (too monotonous/going through the motions).


Final Word:

There is A LOT more depth to this game than I have presented here, but I have presented the basic gist of the title. While the game is unique and original, it lacks engagement. There isn't much of a story and the gameplay is simply too repetitive.  I'm very torn on this title, as I want to recommend it but the game just isn't fun. The gamplay isn't strong enough and it becomes repetitive very fast.

I highly recommend this game on several different levels, but there are also a couple tidbits worth noting.

First of all, let me say this is a game that strives to speak with a concious about the reality of war for civilians -- something that is meaningful when you consider the bulk of the games we play involve simply running through worlds blowing stuff away (and often gaming the NPC “civilians” to our advantage as we gun down “the bad guys.”) So, I appreciate the attempt to bring a different voice to war in gaming. That said, this product is a game and I believe it should be evaluated as a game. If you really want to delve into the humanitarian side of things, you’re far better off spending an hour a week as a volunteer or donating the full game price to the charity instead of just the % of the sale price that goes to charity. The game creators should absolutely get credit for their social efforts, it’s just that to me, at the end of the day, it’s a game and we shouldn’t confuse “good works” in a game with the impact we might have doing actual volunteering or donating to causes. 

As a game, this is a great little resource management time waster. It’s divided up into phases where you spend the day hours crafting, improving your shelter, and dealing with your character’s needs (food, health, happiness, etc). The night hours are spent scavenging with a single character who makes scavenging choices for the team. Stealing can have a huge impact on character moods, combat is very risky,  and the limited backpack space often means each night presents tough choices about what to take or leave behind. There are multiple characters to play, each with their own pros and cons and unique backstories and you have a limited ability to create your own characters as well. There are limited types of “events” where your shelter can be raided at night and the impact of those raids will be affected by things like who you left on guard duty, what weapons you’ve got back at your base, and how much you’ve improved your shelter, etc. Other types of “events” include neighbors visiting to offer help, or ask for help, a trader that comes to barter, outbreaks of crime or Winter temperatures taking a sharp turn colder. Winter and violence are the two biggest factors of difficulty in various scenarios. 

The game has a great deal of replay value with a few hiccups. There isn’t really much variety in terms of crafting or dialog, so after a game or two those elements get repetitive. There also isn’t much strategy regarding crafting outside of resource management, so that feels flat after you figure out what order you want things to go in. There are a variety of locations, many with multiple variations, so you can experiment with sneaking or combat strategies. However, these mechanics are extraordinarily simplistic -- combat is far more about having protective gear and/or the right weapon or staking out a hiding spot for a backstab rather than anything remotely resembling an active combat tactic. Further, you cannot spend the day hours training your characters, so if they start the game with lousy combat abilities (or cooking, or crafting), they stay that way. This lack of character skill development is a bit disappointing, but reasonable given the setting. 

My biggest “complaint” of the game is the carrying capacity limitation. Each character gets assigned a number of backpack slots and there is no way to improve them. While I appreciate that it’s a balancing mechanic (and one that makes your early games challenging) on replay it becomes tedious. In fact, if not for different mods that exist to address this, I’m not sure how much replay value the game would have. There’s no attempt to make this extremely limiting mechanic more strategy based, or to address it in settings. You cannot swap types of backpacks, for example, to choose one that would be better for carrying large heavy items (like wood) or small objects (like gears) to make different kinds of items stack better. Also, the loot nodes at locations never respawn which, in my opinion, makes the game a little flat. Once you clear a location there is never a reason to return (unless you’re going to chop up furniture for wood, or the location has a trade vendor). I think it would add a level of choice to have nodes randomly respawn so that in later stages you have to choose whether to continue clearing out a location, or risk a return to a previously visited location in hopes there’s been some kind of respawn event, etc. 

All those are ways the game could have been better or more dynamic, but none of those hinder my overall enjoyment. I really like this game, have spent many hours on it, have purchased it for friends, and find it to be one of the best casual game offerings of the last couple years. I don’t just recommend it, I enthusiastically recommend it, even at full $20 price (though you can regularly get it on sale).

When trying to summarize my thoughts on a game, I usually ask myself "Was this fun to play ?". If the answer is no, I then ask myself "was this compelling and immersive enough to make up for the lack of pure fun, by providing a memorable and unique experience ?". By the 40th, I was banging my head against a wall and listening to podcasts to keep myself awake. 

So in the end, I cannot recommend This War of Mine. It has some undeniable qualities, and someone else might enjoy it far more than me, but in the end it didn't do it for me.

This game is not the sort of thing everyone is going to get the intended effect with. It's not a survival horror game, it's not even really a game. I don't mean that in the way that it is lacking in any sort of gameplay elements.  Rather, I mean that if you go into it thinking it's just going to be a thematic 2D "The Forest" or any of those 'craft and escape the island' games, you're not going to leave with that same impression. The way I see it, there are two types of responses. "This game was boring" and "I'm emotionally scarred that was so sad". Part of that difference lies in how much you are willing to invest yourself in making stories for each character beyond what is given to you. If you take the speech bubbles as ALL your characters ever think, of course you're going to feel this is flat and unenjoyable. But if you look at this game, and try to imagine yourself and the people you care about as being in this situation, and twist the events and experiences into true moments in the world, it's going to be a hard play. Maybe you'll cry when a friend who you've been trying to save finally dies from sickness, because you couldn't keep the shelter warm enough. Maybe you send a reliable scout out to gather materials and he ends up getting shot and killed. Maybe you see a pair of children, trying to get medicine for their sick mother, and sadly tell them there is no way you can help them. Maybe they walk away, and you watch them go, knowing they'll never make it. Hoping against hope that they might. Wondering, as you lay in your home with nothing but the bite of cold and the sickness and barely enough strength to make it to the door as you hear the knocking again, how this is going to end.
If you go into this with a vivid imagination and compassion. It's going to crush you more than once. If you go into it expecting it to be a fun little crafting survival game and take only what it gives you, it's going to bore you. You get out of this what you put into it.

I'm gonna' have to say 'no' to this game. I realize some of you might think I'm crazy or whatever, given the amount of glowing reviews on here (93% is a very high % for any game -- 95 % overall). But, you should realize that nearly ALL of the positive reviews come from people with less than 10 hours, and well over 50% of those have less than 5 hours. . . . for a 20 dollar game? Yeah, I don't think so.  

But there's a very simple reason why I can't recommend this game: it's not procedural at all. 

Everything in this game is pre-determined, and how you beat it is also pre-determined. The claim of 'random events' is bogus, because in the short time I played this game, I was able to predict the time a trader would show up. Also, every building is the same each time you play. All of the items in the game seem to be the same kind/amount every time you play. 

The game does give you that eery feeling, and it does put you on the edge of your seat... until you realize how repetitive the game is. In 3.3 hours of play, I wound up doing the same thing over and over and over and over again - that's sad. 

Also, the game just isn't fun. The game is cool for about 2 hours, then the novelty of it wears off and then you realize you sank  20 bucks into a game that gives you about 1.5 hours of 'new stuff' to do. Seriously. After about an hour and a half, you will have done just about everything there is to do in this game. Do that for 20 more, then you'll start to understand why it just isn't that great. 

If this game was $5, I'd recommend it in a heartbeat, because this feels more like an interactive novel than anything else, given its lack of content. 

So that just about sums up what I don't like about this game and why I regret purchasing it. If you want a survival game that gives you an eery feeling, then get Project Zomboid or 7d2d.

This game is hard, without a doubt. From the perspective of suffering civilians, This War of Mine is something you typically set out to play for the survival tactic and the interesting change of story; the portrayal of not soldiers, but the lesser-seen gameplay of civilians in war-strewn cities. 
The connections grown with each individual character and their situation grow stronger and stronger throughout the game. Reading their growing biography with every passing day, seeing their moods alter based off of current events. If needs for supplies are not met in time, the death impacts everything and it really is powerful. I'm honestly excited to see how The Little Ones DLC plays out and curious to see how it effects the overall gameplay.

The atmosphere itself is powerful as well, with an art style that is both aesthetically pleasing but suiting the core aspect of the game; the grimy, cold struggle for survival. The music is the most fitting (and indisputably catchy) music possible. Everything about this game is beautiful and terrible, and I love it. Would recommend to anyone.

In war, not everyone is a soldier. This War of Mine shows you the horrors of war through the eyes of a group of civilians. Taking quite an influence from the Siege of Sarajevo during the Bosnian War, you are put into a city under siege and forced to survive. Though the gameplay is nothing special, what truly shines about This War of Mine is the message behind it. Survival is tough in this city, and you must do whatever you can to survive. This leads to you quite often making terrible choices to survive, such as [spoiler] robbing a hospital or a church just trying to help innocent people like you survive [/spoiler] and [spoiler] stealing from an elderly couple, and if you come back to where the couple was, you find out that they have starved to death because of you. [/spoiler] Ultimately, This War of Mine is more of a work of art than a game. It excels at showing you the savagery of war through the ones most affected by it, but the raw gameplay is honestly not the most fun or enjoyable, at least during the daytime. At night, however, comes the real fun of the game. You must send one of your playable characters to a location in the world to scavenge for food, medicine, and anything else that your group needs to survive. If you're a roleplayer, you'll be delighted to know about the character creator where you can upload a picture and create a description for your own custom character. But if you want to stick to the base game, it can get a little boring. There isn't much replay value, and once you've seen a location you've seen it all. If you're looking for a  gritty Call of Duty style shooter, look elsewhere. But if you're looking for a fascinating tale of how life under siege affects innocent civilians, this is for you. I don't believe that the current price tag is worth it for such a short experience, but if you can get the game on sale, it's definitely worth it.

It is an amazingly entertaining walk through surviving a warzone as a civilian, not a super-soldier, not a hero, just a civilian. Like in real life, if you get in to a fight with a stranger, you will probably die. When you die, you are permanently dead. It really brings a flavor of warzone survival to those of us fortunate enough to have never known it in real life.

On your first run through the game, you will likely cower in the shadows when you encounter strangers in trouble. When you get comfortable with the game, you may try to save them. Maybe you save them. Maybe you die trying, to be forgotten in a mass grave, just another victim of the war.

I'm really, really passionate about the power and potential video games have as an entertainment, educational and artistic medium. 'This War of Mine' was one of the most emotionally draining and frustrating experiences I've ever engaged in - by deliberate design.

The game simulates the struggle of civilians living amidst the urban destruction of a conflict. Day by day contending with acquiring food, evading bandits, dealing with sickness.

The circumstances of the setting are never elucidated, nor are they actually relevant. This is because 'This War of Mine' is at heart a game about the difficult, often horrible choices people are put through in situations of armed and civil strife. It's about the impact war has on the human spirit.

The decisions you make weigh on you, and as the time progresses the game itself narrows - less resources, frequent illness, increased danger to your 'family' of survivors, multiple morally dubious but necessary decisions you're forced to make in order to break even. This occurs to the point where literally playing the game feels like a strain and burden, even surviving till the next day is an achievement itself - much like the lives of those actually trapped such circumstances.
Eventually, you're faced with a choice. Most of the game has you avoiding capricious and hostile bandits, fellow survivors who have abandoned, or forced to abandon dictates of common decency and who rape, pillage and even thrive in the setting of the game.

As survival gets more difficult - the easy, and logical and natural path to take is to take by force what your group needs. But in doing so, you inadvertently warp into those whom you once cursed and feared. That's the moment when the game really hits you. You've turned into your own worst nightmare, war has ripped apart all that was once considered sane.

'This War of Mine' isn't a video game in the traditional sense, where you play for fun and enjoyment and relaxation. 
It was awful and dark and depressing and stressing and playing it made me feel awful and reflective.

 It was brilliant.

If I had to sum up This War of Mine in one word, it would be "powerful". It is a touching reflection on the suffering caused by war, but through the eyes of civilians rather than soldiers. I actually showed it to a professor of mine who survived the Yugoslav Wars, including spending over three years inside besieged Sarajevo. He was caught there when the Siege started in April 1992 as he tried to help a friend flee the city and ended up being stuck there until 1996, and he has a number of... troubling... stories to tell about the Siege. He actually bought and played This War of Mine for a while and it made him so emotional that he started crying (and he is a very tough, "old school" sort of fellow). I think that pretty much sums up what this game is like, in my opinion.

As you have likely guessed, this game is not really "fun" by any standard, but you should play it anyway, I think.

Now for a forlorn tale of three people. 
(Pavle, Anton and Cveta) 

We began the day just as we would any other, except Anton developed a small cold, he was promptly put in a bed to rest. 

Cveta was allocated the job of clearing as much rubble as possible whilst Pavle rested for the night ahead... 

Come the night, Pavle was preparing his backpack for the long and probably dangerous night ahead, with him he took a lockpick and one shovel, his target location was an abandoned apartment complex from which he was able to loot a large amount of supplies and some food. 

Cveta stood guard in the homespun mansion we had took asylum in, very little occured during her night apart from watching over Anton, who's condition was slightly worsening. 


Pavle returns and promptly crafts himself a bed to rest in whilst Anton prepares a small gas cooker and Cveta takes Anton's bed (Not a good idea, considering he is ill) 

***Three Days Later***


Whilst on a routine supply run, Pavle came across a building armed with thugs, he was warned of this place and contemplated returning empty handed. But his persistence to find medicine and bandages for Anton, who was severely wounded in a raid, during the night. 

Pavle silently enters the complex, his stomach rumbling and his eyes red from exhaustion. He loots several cupboards before hearing footsteps nearing his position. He took what he could from the cabinet and hid in a small crevice in the wall, noticing this guard was armed with a shotgun, Pavle did not wish to run the risk of being seen, so he remained still for what seemed like hours. 

Eventually he departs from his hiding place, still determined to find bandages and and Medicne, climbing through a hole in the roof led to an area which held several cabinets and a pile of garbage. Pavle began to loot the area for what he had been searching for. But to no avail, the night was nearing the end, and there was but one room left on this side of the building, Pavle tries his luck, but in his anticipation to return home, forgot the golden rule. "Always ensure the room is empty before entering" The door swings open, and Pavle steps in, he doesn't notice the armed guard stading near the edge of the room. The man aims his weapon at Pavle and implores he leave immediately Pavle knows this gaurd will put him down regardless... 


Pavle unsheathes his shovel and lunges for the man, surprising him and knocking him back a fair way, the man stumbles near the edge and cries out for help. Pavle can already hear the footsteps of running guards as he lunges again at the man, missing this strike but forcing his rival to step back, further towards the edge. The man, slightly dazed raises his weapon and fires, slightly injuring Pavle. 

Pavle in a blind rage relentlessly bludgeons his attacker with the shovel, just as the man begins to beg for his life, Pavle swings and the shovel connects, the man flails back, tettering on the edge, before plummeting, the sound of flesh and bone hitting the floor rings out in the almost silent room.. 

Pavle, now unable to sprint fast, as he once could, has mere seconds to relish in his victory before the door is opened and two men enter, with weapons raised. they fire but miss as Pavle descends down the very gap his attacker fell through, and begins to limp for the exit. But the two armed guards have now caught up to him, yelling obscenities as Pavle nears the exit. He is about to stumble through the final room before a burning pain spreads swiftly across his back, and another across his thigh, Pavle stumbles and falls. 

Upon the floor Pavle breathes his final breath. 

***The Next Day***

Anton has passed away in his sleep from his injuries.  

Cveta disposes of the corpse before becoming hysterical and collapsing upon the floor. 

***Day FIfteen***

Cveta decides to sleep for the entire day, only waking to eat the remainder of the food. She is still starving. 

During the night Cveta is raided by bandits, and wounded, not before they purloin the last of her water and material. 
She is left to bleed out.

***Day Sixteen***

Cveta loses her struggle with her injuries and passes away, a former shell of her once jocular self.

What eventually happened to them, is unkown.

This War of Mine is a survival game made by 11 bit studios, who used to be known mainly thanks to the Anomaly series ("tower offence" games). This time they went with something completely different, as you'll have to get into lives of people who try to survive in partially destroyed house, in the middle of a war zone.

To survive all the terror outside your house, you have to keep people in healthy state (to the extent possible) - you have to fight their hunger, thirst and depressions, but also keep them prepared for raids - being armed is helpful. From morning to evening, you'll be taking care of all basic needs of your characters by reasonable use of your collected resources like herbs, meat, wood and metal. It may seem complex but the whole crafting system is pretty simple and there isn't a huge amount of items you can have; you'll get known of most items in first hours. But where you'll get all those important resources? At the beginning, you'll find them in the ruined house you try to live in, but sooner or later you have to send out your characters to scavenge the other houses during the night. 

That's the phase where the game swaps from resource management to 2D stealth game, where the whole outcome is only up to you. You can try to rob army deserters, or you can be afraid of them and rather pick the house where ill and old people live. But what will you do if somebody finds you and protects their property? There comes the important part of This War of Mine - all your scavenging brings even more depression to all characters that you control. Even though they have pretty limited amount of dialogues among themselves, you'll still feel the emotional press coming from your actions. Let's say that you won't mind killing other people for food - congratulations, character who kills will get truly depressed and other will be disgusted of him. And what if you don't kill? Congratulations, character will feel depressed because of stealing other people's things, and other will also get disgusted. Or you can just let them die, if you feel that's the better option.

Graphic style of the game is a great one, it doesn't require a strong hardware to play it since it's a combination of 3D models and drawn textures and effects with a really specific style ([i]you can see it in screenshots[/i]). Low HW requirement is also the positive fact for players not just on Steam, as This War of Mine is also ported for mobile platforms (Android, iOS) - that seems obvious from the controls, as they are really touch-friendly, maybe too much for PC standards. All movement is done just by clicking to a specific place, and all actions are done by clicking on small icons over every object that you can interact with.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
This War of Mine isn't overall much complex and isn't even long (few hours for a single scenario is enough), but the game's quality tops at the atmosphere and story based on despair. You may think that you can survive without hurting others (somehow) but you'll be forced to compromise pretty soon. There's no good way, there's only "wrong" and "somehow lesser wrong" way, but at least you can manage to survive the war.

I have played a lot of games in my 30+ years of life. I've played fun, casual, silly games that make me laugh, I've played highly technical games requiring skill and accuracy that make me rage, I've played puzzle games that really make you think and slap your forehead once you figure something out that's taking you too long, I've even played horror games meant to scare me, and I some have really made me scream. The point is that all games touch some emotional side of us, some hit their intended nerves deeper than others, but regardless of how much a game has affected me in this past, I've been able to get past my emotions and continue playing.

This War Of Mine is the exception. After I killed an elderly couple to survive, I had to stop playing. I can't even pinpoint what certain mechanic in the game managed to ring this bell in me, but I have never had such a deep emotional reaction to a game. I felt digusted with myself, completely lost and buried under a mountain of despair. As I clicked the buttons to bash their heads in with a shovel, I felt my soul turning black. I try to think of all those koopas I used to eject from their shell as Mario and wonder why I didn't empathize on the same level because, at the root, the two actions are the same: [i]preying on the weak to succeed.[/i] So, why does it feel so much worse when I do it in This War Of Mine?

For this reason alone I am recommending the game, because no other game has ever been able to strike this sort of reaction in me, but I will never play it again.

This War of Mine is a micromanagement simulator. You are given several survivors and a shelter to maintain and upgrade. You must manage survivor's health, food supply, shelter heating, and supplies for crafting to further your survival. Crafting is a huge gameplay component and you spend half the game scavenging materials from various locations outside your shelter. Outside your shelter, different scenarios play out presenting the player with decisions; decisions that greatly affect your survivor's moral compass, happiness and health.

The goal of the game is to make the player feel the sadness and rawness of war. To this end, the game employs a heavy, dark shading filter that works hand in hand with the music to provide a solemn ambience. Combined with the character's happiness meter and moral compass, decisions to kill or rob for survival cannot be made lightly.

[h1]Overview (sorry for the weird organization, I'm lazy)[/h1]
Being 2D, this game can accomplish things much more easily than 3D games can. This War of Mine is very accessible; character’s actions are controlled by a simple click of your mouse and screen adjustment by using the scroll wheel to zoom in and out and the mouse to position the camera (by dragging the cursor to the edges to move the camera up, down, left, right).

A micromanager’s dream. Starting out with 3 people, you are tasked with keeping them well fed, healthy, happy, well slept, and safe from bandit attacks. Any one of these variables, if left unchecked, can lead to the death of a person in your care. The constant need of each of your survivors forces you to manage our resources wisely. I found food to be my biggest struggle.

Each playthrough will be different. When you start anew, characters and environments will be randomized. Included in this randomization are characters that come to your front door. In search of shelter, help, or trade (they can have some very useful items).

The characters are detailed; each has his/her own traits. Some characters are good at coking, others excel at running, some are good at bartering, and there are even characters who can help keep your civilians happy by boosting morale. The latter character trait is invaluable for keeping your group from spiraling into depression.

Simple questions can force you to really think about what the consequences would be and if the cost is worth it. In many areas that you can visit to scavenge for materials, there are people just like you, trying their best to survive with what little food and other supplies they have. Will you steal the food from them or will you look in another, less occupied place in hopes of finding food? There are only so many abandoned areas, so you will eventually be forced to steal some rations from your next door neighbors or try your luck in more dangerous areas.

Varied resources with in-depth crafting system. There are 8 workshops you can create that help you generate resources.  They are as follows: stove, garden, herbal workshop, moonshine still, alcohol distiller, metal workshop, animal trap, and rainwater collector.   For example, with the metal workshop you can make the crowbar, knife, lock pick, and many other useful tools by using weapon parts and scrap. These tools are a necessity to scavenge through the places that you visit at night.

After the day cycle is over, the night comes upon you and you can choose to send one of your survivors out to scavenge nearby locations. In these areas there are valuable materials such as weapon parts, food, and medical supplies. Backpack size determines how much a person can carry back from scavenging. Most characters have a backpack size of 10-12. There are unoccupied areas, which require no caution, and also occupied areas where you will have to be careful what you take. 

When you aggravate people in an area (stealing valuables or attacking people), each time you go back to that area at night they will remember what you did. They will sometimes shoot on sight or give verbal warnings telling you to leave. This is where stealth becomes vital. There are also naturally dangerous areas occupied by soldiers and snipers. Previously unoccupied areas may become occupied by survivors such as yourself, looking for shelter.

When snow comes, several things change. Most notably, the temperature drops to bone-chilling levels. It is advised to build multiple heaters and upgrade your existing ones to provide for the most efficient heating. You cannot collect water using conventional methods any longer. Instead, you have to go outside and collect snow, which can be melted and purified by using the stove.

The Child Charity DLC is a great way to contribute toward a worthy cause and will unlock an extra achievement (but you would buy the DLC to support the children and not just for an achievement, right?).
