This War of Mine is a game like no other, taking a surprisingly real (well, ish) look at what it would be like to have war engulf your home. It's a survival management game full of tension and atmosphere that is worth playing through completely at least once if you're even remotely interested in the concept.

During the day time you are restricted to your shelter due to the conflict and can build new tools for survival and see to the needs of your survivors such as food, sleep and trying to keep their morale up. During the night phase you have the option of sending one of your survivors out to scavenge for building materials and vital resources. This is an essential part of survival, but an increasingly dangerous and intense undertaking. Your goal is simply to survive, but there is no way to know for how long, and as the game progresses resources become more and more scarce.

As far as replayability goes, you can opt to start with a random selection of different survivors and the locations may be ever so slightly reshuffled, but on the whole the game takes you through the same scenarios every time so you're likely to get two or three playthroughs at most out of it.

I look forward to "The Little Ones" expansion when it comes out for PC, which will hopefully add some interesting new content to explore.

Without a doubt, This War of Mine has been one of my favorite games. I purchased this knowing it was possible an interesting concept, and decided to give it a go. After playing it for some hours in the past 10 days, I have to say that it's probably the best emotional game.

The first thing you notice when you start this game up is the very minimalistic design. The game plays out in very simple 2D environments that look almost like pages from a sketchbook. If you're anything like me, this might take you aback. Call me shallow, but graphics are important to me! They're not everything, but they go a long way in immersing you in the storyline. As the game unfolds, however, you realize that the simple, drab art actually matches the "survivors in a war-torn city" theme quite well. Before long, you're completely lost in this world.

Like the art, the gameplay mechanics are simple to grasp but far deeper than they appear at first glance. You start out in your shelter--a dilapidated, abandoned house--and you notice icons over the various things you can interact with. Click on a pile of rubble, and you find some wood and nails. Open a cabinet and you find a few pieces of jewelry and a lockpick. You'll need all of these things. This isn't like Skyrim where half the stuff you find is junk, and it isn't like Fallout where you can beat the game without even dealing with the crafting components. Here, everything you find has a purpose that can save your life. Those old electrical components will be used to construct a radio that will clue you in to what's going on in the city; that empty pill casing can you be used to make critical medications later in the game. Even stuff like old books are useful. Your characters can read them to stay entertained and happy (more on that later), you can burn them for fuel to stave off the chill of winter, or you can trade them for things you need. The challenge comes in choosing what to take with you. As the game progresses, you must venture out into the city to scavenge supplies, and your squad members have very limited backpack space to carry things in. Do you bring back the the gunpowder to make the bullets you'll need to clear out the bad guys in another area, or do you pick up the food that's as scare as it is critical? Finding the right balance is essential, and you'll likely have to start over a couple times before you know what works best.

No matter what style of play you choose, the game is always challenging. That's a good thing! In other games, you might just kill everyone you see and take their possessions until you build up enough wealth to coast through the game. Better them than you right? Not so here. Killing innocent characters or even stealing from them will cause your squad to suffer guilt. You'll see little thought bubbles appear of their head sharing their lament with you: "Those patients at the hospital are probably going to die because of me." Kill too many non-bad guys and one of your squad members may even commit suicide. Most other reviewers are using the term "pulls no punches" a lot, and that's definitely true.

The only drawbacks are in the minimalistic design. While it works well, you can't help but imagine how much better the game could have been with a little more depth. Since emotions play such a big role for your characters, it would be nice to have some kind of dialogue system you could use to cheer each other up, or maybe even ask for help from other non-team members. Also, there's a lot of room for the storyline to really develop and add to the emotional impact you feel. Even lacking this, however, this is still a great, challenging game.

It’s odd to play such an aware title especially after playing Call of Duty or Battlefield where you play as Captain America or some other bullhonkey over-powered character.  I wouldn’t recommend playing the game for the gameplay, no, but for the experience.  This game can take you from “we’re gonna make it” to “we’re barely surviving” and I’m okay with it. The game starts off with usually 3 survivors in what looks to be an abandoned apartment building, as it's too dangerous to scavenge during the day due to snipers the survivors are stuck in the shelter during daytime, this is the time where the player must manage his survivors by cooking and feeding them, building workshops, stoves, heaters and any other necessary household equipment to keep the survivors going but all of this requires materials and parts which you can start off by scavenging your own shelter in the beginning of the game but when 8pm arrives that's when it's time to go scavenging for weapons, meds, food, materials and any other essentials to survive the war, during this time only one character can go scavenging as the rest have to stay back at the shelter to either get rest or stay guard against any other rebels that try to break in and steal your supplies.

Scavenging areas unlock randomly and simultaneously and when you select one it will tell you what loot is available in that area and if it's dangerous or caution is advised when trying to scavenge the area, it will also let you know if the place is currently occupied by any miltia or armed thugs so the player can best prepare with the appropriate equipment before the player commit's to the scavenge.

The hardest part of this game is the decisions that you make because each decision has and can have a huge impact on your shelter and the survival of your survivors, several times during the game you'll have random people knocking on your door asking for meds, food, assistance in helping them and if you choose to assist someone in need of help then you'll lose 1 survivor in your shelter for 1-2 days which means one less person to guard your shelter while you go out and scavenge and you don't always get a reward for helping, it's a risk that the player has to take if they decide to help someone else in need while it is useful to get a survivor out of a depressed state and generally uplift the mood inside your shelter, especially if you've had to kill another innocent to steal their supplies. You're pretty much forced to be the good guy in this war as bad decisions to steal too much from innocents or murder innocent people can and will most likely have a negative impact on all your survivors in the shelter and if any of your survivors go from a depressed state into a broken state that survivor will render useless for the whole period of being in a broken state and there is the risk that they will leave the shelter or go down the path of suicide.

It's important to time manage well especially during the daytime hours, make sure that survivors are getting enough food, rest, build anything that your survivors currently need, manufacture moonshine and alcohol if needed, put some more food inside your rat trap to catch some more rats for meat, always have at least one survivor rest during scavenge time that way you'll always have at least one survivor to do the daytime chores while the others rest.  it's advisable to get your hands on a firearm as quickly as possible as firearms help in a great deal to avoid being raided during the night, if you don't have any firearms, knives or an axe will do the job, it's important to get established early in the game, build a heater before winter comes, upgrade your metal workshop as early as possible so you can craft an axe to destroy the desks and wardrobes inside your shelter for wood, this will be important for surviving through the cold during the winter time and to build more things for your shelter early on in the game.

The player has to survive until a ceasefire which can happen randomly on any day (usually between days 40-50 but it can happen as early as day 25) also the winter usually happens during days 20-30 but it can be random as well, same with crime waves they can happen during any time and usually last at least 7-10 days which increase the chances of being raided each night, during this time especially it's very useful to have firearms. This game has quickly risen to one of my all-time favorite video games. I ended up clocking in 12 hours in one weekend once I started the game. The atmosphere is intence and affects you almost immediately; you feel the weight and depression that comes with the war atmosphere. The gameplay is simple and stream-lined. Overall, the game is genuinely addicting and fun to play. 

The main downside is that there is a bit of a learning curve with the game. The first couple of playthroughs were incredibly difficult and I could not figure out get through 15 nights, let alon the whole war! But after some trial-and-error and help from the internet, I was able to figure out how to play, the best strategy, etc. Pro tip: If you are having trouble with the set storymodes, just create your own story/game mode with the survivors you think are best, adjust the war settings, etc. That was the best way to get over the learning curve and become comfortable with the gameplay. After that, I felt like I could handle any of the other story modes. 

Finally, the story and background is interesting, but I wish there was more! You never get a full story about the war, why it started, or in-depth details about the world outside. Any information you get is through short clips from the radio, clues found across the locations, and some comments from the survivors themselves. Honestly, this just adds to the experience! It drives home the point that war is just universally pointless and awful; it does not really matter how the war started or who is in the "right" because it is innocent people who suffer. I do wish there was more meat behind the characters: The diary entries are nice, but a lot of the characters just come off bland and forgettable. I would love if there were more diary entries that shared individual character experiences and thoughts so that they were more fleshed out. But that is just a nit-picky issue for a game that is really great.

Ultimately, this game is wonderful experience that makes you want to put so many hours into it without realizing it. I recommend it to anyone who is looking for a unique, emotional game that is sure to affect you on so many levels.

This will probably get lost in the sea of positive reviews, but I had to add to them. This War of Mine is a great game, and one that's hooked me in solidly for the past two days. On my first playthrough my main scavenger was quickly killed after I tried to prevent a soldier sexually assaulting a civilian. Clearly this game is not shy about throwing you straight in, and this is one of many moments that highlights that the morally correct decision is not necessarily the one that's going to get you through the war. This, combined with overnight bandit raids on my shelter left the remaining survivors wounded and depressed. One died of sickness, and the last one was then driven to suicide by day 14. 

At this point I didn't think I'd ever pick the game back up - it was harrowing and felt legitimately futile (intentionally so, I'm sure). However, on a second playthrough you'll most likely get to grips with the game mechanics and start to learn to scavenge and trade effectively, allowing you to build utilities and structural improvements to your shelter. Eventually, you'll even become self sufficient to the point that food is no longer too much of a concern when scavenging. It's not all plain sailing though, as the game progresses you'll need to traverse increaslingly dangerous areas to continue collecting supplies, and you'll face tough choices on whether you can afford to help people. You'll also inevitably be faced with the moral dilemma of whether to steal or not. And you probably will.

I have only a couple of minor negative points to mention about this game. First is that the combat is very unintuitive. Some kind of tutorial system for this aspect is badly needed, given that one wrong move will almost certainly end with your death. Second is that if you do well in the early game, the mid to late game can become a bit of a formality, You'll have all the food and meds that you need and plenty of luxuries to trade, which can result in a 15 or so day period where you're kind of just waiting for it to end. It still manages to be fun, but the variety is gone by this point.

All in all, however, the positives FAR outway any minor drawbacks and I highly recommend giving this engrossing, thought-provoking game a go.

However, the game wasn't designed in order to 100%-assuredly force a miserable experience. After some runs, I've grasped that killing won't always make everyone sad. If you kill the bandits in the warehouse, no one will be sad, and you'll look like a badass (no one will be sad if you kill the soldiers in the construction site too. Screw the rebels, screw the military!).  Plus, by killing said bandits, you'll hit the jackpot, since you'll get their firearms, ammunition, protective body suit and all of the contents of the warehouse. It'll be easy to purchase what is needed, and everyone of the four people in the house will easily have the status "Well  Feed" and "Content". 

In fact, on one run, by using the strategy above, my team became so wealthy that I decided to be generous and give all of our medical supplies (five bandages, three medicine bottles, four herbal meds and, as a bonus, two food cans). After giving the generous donation for the hospital (and receiving a few cigarettes), I've then resumed my business of collecting materials from the hospital debris. While walking in the hospital, I've saw someone (from his blue, pajama-like clothing, I guess it was a patient) poking around a nightstand (which, apparently, he wasn't supposed to, since it had the "private property" mark). I, still in character, felt stung by this outrageous act! My donation was to the hospital, and the doctor will decide how these medicines will be used. So I decided to give him a punch, just to stop his theft attempt. And guess what? [i]A single punch killed him[/i]. And, all of a sudden, I'm a murder in the middle of the hospital, and everyone else is scared of me, and a guy with a shotgun starts to pursuit me.

Have I just overcalculated things, by being too much in character, or have the developers indeed placed a trap like that to me? This is what motivated me to do a review.

I'm sorry I didn't play this game when I bought it, I've been totally addicted to it all week and played it every night... finally completing it this evening. The concept for the game is refreshing and quite frankly excellently executed. It's a survival game set in a war torn eastern European city, you must guide the fate of up to four civilians and try to keep them all alive until a cease fire is called. The focus of this game is very much on scavenging, base building and resource management. Combat is possible during the game but should be avoided at all costs because you are almost always outgunned and / or outnumbered! It is possible to get weapons in the game, on my final playthrough I think that game completion was secured by getting a shotgun on about day 4 which I used to protect my home to great effect during an ensuing crime spree. The game has a great level of depth and requires micro management and resource planning. There is a strong trading and crafting element to the game and is arguably its core mechanic alongside stealthy scavenging.

The big plus point of this game from my perspective is being a mature gamer you can play this game in a day and night cycle at a time as it saves the game each morning. This effectively happens in 10 minute chunks so it's easy to pick up and put down. I'm not going to give this game a score, I will simply say that as a game from a small company the finish and stability would put some big studios to shame. The graphics and sound effects are top notch. This game is a must play, regardless of the type of game you enjoy. Pick this up and try it you won't be disappointed, the one caveat being that it is intended for a mature audience.

I've had this game for a while and I still love it, which can't be said for a lot of games.

Not only are the visuals aesthetially pleasing, they also fit the theme of the game really well. Every single time I play, I go through every single emotion imaginable. The way individual events play with your heart and how each character has their own storyline and what makes it even better is that at the end, it's not an immediate cut off; you're told what happens to them after the ceasefire. This game is one of the most dramatic, exciting and heart wrenching games on the market and is worth every penny. 

Not only that, there's an additional DLC that you can buy which adds artwork to the game and the money goes to charity (you can also decide how much you spend, to a certain extent).

However, there are a few things that I would like to see improved in the future as I believe it was touched on but not competely developed. Each character has a certain personality, explained in their biography. When certain events happen, their biography is updated with how they feel about the situation that happened, for example, if you choose to kill an NPC for supplies, some don't care while others actually do. What bothers me is that even though certain characters aren't affected by these, they still become sad, depressed and broken, leaving them completely useless. I would expect a character that actually understands the concept of self defense and the fact that sometimes we must kill for supplies and even says that they understand it, to not become so depressed. Another thing is during the day, sometimes there are events in which a survivor has the choice to leave the base and help an NPC out. It would be nice to add another choice to go with them, perhaps for an extra reward where you can physically help them out, such as clearing rubble, fixing up a base, healing people etc. (You could see it as a minigame during the day).

All in all, I really recommend this game and I believe there is also room for improvement. If you're even thinking about it, buy it. You will not regret the decision and the replayability immense, with the difficulty changing every single time.

"This War of Mine" is an experience where all you want is for your handful of civilians to survive. You don't play this game to brag about how many days you made it. You don't play this game to play God and shape people's lives at your whim. You play this game if you want a bleak and often tense simulation of the trials faced by non-combatants stuck in a lawless city, trapped in whatever shelter they've found because war has made normal life an impossibility. Note that the developers drew heavily on accounts of the Siege of Sarajevo, which took place from 1992 to 1996 during the Bosnian War.

While there are imperfections, 11 Bit Studios has absolutely hit the right note. The characters are neither superheroes nor survivalists. Every morsel of food or fuel becomes a precious commodity, every wound sustained becomes a source of dread. You'll feel despair and irritation as you wait for the harsh winter to end, wondering each night which of your people will succumb to illness, and each chance encouter that turns to violence will leave you with anguish, relief, or maybe a combination of both.

The tone is sublimely melancholy, with the music in particular worth listening to long after you're done with the game. The DLCs, also, are of the perfect kind: a free editor's workshop, and a priced art package where 100% of the proceeds go to a charity for children victimized by war. 11 Bit Studios isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ around: "This War of Mine" is not just a game, but a symbol of what a game can represent. It's an empathetic opportunity to imagine what people throughout history have faced in their darkest days.

If you love playing a badass with special powers who can rip through enemies with ease, this game may prove hard for you to adjust to. What makes this game special is that you direct the actions of a group of survivors who each have some unique skills and personalities, but otherwise they're just ordinary people, trying desperately to surive the horrors of a modern day urban warzone. You will never feel 100% on top of things and you will regularly face tough moral and ethical decisions, the consequences of which genuinely shape the progression of your story. You will always be short of the exact component you need, and just when you think everything's going smoothly something terrible will happen to rock your group's morale.

So, here's the story of my first playthrough with as few spoiler details as possible. Happily, I made it through with all three of my initial survivors alive and happy, though not without incident. I managed to get by without resorting to too much stealing, and the moments when I did take stuff from other innocents really felt like a major moral decision. I did my best to help my neighbours whenever they came to me begging for assistance. Sadly, two others who came to live with my group were killed along the way; both Marko and later Roman perished trying to break into a gang-controlled brothel, of all places. Both deaths hit me surprisingly hard. It's a triumph of this game that it really makes you care about the members of your group. The game's combat system is really tough to get to grips with, but this seems fitting; again, you're in control of ordinary folks trying to survive rather than kick-ass superheroes. Both times, my guys took down a couple of the thugs before meeting their ends. In retrospect I wish I'd played it safer on those occasions, but a part of me wanted to see how the combat system worked!

The memory of my first time through this game will stick with me and resonate in the way a good movie often does. Just like with a movie, you'd be spoiling it for yourself by reading up on it too much before seeing it, so again, do yourself a favour and play this game through at least once before using any mods or reading any guides! This war of mine takes you to the other side of conflicts and looks at survival in a conflict from the side of the civilians. 
If you have ever wondered what was going on behind those windows when you were driving your tank through the town, then this war of mine is able to show you the harsh reality of being a non-combatant in a war zone.

You start off in a house with up to four survivors and around three and a half walls, a roof and a few areas in the house to scavenge for supplies.
This building is your home and it is where, during the daytime, you get your characters to perform actions. These range from building items, tools or workstations/furniture and to also perform tasks like cooking, gardening, or even sleeping (an important task). 
These actions happen during the daytime hours but when night falls then the game changes where you get to choose which of your characters goes out into the night to scavenge, who sleeps and who goes onto guard duty.
The scavenging destination is chosen on a simple map of the city which gives an overview of the area you choose to visit including a basic description of what you might find.
It is during the scavenging that the game throws some difficult decisions at you and there was one area that I was faced with a dilemma.
I found an old couple in their house, the old man followed me around asking if I was going to rob them, he also asked me not to hurt his wife as she is sick. I managed to give the old man the run around and when I was out of site of him, I stole from the old couple. I actually felt bad that I took things from the old couple in a game, I didn't take much from them and when I went back to my home the rest of my group seemed to accept what I did, I haven't been back to their house to clean them out and I think I will leave them alone from now on. The choices you make affect your fellow survivors in different ways.
This is just one of the ways that this game sets its self apart from most games as you initially think that you will always look out for your own group, but it works on your mind when you are scavenging and you listen (well read) what the NPC's in the area are saying and you start to think that my group does not need this as much as these people as they are just like you in that they are trying to survive as well.

The graphics of the game are gritty and drab and work well to immerse you into the setting, there is the sounds of conflict in the background to improve the immersion.

For me the standout point of this game is the way it brings you to the other side of the conflict and it does thins in a way that makes you think about what you are doing, it no longer feels black and white as your decisions have consequences.
To me this game is one that should be on your list and I am very happy that I bought it.

This is one of the hardest decisions for a review I've had in a very long time.  Overall, I'm giving it a thumbs down primarily due to "my" perception of a lack of proper basic training provided by the developer and a community I found to be a majority of cruel fanboys.

What I enjoyed:
First off, major kudo's for the developing team for concieving and delivering a simulation of the realities of war, as told by the innoncent bystander.  So many war games give the player a sense of immortality and reward for senseless and mindless destruction, war is quite devistating and this simulator portrays this extremely well.  The graphics are quite good, they're crisp and clear yet dark and hazy...  perfect!  The human stories you encounter help a great deal to pull you into the story line, well done.  The activities in the game seam quite realistic for the environment and was pleased to see that fear, concern, empathy, and hatred all exist within the encounters.  Each game is different, so there's plenty of replayability in this simulator.  There's not much help in the way of instructions, no list of commands to look up, you just get tossed into the game and have to figure it out.   I both liked this and hated it at the same time.  The first day you are introduced to several game play mechanics which do an excellent form of learning the game mechanics.  You're digging, scavenging, building, breaking into all sorts of things.  You get used to the interface pretty quick, but there are several things it doesn't teach you, which brings me to what I didn't like...

What I didn't enjoy:
Since there are no instructions (and again, I partially like that fact), I spent a good deal of time searching YouTube for instructional videos and tips.  Enduring several hours of listening to fanboys who love to hear themselves talk on and on about the most mundane of thoughts, I was able to pickup that in the game there is combat, the ability for characters to interact with each other, a few things that help you and your group suvive.  These abilities are not intuitive in the game and appear to have some combination of setting or events to make them happen that are not obvious, I've figured out combat finally, but little else.  Despite all the videos, all that I've seen is that you need to do these things, none cover HOW to do these things.  Aside from gameplay, these missing lists of commands would be very handy when setting up a custom game.  I am unable to create one because the map requires I pick some 24 city locations and I can't get the interface to do anything more than toggle to loctions I pick and won't maintain my selection.  

So like many other players have posted, the game sets you up to fail and it's down right fustrating.  Having a house full of squatters/survivors you would think you could send out a large party to bring home several scavenged items.  Nope, only one person can go out for supplies a night, while the rest sit around and complain about how hungry, wounded, and sad they are.

Overall, it didn't take long before I felt like playing this simulator was just pointless and a waste of my time.  Despite really being drawn to the game concept, I'm just not enjoying this game and as such can't give it a thumbs up.

This War of Mine is an excellent little gem that takes on a different perspective. Instead of surviving the 'zombie appocalypse' and running around causing hell, you're trapped in a city besieged by war. Every decision will affect the outcome later down the road; so you must carefully plan your moves; much like a game of chess.

First, I don't think I can say enough praise about this game. I fell in love almost instantly with the concept, characters, setting, music, and even the 2.5d gameplay. 

Second, this game is HARD at the start. It took me until my 5th try to beat the game; almost 20 hrs in. This is not for people who get frustrated easily; as there's a lot of trial and error involved with your first few playthroughs; at least until you get the hang of how stuff works. There is no tutorial or walkthrough; they throw you right in the middle and you must learn to overcome any obstacles.

There's a very delicate balance of risk vs. reward, so as I said earlier you must plan each day out as best as possible so you don't waste time\resources going to places that won't benefit you the most. A lot of times you won't even be able to do a "recon" mission because you will be pressed to find food, medication, or materials so you can survive another night. 

During each day you must stay in your shelter and build equipment, upgrade your house, cook food, comfort other members, etc. There's plenty of stuff to keep you busy, and usually you will be pressed by time to finish any tasks before nightfall.

 At night you use the cover of darkness to travel to different areas of the city gathering supplies. Some will be abandoned; but most will still have occupants. Some will be neutral or even trade; but most will attack if provoked. Levels have multiple paths that you will need to navigate thru, using shovels to clear debris piles; or a saw to cut metal bars. Each action makes sound; so (for example) if you're trying to be sneaky, use a lockpick instead of a crowbar to open a door. 

It's also not wise to kill everyone you come accross; as this will send some members over the breaking point. and they will refuse to take orders; or they may just leave; making survival even tougher. In some situations, killing is inevitable; so you must be prepared for the concequences.

 The game does an excellent job at connecting the player with the characters; so when (not if) a member dies, you actually feel like you lost a friend. But, it's at this point you must press on; because sooner or later the war will end.

Game design is top notch. The music is fantastic, with a Metro2033 vibe that adds a lot to the mood. The interface is simply point\click, with icons highlighting interactive spots; very simple and easy to use. The level design helps with the mood as well, with excellent graphics detail of partially destroyed buildings; lighting, and the overall feel of a war-torn city. 

The main story even has randomn events and characters, so each playthrough is a little different. Once you've played the main story, there's also custom "stories" that you can either build from within the game, or dl via Steam Workshop; so there's many hours of play from this great game.

--Bottom Line--
Don't pass this up, the game has a little bit for everyone IMO. This proves that you don't need the latest 3D engine and hundreds of staff to make a good game. If you can look past the lack of tutorial\instruction, then this game will not disappoint.

The backstory to the game is fairly simple, you are a small group of people (Normally 3, but you can expand through the game.) who have survived the short amount of shellings in your area, you have grouped together to survive as long as possible, with no end in sight to the war. This game is an absolute treasure. I cannot even begin to imagine what it would be like to be involved in war as a civilian, but This War of Mine provides a wonderful start. In fact, since the only DLC is literally a donation to help children in war, it's probably the best DLC you'll ever purchase. It adds art to the game for free, since all the money you spend on it is a donation, which I assume you can continually buy if you want to donate more.

Of course, the gameplay can be incredibly challenging depending on who you start out with, and each civilian (you can make your own character, by the way) has their own skills, personality, and possibly an addiction. Every character has an autobiography that tells you what kind of life they lived before the war broke out. Each story is just as heartbreaking as the last, and it makes the whole experience that much more real.

Your household can grow if you allow new people to take shelter with your group, and it can shrink a whole lot faster while scavenging for supplies, illness, or attacks for robbers during the night. However, since you yourself can go to other houses that may or may not be empty, it's a painful revelation that you're just as bad as the people who attack your group. Your group realizes this no matter how stoic they are, but the more sensitive characters are particularly affected by this, just as it would be in real life. It can be so easy for some characters to become depressed, especially if they're doing something they feel uncomfortable doing.

The atmosphere for the game is absolutely spot-on, and the world is almost devoid of all colour, save for red and some orange for fire. The graphics are a blurred grey for the backgrounds, and it's reminiscent of a watercolour painting or charcoal drawing. There is a sombre theme established through the background music, but you are able to change that through a radio that you can craft during the day.

During the night, you scavenge or trade for food, water, and materials, but in the day you're cooped up inside for safety and, therefore, carry out basic needs. This would be the time to feed your group, heal them, console each other, or craft new objects out of materials to make your shelter a more liveable place. A radio can be crafted to hear about shortages, the weather, and of course, listen to music. Beds can be made for sleeping and recovering from injuries or illness. Weapons, animal traps, home security systems, tools, medicine cabinets, and other objects can be created to aid in survival, and deciding which one to build first is incredibly difficult.

Personally, I like to play this when I'm feeling depressed and can't see anything positively, because despite being a melancholy game about the horrors of war, I find it to also have hope for survival. Every time I play this, it makes me feel the same way: pensive. I feel as though I have realized something great - yet sad - about humanity. As strange as it sounds, focusing on survivng is incredibily helpful for me to take a step back, although I doubt everyone will feel this way.

Honestly, this is a wonderfully challenging game for fans of strategy, war, or crafting genres, and I could see it appealing to a much larger audience.

Too often in games I can be cold and very heartless. I relish being the 'bad guy' in a lot of games, often opting for the 'easy choice' of choosing the mentality of 'the needs of one, outweighs the needs of the many'. This War of Mine is in a word; Brilliant. It's art style is very monochromatic, dark and pencil drawn, something which compliments the game's overall feel and direction. The musical score works really well with certain types of situations and often helps set the mood of a wore torn country that had clearly seen better days.

But for me, while all of the details are important in the art style and music, the real impact this game has had on me is it's core mechanic; it's game play. 

Too often in modern games, players are not confronted with tough choices. When there are choices in games, they are often very clean and cut (do this and this will happen, don't and it won't - etc). I feel that because of this, players are not given the true consequences of their actions in games therefore making it much easier for players to turn 'bad' and reap the rewards. For me this is often why I went rogue. In This War of Mine, I simply cannot do it and when I have to, I feel terrible about it.

Taking charge of a group of three survivors in a worn torn city who have shacked up in a abandoned building, the player is immediately confronted with a wide selection of problems right from the offset. One of your group may be sick, hungry, sad or simply tired and it is up to you to provide the fulfillment of their most basic needs in order to keep them alive. Sure, you can scavenge for stuff in your own dwelling but the resources found there will only get you so far so you must find additional materials/food from other areas around the city. Venturing into the city gives you no promises and it thrusts you into situations that make you question your morality. An example can be that you have a sick friend back at your shelter and you have gone into a home that you know has an elderly couple inside, one of which is very ill. Do you take their medical supplies to save your friend and risk destroying the morale of your group (because you stole from people who truly needed the supplies), or do you leave them be and potentially lose your party member, which in turn could create the same amount of dismay within the group? Other examples can simply come from making a bad call, i.e. getting your scavenger into situations that they went prepared for and killed, not returning back to the safety of your 'home' in time before the sun came up, or choosing to take additional survivors into the group whom of which you couldn't really provide enough resources to cover their basic needs.

Because of the choices that you have to make and the knock-on results that they can bring, you pay the consequences or enjoy the rewards of your choices. Personally, it's refreshing to play a game that questions morality and adequately changes the gaming dynamic because of these calls.  

This War of Mine gave me that new challenge in the choices that I make in games. I no longer wish to be the bad guy and when I do it in this game, it's not without reason. 

I really recommend this game to players of fifteen years older or more.

Dear Devs: Excellent artwork, music, and mechanics, except for the one that is the most basic of them all, at which you utterly fail. What a waste. With proper time management mechanics, I would be engrossed in this game for months. Instead, I was engrossed in it for about 3 hours until I realized the gig was up, played a few more hours until my patience ran out and annoyance level peaked, and uninstalled.

I'd also like to say a bit about time management in night cycles, as this further highlights the complete brokenness of time management in This War of Mine. Upon your first visit to a location, you generally have more than enough time to completely loot every item and place all of your loot in a single cache, right by the entrance of the location. This means that you're not really pressed for time (not sure if time moves at the same rate at night, but even if it does, you rarely run into a time crunch at night) and upon subsequent visits to areas you've already full plundered and gathered all the loot by the entrance that you arrive at the location at 9 PM, loot a single cache, fill your pack, and leave the location by 9:10 PM.

In this scenario, you can't visit another location the same night, and the daytime travesty of time management just infuriates you even more. Also, it takes exactly one hour to travel to any location, regardless of how far away it is.

Night time should have been fleshed out way more, with varying travel times to make it to a location at the very least, as well as the ability to return home, and go back out. It makes no sense to limit us to one trip out at night, especially when the time spent at the location is typically only 10 minutes of the evening.

I'd much rather have to spend between 10 minutes and 2 hours to actually make it to a location, have to leave in enough time to account for return travel time, and be able to make additional trips out. This would add a whole new level of complexity and risk versus reward to night time, instead of it just being the "gimme" portion of the game's time management, while you spend more time during the day to walk up the stairs than it took you to do your overnight haul of goods.

This War of Mine is, in my opinion, the most important and most value for a game on Steam presently. The game is loosely inspired by the siege of Sarajevo from 1992-1996 during the Bosnian war. That being said, this is not a historical game. You will not learn anything about Bosnia, Herzegovnia, Yugoslavia, or Srpska in this game. If this was a historical representation of that war, it would be susceptible to many counter-claims of realism. People did not raid the homes of old people, you might say; the survivors of the conflict came together. People did not scavenge at night, it was too dangerous. So and so forth.
 
All of that is to miss the point. This game immerses the player in a cohesive framework that presents a compelling attitude toward war: that for non-combatants, war is wretched, a disruption to life that even among the survivors might not be recovered from. In a strange way, this makes the game all the more compelling as a game. Yes, you can get better at the game. You can learn to play the mechanics. You can scavenge more efficiently and perhaps if you play enough you will learn how to attack some of the belligerents hurting the civilians. I do not, however, think this game ever becomes a power fantasy, and that is precisely what makes it distinctive, exciting, and even important.  
 
This is a game that should be played, and perhaps the most important game on Steam right now.

This War of Mine tries, and arguably does a good job, to create a realistic take on what life is like for those that have to survive the war instead of 'merely' fighting in it.

The game puts the player in the role of one or more civilians stuck in a besieged city in which they're forced to survive until a peacekeeping force can intervene and break the blockade. Sounds easy right?

WRONG

You're not playing as some legendary war hero posse capable of breaking sieges, nor are you immune to the wear and tear of daily life. Hunger will kill you as surely as a kitchen knife in the ribs, and you won't miraculously shrug off shotgun fire after ducking behind a door for a couple of seconds.

No. You're playing as a rather diverse group of civilians, each with their own skills, moral code, beliefs and strengths and weaknesses. Some can carry a lot, others not so much. Some people will gladly knife some fool for a can of meat, others will sink into depression after stealing a bottle of water. And to top it off there's no easy "reload last save" button to bail you out of terrible choices. Go forward or start again.

Now, this might all sound well and good, but what does this game truly offer you might ask?

This War of Mine, boiled to its essence, is a survival simulator on a day/night cycled basis that focuses on resource management and moral choices. Each day you're stuck in your shelter doing daily tasks like building furniture, crafting tools, making meals or alcoholic beverages, handling visitors and the likes. At night comes the true test: do you venture out into the city proper and try and scavenge what you need to survive? Locations offer a whole variety of loot, events and choices. You might find a trader. or bandits without qualms about filling you full of lead. Maybe it's just an abandoned house full of stuff ripe for the taking instead?


For those that rather have bullet points about what might attract you or turn you off instead:

The Good:
-> Decisions carry weight. Killing, stealing, getting sick/wounded, helping people all have their good and bad results and oftentimes they feel meaningful, even if it's way down the line. That girl you saved from a collapsed building might show up a week later to reward you for your actions, or that stuff you stole from an aid drop might attract investigating soldiers...

-> Lots of choices to be made across the game. Raid every night? Live as looters? Be self-sufficient? Start a cigarette trading setup? Be the local booze dealer? You can succeed in many ways indeed.

-> Plenty of events, locations to scavenge and people to meet(Or murder). Many locations also offer multiple scenarios, so no playthrough is ever the same.

-> While kind of bugged right now, the game features workshop/mod support and can be customised to a reasonable degree at the moment.

-> It's easy to start caring for what your survivors do and get immersed in their plight.

The Love/Hate parts:

-> No save/load. Some applaud it(I do in this case) but it might turn you off. It does make your choices feel more rewarding/punishing though!

-> While there's a lot of replayability, once you've got the 'minmax super build order' memorized the game starts losing its challenge very fast, but if you start doing (self imposed or premade) challenges things might spike up again.

-> The combat/scavenging will be a love or hate relationship. Some feel it's good enough while others think it's way too gamey. AI standing before a hidey-hole wondering why you went up in smoke might get old fast.


The "Maybe skip on this" part:

-> Bugs. The game is buggy, and while the devs try/tried(Unsure if they're still actively trying to fix everything) to fix bugs there are still some pretty annoying ones left. E.G. if you're in Hotel-Bandit version, the game thinks you're in the Hotel-Friendlies version and believes you're stealing(Same with e.g. the Church and Apartments). 

-> Exploits are in the game. Sure, you can opt not to use them, but be forewarned. Katia approves of giving her two bottles of pills and a medkit for her two bottles of pills!

-> AI can be pretty terrible at times, failing to use doors, taking long routes around or occasionally getting x-ray sight.

-> Steep learning curve that once mastered makes the default game a cakewalk.

-> Game has lots of options but little variety. E.G. While the Construction Site has two versions that can trigger, those versions will ALWAYS have the same amount of enemies, the same events, etc.


In summary:
A glowing recommendation if you like immersive survival war-themed games with a bit of management sprinkled over it.
A cautious recommendation if you're a fan of just survival, just war-themed games or just immersive games.
A Big NO if you can't handle a tough start, bugs, a lack of save/load options, thinking ahead, handling consequences or human emotions.

This War of Mine is an anti-war game that knows that even serious games are in fact still games.

The good:
+Every playable character has their own backstory and abilities.
+The day/night cycle of upgrading your home during the day and raiding in the night is an extremely addicting gameplay loop.
+The music is fantastic and the sound design is quite atmospheric.
+The emotional moments are experienced through gameplay and can be avoided by skilled players.
+The many different scenarios change both the story and the difficulty.

The bad:
-Bandit raids become extremely tedious, which might be the point.
-In order to fully understand some characters abilities you need to read the wiki, personally I would never have guessed that the math teacher is better at using cage traps.
-The graphics are blurry and gloomy, which was probably done to sell the horrible situation, but I'm not sure I'm sold on the effect.
-There are a set number of areas to explore and once you know what happens at a certain area you can get through them much faster.
-The inventory system is limited to challenge you, but the it really needed a drop all function, the ability to use bandages, meds, etc. while scavenging, and it would also make more sense if you had a seperate equipment slot for the stuff in your hand, rather than it taking up space in your backpack.

Bottom line:
This War of Mine is a game that doesn't sacrifice game mechanics in order to make a point and it makes for a great merging of story and gameplay about the horrors of war.

This War of Mine is a game that attempts to replicate the difficulties of war. It's premise is designed around choosing a character and playing out the war in that characters shoes. As you progress, there will new characters available to choose from. Some characters comes with perks, such as one guy might be a fast runner while one guy may be a cook. When you first start off, you'll have three characters at your disposal. To move these characters, you simply click their face on the bottom right hand corner or click literally on them, then click where you want them to go. You can also tell them to double time it (sprint) if necessary. There will be actions available throughout the game. This may include cleaning up rubble, breaking down a garrisoned door, pick locking a door, opening/searching through cabinets or even fighting with other survivors. In your own house, you can build things from beds to stoves all the way to shovels to lock picks. 

Upgrading these work station will give you access to better weaponry. Upon ending your day, you will be prompted for further action. As you end the day, you will be asked whether you want to send someone to scavenge, allow someone to sleep or allow someone to guard the door. Just because you have a guard wandering the house doesn't mean you're completely fool proof. When selecting a person to scavenge, you may choose different areas of the city to check out. More locations will open up with their own unique challenges. For example, there is one area where there is a sniper watching over a location. If you don't take the appropriate steps (or cover), you will be shot dead or injured. When scavenging, it is wise to take the proper materials. Most of the time you will need a shovel with you and a few lock picks. Keep in mind though, not all scavengers can carry as much as the other so making use of space is really key. Sneaking around in someone's house does provide a challenge but is more of a waiting game than anything. Red markers that appear in circles will display the location of potential enemies (or even rodents making noise). 

Fighting is pretty basic and can turn into a gun or knife fight if the proper material is available. Some opponents are a lot stronger and tougher than others due to this fact. There is a bit of a thrill while raiding homes but can become redundant after doing it a hand full of times. The game is really minimal when it comes to being immersive in it's works. Meaning, you will be using the mouse a lot in this game and not much else. What provides the pleasure in playing is watching the characters act out what you've told them. 

The graphics are pretty good and the animations do their best to ensure every detail is nailed. When someone is breaking down a barrier to access another room VIA door, you will see material being broken off of the door as your character gets closer to breaking through. The sounds are actually not too bad and the sniper gunshots will initially shoot a shock down your spine. 

Although this game is seen extremely positive, I think it's an OK game. It's neither good nor bad, just there sort of thing. I am not recommending it as it's really not my cup of tea as I'm not a huge fan of point-and-click type things. I also found the game play lacking as they could have given the player more control in sneaking around, fighting or even shooting. There may be some cool RPG elements in it but it wasn't enough to keep me satisfied.

My own personal story:
I had a small group of survivors. We'd been fairly cohesive and effective for the first couple weeks of the war, then we got a new survivor to the group. She was badly hurt and sick but I felt this deep compassion after reading her story. She's barely escaped with her life when soldiers (Never learned if they were government or rebel soldiers) burnt her village and killed her family. I knew we needed to help her, so I sent Marco out to gather some medical supplies so we could nurse her wounds and treat her infections. 
Marco crept through an abandoned hospital to find our desperately needed supplies. There was a chance there would be soldiers but that was the only place left with medical supplies. Marco found the last of the supplies that were desperately needed. He made his way towards the exit when suddenly, a group of soldiers burst in from the way he came. Panicking, Marco sprinted towards the other exit as gunfire and curses were shot in his direction. The exit was within arms reach as two bullets lodged themselves in Marco's back. He collapsed dead on the floor.
I was in shock. This character, this person, I had grown attached to and heard their story was now gone, forever. I sat there and read as everyone in the group tried to come to grips with Marco's death. They cried the entire day, no one could be motivated to do anything, I cried with them. For a solid ten minutes I sat in front of my computer weeping over Marco, this friend I'd felt I'd known was lost. All the while the song from the soundtrack "We keep going" played in the background. 

I cannot recommend this game enough to people but be forewarned, this game will leave you feeling some of the deepest emotions a game has ever made you feel.

Each of the differeing playthroughs has entirely new aspects and storylines to reveal to the player, on one playthrough the hospital has been seriously bombed but is still barely running thanks to the kind doctor there and in another it could be the hideout for a ruthless band of heavily armed thugs, not only that but you have to deal with the changing weather as winter is just around the corner and sitting in a ruin freezing to death is currently not on your survivors wishlists for their future's.

Even taking all of that out of the picture each and every character has their own rich personality and backstory told gradually as the game progresses but not in its entirety, the game simply shows you quotes from the character like you were talking directly too them and their responses to varying events that have occured shows you their characters, the selfish ones who only want to help themselves to those believing that generosity and kindness are the only things that humanity needs, this game will play with your emotions from start to finish and is a must buy for anyone that is a fan of wartime simulator games.

So, I tried Fallout-what-ever-on-android-ios which was... well, let's be kind and say disappointing. Then I tried "This War of Mine". This game convinced me that it wasn't the gameplay or the genre that was at fault, it was just the execution of the two other games.

I'm about halfway through the first campaign. So far, I haven't had any real problems which is a bit disappointing. I was expecting the game to be difficult, at least to the point where I had to make some hard decissions. It might just be me, but it looks like the game is a bit more lenient that what the fans and the hype tells you. I have yet to be forced into combat, except for a few nightly raids, which are rather easy to handle, food is reasonably easy to get. The only annoying thing is parts -- you need parts for everything and there aren't enough of them. You can get by rather easily without them, but you need them to make waterfilters to get water (even when melting snow) and that's pretty much the biggest drain you'll have. You can get water from other places and, in the end, you can do without it if you have to. 

The attention to detail, regarding needs in wartime, is, to my humble knowledge, pretty good -- you need to manage fatigue, hunger, physical wounds, illness and mental health. All things I would assume are crucial in a warzone (having never been to one, I don't know if anything else should be present, so I won't comment further on that). On top of that you also need to manage an inventory of goods, including food (obviously), water, various materials, weapons, tools, tobacco and alcohol, as well as medical supplies. How you spend your resources also determines how you aquire resources; you can make yourself independent of food resources by making traps and growing your own vegetables -- once you've built and upgraded everything, you don't need anything besides water, which you can do without if you must, and firewood for the winter -- which you will have passed once you have build everything anway.

All in all, get the game. It's pretty good.

If you're the kind of person who likes £3-20 indie games and rarely spends £40+ on a big budget blockbuster, then [u]buy this game[/u]. If you are that kind of gamer, and I have absolutely nothing against you if you are, then I whole heartedly recommend This War of Mine and am confident that it will be one of the best games you have played recently.

However, if you're used to big name games and have a lot of experience with strategy/management/base building/economic games then, like me, you will probably find TWoM somewhat underwhelming, often frustrating and all too predictable. The first 15minutes seemed brimming with potential, but after about half an hour I realised that I'd seen and done this all before and there wasn't anything new on offer.

Most of the game is spent staring at the screen, listening to your characters complain that they're hungry or tired or don't feel well or don't have [tool] or wish they still had basic luxuries. A lot of people seemed to find this endearing and heartbreaking, but for me it quickly got annoying. You're in a war zone! I don't care if you'd sleep better if I built you a real bed; suck it up! Between the waiting around, it's fairly repetitive. You spend the day building things with materials you found during the night. That's basically it. If you use all your materials, you can skip forward to the night section, but risk missing out on traders or other survivors visiting you if you do.

The night time looting really should have been the highlight of this game, and in many ways it is, but some odd design choices spoil the fun. For a game which prides itself on generating a more realistic wartime experience, I found the fact that a cigarette apparently uses as much backpack space as two planks of wood slightly confusing. TWoM uses the classic 'box inventory' system, where individual items have their own inventory space and stack to a limited number when you pick up an item of the same type. This works for some games, but because of the variety of items you can find, TWoM should probably have gone with a weight system instead - the frustration of having to decide between a single pouch of tobacco or ten bottles of water because I didn't want to drop four vegetables very quickly wore thin.

Add to this, that you can only visit ONE place, ONCE, PER NIGHT, even if you only spent an hour looting and still have six hours of darkness, and the whole looting process becomes exacerbating. Especially when you then have to sit around listening to your guys moaning all day, even though their problems would be solved if they could bothered to loot a place twice in an evening.
 
For a low budget indie game, TWoM is fantastic. This goes doubly so if you're impressed by 2D games with pencil effect shading, and triply so if you've never spent more than £20 on a game. I don't mean that in a derisory way, I'm just trying to manage expectations.

However, I found it to be overall repetitive, frustrating and, ultimately, not nearly as original as it likes to think it is. Experienced gamers will be able to predict most aspects of this game without requiring a lengthy play through. If you want a really gruelling resource management/suspense & strategy/tough decisions game experience then I’d recommend XCOM on a harder difficulty and/or with the Long War mod over this.

This game is amazing. It took me a few play throughs to really be hit by it but this last one shook me. Let me explain my story without spoiling anything. 

The first several days were going well. The three of us, Arica, Roman, and Bruno,  were scavenging supplies, defending, and resting while upgrading the base. We were lucky enough to have friendly neighbors that would bring over supplies.  When tragedy struck them, we were more than happy to help. 

After sometime, a lonely man, Marko, came to our home begging to join us. Since our home was well established, we welcomed him in. Right about the time our newest member was starting to fit it, tragedy struck and Marko was ripped from our lives. At the same time, supplies were getting harder to come by and we resulted to actions we never thought possible. While it shook us, we were still surviving. 

Everything was going fairly well until winter came.  The first couple of days were fine, but how were we to know the toll winter would have on us? We even relucantly welcomed, Cveta, to our band of survivors. Out of desperation, supplies were being gathered at whatever cost. This is how we lost Roman.  We didn't even have time to mourn Roman when Arica failed to come back.

What was once a solid group of survivors was boiled down to two, Bruno and Cveta. Unfortunately, do to the weather, recent tragedies, and lack of supplies, Cveta became gravely ill. Our neighbors were also struck by tragedy but we were unable to offer them assistance this time. Desperately, we hung to the radio listening for when the winter would end and possibly even the war. Nothing useful was ever heard. 

For days, the cycle continued. No news on the war or winter, Cveta crept closer to death, while Bruno tried desperately to find supplies that were only to be stolen the next night. We even traded away all of our valuables to limp on another day. What's the point of having a gun with no bullets? How long could we go on like this? How have we even survived the last few days in this death cycle?
 
Finally, finally, a reprieve; winter has ended. Bruno had found some medicine and was slowly nursing Cveta back from near death. We were going to make it! All that was needed was for this war to end. It has been so long, how can it possibly continue? Haven't enough died? What was gained? Still, the radio mocked us by providing no useful information.

This hit Bruno hardest of all, he became paralyzed by depression. To the point that Cveta, while still seriously ill, went out for supplies just to keep us going. What other choice did she have? We were still sick, wounded and slowly starving to death. 

Cveta came home late, her injuries made the scavenging very challenging and lengthy. Overall, the haul was ok, but we still needed so much.  Out of all the times I thought we wouldn't make it, this day was the start of a new hope that was squashed before it began. Bruno was gone. The brutality of this hell was too much for Bruno and he gave into the thoughts we tried desperately to suppress. Cveta was devastated. Not only had she risked everything so we could survive, but her sickness had worsened. Reluctantly, Cveta stayed home for the night and never woke up in the morning.

People will suffer and they will die. Others will survive but may not have happy lives afterward. And some will manage to find peace in the end and go on. This is a game everyone should play and experience.

[b][u]Game Information[/u][/b]

"This War of Mine" is a Indie game. The game was developed and published by 11 bit Studios.

[b][u]The Game Review[/u][/b]

Game Visuals

I want to mention that the visuals in the game are well done. The visuals can be adjusted in the game's option menu.

Game Audio

I want to mention that audio for the game is well done. Even though the audio is somewhat simplistic and repetitive. The audio can be adjusted in the game's option menu as well.

Gameplay

'This War of Mine' places the players in a position that they never thought to find themselves in.

'In war, not everyone is a soldier;' a civilian in a war worn country.

This game simulates what it is like to be a civilian trapped in a war worn country. Survival becomes very critical because there is unfathomable danger lurking at every corner. Everyday resources have become a prized possession because the country has been cut off from the outside. The crimes run rampant as rule of law becomes null and void.

There are plenty of pre-generated scenarios for the player to choose from. They can also create their own scenarios and share them with other players.

Morality is heavily presented in the game. Freewill to choose to be a good person and help out other civilians or be a bad person and not help out other civilians. The choices that the player makes have side effects on the civilian.

There are multiple endings for this game. These multiple endings depend upon the choices that the player made throughout the game.

There is downloadable content for this game: 'War Child Charity.' This DLC features various graffiti art from their artists. These artworks are found throughout the game. They reflect the nature of what is happening in the war worn country.

(Please note that this DLC has different pricing. The purchase of this DLC goes to the charity.)

There are twenty-two different achievements that can be unlocked from playing the game. Each of these achievements does come with some requirements that need to be completed before they can be unlocked.

Miscellaneous

There are six different trading cards to collect. Only three of those trading cards are given out by the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam's Community Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and its' Booster Pack Creator.

Final thoughts: I have found the game enjoyable to a certain extent. The replay value for the game is high. I would recommend this game, but not at the game's full price value.

This game is one of the best experiences I've had as a player in my entire life.
I am more fond of survival games than most, but that is irrelevant. It cannot be denied that This War of Mine's depressive setting, heart-felt music and slow-paced while intense gameplay deserve a place among the best of these last years.
It is remarkably original, primarily for dealing with the topic of war, an over-exploited matter when it comes to PC gaming. And yet this is a completely different scenario, for you are not just facing a complicated situation, nor trying to solve a problem through fighting. There is a lot more depth to it, as you first acknowledge when you start the game, encountering a set of characters that will accompany you through your initial (and probably rather dramatic) attempt to survive the cruelty of war.
But there is nothing more charming than a game that gets you to see the enchanting and devastating nature of human error, and that is something This War of Mine excels at doing. It is an unforgettable experience, and one that changes your perspective on bellic intervention, on the sufferings of the people that are at this precise moment affected by them, and, above all, on your own power to change things for the better.
That is why I consider this game more than just a source of cheap entertainment, but a message that was put into the world in the most brilliant manner. 
Above all, if you decide to give it a chance, I hope it makes you have as many good, stressful, sad and intense moments as it did for me, so that you can understand and learn as much of this game as I was lucky to do through my 53 hours of playing (and counting).

I don't like jumping on the hype wagon, but this is such a good game in more ways than one, that I felt it deserved the praise. It simultaneously manages to be engrossing and entertaining, yet also exhausting and emotionally draining. It is both a conventional game with enjoyable gameplay, but also makes use of the interactive potential of games to put players in the shoes of another person, in this case, a civilian trying to survive in an urban warzone. It has a valuable message about the reality of war that is neither preachy nor heavy-handed, showing rather than telling and letting it emerge naturally from the gameplay. It also focuses on the mental and emotional toll of war rather than focusing on the carnage.

There is a lot of debate about whether games are "art" or not. I believe they can be, but often fall short of that mark. This War of Mine is a glowing example of how a game can be a work of art, with the potential to make the world just a little bit better.

I suppose like most stories it started on day 1, and like a number of stories amnesia defines day 1. Being hit by some heavy debris during a shelling that wrecked what appears to have been a multiple story building for a large family, surrounded by a crew of four soft caramel chews. They apparently had got the memo that I was a hard piece of candy, and pledged loyalty to me immediately, as long as I saw them through the mess that was This War of Ours.

Allow me to describe this crew of motley.

There's my workhorse, Bruno. This guy was a grump through and through, would complain all the time, and never stopped bumming smokes. Still he was the most competent individual in that he never seemed to waste any fuel when cooking much of anything. He's the only one who knew how to measure anything, giving you an idea of what I was working with. He was the only one I trusted with establishing our little cartel, because he was the only one I could count on to do the job right.

There's the looks, Katia. She's a pretty thing, who people always want to do favors for. She ran the front desk, handled the interactions with people when a smile, wink, handshake and hug were needed. She wasn't a bad scavenger either, but there's a bit of reluctance to ask such beauty to go picking through rubble and god-knows-what, especially when numerous unsavory characters are about.

Especially when there's Pavle. He's a real night owl. He was sick from the beginning to the end, but it seems I'm the only one who pegged him as a hypochondriac. Somehow when he didn't get his dose of 'medicine' regularly enough, he'd start showing symptoms. I let him sleep all day, at first because of his shakes, but later because he's the guy to send out at night to find and steal all the treasures that have been left behind locked doors and saw-busting grates. This guy moved like a man with purpose. He'd kill if it comes to that, but he won't like it; can't blame him for that, and besides too much killing is bad for business.

Finally, there's, darling Cveta. She filled in a lot of the gaps that would develop. Most of her work was to take work from Bruno when his hands were full, keeping the water flowing, rolling a few not-too-fat ones to be sold, baiting traps, putting another log on the fire,  being another watch as guard, stuff that's hard to mess up. She did have a unique skill in that if someone was bumming the group out too much, she could always make them smile. It's always good to have that around.

We started out small, just wanted to barter a bit, were tired of being hungry and unable to defend ourselves. Cigarettes ran low in the city, addicts never could pace themselves, and so we started bootlegging them. There were no police.  We got a bit of excess capital around, got a taste for the lifestyle, saw our morals slip, started bootlegging high proof alcohol, sold it tax-free. After a while we got even bolder, started making home made bandages, and passed them off as the real thing, though we never got any complaints about them. Eventually we were putting anything that looked like it had an active ingredient, into fresh new pills and selling it as Grade-A pharmaceuticals. There's no guarantee, your mileage may vary.

Mostly we traded with a hood who would come by our door every few days. Always seemed to have a lot of scrap, still don't know where he kept finding it. We admired his resourcefulness, and never asked a question. There were a few other people here and there, looking for parts, weapons, tools, or whatever was still worth half a damn. When Pavle rubbed out our competition we were the best equipped militia in town. Assault rifles, kevlar, medical supplies, state-of-the-ghetto facilities. We went where we wanted and took what we desired. We could make most of it ourselves when we had the gumption.

We always had a mind toward the community though. Helped out our neighbors, helped out the hospital, never killed no one who didn't deserve it, and never took nothing we didn't plan on paying back.

Then the war ended. The newly galvanized crew, they wanted to go back to their lives, friends, and families, have real jobs. They weren't criminals, they didn't want to go up against police, dodge investigations, deal with rivalries. They weren't interested in the power, excitement, or debauchery, had no need for colorful knives and expensive masks. I'd helped them survive the tough times, when that time passed, they wanted to forget what I tought them, forget the kind of person I was. They wanted to forget the kind of person I needed them to become for that short while.

All four people abandoned me shortly after and we haven't interacted since. There's no regret or shame on my end towards them, and I understand why. Friendship was never the objective; I kept them alive.

This is a graphic-lite resource management sim where you walk the tightrope of bare subsistence over the pit of starvation. The protagonists (that you control) consume resources, while you task them with building enough of a surplus that one raid won't leave you all dead.

Some games suffer from obtuse rules or too much RNG. In This War of Mine, the rules are upfront, the RNG is only as crippling as you are impatient, while the randomly-generated locations allow for replayability and starting over without mindless grinding and memorization. Further, you get to control the actions of the people you send scavenging, giving you a sense of ownership superior to a roll of the dice.

Overall the game has great atmosphere, artwork, and gameplay elements. This War of Mine could be improved by voice-acting for all the characters to compliment the speach-bubbles. Further, the game will be a smoother ride if you the player are a fast/comprehensive reader, becuase there are helpful gameplay clues and cues that all come in the form of text. My last gripe is about how slow characters move. It does give a sense of gravity and immersion, but during the day-cycle where you are fortifying and working within your stronghold, it can also be cumbersome if you placed two related items far apart from one another. 

Despite the caveats above, I am very much enjoying this game for doing an excellent job of everything it means for itself to be: an oppressive resource-management story-telling war-time sim selling itself on visual and audio atmosphere.

[h1]A unique look at war, not as a combatant, but as a bystander caught in one. Thought-provoking, challenging, and brutally difficult as it makes you ask important questions about war and one's attitudes towards it, not just in videogame form, but in general.[/h1]

+ Dark and gritty art direction done right, without said gritty feel getting in the way of showing important information to the player.
+ Simple, mouse-based controls makes this a pick-up-and-play game that works for everyone.
+ Solid survival mechanics means that one's decisions mean the difference of surviving, or losing.
+ Losses are meaningful no matter what, or who, they are.
+ Goes above and beyond being a videogame by being a focused lens looking at the effects of armed conflict upon civilian populations, away from being an instigator or participant, but by being someone caught in one.

- Limited fidelity options as well as the rigid camera on top of the dark and gritty art direction view may make this one of the more difficult games to get through visually.
- Mouse-driven completely. Limited hotkey support as well as alternative controls.
- Very difficult.
- Losses can be very punishing, even game-ending for seemingly simple losses that have knock-on effects down the line. Games can be lost long before the player finds out.
- May be a touch heavy-handed in delivery of its message, and the game's focus may not be to the liking of some.

This game goes right in them feels.

A depressing, heart-wrenching reminder of what man is capable of doing to his fellow man in times of utmost necessity.

Would you stick by your principles and morals whilst all around you abandoned theirs? Would you refuse to steal, or to kill? Would you stand by your guns and remain steadfast in your morality, your [i]humanity[/i], even whilst your family are freezing; starving; dying of disease? 

Many wouldn't.

I didn't.

And that, I believe, is the true value of this game. It made me think, a lot more than any other game I've recently played. It made me sit down and think about what I was doing, and why I was doing it.

And it made me realise something:

These characters, these [i]people[/i] represented by pixels on a screen, could be any one of us, given all the wrong circumstances. 

With that knowledge also comes the understanding that, at some point in time, in some oft-forgotten conflict, a real human being decided they had no choice but to do exactly what you just did.

That broke me, personally, for a while.

It's depressing, it's soul-crushing, and yet it's somehow still so compelling.

It's us, as a species, trying to survive the torture that we create for ourselves.

War is hell.
