This War of Mine is an excellent concept buried under a plethora of bad gameplay elements. 

I'll start right off the bat with my first "nitpick," which I've put in quotation marks because of just how bad this concept is: Every single character, regardless of background, upbringing, etc. has the skills and the knowledge required to build complicated appliances that, more often than not, at least require a few weeks, if not months of training in order to even learn how to MAINTAIN. It's a huge stretch to say that a single person studying music understands how to distill moonshine, build an oven, and construct firearms. They do all of this perfectly; the guns themselves don't have any individual stats, unlike Rimworld (a game which I find quite similar in terms of having colonists/survivors that all work in tandem to survive in a harsh environment), which features pawns who are oftentimes only good at a few things but are able to learn new skills as they develop.

This game is long enough to have developing skills and could have at least had a system where people learn how to build more complex things with experience, for example after building X amount of furniture. It's not a perfect system, but it makes more sense than having a news reporter essentially do the same level and quality of work that an HVAC technician can do.

This isn't even the main problem with the game. The biggest problem is that the gameplay is EXTREMELY unpolished. Combat feels terrible and clunky and is very hard to learn given how rare it is in this game, and getting into a fight is VERY punishing if you do not kill your target instantly. A lot of the combat mechanics like cover, hiding, etc. completely fall apart when you are fighting more than one opponent, as most of the time you will be overpowered very easily. Furthermore, NPC aggression is also quite stupid in this game. NPCs will more often than not get angry at you for running towards them or getting too close, but by the time they give you their warning dialogue they will likely turn hostile and try to kill you. It's just stupid and makes this game feel way more unpolished than a game this simple should be. If it weren't for the bad combat and the janky controls (because believe me, this game feels really jank even outside of combat), I would have likely recommended this..

Part two of the gameplay issue features my second critique: The game is way too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ easy. It's the same thing every time. Houses barely differ if at all (I never noticed them being different), you usually get enough resources to make every single station besides the garden, herb bench, and the distillery (these three are barely helpful by the way), and the way the game scales is very anticlimactic. More often than not the game will get progressively harder but then take a huge nosedive in difficulty in the last 10 days. I find this game so easy that I often spend most days making my guys eat food and then sleeping because of how overly abundant most resources are. Of course, it depends on how much risk you're willing to take, but more often than not you can easily win most fights simply by shooting bandits with the shotgun.

The game's scaling is off and it's very hard to actually find yourself in a desperate situation in this game, mostly because it's very easy to bail yourself out of most situations. Sure, stealing is wrong, I get that, but it's often too easy to do (in some areas) and the rewards far exceed the punishment. If I were the devs I'd make the final few days REALLY hard, just as a "final push." Most of my experiences had the final few days be very easy which is very underwhelming and BORING to play through.

That's the main problem this game has. It's not challenging and it doesn't respect your time very well, nor does it allow you to do anything interesting with the micro system this game has. Queuing up tasks or creating bills for your characters to do would make this game far more interesting and dynamic. Unfortunately a lot of the time spent in the house will involve you sitting there and watching. This is the same for items like the shovel. Most of the time you won't need it. Most of the time when you see bars or a locked door it will do nothing but create a sticky note in your head that reminds you to check it out later. All the impediments in this game just serve to slow you down or delay you, thus wasting your time. It doesn't provide a challenge. There's no RISK in making lockpicks, saws, etc. because the resources to make them are cheap and found practically everywhere. There's no reason to invest all your resources into anything other than basic weapons (the assault rifle is horrible and the shotgun is the best weapon in the game), reliably ways of acquiring food, and medicine to heal your units. All of the advanced stuff really doesn't do anything when all it takes to guard your home is a handgun and a few bullets which you will find everywhere.

Killing people is way too easy in this game and most gunfights make no sense. Somebody shot at my unit 10 times and they were only "wounded." I'm pretty sure if I shot someone 10 times they'd either be dead or on the brink of death. Meanwhile I can kill people instantly with a single bullet using a pump action shotgun.

I don't have anything to say about the design of this game other than it's beautiful. Artstyle is cool, I like the polaroid style for the characters, and I love the music and the themes behind this game. It aged very well for me given that I appreciate the mature and realistic themes far more, it's just that the gameplay really hurts this game.

This game still holds a tiny place in my tiny heart because I like the themes and concept behind the game. The core gameplay is good but it needs so much work. I wish it was a lot harder or had difficulty settings. I want to STRUGGLE to survive, and I want the last few days of the game to feel like a huge desperate push where I must do everything in my power to see it through. Instead my colonists are living better than I am in my luxury apartment on the East Coast. This War of Mine is one of the most emotional, grim games I've ever played. There were many moments in this game where I felt absolutley terrible for the things I had to do to survive. WARNING: this is not a happy game in any stretch of the imagination. This is a game about war, and war is hell. Sure there are a couple mildly happy moments in the game, but overhall it's very grim. This War of Mine is a game based on the Seige of Sarajevo that lasted 1,425 days and it is known to be the largest seige of a city in history. You play as a group of civilians trying to survive in a fictional beseiged city called Pogoren. You must deal with starvation, lack of medical supplies, scavangers trying to raid your supplies, and the emotional state of the survivors.

  One of the best things about this game is the fact that I couldn't reload a previous save to undo a horrible thing I've done, the game only auto saves after every night of scavenging and override's the previous save. This makes it more emmotionally gripping and nail-biting since it makes my decisions perminant and that it made me try even harder to not die. And it's not easy, trust me. There are multiple points in the game where I had little resources and my survivors were either starving, depressed, exausted, freezing, or all of the above. All of the abbandoned buildings were either stripped clean of supplies or didn't have the resources that the survivors needed to, well, survive.  There were only 2 options: raid another shelter for supplies or die. I had to rob and/or kill (mostly) innocents for their supplies in order to survive. It's not a walk in the park either, it will be emotionally heavy for both the player (unless they're a psychopath or a sociopath) and their survivors. The one who got to raid and kill the innocents for food and supplies will suffer from severe psychological trauma. And the player will have to deal with that.

   And due to the trend I've seen when people who review this game tell a story from their experience from the game, I'm going to do that too. 
There was one day where my survivors were starving, some wounded and/or exausted. They had little resources, their options were limited. They had no choice but to attack another Shelter full of people. Marko, an expert scavenger, couldn't go because he was emmotionally broken from all the people he had to kill in order to survive. Bruno seemed to be the only one capable to go and steal from another shelter, so he was sent to steal supplies from another shelter while Pavle was to gaurd the shelter from looters during the night. When Bruno reached the place, he looked through the peephole and saw a gaurd. He waited when the gaurd wasn't looking. Bruno then equiped his knife and then stabbed the gaurd in the back. This didn't insta-kill him though, so Bruno had to stab him a second time. Bruno then looted the gaurd's corpse and found a shotgun with some ammo. This caused some noise however, and caused a woman to come down from the stairs. The woman was crying out: "Oh god! Herald, no! No, this can't be happening!" and sat down next to the dead gaurd while sobbing. Bruno couldn't think striaght, he thought it was best to shoot the woman and put her out of her misery. The gunshot alerted two gaurds nearby, they came down and saw the two dead bodies of their comarads. They yelled out "Murderer!" to Bruno and tried to kill him. Bruno killed the two soldiers but was severely wounded. As he looted their corpses as well as the nearby area with no gaurds, he was soaking in the fact that he just murdered innocent people for food. 
I felt like crap after doing that, there are many moments like these that the player will encounter during their playthrough. It's depressing but in a good way, if that makes any sense. 

But the game isn't perfect, the survivors will sometimes say obvious things like "this shovel is doing well." while they're  digging it. And the controls can be annoying at times, I've accidentally closed doors when I was trying to get through them multiple times in the game.  It runs pretty smoothly on my pc, and I haven't noticed any bugs sp far. 

But the game's flaws hardly take away from the experience. This is by far my game of the year. I give This War of Mine a 10/10. I highly recomend it if you're sick of war games from the point of view from a soldiers perspective and glorifying violence.

This War of Mine is an excellent survival game that shows off a different aspect of war. You are not a health-regenerating god with the skill to shoot enemies in the head with a pistol from 100m away. No. You control a group of survivors that are facing the hardships of war: having to scavenge for supplies, fend off bandits, beat the chill of the winter, etc. And trust me, it is HARD!

The controls are simple: click here to walk, click there to search through some trash, click on that guy to punch them, etc. And it is well done too as I never felt like that controls were inadequate or dodgy, so props to the developers on that one. The gameplay is simple too (there seems to be no tutorial, but after 5mins of playing you will surely figure out what you're doing): build up your base with furniture, create weapons, manage your survivors health and hunger, trade with other survivors that approach your shelter, and more, throughout the day. When night comes around, you get to decide who sleeps, who guards (or have no one guard, which is risky due to the possibility of being raided), and who goes out on a scavenging run (e.g. search an abandoned house for materials, or go all out into a military outpost looking for food or medical supplies).

The soft pencil aesthetic is very pleasing too over the top of the 2.5D look of the game. The music and sounds are all well-done too, although the variety of music on the radio is limited (probably due to the war, which is justifiable). The different characters you meet along the way all have their own bio, which changes depending on how they're feeling (e.g. if they have just killed 3 people on the last-night's raid, they may be feeling quite depressed about it). Because of all these factors and the fact that the war could last only 30 days or over 40 days, the potential for replayibility is high.

If you're interested in seeing the side of war that most modern-military shooters don't often portray these days and want to play a rather difficult survival/management game, then definitely pick up This War of Mine. It is truly brilliant!

Enjoy! :D

This War of Mine is an emotionally distressing experience every gamer must play at some point in their lives. Though stylized and simplistic on the surface, it pulls no punches in its gut-wrenchingly realistic depiction of survival amid the unforgiving chaos of war. Inspired by the personal account of a survivor of the 90's Balkan War told on a survivalist forum, the development team clearly did their source material justice. "The War is Over." That's the phrase that pops up when you survive the war, and frankly after playing this game that's all the satisfaction you will ever need. 

This game is indie. It's not funny, it's not known for its fighting mechanics, but it sends a message that can be summed up in three words "war is bad." But of course we already know that right? 9 out of 10 people you ask will probably say that war is bad. They might say support our troops, let the conflict in the middle east end, or hold a moment of silence as a sign of respect. But talk is cheap, actions are what define a person. 

By actions are what define a person I am not suggesting a call to action that every single one of us quit our dayjobs or schooling to go rally and achieve world peace. What I am asking is that you experience a very accurate simulation of what war is truly like, because after this game trust me, you will have a whole new understanding of what war is. Playing this game won't suddenly make you relate to the horrors that the REAL victims of war have seen. But it will make you feel like a human being and if you do it right, you will get some strong emotions in the mix too.

If you do get this game, I suggest you try to play it as realistically as possible and as humanly as possible. What I mean by that is that you keep in your mind that these are real people you are controlling, because eventually there will come a point in the game where you will simply forget that. Everytime your character helps someone, you will feel happy. Everytime you turn away a neighbor asking for help you will feel bad. You will see things in the game that you are powerless to stop. Your morals will be questioned all the way until you either survive or perish. Will you steal from an elderly couple? Will you stand up from those who are being abused even if it means putting yourself in danger? Will you barter with the very people who are responsible for raping, looting, and taking advantage of ordinary citizens like you? You won't know who you really are until you play this game, until you realize that the game is sad for a reason, until you realize that all of the things that happen in this game could and have happened to other people in real life.

You know war is bad. Now experience it for yourself.

TL:DR I was feeling inspired and emotional. War is bad. Get this game if you have a heart and want to learn at the same time that you have some fun. :)

I feel like this is somewhat of a sleeper game that flew under the radar for a lot of people and for that reason I am writing a review. This War of Mine puts you in the shoes of a civilian with one simple goal: survive! You and a few survivors (usually between three and five from a roster of about ten or twelve) are put in a house and need to do whatever you can to survive. During the day you can scavenge around your house or build upgardes such as weapons, stove, animal traps, rain catchers, beds and even a guitar. 
During the night time you must pick one person to venture out into one of the locations where supplies must be scavenged. Early in the game you only need a lockpick or two to search for cigarettes, food, and building supplies. Yet as you start to exhuast supplies you must venture into areas where other people are living, usually armed and dangerous. It becomes a balancing act by ensuring the survival of your group and trying to navigate the tough moral implications of you stealing supplies from other or in extreme situations killing them.
It is a tough game and you must be prepared for members of your group to suffer quite a bit as the strain of trying to live in a warzone takes its toll. It is a visceral and somewhat brutal take on a facet of war that is seldom explored. It is definitely worth a try to see if you can last in This War of Mine.

I will make this review as short as possible, with as little spoilers as possible. 

This is one of the greatest games I have ever played and it is one I hope is expanded upon with either DLC, content patches or sequels. 

This War of Mine is deceptively simplistic to play, yet under the hood is a very detailed, deep and moving game about the horrific consequences of war. The hand drawn look of the game, creates a bleak looking visual interpretation of a war torn world where colour is devoid, as is the love for life for the protagonists. The player is set to make countless life or death decisions for a handful of people who need to be guided through a month or two of what seems to be a civil war in a fictional Eastern Europe style city.  

I don't normally play platform type games, especially ones that look like Snakes and Ladders but after only an hour or two of playing - I found my decision to purchase the game was completely worth while.

You can play this game quite easily with just the mouse and it is easy to pick up and play. It took me about 16 hours to finish the game and did so without any guides or cheats, nor did I watch any "Lets Play's" on YouTube, and in itself made the experience even more rewarding. 

The story while not so deep (ie not very story rich) is still very moving, and one can easily become attached to the people you will be controlling.

The game on occasion reminded me of SIMS, in which you control a persons needs and had a small resemblence to tower defense games or something along the lines of Civilisation where you build, upgrade and defend a base.

While playing the game, I did not encounter any bugs or crashes and the only issue I met was in terms of game play mechanics. I found that I really did not need to upgrade many househole items and instead I decided to hoard materials to trade for food or save stacks of items I could burn, ready for when winter came along.

The game could have lasted longer and had more story - and thus would have required me upgrading certain aspects of my base - but alas I did not need to as the game did not demand it. The game could have had a DLC with different story lines, such as maybe an alien invasion or a zombie apocalypse and of course I would not rule it out happening in the future, and I will be keenly watching an eye on developer news. This is a testament to the game's success, as I rarely keep an eye on specific developer releases once I have finished a game.

At the end of the day, this was a very addictive game - and easy to pick up and play. I was left with a bittersweet feeling when the game ended for me after 46 days. I was happy that I managed to *win* the game on my first try - but I was quite sad because my daily dose of war was over; Quite ironic if you think of it.

I look forward to more games from this developer and hopefully an expansion to this game. I also think if this game allowed mods via the Steam workshop - the games content could be expanded by it's own players giving this game a much longer shelf time.

I give this game a solid A+ or a 9/10. If you are unsure as to whether to purchase this game or not, trust me that you will not be disappointed.

This game is ridiculously addictive, which is strange given the rather dark nature of it. From the simple crafting system to the tense scavenging sections, every game mechanic has been well designed and implemented. There's a somewhat Sims-like survivor needs management - they need to eat and sleep, as well as rest to recover from injuries. You also need to make sure they don't get depressed from the harsh lifestyle that has been thrust upon them. Thankfully it's not too difficult to manage these needs - you just have to make sure you've got the right supplies, whether it be from trading, helping your neighbours out, or scavenging.

Scavenging is where This War of Mine really shines. You pick one of your survivors to go out into any one of up to around a dozen areas of the city, from abandoned homes to bandit hideouts and even a military base. From there, you look for supplies, often whilst avoiding certain undesirable citizens. Each area has an element of procedural generation to it - the overall landscape will be largely the same, but the supplies and inhabitants will differ between playthroughs. When you're out there hunting for supplies, you need to always be on your toes - hide, peek through holes in doorways, make as little noise as possible, and so on - until you can ensure your own safety. It makes for some incredibly tense moments, especially when an armed thug catches you.

Combat's not easy, and odds are you'll die very quickly, so it's best to play it safe and run like hell as soon as someone tries to attack you. This is probably my only complaint with the game, but you're not playing as a group of elite soldiers - these are random civilians brought together (and driven apart) by their need to survive. It's realistic, but can be frustrating at times.

This War of Mine is a great game. The scavenging is tense, and the backstories for the survivors are well-written. Sometimes there's not much to do during the day, but that's mostly down to how you manage your survivors and what supplies you aim to scavenge. The developers have been doing a fantastic job of updating the game since release - you can now choose your group of survivors when you start a new game, and they even added a second hideout for free! I'm sure they'll add more, and honestly wouldn't mind a paid expansion at some point. I strongly recommend This War of Mine to just about anyone - it's an absolute must-play in my opinion.

Before I get into the details of this game, I would like to point out a few key things. You may or may not agree with me, but I will express my opinion on a few issues; you are entitled to your own. - FYI: Final Score is at the end -

First, with the advent of 3D Shooter games and the phenomenal success of names such as Call of Duty and Halo, we as a culture have been led to believe that war is a glorified game, that there are black and white rights and wrongs and that the only lives that matter are our own. When I speak of the culture, I speak for the entire global gaming culture, not just the Americans, Europeans, Asians, etc. 

This is simply not the case. War affects everyone, mostly in a negative way. Can we as humans totally avoid war? No, unfortunately. But we can seek to minimize the negative effects it has on the innocent and the civilian population, as well as supporting our soldiers. Let me be clear, I do not condemn soldiers for serving their respective nations' interests and doing their duty; I condemn war itself as an ugly, sometimes necessary evil to be avoided wherever plausible.

To return to the first point, popular FPS games have de-sensitized the culture to violence, especially violence against the innocent. This is why This War of Mine is absolutely phenomenal. It is more than just a game; it is a drama, a moral statement and a scream to draw people's attention to the horrors that victims in war-torn countries are facing every day. What's even better is that War Child, a charity that the developer 11bit Studios is teamed with, receives proceeds from every purchase of This War of Mine to help people in war-torn countries improve their lives. There's also a link directly to the War Child donation page on the game's main menu, should you decide to take action.

I digress. Now for the part of this review that explains why this game is actually worth purchasing for gameplay value.

- Overview - 

This War of Mine is a survival-strategy game that incorporates time and character management with item development. The game is point and click from a 2D cut-away perspective. This allows you to see for a certain distance until an obstacle such as a closed door or a wall blocks your line of sight, showing only a haze or a black fog. You begin the game in an abandoned house with a few freebie goods to start off with and 2-4 characters, depending on which story you choose to play.

- World Interaction - 

Characters move to where you click, normal/sneak speed with one click and running speed with a double-click. Icons hover above interactable objects: a hand for lootables, open/close door, peek through to the other side of a door, etc. Some doors or cabinets will be locked and will require tools to open, or a door might be barred from one side. You will have to explore cautiously and keep track of time to survive and get a good haul each night.

- Time System -

Time moves rather quickly in this game, 10 game minutes elapses approximately every 3-4 seconds. Daytime lasts from about 7 AM to 8 PM. During this time, you are stuck inside your shelter due to snipers lining the streets. At night, 9 PM to 5 AM, you may choose a character and a location to scavenge for goods. Each character has a different amount of slots of items that they can take, the average number being 10. You can choose to bring tools or weapons along to help or unlock new routes, but that means that you cannot use those slots to bring something new back. The other characters will have to stay in the shelter, getting to sleep or stand guard for the night by your choice.

-Characters and States - 

Characters have realistic needs and personalities. They will get hungry and need to be fed at least once a day to maintain optimal health. They may get injured or sick and will need to rest to heal, preferably in a bed. Depression is also a looming spectre if you choose to go the absolutely self-centered route (stealing, killing, robbing the hospital, etc.), especially if you have kind-hearted characters. Some characters have addictions and will consume items such as brewed coffee or cigarettes. Each one is unique and some have helpful attributes.

- Improvements - 

You will need to construct everything from beds to gardens to water collectors in your shelter to survive and become more self-sufficient. Each improvement has its own cost in materials to build and will inform you the time needed to finish its construction. Stations, such as the workshop, that allow new items to be built can be upgraded, unlocking more designs for construction.

- Music and Art - 

This War of Mine has a very dark, reflective soundtrack comprised of mostly clean electric guitar with strings accompanying. Some have noted that the music is repetitive; they are correct. As a guitar player myself, I do not mind so much and do not believe it is repetitive enough to cause anyone any unmanageable angst. The art style is equally as edgy. The game's colors are mostly greyscale or brown with a splash of subdued color here or there, usually red. The fog where your character cannot see is made mysterious by a soft, wavering pencil sketch effect. The mood is definitely one of depression and hardship. You can hear different music if a character plays a guitar (well) or if you turn on the radio to a punk rock or classical music station.

- Winning -

The game is concluded when you reach the randomly-generated ceasefire day. I've had games last from 25 days to 42, and I'm sure they could go shorter or longer.

- Conclusion -

I don't ever think I've spent a day of my life on something that's made me think about life and war so much. Most of us take a warm bed, three square meals a day and indoor heating for granted. I wholeheartedly recommend this war drama packaged as an enjoyable video game.

This game inspires epics (such as the one below -- modified from my original forum post) and touches lives.

After my first playthrough of this game -- in which my poor survivors were harassed constantly by ruthless thugs and bandits when they weren't being ravaged by the cruel hardships of famine and depression, only to be mercilessly killed off by cold (or in my last survivor Bruno's case, by his own hand) all in a mere 25 days -- I was shell-shocked.

I couldn't sleep IRL.  When I wasn't plagued by grief and guilt at my own naivety in thinking I could maintain my self-image as a principled person who could make it while never committing real atrocities, the lifeless faces of my poor characters still continued to haunt me -- their bloodied or deathly polaroids scraping at the back of my skull for days.

I was angry.  I was sullen.  I was in despair.

"F*** THE WAR"

Those words were mine.  But that was also the point when I vowed to make those words mine more than ever before.

F*** the War.  Indeed.  Oh yes, I will f*** the war.

I relentlessly researched everything I could about the game.  Everything I had done wrong in my first playthrough, Playthrough after playthrough I would scrimp and pinch every last material those first few nights, slowly building up to self-sufficiency each and every time, even when the game characteristically threw those tricky curveballs at my rag-tag group.

Early winter?  To the furniture!  Chop it all!

Murderous thieves attacking EVERY NIGHT for a week?  Every last survivor on guard; your shovel and crowbar strike as swift as the deadliest bullet!

Indefinitely delayed ceasefire?  Let us find strength in numbers and overcome, acting as shining beacons of humanity!

I had gotten the hang of the game.  Times were good.  I would never see those sad faces or read of their tragic fates ever again.

I finally decided on one last moment of glory before I put this game away -- I would go for (what I had hitherto considered) the hardest playthrough -- Emilia + Zlata.  Not enough members to guard your few belongings (thanks to their low carry capacity) against the raids that come in the 10 days you needed to heal their sickness, and with no tangible advantages in their abilities.  (Even the Roman + Katia playthrough had... well, Roman).

It was as brutal as I had imagined.  Constantly wounded and sick, while struggling to stay awake against voracious scavengers, the young women still could not bear to refuse their neighbors' desperate pleas for help.  The first 5 days were nothing if not taxing.

But those words -- those fateful words -- some blessed individual had scrawled outside Our Shelter continued to drive me forward.

"F*** THE WAR!"

"Yes," I decided with dogged determination. "I will f*** the war."

Slowly but surely, after careful management of time and resources, and devoted attention to their health, Zlata and eventually Emilia recovered from their respective ailments and, at the same time, had built up a formidable base, catching more food than they could eat and turning away increasingly violent aggressors.  There was no stopping us now.

Neighbors always knew who they could turn to in the midst of the seemingly endless conflict, in which the spineless "international community" fretted frivolously while accomplishing nothing regarding a potential ceasefire.  Yes, it was haven.

By day 25, Zlata had finally completed work on the broken Pistol, now adding offensive potential to their already respectable arsenal.  Villains, even hardened and determined killers, shuddered at the mention of "Our Shelter" and its heroes.  No one would be bullied on our watch, not in our neighborhood!

Soon, "they" became known as "Hospital Saviors," because even as the hospital was being indiscriminately shelled and its life-saving role threatened, "they" showed up every few days to donate ever-scarce medical supplies and relief.  People were in awe.  Nobody said anything, they simply looked up and watched as the member of Our Shelter walked away after quietly depositing the medicines.

And then, at last, it came.  Day 32.

"Ceasefire"

On that last day, before the war was declared over at sundown, Franko sold his remaining ammo to Zlata and Emilia.  Apparently, their war wasn't over yet.  They still had some more trash to clean out.

People would tell stories of Our Shelter and those courageous youngsters that defied the monolithic war, all while never failing to help every soul they came across -- they would tell them for years and years.

As for me, I took satisfaction in just one thing.

I am no longer a victim of this game, but a conqueror.  And my characters are no longer mere survivors of the war, but its CHAMPIONS.

F*** the war?  I didn't just f*** it, I made it my b****. :D :D :D

Well, after finally beating it, I have to say this is the first survival game I've really liked. Perhaps because instead of zombies or mutants or whatever, this is a real thing that happens on occasion (and is probably happening in one particular country). 

Gameplay:  Well, it's survival. You start out in a house with a number of people decided by the start you choose (no more than four, so far). You manage their happiness, hunger, wounds, illnesses and exhaustion. During the day, you play what's kinda like Sims Hardcore, where you watch your ever-dwindling stock of supplies vanish as you try to keep everyone alive and happy. You build upgrades to the house, things like stoves, a moonshine distillery (no better trade material than booze or meds) and defenses among others. At night, you post guards, figure out who gets to sleep and go on scavenging missions. These missions go to a wide array of places, where you can either loot the place (which will depress your survivors if you steal from innocent people) or trade with the inhabitants there if it's noted on the description. As loot dwindles at these places, you'll find yourselves making difficult choices with your supplies.

During the summer months, you're more concerned with keeping your food and construction supplies well-stocked. During the winter, vermin traps fill quicker (for obvious reasons) and give you more food while you toss every bit of construction supply you own into a heater to keep everyone from getting sick.

If they get too sick, too hungry, too tired, too whatever, they'll die. Yes, even if they get too sad, they'll kill themselves. Were there a problem I had with the game, it's lack of variety. Throughout my starts (to be fair, I've only had the first four characters unlocked until now) there have only been two ways the entire scenario goes down, with everything from house visits to unlocked areas being the exact same along those two starts. Also woulda liked more house models, but I'm being nitpicky here.

On the play I won, I endeavored to NEVER get into combat. There's something odd about the fact that on another play I snuck behind a would-be rapist who had cornered a scavenger, slammed an axe into his head to save her, and he recovered quickly enough to shoot and kill my character before I could take another swing. Combat is incredibly awkward, is what I'm saying. I don't know if that was by design or lack thereof, and if it is by design, I get the point they're trying to make but I'd at least like a sneak attack from an axe to be a one hit kill, like the enemies' bullets typically are. 

As much as it tries to encourage you to build and utilize everything, there were so many aspects of the crafting system I never bothered to use. By design, you have to play the game very conservatively, so wasting resources to grow vegetables, craft armor, craft higher level weapons, craft bullets, make coffee and make medicine is pointless, since you can just set up a moonshine distillery and keep making that to trade for anything that's more expensive to craft freeing your inventory up on salvaging missions so you can go after heaps of the bare necessities. Still, these are just minor complaints about very solid gameplay.

Aesthetic: There isn't a lot to speak about here, and I don't mean that in a bad way. The music is gloomy as hell (and also, is free DLC [Thanks, 11-Bit]), the art style is this kind of washed-out pencil shaded graphic of muted dull colors that really draws you into the game and makes you sufficiently miserable. Which again, is good, as it assists in giving the impact this kind of game needs. 

Story: The game has no real story besides: a civil war has started, survive. That's all it needs, though, because you make your own story. Will you donate expensive and very valuable meds to the hospital or rob it blind while they try to help people? Will you rob an elderly couple for their medicine because that young journalist with you is sick and her only hope to survive are a few pills(I did)? Will you turn a blind eye to a soldier who's about to rape a scavenger because you don't want to get hurt? The story's all on you.

This War of Mine is like nothing I have ever played before. I thought going into it that it was a platformer of sorts, but it’s actually closer to being a real time strategy game. The whole game revolves around keeping a group of survivors alive for the duration of the war, which includes keeping them fed, rested, warm, treated for any sickness (meds) or wounds (bandages) and also keeping tabs on their mental wellbeing, which I learned early on is very important as I lost a character to suicide.

The gameplay basically revolves around activities in your safe house during the day, which include things like building beds, stoves, work benches, etc and then building and managing supplies like food, fuel for the heater, filters for clean water,  and ammo etc.  As night falls, you have to choose which characters will sleep, which will guard and which will go scavenging for supplies. You have to balance sleeping with guarding, as you can’t let your people get too tired, but you also run the risk of getting raided each night by bandits, which leaves you with supplies stolen and possibly wounded characters.

Scavenging at night, now this is where the real fun of it came in for me. You can’t go in guns blazing as you usually scored yourself a pretty quick death. In the end I found the most effective form of combat was to hide in the shadows, and bait each enemy close to me so I could finish them with my knife. But, you have to balance who you kill as killing can have huge consequences on your team’s mental health. In the end it was easier to only kill when needed, as I didn’t have to worry about anyone getting sad or depressed.

All in all I had a heap of fun learning the game, and after having just completed my first play through, I look forward to playing through again with all the tricks that I learnt.  I highly recommend this game for all fans of strategy or even just someone looking for something a little different. Even at full price, I think there is a lot of fun to be had.

This War of Mine has you take control of a group of survivors, up to 4 people, who are just trying to live until the end of the war that's taking place in their city. These survivors each have their own stories, and personalities, some with pros and cons that can help you or make things slightly more difficult through out the game. The amount of days to survive is random. In one playthrough the war may only last a few weeks, in another close to two months (in game time of course). Which really keeps you hopeful as you play the game. Sometimes you can even catch some good news from the radio you have the option to construct. This is a game where you're going to be counting every blessing you get, cause you aint getting many.

One thing this game gets right is definately the despiration, and bleakness of a tragic environment of a war-torn country. There are moments where you will be searching for food or another necessity you need and you may not find it for some time. At that point do you make the decision to sneak into a fellow group of survivors' camp and steal, or ride it out and hope you'll find some, or something good to trade for some. There are also some tough moral decisions as well. There will be moments where people will come to your door, sometimes simply asking for assistance, sometimes for some of your supplies. And thankfully it can sometimes pay of to help these people, you can be rewarded with more useful supplies, or supplies that would be valuable to trade. Also not everyone is a helpless survivor, obviously. Some places you visit are under control of the military or bandits. And if you're desperate enough you could try to steal from them, or if you're brave enough kill them, though I wouldn't advise that unless you have a very well planned out strategy.

The games design is very good too. I love the sketchy black and white art style. And I like the ant-farm-like design of the different areas you scavenge in.

A game that can give you a new perspective on a real-world event, in a way that's different from a movie or TV show, you cant interact with a movie or TV show like you can a game.

I'm really hard pressed to find anything I didn't enjoy in this game. Whatever I found annoying, like supplies not showing up in areas I was expecting them too just made the game more realistic, and intense. Or the combat being a little difficult, the game is supposed to be hard, it's about surviving a war. These are everyday citizens, not soldiers trained in combat.

This is a game that everyone needs to play before they die. With all the Call of Duties and Battlefields dominating the "War-theme" in the game industry, it's easy to forget that, as this game perfectly puts it "In war not everyone is a soldier." In this game you may not have "fun" but you may get a new well-needed perspective on the aspect of war.

I came to This War of Mine having just finished reading a book about the Siege of Leningrad in 1941-42. It turned out to be the perfect preparation.

TWOM is not like other survival games, with an emphasis on shooting your way out of trouble. In fact, it's more than possible to go for an entire game without once experiencing any kind of combat. If that makes the game sound easy or boring, think again. RIght from the outset, your small group of survivors is left to fend for themselves, using any means of staying alive - scrabbling through piles of debris for scraps of food, wood, material, mechanical parts, anything to make their lives in their half-bombed shelter bearable.

During the day it's too dangerous to leave their shelter, so the survivors spend their time building makeshift workshops, eating barely-edible meals made up of dead rats and scavenged vegetables, melting snow to make fresh water, and playing the guitar to relieve the gloom. Occasionally someone comes to the door to offer help, or to barter goods, or to present a risky opportunity with high reward if it comes off.

During the night, one survivor in the group must go on a mission to find supplies. This could mean raiding an abandoned supermarket, ransacking a shelled building with dead bodies still inside, or sneaking through a hotel filled with dangerous, armed gangsters. There's only a limited amount of time, and a limited amount of stuff the survivor can carry - so it comes down to hard choices. Take this extra piece of food, because everyone in the group is hungry? Or sacrifice it in order to take these mechanical parts which will enable the group to build a water filter?

The game never quite gives you enough, so the resources are always stretched, and these hard choices have to be made every day. You find yourself willing a trader to come to the door so that you can barter your precious medical supplies (which you might need one day) just for an extra piece of food. And, of course, as soon as you've done that, one of your group falls ill... The game further complicates things by triggering random raids on your shelter, so that even when you think you're safe the little you have can be taken away from you. You can literally be left without food, and with half your group injured, in a single night.

It's details like these (and the fact that the game gives you no instructions whatsoever) that have led some people to complain that the game is too difficult; and the Steam forums are abuzz with people requesting the developers add in extra options and amendments to make life easier. But, in fact, once you've grasped the basics and played through a few times, a clear path to victory does emerge (although it'll be different each time). The game can almost be too easy for a seasoned player - but the challenge has been increased in the latest version, as you get to try your luck with different groups of survivors, each more helpless and limited than the previous set.

Aside from gameplay, the game is beautifully rendered in cross-section pseudo-3D graphics, with monochrome shading and a highly plausible design. You really do feel like you're in the middle of war-torn Sarajevo (the game is set in the fictional East European city of Pogoren, but the allusions to the war in Bosnia are obvious). The atmosphere throughout is gloomy, thoughtful and just the right side of depressing. You really do become attached to your little band of survivors, each with his or her own skills and drawbacks. To complete the picture, each survivor has a backstory which is revealed gradually thoughout the game, giving them a rounded personality and making the player identify more strongly with each of them.

The emphasis in the game is on realism (which is why it's hard - surviving in a war zone is no picnic, after all). Where realism is sacrificed, it enhances the gameplay, putting limits on the player which would make the game too easy if they weren't there.

TWOM isn't (usually) a heart-thumping, high-octane, shoot-em-up wartime action game; there's no shortage of them around. What it is is something rather more thought-provoking. When you take away the guns and give them all to your opponents, what do you have left? How do the little people, the non-combatants, the citizens with no access to food, warmth or weapons, survive in a situation like this? You'll lose your first few games, most likely - all your survivors dead, your heart broken. But play on, because when you finally get your people through to the end of the war, all the emotion you invested in them will be repaid.

Thoroughly recommended.

You could go the easy route and describe This War of Mine as "The Sims, but set in Hell." And you'd be right.

The game can be better described as an 'entropy simulator': There's plenty of things to pick up initially. Just through initial walks through the area you can find a bunch of resources you can use for initial improvements to make for your war hovel. But eventually, that stuff will start to run out, and you will not be able to play it safe anymore. If you're smart, you'll have someone who is good at bartering and items to supply the demands of rich survivors with, and you might be able to get through the war without blood on your hands.

If you're no longer able to play it safe, that is where the real This War of Mine begins.

It is easy to lose control of your circumstances concerning what your group needs. If you have to keep pushing your wounded and your sick, they will get worse. But there's points where you just can't, because you need to keep a tight budget on what little resources you have. Raiders will come by, you will get a small winter, and your group members will get hideously depressed from having to hide from the war in a cold, destroyed house. All of these things will add up, and not having what you need to keep them sane and healthy will eventually destroy your chances of seeing the end of the game. 

You'll have to be a bastard to get what you need, and the mental tax that your actions will cause will be heavy. Sure, you can poke your scavenging survivor to stab an armed thug in the back, but he will hate himself for it the next day. You can brandish your pistol at the elderly couple hiding out in their nice home to take their supplies. You can carefully sneak through homes and take things that survivors not unlike yourself have been hoarding for a rainy day, putting them in  poverty to get what your group needs. And, of course, you can sneak through shadows and stab people in the back, trying to ignore their frightened pleads as you put the blade in to keep others from noticing all for the sake of some things you could have, in better days, gotten from a supermarket for five dollars.

This game is one of those games where it can make you feel like a bastard for trying to survive, and the more desperate you have to get to feed your group, the more it works. It's a horrible bastard feeling generator when the game is at it's toughest.

This War of Mine, an amazing game that came up on Steam not to long ago, but it gained MASSIVE response. This game explores an area that isn't explored in many other games: what is it like for the citizens of a country that is in the middle of a war. And it isn't talking about militia, or heroes that defeated an empire: These are buisnessmen, chefs, football coaches, and just regular people, trying to survive what seems to be a neverending war.

Now gameplay: You take control of 3 survivors at the start of a playthrough, and you find a large building with a good amount of supplies. However, you will find out that what you start out with, will not be enough. At night, you will have to scavenge different areas of the city, all while trying to stay hidden, get as much as possible, and to not die. Shall you mess up, and you will most likely find yourself in combat. In combat, you are usually at a disadvantage, shall you find yourself with no weapon or tool. However, fighting usually isn't worth it anyway, because if you do end up being the killer of another person or group, your survivors will have real effects from it. They will slowly become more and more depressed as you continue to do morally wrong things. Now, once the hell of night washes over, you get to experience the hardships of day.

During the day, you mainly focus on your "home", building other workbenches, feeding your survivors, and otherwise taking care of them, such as through medical aid, or with just a simple bed. Sometimes, you will encounter a stranger at the door, asking for help, asking to live with you (letting you control them, but it is another mouth to feed.), or even possibly asking for trade. When you choose to go back into the night, you will have to station certain people to do certain things, such as having one person getting to sleep, one on guard at your "house", and one scavenging.

Overall, this game is amazing, the graphics are great, gameplay is fantastic, and while it seems like there is no story at first, one will surely develop during your playthrough.

Rating: 9.5/10

A game born from an exceptional idea, an enticing premise. Finally, I thought, a 'post-apocalyptic' without the zombie-filler, full of moral dilemmas and drama.

But, sadly, it fails in choosing a fitting game formula. It is enthralling for the first... 2 hours, but at a certain point, sooner or later, the facade fades and the underlying game disappoints.

Living in a warzone would mean a struggle for the most basic needs. These would be food & water (which are consumed quite rapidly), tools (which do not degrade as quickly as most modern games would make us believe), warmth (clothing & fuel) and weapons (which are either basic tools or heavily limited through ammunition). These are the things I would expect to fight for.

But just in the resources and crafting system the ugly mechanics of the game show, it is just like playing a mobile game. (be prepared to click A LOT). Food and Water was a non-issue for me (although constantly producing filters to 'produce' rain water was an annoyance) and tools were an annoyance (what are these rapidly degrading shovels made of?). Instead I found myself constantly carting massive quantities of wood and generic 'components' back into my base in order to upgrade my stove. In a post-apocalyptic world, building an independent, self-sufficient settlement is absolutely unrealistic and undermines the core of the setting. Building furniture and tools would be for a me a horrible waste of time and energy, especially if i have to carry wood and 'components' through the entire city first. To cut it short, the resources and crafting system is bloated, is missing a lot of balancing, and it's focus is chosen poorly.

Characters and moral conflicts are present but unfulfilling. The characters feel lacking and uniform, they generally seem to feel the same to any events in the world. The fixed base which is chosen for you takes a lot of opportunity out of the game, and the limitation of a single scavenger at night feels artifical and arbitrary (and reminded me of the new XCOM). Others raiding your camp should be a major event of a game and a situation of life or death for all your companions. Instead, it's a random text event, and a minor wound is allocated somewhere. Even more depressing.

there were two men in my little hovel, a cook named bruno and runner named pavle.  bruno would normally stay at home during the night to cook and guard the belongings while pavle went out scavenging for supplies, but that previous night pavle had been shot while sprinting across a courtyard trying to make it to the abandoned side of a building complex for any chance of food. they were both hungry.  pavle survived and made it back (there was no food to be found), but it was clear that bruno would need to leave the shelter to find food and bandages while pavle nursed his wounds.  even though it was likely dangerous, the best bet seemed a run down supermarket.  shelling from the war had closed off any safer avenues.  

while sifting through toppled shopping carts and piles of rubble, bruno heard a confrontation in an adjoining room: a young woman was also there looking for food, but had been accosted by an armed man.  his implication was clear: he had the food, so she had to do what he wanted.  she sounded so hungry.  bruno (and by extension, i) was unable to ignore it, even though he had literally brought only a knife to a gun fight.  maybe he could sneak up behind him before he noticed.  as soon as the door behind him opened, the girl yelled and ran through it, leaving bruno crouched, exposed, in full view of her attacker. a single gunshot later, and bruno was dead.  at that moment, i wondered something very dark:  the woman had escaped, but she was still hungry.  perhaps she starved to death, because of my intervention.  perhaps she, through a horror i don't even want to acknowledge, would have indeed received food from her attacker. perhaps he would have simply killed her.  there was no way to know.  pavle awoke alone the next morning.

at this point my videogame urge to just start over with new characters and resources was strong, but i kept playing.  i was forced to make more difficult, tense choices for survival, sacrifices, and calculated risks in a way that i would have never experienced if i'd taken the easy way out.  pavle is still alive and alone, many days later.  a man arrived wanting to trade shortly after bruno died, and pavle gave him almost everything of value in the shelter (including his lucky shovel) for a tin of food and some bandages.  he arrives home, dejected, each morning to the unguarded, almost undoubtedly ransacked shelter.  a man on the radio mentions that tobacco is currently in high demand, so pavle spent his entire morning rolling cigarettes with the spoils of last night's haul.  maybe he can find someone tonight willing to trade. maybe they'll have food.

In this highly immersive game you not only test the limitations of what desperate civilians can do, but also test the morality of your own conscious.  Stranded on the battlefield and deserted by the very soldiers that your country had sworn to protect various scavengers come together to fight against rising raids and thugs that have taken over the city when nightfall comes.  Resources are scarce, happiness dwindling, there are no moral decisions on the battlefield, only survival.  The scavengers all have various skills, some are faster than others, some stronger, and others still are good at boosting the happiness of those around them even when blood is staining their hands.

The first game that has ever truthfully brought me to tears, I spent the first part of the game shifting through abandoned houses, taking what little I could find in hopes of just feeding the two friends I had left at the house to guard the small amount we could call our own.  Even from the beginning Pavle became my savior, his speed and his ability to talk others out of depression was what made him my most-played character, where he would sleep and talk to others during the day, and at night he was my main scavenger in hopes of quickly gathering what we needed without drawing any attention.  But once the majority was taken from abandoned houses that were quickly sapped dry of their resources, morality became nothing more than an afterthought.

Pavle had to start making impossible decisions to obtain food, where first he went into armed buildings and got what little he could without engaging others, but once food hadn't come back night after night and Bruno's wounds were only getting more severe from constant raids, Boris began to take the reign.  His strength was my ally, and our first kill was made against an armed man, and where I expected more to follow I was horrified by not armed guards coming to mow Boris down, but rather the dead man's friends, disregarding me as they ran past and wept at the sight of their dead friend (I get chills even as I imagine those horror-stricken voices), however Boris had already fled with the man's gun and other belongings.  So broken upon returning Pavle did what little he could to console the tough man, but it was futile, and Pavle was forced to take the lead once more to find bandages for Bruno's increasing wounds.

It took some adjusting, but gradually I was able to take Pavle into more armed places, having to do nothing more than flash his knife to scare away those that would of otherwise harmed him, and although his own depression quickly set in Pavle charged through it all, sifting through inhabited houses and leaving small amounts of food and a knife for those that remained in hopes of them finding some hope as well.  But soon raids began, and with Bruno incapacitated Boris guarded the shelter at night, armed with a shotgun and enough bullets to fell a few thugs.  But devastation struck when Pavle killed a young man who had shot him, my own desperation for all three to survive kicking in when I had seen the young man with a gun, and knew how useful it could be against stronger raids.  But then the young man's parents came down, tears streaming down their cheeks and their voices filled with horror as the old couple grappled uselessly to their son, as if they thought he would just get up and hug them.

That was what did it, Pavle was broken.  My main scavenger incapacitated by his own mind, where only Boris could console him, but once Boris became my main scavenger due to his strength and his depression seldom ever became broken, I left Pavle to the dangerous task of guarding the shelter, tending to Bruno's severe wounds.  Things only got worse, after things seemed to be getting better, Boris had brought guns, food, bandages and medicine, Pavle was still depressed however no longer broken, Bruno took it all.  He didn't make it far, in the end I know that now, but he took everything, food, shotguns, bandages, medicine, we were left where we were to begin with.  Boris was the second to leave, wounded and hungry I like to think he simply didn't want to have Pavle see another good man die, so he left the young man alone, and what became of depression quickly turned into a mind broken.  I survived with Pavle alone for a good 10 days, taking important things with me so that when the inevitable raid did come, they didn't get much, however I only brought back small things from his scavenging that was becoming more gruesome by the night.  He was broken, I wanted him to sleep it off after getting large amounts of food that could keep him to guard for a few more days at the least, but what it showed on the screen brought me to tears, after hours of making sure Pavle survived, that he helped some people just to take something off of his mind.

Day 27: Pavle hung himself.

What will you do, allow those around you to gradually crumble into their own minds and hands, or throw caution to the wind and fight against everything you have ever been taught about right and wrong?

TLDR;  I cannot recommend this game enough, I am usually very picky (unfortunately) when it comes to games, however I have always been able to appreciate hard work and great graphics or story line, but usually never enough to buy it.  This game just intrigued me to no end, and after playing it for my first time (and certainly not my last) I can truthfully say it is one of the best games I've ever played.  Mechanics is great, character design near flawless, it's a little difficult to begin with to figure out some of the controls and what everything does, but you learn quickly, you have to in order to survive.  It's not tedious, it's enthralling all the way through, not your usual hunt-and-gather mechanics but taken to the next level as something too real to not be labeled as horrifying.  Play at the risk of your own view of the world.

Out of all kinds of survival simulators, this one stands out.

As the game tells you, war games are all about the armies. The soldiers. The countries fighting for glory. But what about the citizens? 

In This War of Mine, you play as a generally helpess civilian alongside your other friends in an attempt to survive during a time of war, where the city you reside in is under siege.

Your survivors can be easily wounded by constant attacks by thugs and bandits on your shelter, finding a good meal is sparse, and each day is a struggle to survive.

Do you have the supplies to make a good meal, or will you eat raw food? Do you have enough items of value to trade in order to survive? Do your medical supplies allow for bringing your near-dying friend to health?

Should you uphold your morals in this time of crisis, or will you murder, steal, and sack just to live? Your decisions lie with you, and the effects they have on your characters will show.

Will you help some children's dying mother get to health, or are you too desperate to live and must preserve what you do have? Will you risk saving a girl from being rap3d by a soldier, or disregard the effort in fear of death? Will you threaten to murder an old couple, just to steal from their supplies?

Survival is a gift in this game, and the strategy, thought, and your own morals will be brought to the test in this game. Not many other games can boast of giving you the challenge of surviving down to the letter.

Would recommend to anyone looking for a challenging, intriguing game, rather than a hack-and-slash one.

This War of Mine is a hard one to recommend. While the game itself is great and i really enjoy the approach the game takes on war, replayability is the huge concern. I have played the game for about 10 hours now, which is approximately the time it takes to get a complete run (I failed my first try in a very harsh fashion but once i got the mechanics i succeeded in my second attempt keeping everyone alive till the end).

The gameplay mechanics in themself are good and the chosen artstyle is amazingly fitting for such a game. If you would like to get an impression of what it would be like to be forced to survive in urban warfare as a civilian this game is the one for you. 
For one walkthrough it is a nice game which really gets you thinking what would happen if you were in such  a dire situation. Especially in times like these in which violent conflicts are getting more common once again i can recommend taking a look into This War of Mine.

With all those positive traits i have to say i don't really like the game. The game offers not much playing time (to get it right once takes about 10 hours) and that's a huge problem. The gameplay is too repetitive and the "randomised" setpieces you get every time you start a new game are way too similar to offer something reminiscent of replayability. Other than that the game is way too easy. The first days seem to be the only ones challenging. As soon as you have upgraded your shelter to the max you can quite easily fend off all intruders and feed, medicate and bandage everyone. 

The run i finished took 41 days. The last 20 days at least the game didn't provide any real challenge other than collecting food for everybody which imo is way too easy once you have 2 traps set up. I was never confronted with real scarcity and tough decisions such as "Who gets to eat?" "Do i let Pavle bleed to death?" "Do i send someone on a suicide mission because there is a desperate need for food?". Thus "surviving" the urban warfare became a pretty dull affair after a short while. Also the game promotes and rewards only one kind of behaviour. Helping others is always good and rewards you with even more ressources and killing and stealing (while being important to survive) are always bad and the characters feel terrible about it or even get depressed. If you hope to get in a run in which you lead your own band of looters and bandits killing and stealing just because you are not a nice person the game will disappoint you. 

Don't get me wrong i like helping other people and I am in no way a sadistic or violent person but I expected the game to provide the full spectrum of human character and a more diverse experience. There are a lot of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up people around town but they are never within your group. While the actual characters you play have different personalities and actually have very interesting backgrounds and stories to tell the game fails to accomplish character development. The characters all stay true to their beliefs and no one is really changed by the horrors of war. Additionally the all so different characters play almost exactly the same and there are just few (and very superficial) gameplay implications of playing the different characters such as larger inventory, faster movespeed etc.

To put it in a nutshell i would not recommend buying This War of Mine for the price they're asking for right now (18,99€ as I write this review). The game just offers too little of everything and fails to reach its full potential. If you ever find it in a nice sale for like 5-10€ or if you have that kind of disposable cash you don't really have to care about too much i would definitely say that you should take a look into it. For the price of a movie ticket you can say that this game offers you  a nice approach on war and surviving it. For the current price of 18,99€ I think it is a bit overprized.

On day 20, Katia started feeling ill. Pavle returned bearing herbal remedies for Katia to consume.  Believing herself to be on the mend, Katia went out on a foraging mission the next night. By day 23, she was severely ill.  Not wanting to steal anything, Pavle searched for a trading partner in order to barter for the pills that would eliminate Katia's pallor.  No one had any to spare, though, so he returned empty handed.  Katia remained bedridden while the other denizens of the meager shelter shot worried whispers to each other.

As day 25 rolled around with no improvement in Katia's condition, Pavle resolved to obtain the medicine for her by any means necesary.  Tired, hungry, and sad, Pavle set out to steal from a warehouse  which was patrolled by heavily armed men.  Furtively dodging the patrols and rifling through drawers, Pavle raced against the approaching dawn to find his prize.  Finally, an hour from dawn, he unveiled a bottle of asprin to bring down his friend's fever.  He raced home.

But it was too late.  Katia died in the night.  Pavle collapsed in the doorway and grieved for his friend the whole day through.

Glancing at my wall-mounted map of the world, my eyes danced between the Middle East, Ukraine, and Africa, and I considered joining Pavle in the splintered door frame.

Let me start by saying that I thought that the "survival" genre was on its way out of popularity before I started playing this game. That being said, This War of Mine is a brilliant minimalist survival experience that will have you playing through multiple times. The basic premise of the game is simply to survive the horrors of a war-torn city experiencing an armed rebellion.  To do this you must control a cast of characters and fortify a shelled out home to endure the coming days. The characters you get are pre set, but you unlock more combinations of characters as you progress through the game. Each character has basic needs; hunger, sleep, and their general health (ie: keeping their wounds treated and sick characters healthy). Some characters also have additional needs that make taking care of them slightly more difficult, such as an addiction to cigarettes. These needs and wants are what will influence your decision making as you progress through the game.

This War of Mine focuses on survival, but also allows players to choose the easy way out of a situation by sacraficing their humanity in order to live. What I mean by this is that you will encounter situations where you can easily obtain food or medical supplies, but you must steal or kill to obtain them. The option to scavenge and create your own supplies exists, but if someone is dying from a gunshot wound, then you may have no choice but to rob the doctor down the street who is doing all he can to treat civilians who are injured in the conflict. Performing such an act will have a negative influence on morale, and has a chance to break the character who performed the deed, rendering them useless for some time and possibly even pushing them to suicide.

The game is not flawless. One big problem that I had was that little to no game mechanics are explained. There is no legend to tell players what icons mean, and combat is a veritable trial by fire that will most likely claim the life of the first character that encounters it. Once you have become a veteran all this will mean nothing, but as a new player to the game it can be frustrating. That is certainly the biggest error I have detected, and it is not enough to stop me from labeling this as an excellent game.

What is being presented to us as gamers is more than just another "get wood, make fire, cook meat, live" survival game; it is The Sims meets Fallout. Control your party's emotions and physical and mental state of being. Juggle your characters needs, make or steal the weapons you need to survive, and ultimately do what you need to in order to live through the war.

[u]Premise[/u]
This War of Mine is a survival-themed strategy game made by 11 bit studios. This game was inspired by the 1992-96 Seige of Sarajevo during the Bosnian War (the longest city siege in modern history), and the story-line is centered around the civilian experience of war (the poor living conditions and wartime atrocities) rather than front-line combat. It was released in November 2014.

[u]Gameplay[/u]
You control a number of civilians trying to survive in a makeshift shelter in a war-torn city. Each civilian has a specific skill, i.e. a good cook, skilled scavenger, and these characteristics need to be taken advantage of in order to survive.

During the day your civilians cannot leave the makeshift shelter due to hostile snipers, so it is during this time that you can get your civilians to rest, build new items for the shelter, make weapons, and also ensure that their basic needs: health, hunger, rest, etc., are catered for.

Night time is one of the most important times of the game - this is when your civilians can go to scavenge for supplies such as food, water, weapons, wood, medicine, etc. This part of the game is particularly stressful as you genuinely feel the pressure of needing to return to the shelter with a good haul of items which is never as easy as you'd like it to be. Scavenging missions are particularly dangerous as the military or other survivors can attack you on sight, other times they could ask you for things to trade you don't have with you, other survivors may also be trying to scavenge in the same location and they may hear you digging through rubble to get the best items, all of which leads to a tense night for your scavenger, and also for you as the player.

You are able to build a radio in the shelter which does help towards planning what to scavenge for trade, or what the surrounding areas are currently like in terms of shelters getting raided, or the likelihood of getting attacked while on scavenging missions, etc.

Your civilians can meet other NPC survivors throughout the game which enables trade for items. The items that you will need the most, however, are often the most expensive, and you will need to really think about the impact it will make giving away half of your items in storage just to get one bandage for a poorly civilian of your own.

Choices are very tough in this game, and I found myself feeling as desperate and anxious as my in-game civilians were feeling towards the end - particularly after my first civilian died during a scavenging mission after getting into a fight. Your decisions are genuinely a matter of life-and-death, and are very much conscious based: save your own civilians, or run the risk of other civilians dying just so you can save yourselves. The decisions you make also affect the mood of the civilians that you control, and once morale within the shelter is low it makes life even more difficult.

The game is 'won', or more completed/finished by managing to keep one or more civilians alive until a ceasefire is called. Even though I managed to finish my very first game, it didn't really feel much of a win, or an achievement considering I'd lost all but one of my civilians, and my last surviving civilian wasn't going to be able to hold on much longer. The ceasefire is called at random, and mine was called on day 42 - it took me around 7hrs of gameplay to get to this point.

[u]Design[/u]
The soundtrack (by Piotr Musial) and 2D charcoal artwork of this game are perfectly matched to the style and genre as they completely capture the bleak, tense and somber atmosphere/situation. The character animation is beautiful, and should you be lucky enough to be able to get a guitar made for your shelter, the music created by the civilians playing the instrument sent chills down my spine.

This game has tons of replay ability as it is random each time you play. You can start with different survivors, different seasons, different locations to scavenge from at night, and a random ceasefire date each play though - all of which will make for a different experience each time.

[u]Summary[/u]
I am still thinking about my first play-through: could I have done things differently, could I have had more civilians alive at the ceasefire? It's not often that a game continues to make me think about it once a few days have passed by after completing it; it's also not often that a game would draw me back for multiple play-throughs. I really adored everything about this game from start to finish.

For anyone that likes The Sims style games, but fancies something tougher, more RPG like, this will definitely be one for you to try though it is no easy ride - it is difficult, brutal and harrowing, but equally fantastic.

This War of Mine is available DRM free from 11 bit studios' website, or on Steam. Current full-price cost is £14.99.

[b]Summary:[/b]
[b]This War of Mine[/b] isn't only about the war in the game but it also has a double meaning, referring to the internal struggle of the player to make decisions. It is a really nice game. I've spent roughly 30 hours to reach the end and it was my second try. None of my survivors died and the only times I really struggled was winter and the military outpost. 
I loved the different scenarios like saving the girl in the supermarket or the two women trapped in the basement. There were a couple of others which were really nice and that's really something I have to highlight.

After killing some bandits and soldiers I was actually looking forward to killing more bad guys and thankfully I didn't end up harming innocent people out of boredom. Kinda scary there.
Unfortunately some locations are locked for some characters so you have to replay the story with other characters to unlock different locations with different scenarios which is kinda a plus regarding the playtime but overall, I wouldn't complete the stories more than twice. 

[b]Was it worth the money?[/b]

Perhaps if they'll add more characters, locations, scenarios and interactions in the future then YES but considering you can have a bunch of better games for less money then NO. I bought this game when it was discounted and roughly $14. I wouldn't recommend buying it for more than $10 unless you want to support the game and its developers.
